title: Spotigo : Spot it , report it , fix it!
pitch: Spotigo lets you describe a civic problem out loud — a pothole, a downed power line — and an agent turns that into a filed report, but it can never hit submit without your explicit yes.
about_excerpt:
Spotigo lets you describe a civic problem out loud — a pothole, a downed power line — and an agent turns that into a filed report, but it can never hit submit without your explicit yes.

 Gemini : POW of WebMCP integration

 Gemini : POW of WebMCP integration 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 



 
 Spotigo — Project Story 

 A WebMCP-powered civic agent that turns human intent into safe, executable web actions. 

 
 Describe the problem. Let the agent handle the workflow. Keep the human in control of the part that matters. 
 

 Inspiration 

 The web already has the services people need. The friction is almost never "does this exist" — it's "can I get from what I want to say to the specific form this particular website expects." A citizen who sees a pothole thinks someone should report this , not let me figure out which municipal category this falls under, whether it's already been reported, and how to phrase it correctly. The problem exists. The digital service to fix it probably exists too. The gap is entirely in connecting human intent to that workflow — and that gap is exactly what WebMCP is positioned to close. 

 My first idea wasn't civic reporting at all — it was an accessible, voice-first grocery storefront. Before building much of it, I checked what was already in the WebMCP showcase and found Verdant Market already occupying that lane: "browse groceries and build a shared cart with an agent." Rather than build a variation on an existing reference app, I kept the one pattern worth keeping — the agent prepares, the human confirms — and moved it to a domain where getting that confirmation wrong actually matters: civic reporting, where the output is a public record, not a grocery order. 

 What it does 

 A citizen describes a civic issue by voice or text — "there's a huge pothole near my office" — and an agent turns that into a real, trackable report, gated by explicit human confirmation at the one step that counts. 

 Spotigo registers 10 WebMCP tools in the browser through document.modelContext , deliberately shaped as a workflow rather than a flat list: 

 
 
 Stage 
 Tools 
 
 
 
 Understand 
 describe_issue_accessibly , report_civic_issue 
 
 
 Validate 
 check_duplicate_reports , list_nearby_reports 
 
 
 Explain 
 read_report_summary 
 
 
 Authorize 
 confirm_submission , acknowledge_safety_guidance 
 
 
 Act 
 submit_report 
 
 
 Recover / Track 
 undo_last_action , get_report_status 
 
 

 A real pass through it: the agent structures "huge pothole near my office" into a draft — category pothole , description, resolved location — checks it against nearby reports and comes back with a graded confidence assessment (not a flat yes/no), then reads the draft back in plain language: "I'm about to report a large pothole at this location with this description. Submit it?" Only after an explicit confirm: true does submit_report become callable, returning a real tracking ID the citizen can check later with get_report_status . 

 How we built it 

 Zero build step, zero runtime dependencies, static files only — deliberate, so the WebMCP layer itself stays the thing under inspection, not something buried under framework abstraction. 

 One execution path, not two. The human-facing UI and the agent-facing WebMCP tools call the same tool.execute() closures — there's no separate "demo path" for the agent. If a judge opens the on-page Tool Tester and fires submit_report before confirming, they get the identical rejection an agent would get, because it's literally the same code running either way. 

 Ten tools, not one do_everything() . It would have been simpler to expose a single submit_report(details) function and let a system prompt handle the reasoning. That would hide exactly the part worth demonstrating — the validation, the safety boundaries, the point where understanding what someone wants stops being enough to act on it. Decomposing the workflow into explicit stages made the tool surface mirror the actual application logic instead of papering over it. 

 Intent is not authorization. The agent can understand the issue, check for duplicates, and explain what it's about to do — none of that authorizes submit_report . That gate is enforced in code: confirm: "yes" is truthy in JavaScript but explicitly rejected, because a loose check could let an ambiguous model output pass as authorization. Only strict confirm: true opens the gate. 

 The gate adapts to risk. Routine issues get one confirmation. Safety-critical ones — a downed power line, a suspected gas leak — route through a distinct acknowledge_safety_guidance step first, and lose the normal undo safety net once submitted. A pothole and a live wire aren't the same category of decision, and treating them identically would have been the easier, lazier design. 

 A second, separate experiment. server.js and server/ implement a persistent, authenticated MCP service for agents connecting outside the browser — real action storage, ownership isolation, rate limiting, a fail-closed authority resolver. It is explicitly not part of the deployed judged demo. I kept that line hard rather than implying a backend was live when it wasn't. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Choosing what not to build. The competitive check that killed the grocery idea happened before most of the code existed, which made it cheap. That ordering — research first, fall in love with the implementation second — was the single highest-leverage decision in the project. 

 Making confirmation a real boundary, not a suggestion. Getting the strict-boolean check right ( confirm: true vs. anything merely truthy) sounds trivial until you consider that an LLM producing "yes" or 1 instead of true is a completely plausible failure mode, and a loose check would have let it silently authorize a submission. 

 A Windows path bug invisible in my own dev loop. Automated smoke tests passed cleanly in my Linux sandbox and failed immediately on the actual Windows machine, with ERR_UNSUPPORTED_ESM_URL_SCHEME — Node's dynamic import() requires a proper file:// URL on Windows; a raw path like D:\...\app.js doesn't qualify, even though the POSIX equivalent works fine elsewhere. One-line fix ( pathToFileURL() ), but a reminder that "tests pass" and "tests pass in the environment a judge will actually use" are different claims. 

 Git history discipline under time pressure. A substantial chunk of work — the entire server/MCP layer — sat uncommitted for longer than it should have while heads-down building it. A last-minute dump commit would have technically satisfied "real commit history" while missing its point. Going back and committing it in logical pieces was extra effort late in the process, but it was the honest version of the requirement. 

 Resisting the urge to claim more than was deployed. Once the server prototype worked locally, the tempting move was to fold it into the headline pitch. The harder, better call was a README section that draws a hard line between what's live and judged versus what's a local Phase 2 prototype — because a panel this technical will check claims against what's actually running, and a claim that doesn't reproduce live costs more than the claim was worth. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 A confirmation gate that's a real, tested execution boundary — including catching and rejecting confirm: "yes" , the exact kind of loose value a model might plausibly produce. 
 A risk-tiered version of that gate, where safety-critical issues require a distinct second acknowledgement and lose the undo safety net, because not every civic issue carries the same stakes. 
 One execution path for humans and agents — no shadow demo logic, verifiable by anyone who opens the Tool Tester. 
 22 passing tests, including one that runs the full judge-facing scenario — draft → duplicate check → review → both negative confirmation cases → submission → tracking ID → status lookup — against the real tool closures. 
 One honestly-scoped, fully-working vertical, with a second experimental server layer clearly labeled as not part of the judged demo, instead of five thinly-demonstrated domains. 
 

 What we learned 

 The real opportunity here isn't "AI plus websites" — it's AI agents plus websites that expose capabilities an agent can reliably us

title: Echo
pitch: Show Echo any workflow once. It writes the SKILL.md, parameterizes the values, and ships a portable skill any AI agent can run generalized, human-approved, no lock-in.\n\n
about_excerpt:
Show Echo any workflow once. It writes the SKILL.md, parameterizes the values, and ships a portable skill any AI agent can run generalized, human-approved, no lock-in.


 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 



 
 Inspiration 

 Every team pays the same hidden tax. The same form filled out 50 times a week. The same Monday Slack post. The same five links checked every morning. 

 Today's options are all bad. Code it yourself — and most people can't. Use a no-code bot — and it breaks the first time a website changes a button. Fine-tune an LLM — and you've started a research project. 

 I wanted something simpler: show the AI the work once, and have it generalize from the one example. I had read open-source Skill Recorder watches your screen and ships a portable SKILL.md . It had the right shape, but it was a desktop app, it required GitHub Copilot CLI, and it didn't actually generalize. I wanted the same pipeline on the web, against any service, with a human in the loop at every step. 

 What it does 

 Echo is a platform with two halves. 

 1. The Recorder. A browser page at /record that captures your screen, records your voice if you want it, and ships the whole thing to an AI. The AI returns a structured analysis — the title, the intent, the ordered steps. You review and approve it. Then a second AI turns your steps into a generalized plan — your hardcoded search query becomes a {{job_query}} token, your "for the 3 rows" becomes "for every row", and every step is mapped to a tool Echo knows about. You review and approve that. The final output is a portable SKILL.md file that any AI agent runtime can read and run. 

 2. The Composer. A 2×2 grid at /compose . Each slot owns its own goal, plan, run, and progress stream. Hit dispatch on all four and they fire in parallel — real headless browser, real screenshots, real action logs streaming back to your screen. The runs page shows a "📸 real headless" badge whenever the action came from a real browser rather than a simulation. 

 How we built it 

 
 Next.js 16 on Vercel with the function timeout pushed to 60s so the LLM calls have breathing room. State is local-first (everything in your browser's localStorage), with an optional Firestore mirror when GCP is configured. 
 Real headless Chromium running inside the Vercel function. Not a fake — every screenshot in the runs page is from a live browser session. The browser-executor/ package is a Cloud Run-ready container for production scale. 
 Gemini 3.5 Flash for both the describer and the builder. The code tries Vertex AI first, falls back to AI Studio, and has a fallback chain of three models. 
 A 4-stage pipeline lifted from Skill Recorder (Record → Timeline → Describer → Builder → SKILL.md), adapted from Electron to a pure web app. The describer and builder prompts are ~250 lines each, with strict schema validators. The {{id}} token system is a port of theirs. 
 An eval harness that runs 6 fixture recordings against the real LLM and scores each one on tokenization, tool picks, step count, and side-effect classification. Average score: 64% (above the 60% gate). The harness caught a real prompt regression the first time I ran it. 
 Human-in-the-loop gates between every LLM step. If a step is wrong, you say so in plain English ("step 3 is irrelevant") and the agent re-runs with your feedback in context. 
 

 Challenges we ran into 

 
 Vercel's 10-second function timeout. I pushed it to 60s, warm-started the browser, and split the pipeline into separate routes so each LLM call is its own function. A real production deploy would use Cloud Run with no timeout pressure. 
 Chromium binary stripping on Vercel. The browser's bin/ directory kept getting dropped. Fixed with serverExternalPackages and outputFileTracingIncludes so the binary ships inside the function bundle. 
 Cloud Run worker failed on first deploy because the org blocks JSON service-account keys. I switched to IAM-bound credentials and ran out of time to retry, so the live demo runs on Vercel-hosted Chromium. The Cloud Run Dockerfile is ready when those constraints relax. 
 The LLM kept hardcoding values instead of using the {{token}} pattern. The first eval run scored 30% on a fixture because Gemini wrote "AI jobs" instead of {{job_query}} . I rewrote the Builder prompt with an explicit "Dynamic values are tokens. Period." section. The score went to 60%+ but the LLM still misses abstract-noun tokens about half the time — a self-critique pass is the next iteration. 
 A React hooks rule violation on the agent detail page caused a "This page couldn't load" error. Discovered during a smoke test right before the demo. Fixed in two lines. 
 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 End-to-end pipeline live at echo-one-liard.vercel.app . Record → analyze → build → SKILL.md, with human review gates between every step. 
 Real headless integration, not a mock. Every screenshot in the runs page is from a real browser session. 
 Multi-composer parallelism. Four agents fire in parallel; each one streams its own progress, browser actions, and screenshots. 
 Portable SKILL.md export. Every saved skill is a self-contained markdown file with YAML frontmatter, parameterized body, rules, and error codes. Drop it into any agent runtime. 
 The eval harness caught a real gap before users did. The tokenization regression was visible in the scorecard the moment I changed the prompt. 
 Local-first architecture. The app degrades gracefully without GCP — everything works on localStorage alone. 
 

 What we learned 

 
 The 4-stage pipeline is the right shape. Every alternative I considered — single-shot LLM, fine-tuned model, end-to-end agent — lost the human-in-the-loop gates, and those gates are what kept hallucinations from shipping as skills. 
 The hard part isn't the LLM call, it's the data model. Tokens, plan structure, step kinds, tool mapping, allowed-tools — none of these are free from the LLM. Each one needs a strict schema with hand-rolled validation. 
 Headless browsers on Vercel are real but bounded. 60s is the absolute ceiling. For real production scale, the worker belongs on Cloud Run or Fly.io, not on the same Vercel function as the consumer app. 
 Real-time eval is the only way to know if a prompt change helped. I lost hours to LLM variance on the first run. A 6-fixture suite is the floor; 20+ is what you need for statistical confidence. 
 Browser-level event capture is enough for 80% of use cases. Skill Recorder captures OS-level events via Electron. We can't do that in a web app. But for browser-first workflows (LinkedIn, Gmail, HubSpot, Sheets, Notion), the browser API gives us everything we need. 
 

 What's next for Echo 

 
 A self-critique pass in the Builder — a second LLM call that asks "did you miss any tokens?" before finalizing. Should push the eval from 64% to 80%+. 
 Production Cloud Run deployment of the headless browser worker once the org's JSON-key constraint is worked around. 
 Real OAuth integrations with HubSpot, Notion, Slack, and Gmail. The Builder can already pick these tools; what's missing is the OAuth handshake. 
 A Chrome extension for OS-level event capture 
 Scheduled runs / automations — a Skill Recorder "AutomationBuilder" tier that wraps a plan in a trigger (schedule, webhook, condition). 
 A 20+ fixture eval suite + a regression test for the Builder prompt. 
 A token marketplace — a public library of {{value}} tokens users have already configured, so skills are shareable across teams. 
 

 Echo is open-source at github.com/Prasannaverse13/Echo . Live demo at echo-one-liard.vercel.app .

title: AgentOps
pitch: AgentOps gives AI agents real WebMCP tools to act on the web and a Sentinel security layer that keeps you in control of every risky move.
about_excerpt:
AgentOps gives AI agents real WebMCP tools to act on the web and a Sentinel security layer that keeps you in control of every risky move.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Give AI the web and keep yourself in control 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Give AI the web and keep yourself in control 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Give AI the web and keep yourself in control 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 Every "AI agent that browses the web for you" demo I'd seen was binary, either the AI does everything unsupervised unsettling the moment money or personal data is involved or the user has to approve every single click, which defeats the point of delegating anything. I wanted to build the middle ground: Which is an agent that acts freely on low-risk actions, but hits a real, structural trust boundary the moment something consequential is at stake. WebMCP made that possible in a way ad-hoc browser automation never could because a registered tool is structured data , a security layer can actually reason about what a call means before it runs, not just watch pixels get clicked. 

 What it does 

 AgentOps takes a plain-language goal "book me a flight to Venice under $600," "order pizza for a get-together" and turns it into a mission: a sequence of real WebMCP tool calls. Every one of those calls passes through Sentinel , our trust/policy layer, before it executes: 

 
 Low-risk actions (search, compare, read) run automatically. 
 Consequential ones (bookings, purchases above a user-set threshold, sending messages) pause and ask for a one-click approval, with a plain-English reason and a risk score. 
 A fixed set of categories (credentials, password changes, financial transfers) are never auto-approved, full stop. 
 Anything a tool returns is treated as untrusted content if it contains an embedded instruction trying to override the agent (a prompt injection), Sentinel blocks it outright. Not a setting. A boundary. 
 

 The user sets their own risk tolerance once in a Trust Policy screen; every mission afterward respects it without further supervision. Missions pause and resume in place no restarting and every decision is logged. 

 How we built it 

 The frontend is a Vite/React app with a Three.js "Agent Core" that visually reflects the agent's state (idle, thinking, executing, awaiting approval, blocked). Every mission step is registered as a real tool via document.modelContext.registerTool() / navigator.modelContext native on Chrome behind the WebMCP flag, or through the @mcp-b/webmcp-polyfill package everywhere else, so the same code path works across environments. Before executing anything, the mission engine calls getTools() a genuine discovery step, not a hardcoded list. 

 Sentinel's gate lives inside each tool's execute() , so the enforcement isn't UI-only it applies no matter who calls the tool, our own runner or, in principle, an external agent. Mission plans are generated at runtime by an LLM (via an OpenAI-compatible endpoint) rather than picked from a fixed script, and one mission's flight-search step calls a real (sandboxed) flight-search API through a small serverless proxy the only place any secret key lives, since real commerce/travel APIs explicitly block direct browser calls. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 A few things broke in ways that shaped the final architecture: 

 
 My first pick for real flight data, Amadeus's free self-service tier, was decommissioned mid-build . We moved to Duffel's test-mode API instead. 
 Duffel (like most real commercial APIs) explicitly blocks direct browser calls you cannot safely hold a real secret key client-side. That's what pushed me to add a minimal Vercel serverless function as a proxy: the smallest amount of backend that makes a genuinely real API call possible without leaking credentials. 
 The LLM provider deprecated the model I was building with mid-hackathon, silently breaking AI planning until I caught it and swapped to their current recommended model. 
 The most important bug we found: Sentinel's purchase-risk check used (amount || 0) > threshold , so a step with no amount attached like an AI-planned "order pizza" step that omitted a price silently defaulted to "safe" and auto-approved. I fixed this as defense-in-depth: a missing amount now escalates to "ask" rather than being treated as zero risk, and a second, independent check flags any step whose own description implies a real commitment (ordering, paying, booking, canceling) even if the planner mis-categorized it. Sentinel's judgment isn't purely downstream of a label the LLM chose. 
 

 Accomplishments that I'm proud of 

 Getting Sentinel to feel like a real trust boundary rather than a UI decoration the prompt-injection detection in particular, where content a tool returns is scanned as untrusted data before the agent can act on it, not just the request being sent. And getting at least one mission wired to genuinely real external data (not just simulated), despite hitting a dead API provider and browser CORS restrictions along the way, without ever compromising a secret key. 

 What I learned 

 WebMCP's ecosystem is still very early almost no production site implements it yet, which shaped an honest choice to have AgentOps register its own actions as tools rather than pretend arbitrary sites already support this. I also learned, the hard way, that any security layer built on top of an LLM's own categorization needs a second, independent check trusting a model to always self-report risk correctly is exactly the kind of single point of failure a "trust boundary" is supposed to prevent. 

 What's next for AgentOps 

 Wiring real external data into the Shopping and Finance missions the same way I did for Travel; giving AgentOps a second, fully independent WebMCP surface (a separate site registering its own tools) so the External Agent → Sentinel → WebMCP Tool → Website story is completely literal instead of self-hosted; and letting a real external agent not just our own UI discover and drive AgentOps' tools directly.

title: Heatline
pitch: A tenant and a legal-aid advocate each get an agent on one NYC building's own enforcement record.
about_excerpt: A tenant and a legal-aid advocate each get an agent on one NYC building's own enforcement record. Like Comment Story Updates 52 degrees at 7am, eleven mornings in a row That was the reading in a fourth-floor apartment on Barnes Avenue in the Bronx this winter. The landlord stopped answering in January. What the tenant did not know, and what I did not know until I pulled the data, is that the city already had a file on the building: 102 open class C violations. Class C is HPD's word for "immediately hazardous." The oldest has been open 601 days. All of that sits on NYC Open Data. No key, no login, one SODA query. It has never been in the same room as the tenant. What Heatline does with it Two people open one case page from two different links. The tenant gets 12 WebMCP tools; the legal-aid advocate helping them gets 9. Same origin, same deployment, different agents. I want to be precise about the difference because it is the whole product: Only the tenant's window has log_condition , file_packet , answer_evidence_request , share_case and the 311 form. Only the advocate's window has assemble_hp_action_packet and request_evidence . Open DevTools, Application, WebMCP in both windows and the lists are not the same. The role is a capability key in the URL. The server re-derives it on every write, so when the advocate's agent forges a file_packet call (I tried) it gets a 403 that reads: "Only the tenant can file packet. You are the advocate: this stays with the tenant's session." The hidden tool is a convenience. The server is the boundary. A tenant does not know what a BBL is The first version of building_violation_history required a 10-digit borough-block-lot number. The advocate's agent called it with {} and got "bbl is required." That is a tool written for a database, not for a person freezing in an apartment. It now reads the BBL off the open case and only takes one if you want a different building. Fixed the same hour, in the commit log. The same instinct runs through the rest. The tenant types "no heat again, 52 degrees at 7am." match_condition_to_code returns section 27-2029 with the rule in plain English: 68F from 6am to 10pm when it is under 55F outside, heat season October 1 to May 31. log_condition then stops inside a confirmation card until the tenant presses Confirm. The agent proposes; the person decides. Every number on the page carries the SODA URL that produced it. Paste the URL and you get the same 102. Four NYC Open Data feeds become one per-building index, the page registers a different tool set per link, and the server re-checks the role before any write lands. The loop the two agents run The advocate's agent asks for a photo of the thermostat at 7am tomorrow. That request lands in the tenant's window over a live stream, no reload. The tenant's agent answers. The advocate's agent then calls assemble_hp_action_packet , which writes five sections from the case plus the city record: parties (owner name and portfolio size from the HPD registration), conditions with code sections, the building record with a block comparison, a timeline, relief sought. It saves a draft. In the tenant's window, file_packet 's description now says "one draft packet waiting"; the agent calls it, a person presses Confirm, the packet is filed. The 311 complaint is a real <form toolname="draft_311_complaint"> with toolparamdescription on each field and deliberately no toolautosubmit . The agent fills it. Only a human can press Send. You cannot do this with a chatbot wrapper or by scraping the page. Nothing else knows which window is asking. The tenant's window and the advocate's window on the same case. The gate in the middle is the server, not the tool list. The parts that are not glamorous document.modelContext.registerTool , never navigator.modelContext . Native first, @mcp-b/webmcp-polyfill as fallback, and a badge on the page says which one is live. Fourteen tools. untrustedContentHint on list_conditions and build_timeline , because those return text another person typed; that text is wrapped in <untrusted-user-text> on the tool path, the REST path and the SSE stream. Confirm gates are built inside each mutating tool's execute , since WebMCP has no destructive-action annotation. Seventeen eval fixtures. The negative ones assert the denied tool is absent from that session's toolsForRole , so "just file it for them" from the advocate expects zero calls. 125 tests. Read tools fetch through /api/building/* so the 1.3 MB index stays server-side; importing it into the client broke the production build on day one, and that fix is in the history too. The index covers 40 buildings in zip 10467, the Bronx zip with the most open class C heat violations, 6,077 rows. The build script and every query URL are in the repo. Everything here was written on 4 September 2026 with Next.js 16, TypeScript, Tailwind 4, Upstash Redis, Vitest and NYC Open Data. The build script, every SODA query URL and the eval fixtures are in the repo. Built With next.js tailwind typescript upstash vercel vitest webmcp Try it out heatline-nyc.vercel.app github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Aarav Raj Like Share this project: Updates Aarav Raj started this project — Sep 04, 2026 03:33 AM EDT

Heatline is a shared case page for a tenant and a legal aid advocate. Each of them gets their own agent on the same page with different tools. The data is New York's own housing enforcement record. HPD violations, complaints, 311 heat calls, and owner registrations pulled by soda query with the exact URL kept beside every number. Here is the tenant's window. Only a human presses send. Touch wrapper can do this because nothing else knows which window is asking. The page declares its own tools. The roles are capability keys, and every right goes through a person. The city's own record was always public. Now the tenant's agent can read it, and the advocate's agent can build the case from it. That's Heat Line.

title: MusterMind - The wearability agent — buy, restyle, or skip
pitch: The first shopping agent that can tell you not to buy. Buy, restyle, wait or skip — every verdict cited to you, to product data, or to the rules, live over WebMCP.
about_excerpt: The first shopping agent that can tell you not to buy. Buy, restyle, wait or skip — every verdict cited to you, to product data, or to the rules, live over WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration We started somewhere else. The first idea was a size recommender — obvious fashion-commerce problem. Then we opened DevTools on a live AJIO product page and found something that reframed the whole project. Sitting in window.__PRELOADED_STATE__ , invisible to any agent driving the DOM, was a size chart already converted to centimetres , an explicit measurementType: "Garment Measurement" provenance flag, live per-size stock counts, and — the thing we didn't expect — a crowd fit distribution: Perfect 64% · Tight 15% · Too Tight 5% · Loose 11% · Too Loose 3% over 2,100 raters The page already knew this garment runs small. It had no way to tell an agent. But the moment that actually defined the product came later. Our first working version ranked a ₹320 polo as the top buy for a client dinner. It was cheap, in stock, not a duplicate, and technically satisfied every constraint. It was also completely wrong — a polo does not become client-dinner appropriate because it is cheap. That is the failure mode of every shopping agent we've used. They can only say buy , so they optimise for the one signal they can read: price and availability. We rebuilt the engine around a different question — what if the agent could say no? What it does Mustermind is a wearability decision layer. You give it an occasion, a budget, a PIN code, a deadline, fits you avoid, and a rough list of what you already own. It scores live AJIO products on four axes: product facts, your constraints, purchase risk, and rewear value. Every garment gets one of four verdicts: Verdict Meaning buy Worth buying for this occasion restyle You can already assemble this look from what you own wait Right piece, wrong price or arrives too late skip Violates a stated constraint, duplicates something owned, or can't be delivered Every verdict carries the factors behind it, and every factor is tagged with its source — you, product data, or the rules. A real card from the running app: RESTYLE — You can get this look from what you own U.S. Polo Assn. · Men Button Down-Collar Tailored Fit Shirt · ₹1,175 + Within budget [user] ₹1,175 against a ₹3,000 ceiling − Close to what you own [rules] You already have White Shirts; this adds a colour, not a category · Rewear value [rules] Pairs with 1 item you already own + Right register [rules] Shirts suits client dinner + Fit confidence [product] 90% — garment measurements published, 77 fit ratings + Suggested size M [product] 16% of 77 raters found this loose vs 5% tight, so one size down · Deliverable, no date [product] Serviceable at 560029; the delivery API did not return a date That last line matters as much as the verdict. The delivery API returned no date, so the app doesn't invent one. Load the default brief and Mustermind recommends nothing. Two restyles, five skips, four different skip reasons. Then tell the agent "I could stretch to ₹5,500" and a blazer becomes the single buy — on screen, with the reason visible, and the change written to a Decision Ledger showing that you made it. How we built it Zero npm dependencies. Node 20 and vanilla HTML/CSS/JS. Nothing to install, no lockfile, no bundler — a judge can read the entire thing. It ships as a ~55 MB Alpine container running non-root. Five WebMCP tools , registered on document.modelContext with navigator.modelContext as a fallback probe, behind feature detection: Tool readOnlyHint untrustedContentHint get_current_style_brief ✅ — get_product_truth ✅ ✅ evaluate_wearability ✅ ✅ record_user_tradeoff — — prepare_purchase_handoff — — Five, deliberately. Tool selection degrades as the set grows, and each description is written as product surface — when to call it, what changes state, and when to ask instead of assert . The verdict engine is a rule engine, not a model. This was a deliberate constraint: the agent has to narrate why a verdict is what it is, and a scorer you cannot read gives it nothing to say. Gradient boosting would have scored marginally better and been useless on camera. Crowd fit becomes a directional prior. Too Tight and Too Loose count double — they signal a full size off, not a preference: $$\text{skew} = \frac{\left(t + 2t^{+}\right) - \left(l + 2l^{+}\right)}{100}$$ where $t, l$ are the tight and loose percentages and $t^{+}, l^{+}$ the too tight / too loose ones. We call RUNS_SMALL above a weighted gap of 6. At the rater counts these products carry, the standard error on a $p \approx 0.20$ proportion over $n = 2100$ is $$\sigma = \sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}} \approx 0.0087 \approx 0.9\ \text{pp}$$ so a 6-point weighted gap is several standard errors — signal, not noise. Below 50 raters we return INSUFFICIENT_DATA and refuse to call it at all. Two public AJIO sources , called server-side only: the PDP aggregator and the delivery-promise API, with a 60-second cache and hard timeouts. The style-code invariant is strict — only codes this server obtained from AJIO's own search, or ships fixtures for. Never a code supplied by the browser. No anti-bot sensor header is sent, stored or committed anywhere. If a call would need one, the app falls back to clearly-labelled fixtures instead. There's a grep in the verification step that fails the build if such a string ever appears in the tree. 55 assertions, no test framework. node scripts/selfcheck.js . Challenges we ran into The WebMCP API is not the MCP API. Our tools returned {content:[{type:'text',text:...}]} — the envelope a remote MCP server uses. Chrome's execute returns a plain string . Every result would have arrived as a stringified wrapper the agent had to unwrap. We also assumed an unregisterTool method; there isn't one — unregistration is an AbortSignal passed at registration. Both were caught only by reading Chrome's docs against our own code. The silent one: origin isolation. WebMCP is only exposed in origin-isolated documents. Without Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 , document.modelContext is simply undefined — no error, no warning, nothing to debug. You'd naturally blame your Chrome version and go chasing an upgrade that was never the problem. Real data is hostile in small ways. numUserRatings is "2.1K" , a display string — parse it naively and you fabricate a rater count. Percentages arrive as "15 %" , with a space. The size chart is a superset of what's purchasable (8 charted, 5 buyable on one real product), so recommendations must come from the intersection. One live product returned a fittingType of " " — whitespace, which is truthy, and rendered a factor row with blank evidence. A truthful API answer that was useless. Our demo fixtures had invented SKUs. The live delivery API dutifully returned "not serviceable" for them — which is true, and means the SKU doesn't exist , not that the garment can't be delivered. We were putting fabricated products on real-looking hard fails. Fixture products no longer consult live delivery. A regression we caused ourselves. When live search landed, it loaded eight real style codes — and the PDP allowlist, which only knew about fixtures, rejected every one. The app rendered empty under a confident "Live AJIO data" badge. Fixing it meant sharpening the invariant rather than loosening it: codes AJIO's own search returned are server-obtained, so they earn a session allowlist; browser-supplied codes never do. Then the fix had its own bug — the search cache outlived the session allowlist, so the first Reset handed back codes the adapter then refused. Both are now regression-tested. Knowing when to stop being clever. The hardest call was making wrong register a hard stop instead of a weighted negative. Softening it makes price pull junk back to the top of the list, and the whole argument collapses. Accomplishments that we're proud of It opens with zero buys. A recommender that cannot say "you already own something that works" will eventually sell you a fourth white shirt. Getting the rules honest enough to recommend nothing — and then having that be the most compelling thing on screen — is the accomplishment. Four skips, four different reasons. Wrong register, already owned, avoided fit, undeliverable. Not one score threshold wearing four hats. The agent cannot spend your money. prepare_purchase_handoff is two-phase: it returns AWAITING_CONFIRMATION , a card appears, and only a real DOM click mints a single-use token — bound to style code and size, expiring in 60 seconds. Guessing an ID, replaying a used one, or swapping the size after confirmation all fail, and all four are asserted. There is no cart, checkout, login, orders or payment access anywhere in the codebase. It degrades honestly. Fixture mode is labelled in a banner, a header badge, and a per-card pill, and tool results carry dataSource so the agent discloses it. Serviceable-with-no-date says exactly that. title: DevSmith
pitch: DevSmith forge ideas into software with AI-powered project planning.
about_excerpt:
DevSmith forge ideas into software with AI-powered project planning.

 Dashboard

 Upload files section in AI Assistant 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Project roadmap generation 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 



 
 From AI Assistant to AI Teammate 

 Inspiration 

 As developers, we use a lot of different tools to build software: an AI assistant for questions and code generation, a task manager for planning, a code editor for implementation, and documentation for figuring out how everything fits together. 

 I wanted to build something that brought the planning and AI development workflow into one place . 

 That idea became DevSmith . 

 DevSmith lets a developer create a project, generate an AI-powered roadmap of milestones and tasks, and then use an in-context AI assistant to ask questions, generate code, explain code, and fix problems. 

 But while building it, I realized there was another interesting problem: 

 AI agents can interact with websites, but interacting with a website through the UI isn't the same as understanding the application's actual capabilities. 

 An agent shouldn't have to guess which button creates a project or determine whether a status badge means "Planning" or "In Progress" from a screenshot. 

 That's where WebMCP became the most important part of DevSmith. 

 

 What I Built 

 DevSmith is a local-first AI development workspace designed to be usable by both developers and AI agents . 

 The workflow is simple: 

 Idea → Project → Roadmap → Tasks → Development 

 A developer can start with an idea and use AI to turn it into a structured development plan. 

 For example: 

 
 "Create a project for a habit tracker API and plan it out." 
 

 With WebMCP, an AI agent can perform that workflow using DevSmith's actual capabilities: 
 create_project
 ↓
generate_roadmap
 ↓
get_roadmap
 ↓
create_task
 
 DevSmith currently exposes tools including: 

 
 list_projects 
 create_project 
 get_project 
 generate_roadmap 
 get_roadmap 
 create_task 
 update_task 
 ask_devsmith_assistant 
 

 Instead of an agent trying to navigate the DOM, it can call a structured tool with a defined schema. 

 For example: 
 document . modelContext . registerTool ( { 
 name : "generate_roadmap" , 
 description : 
 "Generate an AI roadmap (milestones and tasks) for a project." , 
 inputSchema : { 
 type : "object" , 
 properties : { 
 projectId : { type : "string" } , 
 model : { type : "string" } , 
 } , 
 required : [ "projectId" ] , 
 } , 
 execute : async ( input ) = > { 
 const res = await fetch ( 
 ` / api / projects / $ { input . projectId } / roadmap / generate` , 
 { 
 method : "POST" , 
 headers : { 
 "Content-Type" : "application/json" , 
 } , 
 body : JSON . stringify ( { 
 model : input . model ? ? "default" , 
 } ) , 
 } 
 ) ; 

 return res . json ( ) ; 
 } , 
 } ) ; 
 
 This means the agent interacts with the capability rather than the visual representation of the capability. 

 

 Why WebMCP Matters 

 Before WebMCP, an agent interacting with DevSmith would essentially have to behave like a human using a browser: 
 Agent
 ↓
UI
 ↓
DOM / Screenshots
 ↓
Guess what to click
 ↓
Application
 
 With WebMCP: 
 Agent
 ↓
WebMCP
 ↓
Structured Tool
 ↓
DevSmith API
 ↓
Database / AI
 
 This makes the interaction more reliable and meaningful. 

 For example, instead of: 

 
 "Find the Generate Roadmap button and click it." 
 

 the agent can perform: 
 generate_roadmap({
 projectId: "...",
 model: "..."
})
 
 The agent doesn't need to know where the button is. 

 It needs to know what capability it wants to use . 

 That is the part of WebMCP that I found most interesting. 

 

 How I Built It 

 DevSmith is built with: 

 
 React + TypeScript + Vite for the frontend 
 Tailwind CSS for the UI 
 Express + TypeScript for the backend 
 SQLite + better-sqlite3 for local project data 
 Ollama for local AI models 
 WebMCP for agent interaction 
 

 The application is designed to run locally with Ollama. 

 The local architecture looks like: 
 ┌──────────────────┐
│ DevSmith UI │
└────────┬─────────┘
 │
 ▼
┌──────────────────┐
│ Express Backend │
└───────┬──────────┘
 │
 ┌────┴─────┐
 ▼ ▼
SQLite Ollama
 │
 ▼
 Local LLM
 
 For the WebMCP integration, DevSmith exposes its important application actions as tools. 

 The tools communicate with the same backend functionality used by the application itself. 

 I also created a cloud LLM fallback for the deployed version so that someone visiting the live demo doesn't need to install Ollama or download a local model. 

 This allowed me to keep the local-first architecture while still making the project accessible to judges. 

 

 What I Learned 

 The biggest lesson I learned was that adding AI to an application and designing an application for AI agents are two different things . 

 Initially, I was mostly thinking about AI as an assistant: 
 User → AI → Response
 
 WebMCP made me start thinking about AI as an actor that can interact with the application: 
 User
 ↓
AI Agent
 ↓
WebMCP
 ↓
Application capabilities
 
 That changed how I thought about application architecture. 

 I had to think about: 

 
 What capabilities should an agent have? 
 What information does an agent need? 
 What should each tool's schema look like? 
 Which actions should be separate tools? 
 What information should a tool return? 
 How can agents modify application data safely? 
 

 I learned that a good agent interface isn't just a collection of API endpoints. 

 The tools need to represent meaningful actions that make sense to an agent. 

 I also learned more about integrating local LLMs into a full-stack application and designing the application so it can support both local and hosted AI providers. 

 

 Challenges 

 One of the biggest challenges was making WebMCP more than just a checkbox feature. 

 It would have been easy to expose one simple tool and say that DevSmith supports WebMCP. 

 Instead, I wanted the tools to represent actual development workflows. 

 That meant connecting: 
 AI Agent
 ↓
WebMCP Tool
 ↓
Backend API
 ↓
SQLite / AI
 
 Another challenge was balancing the local-first philosophy with the need for an accessible live demo. 

 Locally, DevSmith uses Ollama: 
 DevSmith → Ollama → Local Model
 
 But requiring every judge to install Ollama and download a model would create unnecessary friction. 

 So I implemented a hosted LLM fallback: 
 DevSmith → Cloud LLM
 
 The result is an application that can be fully local for developers who want privacy, while still being easy for someone to test through the live deployment. 

 I also had to work through the normal challenges of building a full-stack application while integrating a relatively new agent interaction model: connecting frontend and backend state, generating useful AI roadmaps, managing tasks and milestones, handling different LLM providers, and making the WebMCP tools work with the existing application. 

 

 What's Next 

 DevSmith is currently focused on project planning and AI-assisted development, but I see WebMCP as the foundation for much more. 

 Future possibilities include: 

 
 GitHub repository integration 
 Codebase-aware AI assistance 
 Git operations through agents 
 Automated task implementation 
 Pull request generation 
 Local code indexing 
 Automated testing and debugging 
 Agent-driven roadmap updates 
 Specialized development agents 
 

 The long-term goal is not to replace the developer. 

 It's to create an AI teammate that understands the project, the roadmap, the tasks, and the tools available to build it . 

 DevSmith started as an AI-powered development workspace. 

 With WebMCP, it became something more interesting: 

 a development workspace that an AI agent can actually operate.

title: Paperwork - a form your agent fills while you watch
pitch: A gnarly insurance form the agent fills from plain language while you watch - pending until you accept, and the legal attestations have no tool that can touch them.
about_excerpt: A gnarly insurance form the agent fills from plain language while you watch - pending until you accept, and the legal attestations have no tool that can touch them. Like Comment Story Updates The renters-insurance form: six steps, one pending layer Tool console: get_form called live via WebMCP WebMCP surface: three legal attestations are structurally unreachable by any tool - human-only fields enforced in the data model itself, not by prompt instruction. Inspiration Nobody's brain fails at forms; their patience does. A renters-insurance application asks forty questions, a third of which only appear conditionally, in the form's own order - even though the applicant already knows all of it. What it does Tell the agent what happened in plain language; it drafts answers onto the real six-step form, in front of you. Nothing the agent writes is an answer yet - every draft lands in a pending layer, highlighted, tracked by provenance (empty / human / pending / accepted / uncertain), and only counts once you accept it. Three legal attestations - fraud acknowledgement, an animal attestation, final accuracy - are marked human-only in the data model itself: no tool can reach them, structurally, not by instruction. How we built it One file, vanilla JavaScript. Every tool writes through the same setField() the inputs commit through via one invoke() chokepoint, so conditional fields, repeaters, and validation behave identically whichever side acted. fill_field / fill_section draft into the pending layer; review_submission is read-only and there is no submit tool at all - Submit is a human-only button. Challenges we ran into An edge case in add_repeater_item : when a conditional trigger (e.g. "any claims in the last 5 years?") auto-spawned an empty repeater row, the tool would add a second row instead of reusing the empty one the UI had already created - a subtle UI/agent-state drift caught by explicit testing of the conditional-field interaction, not the isolated tool call. Accomplishments that we're proud of A form where the agent can genuinely say "I'm not sure" - a flagged, visible uncertainty on a field, not a silent guess - and where three specific legal fields are unreachable by any tool, not merely discouraged by one. What we learned Provenance tracking (who wrote this field, and is it still pending) turned out to be the real product, more than the fill-from-text trick itself - it's what makes it safe to let an agent write into a legal document at all. What's next Multi-document support (a second insurer's form with a different question set) to prove the provenance model generalizes beyond one carrier's application. Part of a seven-app portfolio Each entry proves a different WebMCP capability: Tablemap (dynamic tool registration), Signoff (a tool that only exists once a human approves it), Shortlist (a tool schema generated live from the catalog), Jhola (genuinely cancellable long-running tools), Almari (quarantined untrusted content), Dhwani (declarative, no-JavaScript tools). title: TripRescue
pitch: Human-controlled flight recovery with typed WebMCP tools, constrained search, exact-price preview, and verified booking changes.
about_excerpt: Human-controlled flight recovery with typed WebMCP tools, constrained search, exact-price preview, and verified booking changes. Like Comment Story Updates What it does An airline moves your flight. TripRescue lets a traveller—or a browser agent working with them—inspect the affected booking, state recovery constraints such as arrival time, maximum extra cost, and stops, compare ranked alternatives, preview the exact itinerary and price difference, approve the change in the page, and verify the updated booking. It runs against a real Duffel test-mode order. Duffel's sandbox generates the airline change, the booked airline supplies the change offers, and the app verifies the confirmed order change by refetching it. Why WebMCP fits Trip recovery is a high-stakes, multi-step, stateful task where guessing buttons from pixels is unsafe. The agent needs the current booking, must obey explicit limits, must never confirm without the traveller, and must prove the result. TripRescue registers five focused tools from the top-level page with the imperative document.modelContext.registerTool API: get_trip find_recovery_options preview_trip_change apply_trip_change get_change_status The tools use the page's signed session. Booking IDs, provider tokens, and passenger data never enter the prompt. Read, search, preview, apply, and verify remain separate operations with appropriate annotations and compact normalized outputs. A better human-agent experience Every tool call updates the visible page before resolving, so the traveller sees the same state the agent is reasoning about. An Agent Activity log records each call and its purpose. The consequential write is protected by a server-issued preview, order fingerprint, expiry, exact-price revalidation, and single-use idempotent confirmation. Calling apply_trip_change opens an in-page confirmation dialog. The traveller—not the agent—must review the itinerary and explicitly confirm it. This lets the traveller state intent once—“direct, arrive by 1 PM, no more than $150 extra”—while the agent converts it into a constrained search, ranks valid options, stages the best one, and hands control back exactly when the booking and test charge would change. Success is defined by the refetched provider booking, not merely an HTTP 200. How it was built TripRescue uses Next.js 16, TypeScript, Zod, Tailwind CSS v4, the WebMCP imperative API, and the Duffel Flights API in test mode. It is deployed behind nginx with pm2 on Hetzner. GitHub Actions runs lint, typechecking, tests, and a production build before deploying, then verifies the public URL. Testing Open the live app in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled. Create a sandbox trip, simulate an airline change, and ask the browser agent to find a nonstop replacement arriving before 1 PM for no more than $150 extra. Preview the best option, apply it, approve the in-page confirmation, and verify the refetched booking. Honest limitations Duffel test mode only. Schedules and prices are synthetic, and the airline change is simulated by Duffel. No live bookings or real payments occur. The demo uses the LHR → LTN Duffel Airways scenario supported by Duffel's sandbox. Built With duffel-flights-api github-actions next.js nginx pm2 tailwind-css typescript vitest webmcp zod Try it out triprescue.slate-app.online github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by varun a Like Share this project: Updates varun a started this project — Sep 03, 2026 06:04 AM EDT
video_transcript_excerpt: Trip rescue turns a disrupted flight into a safe agent assisted recovery. The browser agent can search and prepare the fix, but it cannot make the irreversible change on its own. We start with a real sandbox booking, then simulate the disruption inside the page. Before the recovery can work, the page needs a signed in trip and a browser session that the tools can reuse. The agent can read the trip, search options, and stage a change, but the traveler still owns the final approval. The booking ID and provider token stay out of the prompt, so the model works inside a constrained boundary. The demo opens on a Duffel sandbox booking, and the page confirms that five web MCP site tools are registered. A browser agent reads the signed in trip, then the schedule change lands, and the itinerary shifts from the original departure to the disrupted one. The agent gets real state, not a mocked prompt. The agent reads the signed in trip, then searches for non-stop alternatives that arrive before 1:00 p.m. and cost no more than $150 extra. It ranks the results instead of grabbing the first match. That matters because constrained search turns a broad travel problem into a narrow auditable choice. Trip rescue previews the best option as an earlier Duffel Airways flight, but nothing changes yet. The important distinction is between a proposal and a booking. One is comparison, the other is an actual mutation. That separation keeps the agent useful without letting it silently commit the change. The preview shows the full $125 test charge before anything changes. Trip rescue stages the exact itinerary, the fare difference, and the penalty in one place, so the traveler sees the real cost up front. The agent is still asking to apply the change. When the agent asks to apply it, Trip Rescue opens an in-page confirmation dialogue. The traveler, not the agent, reviews the itinerary and explicitly approves the mutation. That is the irreversible step, and it happens under human control inside the browser. After Duffel accepts it, the agent calls get change status, re-fetches the order, and checks that the new itinerary is truly booked. The post-change read-back is just as important as the approval because it proves the mutation actually stuck. Without that verification step, the workflow would only be optimistic. The booking ID and provider token never enter the prompt because every tool reuses the page's signed session. The verified state shows the new itinerary booked and rechecked in the browser. That is WebMCP with real utility and human control at the irreversible step.

title: Orbweaver
pitch: An agent-native semantic workspace where ChatGPT proposes validated visual structures through WebMCP—and the human retains authority to accept, export, or undo.
about_excerpt: An agent-native semantic workspace where ChatGPT proposes validated visual structures through WebMCP—and the human retains authority to accept, export, or undo. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Complex systems do not need more interface. They need better structure. Architecture diagrams, workflows, data models, and knowledge graphs already contain meaning, but turning that meaning into a useful visual usually requires authored coordinates, diagram syntax, manually positioned shapes, or generated output that is difficult to inspect. I built Orbweaver around a simpler principle: Understand complex systems while showing less. What it does Orbweaver turns coordinate-free semantic graphs into deterministic, inspectable visual structures. The input describes meaning: what exists; how things relate; which relationships matter; what evidence and claims support the structure. Orbweaver validates that meaning, computes the layout, and renders an accessible SVG artifact. The proposal contains no authored coordinates, SVG, HTML, CSS, or executable markup. The WebMCP playground extends this into a shared human-agent workspace. ChatGPT can read the live workspace contract, create or revise a semantic proposal, inspect an entity, and focus it in the visible diagram. The agent can propose meaning. It cannot accept its own work. Why WebMCP Without WebMCP, an agent would need to infer interface controls and repeatedly manipulate a large JSON editor. That is slow, fragile, and disconnected from the application’s actual domain model. With WebMCP, Orbweaver exposes six bounded, page-local tools: read the current workspace and revision; read the supported semantic contract; create a complete proposal; revise it using conflict-safe operations; inspect semantic identity and provenance; focus an entity in the visible workspace. The tools reuse the same application controller and validation boundary as the human interface. WebMCP does not introduce a second, privileged execution path. The human-agent experience A person describes an order-fulfillment system in ordinary language. ChatGPT discovers Orbweaver’s tools and supplies entities, relationships, groups, claims, and evidence—not pixels or drawing instructions. Orbweaver validates the entire proposal atomically, derives the geometry, and renders revision one as a validated but untrusted preview . The person and agent then work with the same live state. ChatGPT can add Delivery tracking, focus it, and expose its relationships for inspection. Expected-revision checks prevent stale writes when the shared workspace changes. Acceptance remains a human-only decision. The agent cannot accept a revision or enable export. The person can inspect, reject, or undo the change. In the demonstration, I manually undo the agent’s revision and Orbweaver restores the previous graph. How I built it Orbweaver’s core is a provider-neutral TypeScript library. A strict GraphProposal contract represents semantic content without layout coordinates. ELK.js computes the visual structure, while Orbweaver produces accessible SVG, stable semantic identities, selection behavior, provenance, and inspection details. The playground’s WebMCP adapter registers six tools through the browser’s page-local model context. Tool inputs are treated as untrusted data and pass through the existing validation layer. Create and revise operations are atomic, revisions are versioned, and semantic writes never bundle human acceptance. The implementation is tested with Vitest, Playwright, and axe-core accessibility checks. The npm package contains no AI provider, account requirement, telemetry, or cloud runtime dependency. Challenges The hardest problem was not drawing the graph. It was designing the authority boundary. A useful agent needed enough access to create meaningful structures without gaining the ability to silently approve its own output. This required explicit trust states, expected-revision conflict protection, atomic validation, reversible mutations, and accepted-only export. The other challenge was visual restraint: presenting enough information to understand a complex system without turning the workspace into an aircraft cockpit. Orbweaver keeps the interface secondary to the structure being examined. Accomplishments I’m proud of Published a provider-neutral open-source TypeScript library rather than embedding an AI service inside the product. Built six bounded WebMCP tools around the application’s existing controller and validation boundary. Made agent-authored changes versioned, atomic, inspectable, and reversible. Preserved human-only authority over acceptance and export. Produced deterministic, accessible SVG from semantic proposals containing no authored coordinates. Published the beta package, live playground, documentation, source, and reproducible demonstration. What I learned WebMCP is most valuable when it exposes an application’s domain semantics—not when it simply recreates button clicking as tools. The strongest human-agent experience is not full autonomy. It is shared context with asymmetric authority: the agent contributes reach and synthesis; the application enforces structure; the human retains judgment at the moment of consequence. What’s next Orbweaver is open source and currently available as @semanticintent/orbweaver@0.2.0-beta.1 . Next steps include stabilizing the beta API, expanding semantic lenses and comparison views, and continuing to develop portable artifacts that preserve their meaning, provenance, and accessibility outside the original application.  1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 

 Haoku came from a problem I kept running into while learning about AI and languages. I usually study from multiple papers, articles, notes, and diagrams, but over time it becomes difficult to remember where each idea came from and which source supports it. 

 I wanted a workspace where you and your AI agent can study sources together without losing track of their provenance . Instead of making chat the center, Haoku makes the document the shared workspace. 

 What it does 

 Haoku has two modes: Study and Practice . 

 In Study, you add PDFs, text, images, or pasted content and build a structured Markdown sheet with your agent. Every claim can stay connected to the exact passage it came from. 

 In Practice, those same sources are turned into questions to reinforce what you learned. 

 How we built it 

 Haoku is browser-first: sources and workspace data stay locally in IndexedDB. 

 Through WebMCP, Haoku exposes tools that let the browser agent read the sources, edit the workspace content, link citations and generate practice questions. 

 The document is stored as Markdown, with interactive blocks implemented as web components so it remains portable outside the app. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 One of the challenges was designing the WebMCP tools correctly . The tools needed to expose enough context and structure for the agent to search sources, edit the document, link citations, and recover from errors reliably. 

 Another challenge was designing one workspace that works naturally for both a human and an AI agent . 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 I'm proud of having built a tool around how I think people will work with AI in the future: humans and agents sharing the same workspace, context, and tools instead of interacting only through chat. 

 What we learned 

 One of the biggest lessons was learning where agent tools are actually useful and where they are not . 

 Designing Haoku forced me to think differently about product interfaces: not only about what a human should click, but also about what an agent needs to understand, manipulate, and act on reliably. 

 That shift changed my perspective on future products. Instead of treating agents as an extra feature, I started thinking about how products themselves can be designed to adapt to agents as first-class users . 

 What's next for Haoku: Study workspace driven by your agent over WebMCP 

 Next, I want to expand the workspace with more interactive elements that the agent can create and manipulate while you study. 

 I also want to make conversations themselves usable as sources , so useful context from previous discussions can be brought into the workspace, connected to other material, and studied alongside papers, notes, and documents.

title: Keydler
pitch: A shared memory for you and your AI. Keeps completed work, rules to follow, and mistakes not to repeat, exposed to agents over WebMCP. Browser-local, no account, no server.
about_excerpt: A shared memory for you and your AI. Keeps completed work, rules to follow, and mistakes not to repeat, exposed to agents over WebMCP. Browser-local, no account, no server. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration An agent loses its context, and it does not just lose information. It loses the prohibitions. The approach you ruled out last week. The dependency you refused. The step it already finished. A conversation summary keeps the highlights and sacrifices exactly what constrains, because a constraint reads like a detail right up until someone breaks it. So you explain it again. And the agent proposes, with confidence, the thing you eliminated together on Tuesday. We wanted to know whether that was actually measurable, or just a feeling. It is measurable. What it does Keydler takes those constraints out of the conversation and puts them on a web page that an agent reads and writes through WebMCP: rules in force, work done with its evidence, approaches ruled out with the reason , and the next action. The part that matters is not that the human approves things. It is that the human can change the rules while the agent is working, and the page guarantees the agent finds out. Every agent write carries the version it read. A human write never does. So when you add a rule mid-flight, the agent's next write is refused: STALE STATE You are attempting to log work based on task state v5. Current state is v6. No write took place. Call what_changed with since_version: 5 to see only what moved. It asks for the delta, reads the new rule, and adapts. Without that refusal it would overwrite the rule you had just set, and neither of you would know ; you would find out from the result. Fourteen tools, four read and nine write, plus one that opens the log when none exists. Browser-local: no account, no server, nothing leaves the device. The measurement Without the log, an agent proposed the ruled-out approach again in 8 cases out of 8. With the log, in 0. Eight tasks, two conditions, one binary question. We got the design wrong first, and that failure taught us the product. Our initial tasks ruled out classic anti-patterns ; localStorage for tokens, OFFSET pagination. The control scored zero : a capable model avoids those unprompted, and rules them out by name without being asked. There was nothing to measure. So we inverted it. What has to be ruled out is not the bad answer. It is the good answer, set aside for a local reason. Ban the Redis token bucket because operations refused Redis. Ban cursor pagination because a backfill broke id monotonicity. Those are the right answers everywhere except here, for reasons no model can deduce. That is when the control started failing 8 out of 8, and it is the whole content model of the product. What the number hides is worth more than the number: no agent dodged a keyword. They read the reason and kept the part still valid ; "what was rejected is the Redis backing, not the bucket algorithm." And its limits, stated plainly: eight runs per condition, one model, correlated results. Exploratory, not statistical. No percentage is derived from it. How we built it TypeScript, one runtime dependency, IndexedDB, no framework. The domain is pure ; no DOM, no storage, no WebMCP ; so the guarantees are testable without a browser. The core is a versioned write queue. The version comparison happens inside the IndexedDB transaction, so two tabs cannot silently overwrite each other. Each write carries a mutation_id and an argument fingerprint: the same id with the same arguments replays the original reply verbatim; the same id with different arguments is refused and audited, rather than acknowledged as work that never happened. The interface is Material Design 3, implemented from the specification. The page keeps a default-src 'none' content policy. Challenges A fake cannot fail in a way it was not written to fail. Our 946 tests run against a ModelContext written from the spec IDL. Every time we opened a real browser, it told us something the fake could not: executeTool refuses a tool name and wants the object from getTools() ; its arguments must be a JSON string; its answer comes back serialized. Four times. The most useful bug was found by an agent, yesterday. In ChatGPT's built-in browser, GPT-5.6 Terra found the tools, then stopped and asked the human for permission ; because it believed creating a task would send the project details to keydler.com . The caution was right. The premise was wrong: nothing leaves the page. We added that fact to the tool description. It still asks. And it should: passing arguments to code served by a site is giving that site data, and our claim that we do nothing with it is unverifiable from where the agent sits. An agent that took a website's word for "I don't send your data anywhere" would be a worse agent. So we stopped writing copy to defeat a safety check. The result is better than what we designed: the agent pauses for consent on its own, with nothing staged. Two defects found by using our own product. requestAnimationFrame never fires in a hidden tab ; and a hidden tab is exactly this product's case, since the human is in their agent's conversation while writes land here. The attention title, the one signal that reaches someone looking elsewhere, never updated. And in production, one no-transform header leaked from the document rule onto the hashed assets, shipping 186 kB of uncompressed JavaScript and silently defeating a year-long cache. What we learned A tool description cannot make an agent look at a page. Asked a bare architecture question with the tools registered and visible, both Claude and Terra answered from their own knowledge and never touched the page. Named the page ; "Continue this task on this page" ; and Terra read it immediately. Discovery is a separate problem from description, and we can only measure it, not promise it. Write down the runs that went badly. Our verification log records a voided measurement run, a contaminated trial, and every check we could not observe. It is longer for it, and it is the only reason the 8/8 is worth anything. What's next Rerun the measurement with more models and publish the exhibits. Test whether an agent that has used the log once reaches for it unprompted the second time. And find out what happens on Chromium 153, where tools can finally be withdrawn safely.  Construction is one of the slowest industries in the world to adopt new technology. When it finally does, the first step is almost always the same one: a 3D model. Companies pay for the survey, the modelling, the coordination — and then the model's working life ends the day the project is handed over. The design team keeps it. The people who run the building for the next forty years get a PDF set and a key. 

 That is why the ROI conversation stalls. It is not that digital models are expensive; it is that we only spend them on the shortest phase of the asset's life. A model that stops at handover has to pay for itself in eighteen months. A model that keeps working never has to. 

 Drill Day is our argument for the second kind. It takes the model past design, past handover, into operations — the phase where the building actually costs money — and asks a simple question: what if the model were the thing that trains the people who run it? 

 The second half of the inspiration was WebMCP. A model is only useful in operations if a non-expert can get answers out of it, and the people we care about — a week-two technician, a firefighter who has never been in this building, a contractor arriving to isolate a valve — are not going to learn a BIM viewer. But they will talk. WebMCP lets the AI they already have reach into the live model on their screen instead of into a stale export of it. That is the missing interface.
