title: AgentPerf
pitch: The ecosystem quotes "10x faster" for WebMCP with no methodology behind it. AgentPerf measures it: 2.4x on a small page, 13.8x on a real one. And it ships the React layer that produces the gap.
about_excerpt: The ecosystem quotes "10x faster" for WebMCP with no methodology behind it. AgentPerf measures it: 2.4x on a small page, 13.8x on a real one. And it ships the React layer that produces the gap. Like Comment Story Updates What it does AgentPerf answers the question every frontend team is about to be asked: if we build and maintain a second surface for AI agents, what do we actually get? Three pieces answer it end to end. agentperf, the benchmark CLI. Runs the same task, on the same page, with the same model, twice. Once by DOM driving, an accessibility-tree driver that reads, clicks, fills and selects, the way browser agents work today. Once through the page's WebMCP tools. Identical agent loop, identical prompt, identical verification. It reports wall-clock, tokens, round-trips and success rate, per run and aggregated. @agentperf/react, the fast lane. Three primitives that turn an existing React app into a WebMCP surface without touching the human UI. Two instrumented demo pages and a landing page, all live, all publishing their own tools. The landing page will hand your agent its own benchmark data with the caveats attached. The measurement gpt-5.6-luna, n=5 per lane, both lanes 100% successful on both pages: page accessibility tree lane wall-clock tokens round-trips salon booking 1,010 chars DOM driving 7.5s 10,079 5 salon booking WebMCP tools 5.0s 4,268 4 72-product catalog 32,916 chars DOM driving 24.3s 102,537 7 72-product catalog WebMCP tools 6.0s 7,434 5 2.4x fewer tokens on the tiny page. 13.8x on the realistic one. Make the page 32x heavier and DOM driving pays 10x more, while the tools lane barely moves, because it never reads the page. It asks. That is the finding, and it is not the one anyone is quoting: the gap is a property of the page, not of WebMCP. A single number for "what WebMCP saves" is meaningless without the page it was measured on. That is why this ships as a harness you point at your own site, not as a headline. It replicates across model families: claude-sonnet-5 via OpenRouter, with no vendor-specific workarounds, pays 2.5x on the small page with identical round-trip counts. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP Most WebMCP demos show that an agent can drive a site. The open question is whether a team should pay to build that, and nobody could answer it with data. The "10x faster, ~90% fewer tokens" figures in circulation trace to one methodology-free blog post and to token-only counts measured against screenshot baselines by the ecosystem itself. Google's own WebMCP Evals guide covers correctness (does the agent pick the right tool) and explicitly provides no metrics, no harness, and no comparison against DOM automation. So the fit is direct: WebMCP is the thing being adopted, and the missing artifact is the evidence for adopting it. AgentPerf is built on WebMCP twice over. The demo pages publish tools through document.modelContext, and the harness implements the other half of the protocol, acting as a WebMCP host so it can measure any page that speaks it. How it creates a better experience For the person: the agent's work happens in their tab, in their UI. When it searches, the grid filters. When it orders, the confirmation appears where they can see it. A dock states plainly how many tools the page has exposed. Agent-readiness usually means a headless side door the user cannot observe; here it is a visible second doorway onto the same app. For the developer: the fast lane is additive. Delete agent-surface.tsx from either demo and you have an ordinary React app. In a browser without WebMCP, everything no-ops. For the agent: it stops guessing. It gets typed actions and a state snapshot pruned to a token budget, with explicit "+N more" markers wherever a list was elided, so a partial read is legible as a partial read instead of becoming a confident hallucination. What people and agents can now do together that was hard before Buy correctly from a real catalog in four tool calls. On a 72-product store, "find the cheapest in-stock wireless keyboard rated 4.5 or higher and order it" is a filter, a comparison and a checkout. Through tools that is search_products, add_to_cart, place_order, for 7,434 tokens. By DOM it costs 102,537 tokens of reading and re-reading the same grid. Let an agent write to an app without letting it corrupt the app. Every action is zod-gated. A malformed email never reaches the handler; the agent gets back the exact violated field paths and a deterministic fix-and-retry instruction, and corrects itself in one turn instead of re-sending the same bad call. Ask a marketing page to justify its own claims. The landing page publishes get_benchmark_results. An agent reading it gets the numbers and the caveats (n, model, page sizes, known biases) instead of adjectives. Benchmark a WebMCP page you did not write. The harness supplies the host, so it works on any page that speaks the protocol, in stock Chromium, with no flag and no origin trial. How I implemented WebMCP Publishing side, @agentperf/react: useAgentState(key, value): every slice flows into a single get_page_state tool, serialized within a token budget (default 1,000) with deterministic pruning and explicit elision markers. useAgentAction(name, config): registers a tool whose input schema is generated from a zod schema via z.toJSONSchema, so the contract and the schema the agent sees cannot drift. readOnly and destructive map to WebMCP annotations. A reserved, currently inert price field anticipates x402 settlement without a future breaking change. AgentBoundary: scopes state keys and tool names the way the component tree scopes the UI. Registration hygiene: handlers, descriptions and values are read through refs at call time, so re-renders never tear down and re-register a tool. Each tool holds an AbortController and unregisters on unmount, which fires toolchange so an idle agent learns the surface moved. Host side, the harness: WebMCP lives behind an origin trial and a Chrome flag, which makes reproducible measurement painful and CI impossible. So the harness ships a host shim and injects it with Playwright's addInitScript before page load. The page registers into that shim, and window.__agentperf.listTools() and .call() bridge those tools into the agent loop as function tools. Verification is the benchmark. A run counts as a success only if the model calls task_complete and the rendered page matches the task's successPattern. For the catalog that pattern pins the product and the price, so ordering the wrong keyboard fails the run instead of passing on a bare order number. A task whose pattern already matches at page load is rejected outright as unverifiable. Challenges I ran into My own benchmark was unfair, and I published it before I found out. The launched numbers were 2.4x tokens and 2.6x wall-clock. Then I had the methodology adversarially reviewed, and the review was right: the DOM lane's click returned only "Clicked button X", forcing a separate read_page to see the result, while every real accessibility-tree driver returns the post-action snapshot with the action result. I had doubled that lane's round-trips by design, then billed it for re-sending the transcript each time. Fixed and re-ran: the token ratio survived unchanged at 2.36x; the wall-clock claim did not. 2.6x was wrong, it is 1.5x. The correction is on the landing page and at the top of the README. Then it nearly happened again, in my favour. The first heavy-page run was spectacular: the DOM lane succeeded 1 time in 5, ordering a keyboard rated 4.2 when the task demanded 4.5 or higher, and announcing success every time. "DOM driving doesn't just cost more, it buys the wrong thing" is a far better headline than any cost ratio. It was also my bug: the catalog's rating filter is a select element and my DOM lane had no way to operate a dropdown. Adding select_option took it from 20% to 100%. Two rules came out of that: a lane is only a baseline if it can do what the real thing can do, and a result that flatters your conclusion gets audited harder, not published faster. Rate limits were silently biasing the result. A 429 failed a run outright, which penalizes whichever lane spends more tokens, the lane under measurement. Retries now back off exponentially. Crashed runs also used to record zero tokens and get averaged in, dragging a failing lane's cost toward zero; central tendencies are now over successful runs only, with failures in the success rate. gpt-5.6 returns a 400 on function tools unless reasoning_effort is "none". My first instinct, swallowing provider errors so a run doesn't abort, was exactly wrong for a benchmark: it turns a broken configuration into a plausible-looking failed run. Accomplishments that I'm proud of Every number that moved, moved against me, and I shipped it anyway: on the landing page, in the README, and inside a WebMCP tool the page itself serves. benchmarks/METHODOLOGY.md: the full adversarial review of my own harness, both

title: Agent-Readability Lab
pitch: Agent-Readability Lab lets an AI agent score any web page's readability, prove which real questions it can't answer, and rewrite it to be agent-ready, live, on the same page you're both looking at.
about_excerpt:
Agent-Readability Lab lets an AI agent score any web page's readability, prove which real questions it can't answer, and rewrite it to be agent-ready, live, on the same page you're both looking at.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 The agent scores a page, tests real customer questions, fixes it, and rescores, live. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 The agent scores a page, tests real customer questions, fixes it, and rescores, live. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 The agent scores a page, tests real customer questions, fixes it, and rescores, live. 
 
 1 2 



 
 Your website might be easy for a person to read. But can an AI agent actually understand it? As more people use AI to research products and services before they buy, that question decides whether your page turns up in an answer or gets skipped. Agent-Readability Lab shows you exactly where a page breaks down for an AI agent, and fixes it with you, live, on the same page you are both looking at. 

 Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP 

 The point of WebMCP is to let an agent act on a live page instead of guessing at it from the outside. Agent-Readability Lab turns that inward: the thing being measured is the agent's own ability to read a page, and the only honest way to measure it is to have the agent work directly on that page's live, in-browser content. 

 A scraper or a screenshot-driven browser agent cannot do this. They see fetched HTML or rendered pixels, not the working copy a user is editing in real time, and they cannot run a scoring pass, apply a fix, and immediately re-measure inside the same session. WebMCP is what turns the page itself into a set of tools the agent can call: analyze it, test it against real questions, rewrite it, and rescore, all against state that lives entirely in the browser. This is not "agent fetches data." It is "agent and page collaborate on the page," which is exactly the primitive WebMCP introduces. 

 How it creates a better user experience 

 Today, making a page readable for AI agents is guesswork. You publish, you hope agents parse it, and there is no feedback loop. This tool replaces that with a live, agent-verified audit: 

 
 You paste a page and ask, in plain language, how agent-readable it is. 
 You get a concrete score out of 100 with a per-signal breakdown (headings, structured data, direct answers, link clarity, scannable structure, metadata) and a ranked list of gaps. 
 You watch the agent test real customer questions against the page and show you exactly which ones it cannot answer. 
 You tell it to fix the problems, and the page rewrites itself in front of you as the score climbs. 
 

 The user never leaves the conversation, never opens a config screen, and never writes the structural markup themselves. They steer in natural language while the agent does the mechanical work on a shared, visible surface. It closes a feedback loop that, until now, simply did not exist. 

 What people and agents can do together that was hard or impossible before 

 Before this, you could not sit an AI agent in front of your page and have it tell you, specifically and honestly, "here are six questions a customer would ask, and here are the four I cannot answer from this page," then fix the page with you in the same breath. 

 That collaboration needs three things at once: the agent reasoning like a real reader, a deterministic measurement of the page's structure, and the ability to edit that page live and re-measure. WebMCP is what lets all three happen in one place. The human brings judgment ("focus on pricing and shipping"), the agent brings language and reasoning (writing the FAQ answers, catching the vague link), and the page's own tools bring the objective score. The result is a page rewritten for machine-readability, with the agent proving, in the same session, that it can now answer what it could not before. 

 The agent also stays grounded: in testing, it fixed the structure but flagged that exact pricing and warranty details still needed real product information it did not have. That kind of self-aware collaboration only works when the agent is operating on the real page, not a copy. 

 How WebMCP was implemented 

 The app is a single self-contained page that registers its tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . The page's editable content area is the single source of truth (the "working copy"), and every tool reads from and writes to it, so the human always sees exactly what the agent is doing. 

 Five tools are exposed to the agent: 

 
 analyze_readability runs a deterministic, structural scoring pass out of 100 across six weighted signals and returns the score, a breakdown, and a ranked gap list. 
 check_answerable takes questions the agent proposes and reports, per question, whether the answer is present and well-placed (answerable), present but buried, or missing. 
 apply_fix applies one structural improvement at a time: add a direct-answer summary, add a descriptive heading, append FAQPage JSON-LD, rewrite vague link text, or add page metadata. The agent writes the wording; the tool handles the structure, which keeps the scoring deterministic. 
 rescore re-runs the scoring pass and reports the delta so the improvement is visible. 
 export_optimized returns the improved page along with the before and after scores. 
 

 The division of labor is deliberate: the agent supplies reasoning and language, the page supplies an objective, repeatable score. That keeps the numbers defensible while letting the agent do what it is genuinely good at. 

 What's next 

 Next steps are live URL ingestion through a lightweight proxy, so any published page can be audited in place; a rendered before-and-after preview; and one-click export of the generated JSON-LD. The scoring signals map directly onto how real AI answer engines select and cite sources, which is where this becomes a daily tool for anyone doing SEO, AEO, or GEO work.

about_excerpt:
Teach students with your agents on Chalkboard: a collaborative infinite canvas where 23 WebMCP tools let your AI co-teacher draw, write, highlight and react live as you teach together.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 



 
 Inspiration 

 A real classroom isn't a lecture; a board everyone can point at. 

 Online, that feeling disappears. A teacher talks, students watch. The board is gone. 

 We built Chalkboard to bring it back: a shared infinite canvas where a teacher and students draw, write and react together, live. 

 Then we wondered, what if a third participant could join? Not a chatbot on the side, but a classmate who can use the board. 

 Teach students with your agents. 

 What It Does 

 Create a room, share the link, and everyone sees the same chalkboard. When someone draws a line, it appears for everyone. When someone sends a ❤️, it floats across the screen. 

 Now invite your agent. 

 Say: “Teach the Pythagorean theorem.” 

 Your agent doesn't just reply in text. It opens the same room as you, picks up the chalk, writes $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$, draws the triangle, labels the sides, and highlights the proof stroke by stroke, while students watch. 

 It’s not controlling a copy of the classroom. It’s in the classroom. 

 Why WebMCP 

 We could have built a separate API for every agent action one for drawing, one for writing, one for reacting. Instead we let the website speak for itself. 

 With WebMCP , Chalkboard simply says: here are the things I can do: draw, write, highlight, react, raise a hand, manage the room. 

 The browser exposes those capabilities at navigator.modelContext . The agent discovers them and calls them like any other tool. No custom wiring, no shadow app. 
 Your Agent → WebMCP → Chalkboard → Everyone's Board
 
 The agent doesn't need to know how our canvas works. It just knows what the classroom allows. 

 How We Built It 

 Chalkboard is a web app: a canvas for drawing, Socket.IO for real-time sync, and LiveKit for voice. 

 We wrapped every classroom action — drawing a stroke, writing text, sending a reaction as a simple tool. The browser gathers those tools and offers them through WebMCP, the new web standard for agents. 

 When an agent joins a room, it joins like any student over a websocket. It listens to the room, remembers what's on the board, and when asked to teach, it chooses tools and emits the same events your browser does. A reaction tool even opens the emoji picker and picks one, so you see the interaction, not just the result. 

 If a viewer asks the agent to do something only an editor can do, the agent politely refuses it borrows your permissions, not its own. 

 What We Learned 

 The moment an agent can act instead of just answer , everything changes. A lesson feels real when you watch it being made. 

 We also learned that the web doesn't need a separate world for AI. If a site can tell an agent what it can do, the site itself becomes the interface. 

 Challenges 

 Making a remote agent feel present was hard. It had to join the same room, see the same board, and act through the same browser tools, without lag, without breaking the live sync, and without giving it more power than the student who invited it. 

 Getting browsers, real-time sync and WebMCP to agree was the puzzle. Solving it meant the agent is no longer outside the classroom looking in. It's sitting at the desk next to you. 

 What's Next 

 We started with drawing. Next is understanding an agent that watches the board, notices a mistake, circles it, and offers a hint. A classroom that is collaborative and agent-accessible by default. 

 Chalkboard is our small experiment in that future: where you don't build a separate app for your agent — you just bring it to class.

title: Woven
pitch: Seven site tools. One complete choice. Human-only confirmation.
about_excerpt: Seven site tools. One complete choice. Human-only confirmation. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Woven — one mission, two verified compatible carts. Woven - From model request to user-confirmed pickup receipt. One request, two complete carts. From one request to a pickup-ready order. Ask once. Review once. Confirm once. Why Woven is a strong fit for WebMCP Shopping agents can recommend individual products, but a real mission still requires quantities, compatibility, budget, current stock, pickup, and consent to work together. Woven turns that multi-step job into a structured collaboration between an agent and the person already using the page. On the fictional Woven Trail Market storefront, the agent does not guess at buttons or scrape the interface. Seven purpose-built site tools let it start or inspect a mission, rerank the visible cart comparison, select an offered cart, apply only a merchant-approved compatible alternative, refresh current price and stock, and verify an existing simulated receipt. How it creates a better user experience The canonical request asks for a rainy-weekend camping kit for two first-time campers that fits in one car boot and is pickup-ready today. Woven Trail Market shows the best two complete carts, each from one merchant and one pickup location, and explains how every quantity and component satisfies the brief. The lead proof is exact: 7 units, 5 categories, 89 L packed, and a 3,000 mm rainfly. Agent calls update the same React storefront the person can see. When the agent calls compare_carts , Woven reranks the visible inline kits rather than returning a disconnected text result. The person can review the same carts, prices, stock, compatibility proof, alternatives, and selected state. That removes repeated searching and cart reconstruction without hiding the decision from the person. What people and agents can do together now The agent can translate one outcome-oriented request into bounded, reversible preparation work across product choice, constraints, current catalog facts, and comparison. The person can inspect and steer that work in the same page, then retain sole control of the irreversible step. That boundary is intentional. Woven does not register identity verification, checkout preview, confirmation secrets, or purchase authorization as WebMCP tools. The agent may prepare and recommend; the person must complete the clearly labeled demo identity handoff, review exact expiring terms, and directly confirm or continue to a merchant. Inventory, identity, merchants, and payment authorization are simulated, Woven accepts no card credentials, and it cannot make a live charge. How WebMCP was implemented The dedicated top-level /webmcp storefront document registers seven imperative tools through document.modelContext.registerTool : start_mission , get_mission , compare_carts , select_cart , swap_cart_item , refresh_carts , and verify_receipt . Each tool has a closed JSON schema. Read-only operations carry read-only annotations, content-bearing results are marked untrusted where appropriate, and every registration is attached to an AbortSignal so navigation removes the page's tool surface. The server sends Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 and Permissions-Policy: tools=(self) . Human submission, WebMCP, and the existing MCP App enter the same server-owned mission router, deterministic commerce verifier, SQLite state, and checkout controls. The agent cannot mark a cart checkout-eligible. Connected catalog facts may support a cart; cited web research remains research-only. Price, stock, compatibility, identity session, exact amount, nonce, expiry, and idempotency are revalidated at the human confirmation boundary. Inspiration Search gives links, but buying still takes work. A first-time camper has to size the shelter, duplicate sleep gear, check rain ratings, fit everything into one car, find one pickup location with stock, and rebuild the cart at checkout. Woven was built around a simple product promise: everything works together. What it does One natural-language mission becomes verified complete carts; the storefront shows the best two in solid comparison cards. The agent and person share a visible storefront state, current selection, merchant-approved alternatives, and refreshable catalog state. The agent can do reversible preparation through WebMCP while identity and exact transaction confirmation stay human-only. How we built it Woven is one Node.js and TypeScript service with a dedicated React storefront, seven top-level WebMCP site tools, HTTP and stdio MCP transports, deterministic cart verification, bounded LangGraph.js orchestration for non-camping missions, SQLite persistence, and a simulated payment adapter. Tests assert the exact tool surface, schemas, cleanup lifecycle, shared UI behavior, security headers, and absence of identity or purchase tools. Challenges The hardest design decision was deciding what not to expose. Treating a tool call as payment consent would erase the trust boundary. Woven exposes only reversible preparation work and keeps identity, exact terms, secrets, and final confirmation outside the agent's tool surface. The second challenge was preserving one source of truth across WebMCP, the MCP App, and the browser experience. All surfaces now share the same server routing, validation, persistence, cart rules, and confirmation boundary. Accomplishments Seven browser-discoverable WebMCP tools over a complete product workflow. Tool calls update the visible storefront instead of a parallel agent-only state. Two visible complete one-merchant kits with exact budget, volume, weather, quantity, stock, pickup, source, and verification proofs. One truthful glass activity surface; commerce cards and authorization controls remain solid, and total connector failure never fabricates a result. Merchant-approved substitutions, refreshable facts, signed simulated receipts, and deterministic failure behavior. Human-only identity and purchase confirmation enforced by the server and omitted from WebMCP. Automated tests plus desktop and mobile verification. What we learned WebMCP is strongest when the browser is not merely another API client. Its value is shared context: the agent can act through precise tools while the person sees and controls the same product state. Tool omission is also product design; the absence of a purchase tool makes Woven's consent model clearer and safer. Challenge-period provenance Woven was created during the challenge period. The challenge opened on 25 August 2026; the first public repository commit is dated 29 August 2026, and the dedicated WebMCP implementation is dated 31 August 2026. title: WebMCP Operator Workspace
pitch: A shared workspace where WebMCP agents discover context-aware tools, prepare visible work, and apply sensitive actions only after human approval.
about_excerpt: A shared workspace where WebMCP agents discover context-aware tools, prepare visible work, and apply sensitive actions only after human approval. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration## Inspiration A website should be able to tell an AI agent what it can do, rather than making the agent infer every operation from visual controls. We built WebMCP Operator Workspace to explore a practical question: how can a human and an agent share an operational workspace while keeping capabilities contextual and sensitive decisions human-controlled? What it does The application presents a fictional hotel refrigeration incident across two pages: Case Workspace and Asset Inspector. In Case Workspace, an agent can read the incident, prepare a work plan, draft a customer update, select equipment components and prepare contextual observations. Prepared work appears in the interface for the human to review. The capability surface changes with context: Case Workspace initially exposes 11 tools. Selecting a component activates two additional tools, bringing the total to 13. Clearing the selection withdraws those tools, returning to 11. Navigating to Asset Inspector exposes six tools for that page. For sensitive proposals, the application separates preparation from approval. Applying a pending proposal is blocked. A human reviews it and clicks Approve in the page. The agent can then apply that proposal once; repeating it is rejected. There is no registered WebMCP tool to approve a proposal. On Asset Inspector, the agent can prepare an inspection note, but the final form save remains a human UI action. How we built it The project is a standalone application built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, hosted on GitHub Pages. It registers structured capabilities through document.modelContext.registerTool(). Contextual tools are withdrawn using AbortSignal, and each document registers its relevant tool surface. A semantic capability tree describes declared pages, interface regions and capabilities. It distinguishes application contracts from runtime observations: observing an unexpected tool does not automatically add it to the application's authorized surface. Navigation uses declared page identifiers rather than arbitrary URLs. Proposal handling uses explicit states and single-use approval consumption. The reviewed candidate passed 49 automated tests covering application contracts and behaviors, including approval states, replay rejection and contextual lifecycle scenarios. GitHub Actions runs the test suite. Challenges we faced The main challenge was separating three concepts: discovering a capability, preparing work and having authority to apply a sensitive proposal. Contextual tools must disappear when their context ends. Registration failures must not leave a partially active surface. Navigation must expose the destination page's capabilities rather than preserve stale assumptions. We also needed the interface to distinguish a prepared draft from a saved note, and an approved proposal from an applied action. What we learned WebMCP is useful not only for exposing operations, but also for making the agent-facing interface reflect the current application context. Visible shared state helps the human understand what the agent prepared. Explicit approval states make the transition from proposal to application understandable and testable. Accomplishments We combined contextual tool registration, a multipage capability surface, visible agent-prepared work and a human approval workflow in one publicly accessible application. The result demonstrates a complete application-level sequence: proposal, blocked premature application, human approval, single application and replay rejection. How to try it Open the live application with a WebMCP-compatible agent client and enter the workspace. Ask the agent to read the case, select condenser_fan, prepare an observation and clear the selection. Next, request a sensitive-action proposal and observe the blocked attempt before approving it manually. Ask the agent to apply the approved proposal and then repeat the same proposal to test replay rejection. Finally, navigate to asset-inspector and prepare an inspection note without submitting the human form. The application does not require our developer tunnel, proprietary Universal MCP runtime or credentials. An ordinary browser can display the human interface, but agent invocation requires a WebMCP-compatible client. Scope and limitations All incident, customer and equipment data is fictional. State is in memory and local to the active page; reloads and navigation do not promise persistence. Drafts do not send messages. Applying a proposal records a local demo event; it does not dispatch a technician or operate real equipment. The approval boundary demonstrates application workflow enforcement, not server-side authentication or protection against arbitrary browser automation. The accompanying video is an AI-generated explanation created with NotebookLM, not a screen recording of execution. What's next We would explore further usability testing and carefully scoped operational integrations. Persistence, identity and server-enforced authorization would require additional design before production use. title: Marginalia
pitch: Marginalia is an agent-driven epistemological margin for the web: it knows what you know, ingests what you read, and bridges them — connections, meaning, citations, assistance, integrated knowledge.
about_excerpt: Marginalia is an agent-driven epistemological margin for the web: it knows what you know, ingests what you read, and bridges them — connections, meaning, citations, assistance, integrated knowledge. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every AI reading tool today is a chat box beside the text: ask, get a smooth answer, move on. That smoothness is the enemy of understanding — and it never knows what you already know. Two of my own projects had already designed the fix twice without a surface for it: an expand-and-annotate reader in an open-source LaTeX research environment, and "annotated reading versions" of papers in a learning system I'm building around evidence-gated mastery. The missing piece was a way for an agent to work inside the reading, live, while I read. WebMCP is exactly that piece. The name is a homage to the oldest form of this idea: marginalia — commentary written in the margins of a text, never in the text. What it does Marginalia is a reader where a human and their agent work on the same page. The page holds the document, your marks, and your own notes; the agent brings what it knows about you; WebMCP tools are where the two meet. No tool can write to the source. The agent lives in the margin. Open a paper, an article, or a docs page. Tell your agent what you already know — it records that as proposed knowledge you confirm with a tap — and the document reshapes around you: sections you've mastered fold to a stub with a reason , sections you haven't get expansions, glosses, [figures,] and connections to your own notes. Density isn't a global dial; it's a function of what you know about the concepts in each section. An expert in one domain and a novice in another is the normal case. Three layers, never merged, each toggleable: source (immutable), you (your marks), agent (its artifacts — attributed, reasoned, removable, with one button to remove them all). Switch the agent layer off and you are looking at the untouched text. The demo reads across a century: Rutherford's 1911 scattering paper (public domain), a 2025 Curious Kids essay from The Conversation on where atoms come from (CC BY-ND — and the layer rule is ND-compliance by construction: the text is byte-identical, everything else is margin), and Chrome's own WebMCP documentation (CC BY 4.0), which the agent annotates using the very tools registered on the page it's reading. How we built it Vanilla ES modules, no build step, one static page deployed on Netlify. Page state is a single frozen-source / mutable-margin store; every WebMCP tool validates its input and then calls the store, so the rules are enforced in code, not in a prompt. Tools registered via the WebMCP imperative API: get_reading_state , get_section_text , get_knowledge , upsert_knowledge , set_section_depth , annotate , search_notes , insert_figure [adjust to what shipped]. Every tool returns structured errors with a next_step written in coach voice for the agent to relay ("hiding a section requires a confirmed knowledge entry — ask the reader to confirm first"). [Your notes never leave the browser: drop a folder of Markdown and the agent queries a client-side index through search_notes .] [Math renders with KaTeX in both source and margin.] [SVG figures pass a sanitizer before rendering.] Two rules do most of the work: the layer rule (there is no write-to-source tool — enforcement by absence) and the pending-reshape rule (the agent never reshapes the section you are currently reading; changes land as pending and apply when you arrive). The document never moves under you. Why WebMCP and not an MCP server: the state that matters — the document, the click you just made, your notes, the artifacts already in the margin — is page state you are editing live. A server can't see it; the page can, and hands it to the agent on the next call. And the layer rule is only enforceable where the tools live: a page can simply not register a write tool. A prompt can be argued out of; a missing function cannot. Challenges we ran into Building against a protocol that is a week old, in a few hours, with a team of one human orchestrating several coding agents in parallel: one file per lane, an integrator merging, "tested" meaning a screenshot in the PR. [Getting tools visible in the ChatGPT in-app browser vs. the Chrome inspector extension — the API surface is still moving, so we register on both names and log which one took.] Licensing was its own design problem: the demo content had to be legally copyable into a public repo and shown on video, which is how a 1911 paper, a CC BY-ND essay and CC BY docs ended up sharing a stage. Accomplishments that we're proud of A document that visibly reshapes as you say what you know — with a reason under every fold. An ethical constraint (AI never writes into human text) that is also a technical guarantee and, incidentally, what makes CC BY-ND content legal to read this way. Honest states everywhere: refusals explain themselves, "no notes loaded" is a state, not an error. What we learned The interesting WebMCP apps aren't the ones where the agent fills in forms. They're the ones where the page holds something the agent can't have — here, the reader's live behaviour and their own archive — and the tool schema encodes a relationship: the agent proposes, the page referees, the human decides. What's next for Marginalia Integration with knowledge bases, memory systems and testing. title: Unfolded
pitch: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself
about_excerpt: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself Like 1 Comment Story Updates Mobile screens ( Dark mode ) Light mode ( Desktop ) Dark mode (Desktop) The problem we are solving Design initiated by Chat-GPT Design initiated by Chrome tab more mobile screens ( light mode ) mobile screens ( light mode ) Light / Dark mode From a printed template back to a design The exported printable PDF template ( multi page ) webMCP tools available ( 1 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 2 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 3 of 3 ) Design system ( Dark mode ) Inspiration I've been cutting pottery templates out of cereal boxes for years now. AI chats are great at generating shapes and make complex changes with unusual requirements, but their non deterministic output produce unexpected and misaligned PDFs, especially during the discovery phase of a new piece where the requirements constantly changes. The problem is, the potter notice the failure only after hours of building in the studio. Try for yourself to generate with any AI agent a multipage template for a simple mug, same prompt in 3 separate sessions. The result is always different, most of the time fail silently where it matters the most. I have created Unfolded to move the template generation part of the workflow away from the AI chat into a more deterministic output I can control. The output is a multi page PDF template that always work is always true to the 3D shape you have built. The idea is to retain AI for complexity, difficult math calculations and things that are practically impossible to do in a deterministic UI. When is connected to unfolded, you can ask AI things like: Keep the same vessel style but change the volume to 500ml Prepare a template inspired by this photo, for a porcelain vase with thin walls This container should hold a large americano comfortably 10 bowls like this should be stackable and only 1cm of each one should be visible when stacked What Unfolded does Unfolded is a parametric 3D builder that helps with both the template generation and the decision of what to make. It's a shared 3D workspace where a potter and an AI agent shape a vessel together: the potter keeps the creative decisions, the agent inspects and revises the live design through WebMCP, and Unfolded guarantees the geometry: clay shrinkage, clay type wall thickness, mid-surface-developed. It was thought from the ground up with the potter workflow in mind and its strenght is how flexibly it is and can adapt to many unexpected use case and workflow without letting you down. Most problems related to pottery known how, PDF generations and cross browsers workflow are automagically prevented under the hood without anyone noticing. My favourite features ( try them in the app, especially on mobile ) I've worked a lot at the UX flow for the cross-device handshake . The potter can also design and work with agents on non webMCP capable browsers. One tap on Open in ChatGPT hands off into the ChatGPT app with a prompt that already carries a single-use pairing code; Chat-GPT hidden browser joins the potter's live session over WebSockets. From then on every agent edit appears in the browser within about a second, every browser edit is visible to the agent on its next tool call, and every change ( human or agent ) is a shared undo step. Undo/redo work for both humand and AI changes, no matter what device pushed them. The handover works both ways ( or even 3 ways! ): The agent reads the current design, changes the form, sees the same 3D preview the potter sees — and solves problems that are genuinely hard at the workbench. "Make it hold exactly 350 ml but keep the proportions" --> one sentence for an agent, an afternoon of guesswork by hand. The generated PDF is really well thought ( if I say so myself! ): True-scale printable templates and a calibration ruler on every sheet, QR code to reproduce the design in the browser even after it was printed, seam allowance to glue the template together. This is fully designed around the potter's workflow. The app registers 13 typed WebMCP tools on document.modelContext the moment it loads. The reasons there are so many tools is that I got a little carried away about performance measurament of webMCP. I even made a npm package called MCP-profiler to measure everything from the tools speed to the agent harness time. Most of the slowness in my app ( 30seconds to connect the tools at times ) is unsurprisely caused by my 3D model and the whole context I am passing over with each tool. Something I will definitely look into after the hackathon. How I built it React, TypeScript, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Zustand, Zod, Tailwind CSS, and shadcn/ui, with jsPDF generating the true-scale multi-page templates. Live cross-device sync runs on a Cloudflare Worker with a per-session Durable Object; pairing invitations are single-use and short-lived, so no URL ever carries a durable capability. The interface and the WebMCP tools share the same Zustand store and Zod schemas, so human and agent edits stay synchronized by construction . Everything sits behind a test gate (geometry, schemas, sync protocol), end-to-end suites running real Chromium against the production bundle and two deeper suites that spin up a local Worker to exercise the pairing protocol with two real browsers. Along the way I published webmcp-profiler , also sitting in this repo, an npm package that benchmarks every tool's execution time and payload size. Profiling my own app with it caught a ~20% trim in tool-definition metadata that every conversation was paying for. Challenges and lessons The geometric challenge: complex curved surfaces cannot be flattened without distortion, so for the demo I focused on symmetrical, faceted forms built from planar slabs, where the unroll is exact , not approximate. But my ambitions are higher for this tool and I already have a full plan for complex shapes and things that were not really possible until now. The UX challenge was one I haven't seen discussed anywhere: when ChatGPT drives a WebMCP page, it does so in a built in, hidden browser. Solving the two-way conversation between that invisible tab and the browser the user actually looks at — live sessions, one-tap pairing prompts, agent share links carrying single-use join tokens — became the heart of the project. Here is a page with a nice breakdown of the different user flow the user can face (I have done this for myself, but could be helpful for someone judging the project): User Flows mapped out I am not satisfied with the solution I have found for the pairing, In the future my goal is to merge the link with token, pairing, webMCP concept into a single binary flag. The user does not need to know about webMCP at all, it should simply copy a prompt on his agent to start building from anywhere. The bigger lesson is that WebMCP shines with a clear division of labour: the agent is brilliant at intent and connected constraints, the app owns the deterministic math, and the human keeps the creative decisions. The agent chooses the parameters; the geometry is always right. What's next Better UX. Curved profiles, more construction types and layers, performance optimisation of webMCP and assembly guidance. Maybe a login, and reusable studio presets and lids and matching sets, where the shrinkage math matters most. Most of the backend code is AI written and went through many iterations and adversarial reviews. Luca Gugliemi Product designer with front-end superpowers. title: Agentready Network
pitch: The login you already have is the API. Agents investigate, humans authorize, receipts prove it.
about_excerpt: The login you already have is the API. Agents investigate, humans authorize, receipts prove it. Like Comment Story Updates The problem nobody has budget for Every operations team lives inside sites that will never ship an API for them. Monitoring in Grafana. Customer commitments in Cal.com. Payer portals, vendor consoles, admin dashboards. The person holding the session can see everything and change anything, but their agent can do nothing except screenshot the screen and guess where to click. WebMCP fixes this for sites that adopt it. Today that is roughly none of them. We measured three real open-source products, 522k lines of code, 429 places where a tool obviously belongs, and zero WebMCP registrations. So we asked a different question. What if the user adopts WebMCP for the site? The reframe WebMCP turns the login you already have into an API. A signed-in tab already carries every credential and permission the human has. If that tab registers tools with document.modelContext.registerTool , the agent gets a typed, narrow, inspectable interface to the site, and the vendor never has to ship a line of code. Adoption inverts. It no longer waits on ten thousand vendors. It happens one user, one tab, one reviewed pack at a time. What Agentready Network does Agentready Network is a local-first registry and runtime of reviewed action packs . A pack describes what a site can do, on exactly which origin, with which risk labels. The runtime turns that pack into live WebMCP tools inside the user's own signed-in session, then wraps every call in the safety the vendor never provided: Exact origins. A pack binds to one host and a reviewed fingerprint. Drift fails closed. Declarative, never executable. Manifests are JSON. The registry cannot ship code into your browser. Bounded, untrusted output. Results are allowlist-projected, byte-capped, and labeled contentTrust: "untrusted" . Tool output is content, not instruction. Human authority on consequences. Reads flow. Writes need a preview. Consequential actions need one exact, single-use approval bound to origin, tool, and normalized arguments. Change an argument and the grant is void. Verified closure. After a consequential action an inspector reads authoritative state and issues a receipt with no cookies, secrets, or raw bodies. Unknown outcome is reported as in_doubt , never as success. One concrete job, end to end The demo is not a feature tour. It is one incident. An alert fires in Grafana. Customer bookings in Cal.com are about to be affected. Neither site has WebMCP. The agent discovers the reviewed Grafana and Cal.com packs, installs them for this origin, and reads authoritative state. It never receives a credential. The agent prepares the exact continuity action and states what will change and how it will be inspected. The incident is still investigating . The human grants that exact action once, from a control the agent cannot reach. The agent executes once. The inspector verifies and issues one receipt. The incident is resolved . We poison the fingerprint. The pack refuses to run. We export the recorder draft. Every secret is gone before it can be published. Agents investigate. Humans authorize. Outcomes are verified. That is the whole product. What people and agents can now do together that they could not before Work a real incident across two unrelated vendor sites with no API contract between them. The user is the integration layer. Let an agent read freely and prepare freely, while every consequential step waits for a human decision the agent physically cannot forge. Hand a reviewer a receipt, not a screenshot, as proof of what changed. Teach a site once by observing its own traffic, then reuse that pack every session. Why WebMCP, specifically Screenshot-and-click pays the full cost on every step: a screenshot, a vision pass, a click that misses when the viewport shifts. We measured it. Creating one Grafana data source took nine browser actions and 55 seconds by DOM driving, and one WebMCP tool call in 20 milliseconds. A whole diagramming task took 44 calls versus 5. These are single-trial measurements from our audit work, not a benchmark suite, but the shape is unmistakable. The cost moves from per-action to per-app, and it never comes back. WebMCP also gives us the one thing a bookmarklet never had: a standard discovery surface. Any agent that speaks document.modelContext finds our tools without knowing we exist. How we built it Registry, Pack Lab, and runtime in plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. No framework. Every tool is registered with the current imperative API, document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { signal }) , so tools unregister cleanly when a view unmounts. A Chrome MV3 extension injects reviewed read tools into the exact controlled Cal.com and Grafana origins and bridges receipts back to the registry. Reviewed adapters for Cal.com and Grafana were reverse-engineered on the wire, not from source. The recorder wraps fetch and XMLHttpRequest , clusters observed traffic, drafts tools, auto-flags mutating endpoints, and strips secrets before anything is published. Approval, inspection, drift, and redaction are enforced in the shared runtime, so every pack inherits them and no pack can opt out. Node's built-in test runner covers the trust boundaries. All tests pass on the submitted commit. What we deliberately did not claim The public judge path is a deterministic fixture so nobody needs an account. The same runtime drives the real Cal.com and Grafana adapters against controlled localhost instances; the video shows the controlled Grafana and Cal.com state alongside the public lab. The extension checkpoint is read-only. Remembered approvals, arbitrary-site install, generic DOM automation, and automatic rollback are out of scope. Figma taught us the frontier. Its control plane is reachable in-session; its canvas rides a binary WebSocket inside a Worker that no page-context patch can see. We published only what we proved and marked canvas manipulation unsupported. What we learned Discovery is observation, not code reading. Every tool we guessed from source was wrong. Every tool we drafted from the wire worked. Minification cannot rename what crosses the network. Injection inverts the safety burden onto the installer. The vendor never audited these tools, so we had to. That is why approval, inspection, and redaction live in the runtime and not in the pack. What is next Persist packs across sessions in the extension. Chain packs across sites so one agent can read portal A and act in portal B. Generalize the approval contract into a policy layer: read anything, never pay, never cancel, never touch what a human pinned. The first vertical we want to ship is healthcare payer portals, the most session-locked, human-attestation-gated surfaces on the web. Testing instructions for judges No credentials are needed. Open the live site in ChatGPT's browser or in Chrome with the WebMCP flag enabled, follow the 90-second path in the README, and use Reset between runs. Local run: npm test , then python3 -m http.server 8788 and open /site/ . Built With cal.com chatgpt-sites chrome css3 grafana html5 javascript node.js playwright webmcp Try it out agentready-network.ajaye901089.chatgpt.site github.com agentready-network.ajaye901089.chatgpt.site Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by AJAYKE Edupuganti Like Share this project: Updates AJAYKE Edupuganti started this project — Sep 03, 2026 02:46 PM EDT

title: Agent-Ready Palm Desert
pitch: AICV is building the Agent Ready City layer. A structured, searchable map that AI agents can use to answer real questions about visiting and relocating. This is the WebMCP City of Palm Desert MVP.
about_excerpt: AICV is building the Agent Ready City layer. A structured, searchable map that AI agents can use to answer real questions about visiting and relocating. This is the WebMCP City of Palm Desert MVP. Like Comment Story Updates Home page Agent cards Agent itinerary Inspiration Most relocations do not begin with a moving truck. They begin with a visit. A founder starts wondering whether life—and perhaps part of the company—might work somewhere else. The founding team comes for a retreat. They tour a few workspaces, meet local people, try to understand the talent base, and pay attention to what an ordinary Tuesday morning might feel like. The Coachella Valley is already familiar to millions of people because of Coachella, the Indian Wells tennis tournament, Modernism Week, and the Palm Springs International Film Festival. People know how to visit here. What they do not necessarily know is how to evaluate the region as a place to build a company, open a satellite office, or begin the next chapter of their lives. The web does not make that decision particularly easy. Search engines and even capable AI agents tend to return familiar hotels, attractions, rankings, and generic itineraries. For the judgment that actually matters, people still call someone local: a commercial real estate agent, an economic development director, or a hospitality operator who knows the area. That human guidance is valuable, but a consequential decision can end up depending on whichever local person happens to answer the call. For the past year, AICV has been mapping businesses, institutions, places, and local signals across the nine-city Coachella Valley so agents can understand the region more accurately. Along the way, we discovered that the technical work was only half the challenge. Local businesses are already surrounded by noise from Google, Facebook, Yelp, Yext, Foursquare, and a growing number of consultants promising that AEO is the new SEO. Expecting every restaurant, hotel, university, workspace, and civic institution to understand the agentic web—and independently restructure itself for it—is technically possible, but culturally unrealistic. At the same time, world-scale platforms are attempting to understand and “agentify” millions of places around the globe. They can provide enormous reach, but they cannot easily capture every local distinction: whether two places are genuinely close, whether an institution requires an introduction, whether a supposed innovation district is a finished ecosystem or still a promising collection of institutions, or whether a recommendation makes sense for the particular human asking. That is where we believe WebMCP changes the equation. Instead of waiting for every local entity to become agent-ready on its own, a trusted regional layer can organize the local context and expose it directly to agents as usable tools. The agent no longer has to scrape a directory, infer meaning from buttons, or assemble a decision from generic search results. It can ask the region for a city brief, search locally curated intelligence, compare options, check routes and constraints, build a scouting itinerary, and prepare the next step for human approval. Getting a region ready starts with getting one city ready. We chose Palm Desert because it sits at the center of the Coachella Valley and brings together many of the ingredients a founder or executive would need to evaluate: business support, universities and workforce, retreat infrastructure, hospitality, culture, coffee, outdoor life, and future growth. For this Challenge, we took a deliberately small corpus of AICV’s mapped Palm Desert intelligence and asked a focused question: Could WebMCP help an AI agent deliver something closer to the judgment of a trusted local—not merely tell someone what is here, but help them imagine whether they could build part of their life here? Agent-Ready Palm Desert is our first answer. What it does Agent-Ready Palm Desert helps a founder or executive evaluate Palm Desert for a leadership retreat, satellite office, relocation, or longer-term build path. A person can explore the website directly. Through five WebMCP tools, an AI agent can use the same local intelligence to: Understand the city Search relevant places and institutions Open individual Agent Previews Compare several options Build a route-aware scouting itinerary Prepare an inquiry for human approval - manual The demonstration uses 22 source-linked Palm Desert records. Each Agent Preview separates the official facts from AICV’s local judgment: why the place matters, when it should be considered, and what constraint the agent must preserve. That local context changes the answer. Rutina Coffee may be a good quiet-coffee stop, for example, but it is not walkable from the Entrepreneurship Resource Center. The routing tool identifies approximately 5.5 miles and ten minutes by car. The result is closer to a white-glove relocation conversation than a generic travel itinerary. It helps someone ask not only, “What is in Palm Desert?” but, “Could my team and I actually imagine ourselves here?” How we built it We built Agent-Ready Palm Desert as a standalone ChatGPT Site using React and TypeScript. Its WebMCP tools are registered directly in the browser with document.modelContext.registerTool() . The visible interface and the agent tools use the same underlying data and decision logic, so the human and agent are not working from two different versions of Palm Desert. The corpus is stored as structured JSON with source links, geographic information, access conditions, local signals, and comparison guidance. Routing uses OpenStreetMap road data through OSRM. Five tools are read-only. The sixth will prepare an inquiry or update request, but it cannot send one. It returns sent: false and requires human confirmation. Currently not enabled. AICV’s regional mapping and source material began before the Challenge. During the Challenge, we turned a focused portion of that work into a standalone WebMCP experience with six callable tools, structured Agent Previews, shared human-agent workflows, routing safeguards, and a confirmation-gated handoff. Challenges we ran into The largest challenge was not registering five tools. It was deciding what an agent needs to know before it should make a recommendation about a real place. Local knowledge is full of distinctions that rarely survive conventional search. Two places may sound nearby but be several miles apart. A resource may be valuable but require an appointment or introduction. An area may be described as an innovation corridor while still functioning as a collection of institutions rather than a finished, walkable district. We had to convert those human observations into structured intelligence without presenting AICV’s judgment as an official fact. A second challenge was scope. The Coachella Valley contains thousands of businesses and institutions across nine cities. Trying to make every entity independently WebMCP-ready would reproduce the same adoption problem we had already encountered. For this experiment, we chose a much smaller question: could one regional intelligence layer make one city meaningfully easier for an agent to understand? The final challenge was trust. We wanted the agent to be useful without allowing it to overstate live conditions, overlook access restrictions, or take action before the human was ready. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that the project became a complete human-agent decision experience rather than simply a technical demonstration. The public Site works without an account. All five WebMCP tools are discoverable and functional. The human interface and agent tools share the same 22-record corpus, and every recommendation remains connected to a source, a local explanation, and something the user may need to verify. We are especially proud that the system knows where to stop. It can research, compare, route, and prepare—but the consequential next step remains with the human. What we learned We learned that making a place agent-ready is not primarily a website problem or a listings problem. It is a context problem. Global platforms are very good at indexing enormous amounts of information. Local intelligence layers can contribute something different: the lived distinctions, constraints, relationships, and judgment that make the information useful for a particular human decision. We also learned that expecting every local business to independently adapt to every new AI platform is unlikely to work. A shared regional layer may be a more practical approach. It can organize local truth once and make it available to multiple agents through a common interface such as WebMCP. Most importantly, we learned that constraints are part of the answer. “Not walkable,” “appointment required,” “not live traffic,” and “not yet sent” are not disclaimers added after the recommendation. They are part of what makes the recommendation tr

Morphe is a form builder designed for both people and AI.

Create a form, publish it, collect responses, and get insights — all through one platform. AI can take care of the work too.

 Inspiration 

 AI integrations don't scale when every tool needs a custom connection to every AI client. Morphe takes a different approach: use a common standard so one integration works across many clients — the "USB-C of AI." 

 We wanted to prove that idea on a real product, not a toy. 

 A form builder was a natural fit for WebMCP. Forms are highly interactive, but difficult for agents to operate. An API can expose data, but WebMCP lets an agent actually operate the application in the browser . 

 What it does 

 Morphe is a form builder originally built as part of a larger platform. For this hackathon, we extracted it into a standalone product and added MCP at two levels. 

 Through backend MCP, agents can create, manage, publish, submit, analyse, and export forms . 

 Through WebMCP, agents can operate the actual web app — opening the form list, entering the editor, viewing submissions, opening previews, and navigating the app via the use of tools. 

 The key idea is that humans and agents share the same workspace . There is no separate agent mode or shadow API. Both use the same data, validation, and business logic. 

 How we built it 

 Morphe uses FastAPI + React/Vite , deployed on Render and Vercel. 

 Because WebMCP is still a draft standard, the frontend detects support through document.modelContext . If available, we register our tools; otherwise, the app works normally. 

 We exposed 20 WebMCP tools across two groups: 

 
 Form operations: create, update, publish, submit, analytics, and export. 
 Navigation: move between the form list, editor, submissions, preview, and other views. 
 

 Navigation uses the application's real router, so agents operate the actual SPA rather than simulating page changes. 

 Challenges 

 The biggest challenge was building around an emerging standard while keeping the product reliable without it. 

 We also dealt with production-only routing failures, a CDN issue affecting a specific API path, CORS between separately deployed services, and extracting the application from its larger codebase. 

 Accomplishments 

 We turned an existing project into a standalone, deployed product with: 

 
 20 WebMCP tools 
 Backend MCP support 
 Agent-driven browser navigation 
 Graceful degradation when WebMCP isn't supported 
 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP isn't just useful for AI. Designing interfaces that are easier for agents to understand can also improve accessibility and usability for people. 

 We also learned that emerging standards require graceful degradation: detect what the platform supports, enhance when possible, and never make the core product depend on it. 

 What's next 

 Morphe will become the foundation for the larger platform. Next we're planning Postgres persistence, authentication, richer analytics, conditional logic, embeds, and a larger agent tool surface . 

 The goal remains simple: humans and AI should be able to operate the same product, without bespoke integrations for every AI client.

title: Persona — The Embodied WebMCP AI Agent
pitch: Persona gives AI agents a body—letting them understand your intent, act through WebMCP, and respond naturally with voice, gaze, expressions, and gestures. Making every interaction feel human.
about_excerpt:
Persona gives AI agents a body—letting them understand your intent, act through WebMCP, and respond naturally with voice, gaze, expressions, and gestures. Making every interaction feel human.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Performs agentic tasks 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Persona — The Embodied WebMCP AI Agent 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 With multiple persona's 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Web MCP tool calling, support 10+ useful tools 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Supports Gestures and Human expressions 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Performs agentic tasks 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Persona — The Embodied WebMCP AI Agent 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 With multiple persona's 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Web MCP tool calling, support 10+ useful tools 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Supports Gestures and Human expressions 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Performs agentic tasks 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 



 
 Inspiration 

 We are at a strange point in the evolution of AI. 

 AI can reason, write code, analyze information, use tools, and increasingly perform tasks on our behalf. But when it comes time to actually interact with it, we are still mostly staring at a text box. 

 Type a prompt.
Wait.
Read a long response.
Type again. 

 It works, but it can feel surprisingly disconnected. 

 I kept thinking about a simple question: 

 
 If AI is becoming capable of doing things like a person, why are we still interacting with it like a search box? 
 

 Humans don't communicate through words alone. 

 We use our voice. We look at each other. We react. We gesture. We pay attention. We pause. We interrupt. We change our expression when something is important. 

 Those small signals make communication easier to understand. 

 So we wanted to explore a different kind of AI interface. 

 
 What if an AI agent had a body? 
 

 That question became Persona . 

 The goal wasn't to create a character that simply talks to you or to make AI pretend to be human. 

 The goal was to explore whether an AI agent could have a presence — a way to communicate its intent through voice, attention, expressions, gestures, and visible actions while still doing useful work. 

 WebMCP made this idea especially interesting. 

 Instead of an AI agent trying to figure out which button to click or how a webpage happens to be structured, the webpage can explicitly expose capabilities that the agent can discover and use. 

 That gave us an opportunity to build something where the agent doesn't just talk about what it wants to do. 

 It can actually interact with the webpage through structured tools. 

 And if an agent can control actions on the web, why shouldn't it also be able to control how it communicates with the person standing on the other side of the interaction? 

 That became the idea behind Persona: 

 
 Give the agent a body. Give that body meaningful capabilities. Then let WebMCP connect the agent to them. 
 

 

 What it does 

 Persona is an embodied WebMCP AI agent interface. 

 It gives an AI agent a digital body that can listen, speak, look, react, gesture, and perform structured tasks . 

 Instead of treating the avatar as a visual layer placed on top of a chatbot, Persona makes the avatar part of the agent interaction itself. 

 A user can communicate naturally through voice, while an AI agent can discover and call WebMCP tools exposed by Persona. 

 The agent can: 

 
 Understand the user's spoken intent 
 Create tasks and missions 
 Read the current task state 
 Update tasks when requirements change 
 Complete tasks 
 Present results 
 Speak to the user 
 Change its expression 
 Direct its attention and gaze 
 Perform gestures 
 

 The WebMCP tools exposed by Persona include: 
 get_user_transcript
create_task
get_tasks
update_task
complete_task
show_result
speak
set_expression
set_attention
perform_gesture
 
 This allows the agent to interact with two sides of the application: 

 What it is doing and how it is communicating while doing it . 

 For example, a user can say: 

 
 "Prepare me for a data science technical interview tomorrow." 
 

 The agent can turn that request into a structured mission instead of simply returning a large block of advice. 

 The user can then change their mind: 

 
 "Actually, focus much more on machine learning." 
 

 The agent can update the mission and continue from the current state. 

 At the same time, Persona can communicate through speech, attention, expressions, and gestures. 

 This creates an interaction loop where: 

 Human intent → Agent reasoning → WebMCP action → Application state → Embodied response 

 The interview-preparation scenario is our concrete demonstration of this idea. 

 But Persona itself isn't meant to be just an interview coach. 

 The larger idea is an embodied interface for web agents . 

 The avatar is not there just to look good. 

 The agent can actually control it through WebMCP. 

 That is what turns Persona from an animated chatbot into an exploration of what an agent-native web interface could look and feel like. 

 

 How we built it 

 Persona is a browser-based application built with: 

 
 React 
 TypeScript 
 Vite 
 Three.js 
 VRM 
 @pixiv/three-vrm 
 WebMCP 
 Web Speech API 
 Web Audio API 
 

 The project combines an agent-facing tool layer with an embodiment runtime. 

 WebMCP tool layer 

 The core of the WebMCP integration is the application's ability to expose structured capabilities through document.modelContext . 

 Instead of exposing arbitrary UI elements, Persona exposes tools that represent meaningful actions an agent can perform. 

 For example: 
 document . modelContext . registerTool ( . . . ) 
 
 The tools cover two main areas. 

 Agent actions 
 create_task
get_tasks
update_task
complete_task
show_result
 
 These allow the agent to work with structured application state. 

 Embodiment actions 
 get_user_transcript
speak
set_expression
set_attention
perform_gesture
 
 These allow the agent to communicate through Persona's digital body. 

 This separation was important to us. 

 The AI agent doesn't need to know how the avatar is implemented internally. 

 It doesn't need to manipulate Three.js objects, animation clips, or VRM parameters. 

 It can simply use a meaningful capability such as: 
 speak(...)
set_expression(...)
set_attention(...)
perform_gesture(...)
 
 Persona handles the underlying implementation. 

 The embodiment runtime 

 The visual body is a VRM character rendered through Three.js. 

 Around that character, we built systems for: 

 
 Voice input 
 Voice output 
 Speech-driven mouth movement 
 Facial expressions 
 Eye gaze and attention 
 Gestures 
 Behavioral state 
 Micro-reactions 
 Interruption handling 
 Session continuity 
 

 One of the most important design decisions was separating agent intent from embodiment . 

 The agent decides what it wants to accomplish or communicate . 

 WebMCP provides the structured interface through which it can do that. 

 Persona's runtime determines how that intent appears to the human . 

 For example, the same agent decision can involve both an actual task action and an embodied response. 

 The agent may update a task while also speaking to the user and directing its attention toward them. 

 This means the avatar isn't just an animation layer. 

 It becomes another interface through which the agent communicates. 

 Why WebMCP matters here 

 Without WebMCP, an agent could generate instructions describing what should happen. 

 With WebMCP, Persona can expose the actual capabilities of the webpage in a form the agent can discover and call. 

 That distinction is important. 

 We aren't trying to make the AI look like it is operating the application. 

 We're giving the agent structured ways to actually interact with it. 

 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The difficult part wasn't putting a 3D character on a webpage. 

 The difficult part was making the character feel like part of the interaction rather than a decoration sitting beside a chatbot . 

 Voice interaction introduced several problems. 

 We had to handle microphone state, speech synthesis, turn-taking, interruptions, and make sure Persona didn't accidentally respond to its own generated speech. 

 Then we encountered a more subtle problem: 

 
 When should an AI agent actually move? 
 

 If an avatar constantly moves, looks around randomly, changes expressions without context, or performs gestures at the wrong moment, the result becomes distracting very quickly. 

 So we worked on behavioral state, attention, micr

title: Local Buzz
pitch: Local Buzz turns a city into a shared workspace for you and your AI agent, helping you discover what’s happening now and collaboratively build, adapt, and rescue your night in real time.
about_excerpt: Local Buzz turns a city into a shared workspace for you and your AI agent, helping you discover what’s happening now and collaboratively build, adapt, and rescue your night in real time. Like Comment Story Updates The agent does not click through the UI. Local Buzz exposes structured WebMCP tools, and the results appear directly in the same interface. Local Buzz combines a live city interface with WebMCP so a person and their AI agent can plan together. The human brings taste. The agent handles complexity. Local Buzz provides the live city. WebMCP enables one shared experience. Inspiration “What should we do tonight?” sounds simple, but the answer is scattered across event sites, venues, ticketing platforms, local calendars, social media, and word of mouth. AI can already recommend events or generate itineraries, but chat is a poor interface for exploring a city. A map is better for geography. A timeline is better for sequence. Visual browsing is better for taste. That led to a different question: What if a person and their personal AI agent could explore and shape a night together, inside the same live web experience? What it does Local Buzz turns your city into a shared real-time workspace for a person and their AI agent (starting with Stockholm and San Francisco). Local Buzz knows the city: what is happening, where, when, how much it costs, and what is currently available. The user's agent can bring something Local Buzz does not need to collect: context about the user. Together they can: discover relevant happenings surface candidates directly on the city map stage an evening on a visual timeline let the human lock, reject, or change individual choices let the agent read those changes and adapt around them repair an existing night when something becomes unavailable The important idea is that Local Buzz is not an AI itinerary generator. It is a shared model of a night that stays alive. It answers the age old question: where can I go have fun right now? Why WebMCP The human and the agent need different interfaces into the same application. The human works visually through maps, cards, timelines, locks, and direct manipulation. The agent works through structured WebMCP tools for searching happenings, showing candidates, reading the current plan, staging changes, locking stops, and repairing the plan. Both operate on the same underlying application state. For example, when a human locks a stop in the interface, the agent sees that constraint the next time it reads the plan. If another event becomes unavailable, the agent repairs only the affected portion instead of throwing the entire itinerary away and starting over. This is the interaction we wanted to explore with WebMCP: Agent acts → interface changes → human intervenes → agent understands the intervention → reality changes → agent repairs the shared state → human approves. How we built it Local Buzz is built as a proof-of-concept web application using the Modeless design system. The application has one shared domain model that powers both the human interface and its WebMCP tools. Human actions and agent actions call the same underlying application functions rather than maintaining separate UI and agent state. For the challenge prototype, we focus on Stockholm and San Francisco and use a small normalized set of real local event and venue data. Local Buzz adds derived metadata where useful for planning. A last-minute event availability change used in the demo is intentionally simulated so the repair behavior can be demonstrated deterministically and is clearly labeled as such. What we learned The most interesting part of WebMCP is that websites can be designed from the beginning for two collaborators with different strengths. The human brings taste, intuition, and judgment. The agent handles search, constraints, timing, and complexity. The website provides the live domain state they collaborate around. What I've been exploring is the surface area of how much a web app can be adapted for the end user based on agentic interactions. In some ways, it starts to become reminiscent of push, or streaming, data if the agent is making a lot of updates. I believe there's a lot of use cases for WebMCP around real-time data.
