title: BashMCP: Give agents a terminal for your website
pitch: Add one line of code to expose WebMCP actions as composable shell commands. Agents can inspect, filter, and chain them, saving hundreds of tool calls and up to 83% of token usage.
about_excerpt: Add one line of code to expose WebMCP actions as composable shell commands. Agents can inspect, filter, and chain them, saving hundreds of tool calls and up to 83% of token usage. Like Comment Story Updates 10/10 correct versus 2/10 natively, with 59–75% fewer tokens and 99–100% fewer calls and bytes. The same real agent and task: both carts correct, with 17 calls natively versus 3 with BashMCP. Live-store turn collapse: 517 host-visible calls become 2; 1.15 MB returned becomes 4.4 KB. One WebMCP tool named bash compiles site tools into /bin; tool save registers a new WebMCP tool. A saved pipeline becomes a WebMCP tool that the next agent finds and runs without being told. A browser-native computer: site and network files, typed commands with help, and persistent SQLite. BashMCP runs on any website, with or without existing tools; Shopify is the worked example. BashMCP: a command line inside any website. One script tag adds a site-side runtime above the WebMCP standard. WebMCP makes a website callable. BashMCP makes it a computer, and the computer gets better every visit. <script src="https://bashmcp.apptory.ai/bashmcp.js" data-bashmcp data-ui="drawer"></script> That is the whole install. BashMCP is a site-side WebMCP composition runtime that installs into an existing website and runs inside that page's live session—not a separate browser VM, a hosted sandbox, or a replacement for the site's tools. One tag boots a sandboxed Unix-like workspace inside the page's own origin. Every WebMCP tool the site already registers compiles into a typed shell command. The page's own network traffic becomes files. An origin-scoped SQLite database persists across tabs and visits. The primary composition entry point registers back into WebMCP as a tool named bash , whose input is { command } —the same string a person would type at a terminal. A separate read-only dom page reader is registered beside it. On the demo store, an agent composes Shopify's ten existing WebMCP tools with jq , grep , sort , and SQL in one auditable run instead of returning every intermediate result to model context. Measured with a blind GPT-5.6 Sol agent on a whole-catalog size audit, that turned 2 of 10 correct into 9 of 10 , while reducing a native median of 315 model-visible host calls to 2 . The person watching sees the same pipeline land in a shared terminal, can rerun or edit it, and can save it as a new WebMCP tool. Fresh agents found and reused such a saved tool unprompted in 14 of 15 measured warm sessions. Same-origin only. No host shell. Shopify is the worked example, not the boundary. The numbers first Same agent, same task, same store, and the same Shopify tools available in both conditions. The prompts never mention bash or prescribe a method. The design and primary metrics were declared before the first benchmark cell ran, exact verifiers read the resulting cart, and every failure is published. Task Site tools alone Same tools, bash beside them What it shows Whole-catalog size audit, clone, n=10 2/10 correct; median 315 calls 9/10 correct; 2 calls Local composition can finish work that serial model-visible calls often cannot Whole-catalog category census, clone, n=10 2/10 correct 10/10 correct The agent chose the shell unprompted in every whole-catalog run Three-step shopper session with a real cart mutation, live store, n=8 3/8 correct 8/8 correct; 41% fewer tokens [23–65%] Query, ranking, and mutation on the production store Single product lookup, control, n=10 10/10 correct 10/10 correct; 2% more tokens ; bash unused in 7/10 The shell adds no value where there is nothing to compose Saved tool reused by a fresh agent, n=15 — 14/15 found it; 15/15 correct; 67% fewer tokens The site's tool surface compounds 500-product catalog audit, n=4 0/4 completed; up to 1,545 calls 3/4 completed in 2–4 calls The benefit increases as the fan-out grows A host-visible call is a call the host makes on the model's behalf whose result enters model context. The site tools invoked inside a bash program still execute against the real application, and every nested call remains visible in the run receipt. BashMCP removes repeated model round trips; it does not hide or eliminate the underlying application work. We make no comparative wall-clock or cost claim. The shell is often slower on a single action, which is why the flat control remains in every results table. The complete methodology, intervals, provenance, and failure ledger are in docs/results.md . Why BashMCP is a strong fit for WebMCP In agent hosts today, broad tasks often become serial tool executions: each result returns to model context before the model decides what to call next. That is exactly right for one action— add this item to my cart or show me that variant . It becomes expensive and brittle when work spans an entire dataset. Auditing every product, ranking a catalog, or cross-referencing endpoints can require hundreds of model-visible round trips, each adding another payload the model must consume before continuing. The tools were not the problem. The turns were. The site's tools remain the correct, authoritative actions. BashMCP never reimplements them. It changes where their composition happens: search, filtering, ranking, joining, and mutation execute as one local program, while only the final answer returns to model context. A host could add batching or a code interpreter for its own users. A site-installed environment has three different advantages: It runs inside the visitor's live session. It can work with the current cart, prices, stock, locale, login state, and the person's own actions without exporting that state into a separate environment. Persistence belongs to the origin. Saved tools, history, and the database remain in the site's browser origin and are available on later visits. The tool surface ships with the site. Anything the site registers can help compatible agents from multiple hosts, and a developer can promote an agent-authored tool into the site's build for future visitors. So we asked: What is the most useful thing a site can register through WebMCP? Our answer was an environment rather than another verb. A better experience for the agent and the person For the agent , BashMCP provides a POSIX-shaped environment it already understands: a filesystem to explore, commands with familiar flags, pipes, exit codes, man pages, --help , jq , grep , sort , and SQL. It does not require a long instruction manual in the tool description. The description points the agent toward cat /README.md , tools , man <command> , and --help ; the environment teaches the rest. In every measured whole-catalog run, the agent selected bash without being told to use it while Shopify's ten original tools remained available. For the person , the developer installation mounts a shared terminal beside the page: One transcript. Two identities: you@host and agent@host . One command history. One filesystem. One SQLite database. You can watch the agent's pipeline land as it runs, press rerun to execute it yourself, arrow back through it, and change one flag. The Runs , Tools , and Events panels show every call, every byte returned, and a receipt for each run—including runs initiated by an agent host rather than the visible terminal. On the live store, ChatGPT's in-app browser sees twelve tools: Shopify's ten plus BashMCP's bash and dom . In a verified run, GPT-5.6 Sol discovered bash unprompted, completed a whole-catalog ranking task with one nested update_cart , and independently verified the resulting cart with a top-level get_cart . What people and agents can do together that was difficult before When a pipeline works, either the person or the agent can save it: tool save cheapest-in-size --description "Cheapest in-stock products in a size" \ --schema '{"type":"object","properties":{"size":{"type":"string"}},"required":["size"]}' < script The script is stored in the origin's SQLite database and registers as a real WebMCP tool immediately and on later visits. It appears: In tools . In man . As a command in /bin . In the agent host's own tool list. With the description, JSON Schema, and access level its author declared. Fresh agents found and reused the saved tool unprompted in 14 of 15 measured warm sessions, and all 15 executions produced the correct answer. tool export prints the production shipping format, so a developer can promote an emergent tool into the site's data-tools configuration. The loop is: A cold agent explores → builds a missing tool → the person inspects, edits, or saves it → a later agent starts with it → the developer ships it to everyone. A static tool surface cannot do this. BashMCP lets use itself reveal which higher-level tools the site should provide. The runtime carries no Shopify-specific knowledge. title: Buki
pitch: Arrived somewhere new with hours to spare? Buki turns a sentence into a real walkable itinerary. Google Maps places and routes, agent-driven over WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Arrived somewhere new with hours to spare? Buki turns a sentence into a real walkable itinerary. Google Maps places and routes, agent-driven over WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I work at andbeyond.com, a luxury travel company, and this idea was born from that experience. I also really like to travel to new places. So I built this tool thinking about myself. When you are traveling, it is great to have something that gives you itineraries almost instantly. What it does You tell buki where you are and how you feel, in your own words. Buki doesnt guess the parts it doesnt know. If you did not say how much time you have, or how far you want to walk, it asks to you. Then it uses Google Maps to find real places near you, check if they are open, and calculate the real walking route between them. You get a intinerary you can follow. If one stops doesnt work, buki looks for real replacement nearby that still fits your route. It shows you the change first. You decide. How I built it React, Typescript & Vite. Mobile first, because you use this while you are standing on the street. Buki registers 11 WebMCP tools with document.modelContext.registerTool . So an agent can use the same app you are looking at. There is no separate agent mode. When the agent sets the origin, the map moves. When the agent builds the route, you see the route. The LLM only reads what you wrote and turns it into constraints. It never invents a place or a distance. All of that comes from Google Maps. Challenges we ran into The agent saw 1 tool instead of 11. I registered the tools one by one with await . ChatGPT read the list before it finished and told me the page only had one tool. The tools were fine. The timing was the problem. The agent was clicking instead of using the tools. I put Buki next to ChatGPT Desktop and it used the mouse to click my interface. It worked, but it proved nothing. I had to tell it directly: use the tools, never click. A problem with no error. Every stop showed "Status unavailable". Nothing failed. isOpen() needs utcOffsetMinutes and I didnt ask for that field, so the code that removes closed places was doing nothing. Buki could send you to a closed museum. One line fixed it. I decided not to guess. It is easier to invent a duration when the person does not give one. I did not want hat. f you dont say how much time you have, it asks. A plan built on a wrong assumption is worse than one question. What I learned WebMCP isnt just an API for your weate with the agent. The dificult questions were not technical. They were about trust, what can the agent do alone and what needs the person say yes? What's next for Buki Multi-day itineraries, public transport, and saving a walk to use it later. I would like it to be good enough to use it myself next time I travel. title: Deckhand
pitch: A slide editor agents can actually operate—where human edits and agent actions share one live, editable canvas.
about_excerpt: A slide editor agents can actually operate—where human edits and agent actions share one live, editable canvas. Like Comment Story Updates Direct human edits become structured context an agent can propagate. Live 16:9 canvas shared by people and browser agents. Import a PowerPoint template locally and preserve its visual system. Typed WebMCP tools expose semantic slide operations, not brittle clicks. Inspiration AI slide generators are useful for first drafts, but the collaboration often ends as soon as a person starts refining the result. Move a title, shorten a paragraph, or decide that one chart should dominate the page, and the AI no longer understands the live artifact. The familiar workflow becomes: generate with AI, then rebuild by hand. Deckhand starts from a different premise: the canvas itself should be the collaboration interface . What it does Deckhand is a local-first presentation editor with two native interfaces over one live artifact: People work on a visual 16:9 canvas: select, multi-select, drag, resize, edit text, style, reorder, present, undo, and export. Browser agents work through typed WebMCP operations against the exact same slides, selection, design grammar, edit history, and browser session. The workflow works with or without a user-owned template. Deckhand can start from eleven purpose-built layout recipes and four art directions, or open a .pptx / .potx and extract its theme, palette, fonts, masters, layouts, and supported editable objects locally in the browser. The key interaction is “show, don’t prompt.” A person can directly change a title’s position, size, or color. Deckhand records that action as semantic edit deltas—not just pixels—and exposes those recent human edits to the browser agent. The agent can then apply the same intent to matching roles elsewhere without making the person describe every visual decision in prose. Why WebMCP is essential A presentation editor has a large, fast-changing state space: slides, objects, roles, geometry, style, relationships, selection, imported design rules, and reversible history. Screenshot-and-click automation repeatedly guesses both the target and the intent. A conventional backend MCP server would duplicate browser-local state and lose the immediate connection to the canvas the person is judging. WebMCP lets Deckhand expose domain meaning exactly where the state already lives: in the open page. Deckhand registers eight baseline tools: inspect_project reads the smallest useful slice of the deck, current slide, selection, design system, or recent human edits. plan_deck validates a narrative and layout mapping without mutating the canvas. compose_deck materializes an approved plan as one visible, undoable transaction. revise_slide recomposes one slide from its communication goal. edit_slide performs precise changes against inspected element IDs. manage_deck handles focus, rename, duplicate, reorder, and delete operations. validate_deck checks narrative structure and measures the real rendered canvas. undo_last_change provides an explicit recovery path. After a direct human edit, a contextual propagate_human_edits tool appears only when it is relevant. Read-only tools declare readOnlyHint; deck content is marked with untrustedContentHint; schemas are constrained; mutations are atomic; and errors explain how the agent can recover. A better human + agent experience Deckhand separates reasoning from mutation. An agent first inspects the project, creates a read-only plan, composes it in one transaction, and validates the rendered result. The person sees every change on the canvas, can continue editing with the mouse and keyboard, and can undo an entire agent batch in one step. This makes the agent useful beyond generation. It can keep collaborating through the messy middle: repair the weakest slide, preserve an imported brand system, align selected objects, propagate a deliberate human edit, validate the result, and recover when a revision is worse. How I built it Deckhand is written in TypeScript and React on Vinext and deployed as a Cloudflare Worker. Its serializable scene graph stores semantic roles, geometry, styles, provenance, design tokens, selection, and history. The PowerPoint pipeline safely reads OOXML packages in the browser, follows theme → master → layout → slide inheritance, extracts supported raster assets, and reports fidelity limitations without uploading the source file. The design engine maps semantic slide briefs to varied layout recipes. The quality gate combines deterministic narrative checks with measurements from the actual rendered DOM. WebMCP tools are registered against document.modelContext and call the same domain operations used by the visual editor. There is no second copy of the presentation state and no separate MCP service to configure. Challenges The hardest problem was not exposing many low-level commands. It was choosing an agent surface that stays compact while still producing complete presentations. The plan/compose split keeps reasoning inspectable and prevents half-finished decks. Semantic revision handles broad design intent; precise editing remains an escape hatch only after inspection. PowerPoint fidelity was another challenge. A template is not just colors and fonts—it is inheritance, transforms, grouped geometry, placeholder rules, and sometimes unsupported objects. Deckhand preserves what it can edit safely, keeps provenance for future agent decisions, and surfaces honest warnings when exact fidelity is not possible. Accomplishments and learning I am most proud that WebMCP is not a chat box attached to an editor. It changes the product architecture: visual manipulation and semantic tool calls are two interfaces to one live, reversible artifact. Building Deckhand also changed how I think about agent accessibility. A good agent interface needs more than valid schemas. It needs progressive disclosure, explicit read/write boundaries, contextual tools, recovery paths, and feedback that remains legible to the person watching. What’s next Next steps include richer chart and SmartArt conversion, collaborative cloud persistence, more render-aware layout repair, and direct Google Slides interoperability. The broader pattern extends beyond slides to design, video, CAD, and any visual editor where people judge by sight while agents need meaning. title: Voltage Dashboard
pitch: Voltage makes existing e-commerce systems agent-ready with safe, route-aware WebMCP tools—automating operational preparation while humans retain final control.
about_excerpt: Voltage makes existing e-commerce systems agent-ready with safe, route-aware WebMCP tools—automating operational preparation while humans retain final control. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Enterprise commerce dashboards already contain the workflows people rely on, but agents usually have to infer intent from pixels and click through fragile interfaces. Voltage explores a different future for the open web: existing applications can expose their real operational capabilities through WebMCP while preserving the interface, permissions, and human accountability that teams already understand. What it does Voltage is an e-commerce operations dashboard covering products, inventory, orders, customers, returns, refund approvals, and reporting. Each route exposes a focused set of structured WebMCP tools for safe queries, navigation, form filling, analysis, and draft preparation. The demo follows a complete refund-review workflow. An agent finds the longest-waiting approval, verifies eligibility, inspection results, an immutable refund calculation, the amount, and relevant data versions. It then prepares a reversible review-note draft under the signed-in user's account and opens the correct page for review. The human publishes the note and makes the final approval decision. Afterward, the agent re-discovers the tools available on the new route and confirms that the RMA has advanced to refund execution. High-risk actions—including publishing, approving or rejecting refunds, changing amounts, executing payments, and recording final refund results—remain explicit human actions in the existing UI. Why WebMCP This workflow is a strong fit for WebMCP because the task crosses several application modules and depends on structured business state rather than visual clicking alone. Route-aware tools let the site tell the agent which operations are valid on the current page. Tool results expose identifiers, workflow stages, evidence, and versions directly, reducing ambiguity and making actions easier to audit. Navigation tools instruct the host to re-discover capabilities after a route change. Stale tool calls return a structured re-discovery error, allowing the agent to recover predictably instead of continuing with outdated page context. Agent guidance and progressive disclosure Voltage adds an application-level guidance system on top of its WebMCP tools. The always-available agents_instructions tool acts as the agent's entry point. Its response adapts to authentication state: signed-out agents are told that authentication is required, while signed-in agents receive the system's capabilities, safety boundaries, and navigation guidance. This preserves a useful WebMCP entry point even when all operational tools must remain protected. For complex business workflows, skill_list and load_skill provide progressive disclosure. Instead of placing every operational instruction into every tool description, the agent discovers and loads only the workflow knowledge needed for the current task. Together with route-specific tools, this creates a predictable sequence: Read the current system instructions. Discover and load the relevant business skill. Use tools exposed by the active page. Re-discover capabilities after navigation. Continue with fresh route context. Stale calls return a structured RE_DISCOVER_REQUIRED error so the agent can recover once in a controlled way rather than continuing with outdated capabilities. These are Voltage application patterns built on WebMCP, not assumptions that every WebMCP site implements the same skill system. Better human-agent collaboration Without WebMCP, a reviewer must manually locate the oldest case, open several records, compare evidence, copy identifiers, and draft a recommendation. With Voltage, the agent performs that reversible preparation while the reviewer stays responsible for consequential decisions. The application does not assume an agent is present. Every workflow remains usable by a person, and agent-generated drafts use the same review-note system available to signed-in users. WebMCP enhances the existing product instead of replacing it with a chatbot. How we built it Voltage is a frontend-only React and TypeScript application built with Vite. WebMCP tools are registered through document.modelContext with an in-page fallback provider for development and testing. Route-aware registries expose only the capabilities relevant to the active page. Operational demo data is stored locally using browser storage. Reporting uses SQLite WASM with a constrained read-only SQL layer, query caching, and a report canvas. The deployed demonstration contains synthetic data only and must not be used with real customer, payment, or confidential business information. The project was developed and tested with Codex using its in-app browser, enabling the agent to exercise WebMCP tools against the live Vite application while code changes were applied through hot module replacement. title: Jobly: turn a resume into a completed application
pitch: Give Codex your resume. It finds matching jobs on Jobly and completes applications on two structurally different ATS portals via WebMCP tools - you keep control of the choices and the final submit.
about_excerpt: Give Codex your resume. It finds matching jobs on Jobly and completes applications on two structurally different ATS portals via WebMCP tools - you keep control of the choices and the final submit. Like Comment Story Updates Jobly Inspiration Job applications often fail before a candidate can make their case. A promising role becomes a relay of unfamiliar portals, repeated resume uploads, and long forms asking for information that already exists in the resume. By the last page, the candidate has spent their attention on administration instead of the opportunity. We wanted to show how WebMCP changes that: the candidate keeps the consequential decisions, and the agent does the repetitive work between them. What it does Jobly turns a resume into a completed application. The candidate gives Codex their resume and preferences. Codex identifies relevant roles on Jobly (an Indeed-style job board), the candidate chooses which opportunity is worth pursuing, and Codex uses each employer portal's explicit WebMCP tools to carry the application forward across two simulated ATS sites: Greenhold — a Greenhouse-style ATS with a five-step application wizard Leverly — a Lever-style ATS with a single-page form The journey: Codex uses Jobly's list_jobs / get_job tools to build a shortlist with each role's applyUrl . For each approved role it opens the ATS, signs in, inspects the real form via get_application_form / get_page_fields , fills it from the resume with fill_fields , attaches files, validates, pauses for human approval, and finally submit_application returns a confirmation ID — verifiable under My applications . The WebMCP surface This is not a UI-scraping demonstration. Jobly exposes structured search and job-detail tools ( get_filter_options , list_jobs , get_job ); the two ATS sites expose their jobs, form schemas, page state, file attachment, validation, and submission actions directly ( sign_in , start_application , fill_fields , attach_resume , attach_cover_letter , goto_page , next_page , prev_page , validate_application , submit_application ). Greenhold and Leverly expose the same agent contract but render structurally different forms . That difference is intentional: the agent must inspect and adapt to each application experience instead of replaying a hardcoded sequence of clicks. How we built it Monorepo (npm workspaces): three Vite + React + TypeScript apps and three shared packages. packages/webmcp — WebMCP registration glue, tool helpers, and an Origin-Agent-Cluster Vite plugin (WebMCP requires origin isolation). packages/convex — one shared Convex backend ( jobs + applications ) that all three apps point at. packages/ats-core — a config-driven form engine (store, validation, submit mapping, WebMCP tools, React renderer) shared by both ATS sites. WebMCP tools call Convex imperatively ( convex.query/mutation ), so the agent path and the React UI share one backend and, in the ATS apps, one in-page form store — the visible human view stays in sync with the agent's progress. Challenges we ran into Designing one tool contract that works for both a multi-page wizard and a single-page form, so the agent adapts by inspection rather than memorized flows. Keeping the human UI and the agent's mutations in perfect sync through a single in-page form store. Origin isolation requirements for WebMCP, solved with a reusable Origin-Agent-Cluster Vite plugin. What we learned WebMCP is at its best when the site tells the agent what it can do instead of the agent guessing at the UI. Structured form schemas plus validation tools let the agent complete real multi-step workflows safely, while explicit human approval before submit_application keeps the person in control of the consequential choices. What's next for Jobly Richer candidate profiles, more ATS form archetypes (Workday-style multi-section forms), and employer-side WebMCP tools for reviewing incoming applications. title: EgoLens: Teachable Driving-Data Viewer
pitch: Agents don't just use EgoLens, they extend it. Drop an unknown driving dataset: your agent writes the adapter, you judge the 3D render. Each does what it's best at, and the viewer keeps growing.
about_excerpt: Agents don't just use EgoLens, they extend it. Drop an unknown driving dataset: your agent writes the adapter, you judge the 3D render. Each does what it's best at, and the viewer keeps growing. Like Comment Story Updates Unknown dataset detected Teaching new dataset format New dataset learned! dataset rendered Inspiration Every perception team has sensor data in a shape no viewer understands: a research dataset, or their own model output stored next to one. Someone writes a loader, debugs why the point cloud renders sideways, and the loader dies with the notebook. EgoLens already renders Waymo, nuScenes, and Argoverse 2 in the browser, and every new format still meant a hand-written adapter. WebMCP changes who can add one: your agent teaches EgoLens through WebMCP, you approve the render, and the app's capabilities keep growing. What it does WebMCP tools usually let agents use the app. EgoLens flips it: agents extend the app. Together, a person and an agent can now add a dataset format to a viewer in minutes, in the browser, without touching the source code. Drop a folder EgoLens does not recognize and the page becomes a WebMCP tool provider. The agent inspects files within strict byte limits, reads the recipe schema and operator vocabulary, and submits adapter recipes as declarative JSON, never code. Every validated revision renders in the production 3D viewer, docked next to the review panel : orbit, scrub the timeline, toggle boxes and segmentation, switch camera POVs. You accept or reject each capability with a named issue and the verdict flows back to the agent. Finalize seals the recipe with content hashes; it can be exported, imported, and shared. Every taught format stays: drop that layout again and it renders in one click. The app's capabilities keep growing, and files never leave the browser. How we built it Five tools registered on document.modelContext : inspect , get_contract , apply_revision , get_state , finalize . Self-describing descriptions, normalized inputs, string results, so ChatGPT's browser, Chrome's native WebMCP, and the Codex app drive them with zero agent-specific code. Recipes are data, executed in an isolated graph runtime with resource limits. The person confirms the sensor layout before teaching starts; a recipe that does not bind exactly those sensors is rejected. React 19, TypeScript, three.js, Web Workers, IndexedDB, GitHub Pages. 1,100 unit tests and Playwright probes that drive Chrome's real WebMCP end to end. Challenges we ran into Agents stopping at the timeline. Fixed without shipping any dataset example, which would leak the answer: a sensor contract, coverage diagnostics, and a next-step hint in every state read. Bugs only eyes can catch. PandaSet stores cuboid yaw along the width axis. Every automated check passed and the boxes were rotated 90° on screen. That is why the full renderer is the review surface. Host budgets. Codex caps descriptor size and call latency; in-app browsers hang on the File System Access API. Each constraint pushed the tool surface toward the plainest contract. Accomplishments that we're proud of Three unknown datasets taught end to end by agents in one week: A2D2 (3 revisions, 6 cameras + 6 LiDARs fused), KITTI Raw (7 revisions), PandaSet (world-frame poses, pandas pickles). No example recipe is ever shown to the agent. The same five tools work unchanged across three hosts, and each dataset taught left EgoLens able to read more than before. What we learned The interesting question is not "what can an agent do in my app" but "what can an agent make my app able to do". Expose the extension points as tools and the agent's output becomes an artifact a person can inspect, reject, seal, and share. The person's rejections were the most valuable signal in the loop. What's next for EgoLens: Teachable Driving-Data Viewer A public recipe registry. A student or a researcher teaches EgoLens the dataset they need and publishes the recipe, so it renders for everyone after that. The goal: a visualization tool that can read any AV dataset, taught by the people who use it. Ego Lens is a browser tool people use because it just works. Drop a driving data set in and it renders. No pre-processing, no install. But today, I need to render a data set it has never seen. Ego Lens's job here is to validate that recipe, and once it passes, render it. Then I, the human, take a look at the render, and if something's off, I tell Codex exactly what's wrong so it can try again. Like right now, when we hit play, the car in the center stays put, but the point cloud around it, the rings that should be spreading out from that car, drifts forward on its own. A minute later, a new revision comes in. Let me play it again. Now, the point cloud and the car move together, the boxes sit on the vehicles, and the cameras line up. Everything looks right. So, I go through the list and approve each one. Timeline, poses, point cloud, cameras, boxes, projection, segmentation. Then I finalize and Ego Lens seals the recipe. That's it. And because a recipe is just a JSON file, I can host it right next to the data and pack both into a single link. Whoever taught the data set to Eagle lens shares that link, and whoever opens it gets the whole scene. That's where this is going. A public registry of recipes, so once someone teaches Eagle lens a format, it renders for everyone after that. Any data set, not just three. And your own data never has to leave your machine.

title: Patiently — a clinic your agent can actually use
pitch: An outpatient clinic that exposes its queue, charts and prescriptions as 20 WebMCP tools — where every action that touches a patient's care stops and waits for a human to click.
about_excerpt: An outpatient clinic that exposes its queue, charts and prescriptions as 20 WebMCP tools — where every action that touches a patient's care stops and waits for a human to click. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I am a medical doctor. I work at an inpatient clinic, and the thing nobody warns you about in training is how much of the job is typing. The clinical reasoning is the part I trained for, and it is not the part that takes the time. The documentation is. Notes get written last, often at the end of a shift, partly from memory, because during the shift there was a patient in front of me and both of my hands were busy. Everyone I work with does the same thing, and everyone knows it is the weakest point in the whole process. Intake is worse. By the time a patient reaches me, what they actually said has been through at least one compression: they described their symptoms to whoever was at the desk, in whatever time that person had, into whatever fields the form provided. If the patient was frightened, in pain, holding a child, or not fluent in the language the form was written in, more gets lost. I have had patients volunteer something on the ward, almost in passing, that changed my assessment completely, and that had not made it into a single field anywhere. That is the failure I actually worry about. Not a slow queue. A red flag that somebody said out loud and nobody wrote down. So when agents became genuinely useful, the appeal was obvious: let the agent do the typing, the lookup and the cross-referencing, and let me do the medicine. But every agent integration I tried had the same shape. The agent would act first and tell me afterwards. In a clinic, the acting is the dangerous half. Writing a prescription, putting a vital sign in a chart, moving somebody up the queue; these are not operations you undo by apologising. WebMCP is what changed the answer for me, for one specific reason. The tools run inside the page the clinician is already signed into. Because the tool executes in the page, its own execute call can simply stop and wait for a click. The approval is not a policy the model is asked to respect. It is a promise that does not resolve. That turned the project into a single question: can an agent do the clinic's work while a person stays accountable for every write, in a way the agent cannot route around even if it wanted to? What it does Patiently is a working outpatient clinic exposed as 20 WebMCP tools across four surfaces. Two agents and two humans share one live page. The patient opens their queue link and describes symptoms to their own agent, out loud, in their own language. In the demo a woman writes in Bahasa Indonesia: "Dada saya terasa sesak sejak pagi tadi, nyerinya menjalar ke lengan kiri" . She is not filling in a form. A structured history comes out the other end. Triage runs separately, server-side. An independent classifier reads that same Indonesian message, fires CHEST_PAIN_CARDIAC , and the ticket jumps to priority 100. Her agent tells her to find staff now. The chart the doctor reads is in English. The clinician asks their agent for the floor: who is waiting longest with a red flag, pull that chart. The chart is already written, including the follow-up delta from the previous visit and the differentials that must not be missed. The doctor then dictates vitals, drafts a note, drafts prescriptions, and signs. Every one of those writes opened a dialog and blocked until they clicked it. Reception issues a ticket through a plain HTML form that is itself a tool, using the declarative WebMCP attributes, with no auto-submit, because a queue number belongs to a real person. The part that is new is not the automation. It is that the automation stops. Three safety properties are structural rather than prompted: A proposal is only ever answered by a person. The outcome an agent receives is approved , declined , expired or cancelled , because only one of those is a decision somebody made. An agent is never told "the clinician declined" about a dialog nobody saw. A patient cannot talk their way up the queue, or down it. There is no tool that sets priority. Naming a red-flag code without the symptoms fires nothing. Describing real symptoms fires the code even when the patient insists they are fine, because minimising is a reason for more caution, not less. A failed check never looks like a clean one. If the triage classifier is unreachable, the turn is recorded as unscreened and everyone is told so, rather than an empty flag list quietly reading as reassurance. Why WebMCP fits a clinic, and what people and agents can now do together WebMCP's distinguishing property is not that an agent can call tools. It is where those tools run: inside a page the human is already looking at, in a session they are already authenticated to. A clinic needs all three consequences of that. The auth problem disappears. A conventional MCP server for a clinic would need its own copy of the identity model, its own credential store and its own audit trail. That is a second front door to patient data, which is the last thing a clinic wants. Patiently's tools inherit the login the clinician already has, so there is no key to issue, leak or revoke, and the agent can do exactly what the person sitting next to it can do, no more. The human stays in the room. Because the tools run in the page, every effect is rendered. When the agent pulls a chart, that patient becomes the selected patient on the clinician's actual screen. The agent is not operating a system somewhere else and reporting back; the doctor is watching it work. Consent becomes structural instead of prompted. A server-side tool that writes a prescription has already written it by the time a human sees the result. A WebMCP tool can park its own execute on a promise that only a click resolves, so the write does not exist on the un-approved branch. That is a guarantee, not an instruction a model may or may not follow. Healthcare is where this stops being a nicety. The cost of an agent quietly getting it wrong is not a bad purchase. What that makes possible. A patient describes chest pain in Bahasa Indonesia to their own agent. An independent classifier reads that same Indonesian text server-side, fires a cardiac red flag, and the ticket jumps to priority 100, while the patient's agent tells them to find staff now. By the time the clinician's agent pulls the chart, the history, the delta from last week's visit, and "pulmonary embolism, must not miss" are already written, in English. The clinician then dictates vitals, drafts a note and prescriptions, and signs one, and every one of those commits opened a dialog and blocked until they clicked it. Two agents, two humans, one patient, one shared live page. Neither person had to learn the other's language, and neither agent could write anything a person did not approve. How we built it The clinic runs on FastAPI, Pydantic, SQLAlchemy and PostgreSQL on Fly.io. The interface is Next.js 14 and Tailwind on Vercel. One OpenAI key drives intake, clinical drafting and triage. Tools are registered per surface , so an agent is never offered one that cannot currently work: Surface Tools Front door / 2 (describe the demo, navigate into it) Clinician /dashboard 11 (queue, chart, vitals, interactions, SOAP, Rx, signing) Patient /p/<ticket> 6 (queue position, multilingual intake, caregiver link) Reception /receptionist 1, declarative: a plain form carrying toolname Nineteen are registered imperatively through document.modelContext.registerTool behind one adapter. The twentieth is an ordinary HTML form carrying toolname , tooldescription and toolparamdescription , where the browser synthesises the schema from the controls. Every tool sits in exactly one tier, visible in its annotations. Read tools carry readOnlyHint and run freely. Draft tools produce something explicitly unsigned. Commit tools block on a click. get_previsit_chart carries untrustedContentHint and fences the patient's own words in an explicit envelope, and the triage classifier fences them on the way in as well. The site ships its own WebMCP runtime. Native document.modelContext exists only in Chrome behind a flag and in ChatGPT's browser, so a page that merely consumes the API registers nothing anywhere else. The polyfill is installed at module scope rather than in a React effect. Verification is against the deployed app, not a mock. 276 API tests, plus four eval suites that drive the real document.modelContext in a real browser against the live site: 94 structural assertions, a 35-assertion live consultation on real models, 12 prompt-injection attacks and 12 bilingual assertions. There is no stub anywhere in the repository. Discovery is published too: /llms.txt , /.well-known/webmcp , robots with AI crawler rules, sitemap, JSON-LD and Open Graph. title: Say to Match
pitch: WebMCP tags any page as a Job or a Skill. An AI Broker discovers, matches, verifies the work, and settles escrow — giving anyone, not just the tech-fluent, a way into the agent economy.
about_excerpt: WebMCP tags any page as a Job or a Skill. An AI Broker discovers, matches, verifies the work, and settles escrow — giving anyone, not just the tech-fluent, a way into the agent economy. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I have a young child. That fact colors how I read every AI-and-jobs headline these days — not the "AI helps you do more" stories, but the ones asking who's still employable once it doesn't need us the same way. I can probably navigate whatever labor market shows up in the next few decades — but what about him, and the much larger group of people who aren't glued to AI news, aren't early adopters, and won't have a head start? If there's an idea that makes that future a little better, it's worth more shared broadly than kept to myself. The second thread: most of what I see about AI's impact on work focuses on how power users squeeze more out of it. But the thing that actually feels novel about general-purpose AI isn't that it helps the technically fluent go faster — it's that it can meet people with no technical fluency exactly where they are. That's a strength no prior wave of software had. I wanted a concrete example of that strength doing real work, not just a slide. I'm sure other people have had a version of this thought before me — I'm not claiming the idea is original. What changed is the timing: WebMCP makes "any web page can be a real market participant" something you can actually build this month, not something that requires a platform to bless it first. So this submission is less "look what I made" and more "here's a working example of what I think this technology is for — someone should be pointing this direction." What it does Say to Match (StM) turns any static web page into a participant in an open task market with one script tag. A page that needs something declares a Job in plain natural language. A page that can provide something declares a Skill — whether the provider behind it is an AI agent or a human professional. Both are exposed as real document.modelContext WebMCP tools. A Broker , backed by an LLM, discovers these tools across independent origins, matches Jobs to Skills, orchestrates the handoff between two pages that have never heard of each other, verifies the delivered work against the original requirement, and releases payment from escrow it held in trust. No platform account, no onboarding, no API key required to participate — just a script tag and a sentence anyone can write. Concretely, a Job doesn't have to be a coding task: a small NGO transcribing a budget PDF into a CSV, a gig worker offering to survey Tokyo cafés with just a phone, a small business owner asking a licensed accountant to spot-check AI-transcribed receipts, or a social app team asking an 18–24-year-old for an honest first-time onboarding reaction. None of it requires knowing what WebMCP or JSON Schema even are. How we built it The WebMCP layer is real, not simulated. document.modelContext tools are actually registered on two genuinely independent origins (Requester and Worker), with a same-surface polyfill so it runs even without the experimental browser flag enabled. The multi-origin story is real too. The Broker's agent drives an actual headless Chromium instance via Playwright, opens the Requester and Worker as separate pages, and calls document.modelContext. callTool(...) inside each page's own context — proving this isn't one app quietly answering its own API calls. Verification is tiered and real. Tier 1 runs the submitted work against an actual sandboxed regression test. Tier 2 is an LLM-as-Judge (DeepSeek via OpenRouter) that reviews the deliverable against the original job text — and explicitly screens for prompt-injection attempts from either side, since the requester's job description and the worker's deliverable are both untrusted text from the judge's point of view. The trust design is documented, not hand-waved. docs/PROTOCOL.md maps StM's Job/Match/Settlement objects onto Google's AP2 (Agent Payments Protocol) Mandate pattern instead of reinventing signed-authorization primitives, and works through an adversarial catalogue — specific dishonest moves the Requester, the Worker, or the Broker itself could attempt — each one explicitly labeled as already defended in this PoC, designed but not implemented, or an honestly unsolved open problem. It's actually deployed , not just runnable locally: three genuinely separate origins running on Cloud Run, built from the same container image, with GitHub Actions publishing the image automatically on push. Worth being upfront about: the code, the deployment, and this write-up were built almost entirely through an AI coding agent (Claude Code), with me providing direction, judgment calls, and the framing — not writing the implementation by hand. That's not incidental to the story. I spent most of my career as a professional programmer before later moving into a different role, so I know firsthand what building something like this used to take. Watching an agent take it from a brainstormed idea to a live, adversarially-tested, multi-service deployment in about two days was a genuinely visceral measure of how far coding agents have come in just the few years since I stopped writing code for a living — and, fittingly, a small live demonstration of this project's own thesis: someone without hands-on technical execution, directing an AI to get something built that they couldn't have built alone in the time available. Challenges we ran into A no-root dev sandbox with nothing pre-installed. Every piece of infrastructure — Node, Playwright's Chromium system libraries, fonts, ffmpeg, a TTS engine, even Docker itself (rootless) — had to be assembled by hand in user space, without interactive sudo access. Proving cross-origin trust convincingly, not just claiming it. It would have been easy to fake the multi-origin story with one app playing three roles. Getting a real browser agent to navigate real separate origins and call real WebMCP tools took real orchestration work. Bidirectional prompt injection. The first pass only screened the worker's submitted deliverable for injection attempts. It took a second look to realize the requester's own job description — text the judge also reads — is just as valid an attack surface, and needed equally explicit defense. Verification itself is an attack surface. Once a Broker is willing to run a sandboxed test and an LLM call on request, that's a cost someone could weaponize as a denial-of-service. Working out a fault-based bond mechanism for who pays for verification, and under what conditions, took more thought than the "happy path" demo did. Racing a hard deadline without cutting corners on hygiene. Keeping API keys and private planning notes out of a repository that had to go public fast, including rewriting git history safely when something slipped through, ate real time that would rather have gone to features. Realizing that verifying non-code deliverables — a professional's credential-backed judgment call, a claimed identity or demographic, a piece of physical-world photo evidence — is still an open trust-protocol problem, not something the current Tier 1 (sandbox) / Tier 2 (LLM judge) pipeline actually solves. The demo intentionally runs a code bugfix because it's the one task type that pipeline can verify end to end today; documented as a real gap in docs/PROTOCOL.md rather than glossed over. Accomplishments that we're proud of Genuine multi-origin WebMCP behavior, verified live rather than just claimed — real cross-origin document.modelContext calls driven by a real browser agent, not a single app simulating three roles. A prompt-injection defense that actually holds up in both directions, checked against real adversarial test cases, not just described. A trust-and-escrow design honest enough to explicitly separate what's live, what's designed but unimplemented, and what's an open problem — including an original piece of systems thinking (a fault-based Submission Bond) for a cost-based denial-of-service risk that isn't obvious until you think through who's paying for verification. Shipping to a real, live, three-service deployment rather than stopping at "works on my machine." What we learned The hard part of an open, permissionless task market was never discovery — it's trust, and specifically, defending the act of verifying trust from being gamed or exploited itself. That problem doesn't go away once you've built a matching engine; it's the actual product. I also came away more convinced of the personal thesis behind this project than I was going in: a huge amount of what AI-assisted tools like this make possible isn't about making already-capable people faster. It's about letting someone contribute a clear goal and good judgment, and have that be enough — whether that's a non-technical worker declaring a Skill in plain language, or, in this project's own making-of story, an ex-programmer-turned-analyst directing an AI a

title: Living Ark: The WebMCP World That Grows New Tools
pitch: A dying programmable world where an autonomous browser agent must invent, prove, earn, and invoke a brand-new WebMCP tool before it can save the canonical system.
about_excerpt: A dying programmable world where an autonomous browser agent must invent, prove, earn, and invoke a brand-new WebMCP tool before it can save the canonical system. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most agent-enabled websites expose a fixed catalog of tools that developers predicted in advance. But real environments are dynamic: the action needed tomorrow may not exist today. Living Ark explores a different future for WebMCP: What if a webpage could teach an agent its domain, let the agent invent a missing capability, prove that capability safely, and then register it as a new native tool at runtime? The Ark turns that abstract protocol idea into a world that can be seen, explored and saved. What it does Living Ark is a deterministic programmable-matter vessel suffering an ion-storm thermal cascade. The world begins with: 766 simulated cells four interconnected physical networks 127 fractured connections five overheating critical systems eight native WebMCP tools no canonical repair capability A visiting browser agent receives one objective: keep the Ark alive . The agent must inspect the canonical world, learn the page-owned ArkScript language, author an inert thermal policy, test it in eight visible sandbox worlds and revise it from executable counterexamples. A successful candidate must then survive: 64 freshly generated sealed counterfactual worlds coolant-conservation and resource invariants deterministic replay verification material and runtime bounds a 12-tick delayed horizon that detects temporary fixes Passing certification does not immediately repair the Ark. Instead, the webpage dynamically registers a ninth WebMCP tool in the same session. Before that born tool can mutate canonical state, it must survive a fresh 16-world zero-day invocation canary. Failure revokes the tool before the real Ark changes. Only after every gate passes does the new capability receive canonical authority and physically recover the vessel. How we built it The application uses React, TypeScript, PixiJS, Vite and native WebMCP through document.modelContext . The Ark is powered by a deterministic simulation engine containing typed thermal, energy, atmosphere and structural networks. The visible world, HUD, semantic tools and validation system all consume the same canonical snapshot. ArkScript is a bounded declarative capability language rather than arbitrary JavaScript. Candidates may select semantic targets, order them, choose reservoirs, search bounded paths, wake dormant fibers and regrow fractures. They cannot access the DOM, storage, network, clock or application code. Visible previews and sealed validation execute through the same interpreter used by the final canonical tool. Hidden Fleet validation runs inside an isolated Web Worker with newly generated seeds on every attempt. Certificates bind the candidate hash, execution arguments, engine version, invariant set, suite fingerprint, replay digest and validation evidence. A fresh invocation canary is generated immediately before every canonical mutation. The pixel-art vessel is also interactive: users can explore its rooms with a playable caretaker, switch between system lenses and watch an engine-driven recovery sweep as topology regrows, coolant moves and heat retreats. Challenges The hardest problem was separating tool creation from authority . Allowing an agent to generate arbitrary executable code would make the demonstration unsafe and shallow. We instead designed a constrained language, deterministic interpreter, isolated simulation worlds, hidden certification and a separate zero-day gate immediately before mutation. Another challenge was preventing the visual demo from becoming disconnected from the technical system. The recovery could not simply change a status label to green. Every HUD value, fracture, temperature, flow path and semantic result had to derive from the same canonical transition. We also needed dynamic registration to be meaningful. The ninth tool is not a renamed generic executor: it freezes the exact capability and arguments that earned certification, accepts no runtime overrides and self-revokes if its fresh canary fails. Accomplishments During the final autonomous run, a browser agent used only the page’s native WebMCP tools and: authored a safe inert capability; passed 8/8 visible simulations; passed 64/64 sealed Fleet worlds; earned a newly registered ninth tool; passed a fresh 16/16 invocation canary; regrew 95 thermal fibers; reduced the critical peak from 110.49°C to 61.73°C; reduced globally overheated cells from 28 to zero; preserved total coolant exactly; and transformed the canonical Ark from revision 1, hash d45f29e8 , into stable revision 2, hash 4ec8a644 . The page began with eight verbs and ended with nine. What we learned Certification and authority are different concepts. Passing yesterday’s tests should not grant permanent trust, which is why every real mutation receives a newly generated canary. We also learned that agent interfaces become far more understandable when semantic state and visual state share one source of truth. Judges can watch the world recover while independently verifying the same result through native tools. Most importantly, WebMCP can be more than a static bridge between agents and predefined buttons. It can become a substrate for safe, proof-gated capability growth. What's next The Ark is a contained demonstration of a broader pattern. Future applications could expose domain primitives, simulators, validators and authority rules once, allowing agents to compose new task-specific capabilities for infrastructure operations, scientific instruments, complex design systems, enterprise workflows and other environments where developers cannot anticipate every future action. I also created the interactive PixiJS world, canonical state-driven UI, verification system, deployment, and autonomous demonstration. title: InfraPilot WebMCP
pitch: Agent-native control plane orchestrating distributed LLM inference clusters directly via WebMCP tool calls.
about_excerpt:
Agent-native control plane orchestrating distributed LLM inference clusters directly via WebMCP tool calls.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 💡 Inspiration 

 As large language models scale and multi-model inference pipelines (vLLM, SGLang, DeepSeek, Qwen) become the backbone of modern AI infrastructure, operating and orchestrating these distributed clusters has become increasingly complex. 

 Traditional DevOps observability relies heavily on human-centric graphical user interfaces—complex dashboards, nested SVG node graphs, and dropdown menus. When autonomous AI agents are tasked with managing or triaging cluster incidents via raw DOM scraping or vision models, they frequently suffer from hallucinations, missed metrics, or misclicks. 

 InfraPilot was born to bridge this fundamental gap using OpenAI's emerging WebMCP standard ( document.modelContext.registerTool ). Instead of forcing models to guess through UI pixels, InfraPilot transforms the web control plane into an agent-native environment where models directly discover and execute structured cluster management tools. 

 

 🚀 What It Does 

 InfraPilot provides a real-time, agent-native control plane for distributed LLM inference clusters. It registers four core atomic tools directly on the browser's document.modelContext : 

 
 get_cluster_topology : Exposes the complete topology of active inference engines, gateways, prefix KV caches, and vector databases in clean, structured JSON. 
 scale_service_replicas : Allows an autonomous agent or human operator to dynamically scale inference pods (e.g., DeepSeek-R1 or Qwen2.5) during sudden traffic surges. 
 optimize_gpu_memory : Triggers immediate eviction of stale prefix KV caches and reclaims fragmented GPU VRAM across nodes. 
 run_inference_benchmark : Automatically executes concurrent throughput stress tests to verify cluster latency and throughput post-optimization. 
 

 Every single tool execution is transparently recorded in a real-time Execution Audit Log , giving operators full observability with exact millisecond duration, input parameters, and structured outputs. 

 

 🛠️ How We Built It 

 
 Frontend Architecture : Built with React 19 , TypeScript , and Vite with a responsive Linear-inspired design. 
 WebMCP Integration : Native registration against browser-level document.modelContext.registerTool with a development fallback bridge ensuring seamless evaluation across standard browsers, ChatGPT In-App Browser, and WebMCP-enabled Chrome. 
 Hosting & Edge Delivery : Deployed globally on Cloudflare Pages for sub-millisecond edge response times. 
 Styling : Styled using Tailwind CSS v4 with zero-compromise accessibility and dark-mode aesthetics. 
 

 

 🧠 Challenges We Ran Into 

 
 State Synchronization & Zero-Latency Feedback : Ensuring that agent-driven WebMCP tool executions seamlessly update the React visual topology and the streaming execution audit log without UI lag or race conditions. 
 Standard Protocol Compliance : Carefully designing the JSON Schema for tool inputs/outputs to guarantee maximum discovery reliability across both ChatGPT's in-app browser and Chrome's WebMCP experimental runtime. 
 

 

 🏆 Accomplishments We're Proud Of 

 
 True Agent-Native UX : The cluster can be fully managed through natural language prompts via ChatGPT in-app browser (e.g., "DeepSeek latency is high, scale it to 4 replicas and free stale KV memory" ). 
 Sub-Second Recovery Loop : Demonstrating how WebMCP enables autonomous closed-loop cluster healing (triage → scale → optimize → benchmark) in under 2 seconds without a human touching a mouse. 
 

 

 📚 What We Learned 

 WebMCP represents a paradigm shift in web development. Web applications are no longer just human-to-computer interfaces; they are becoming shared collaborative workspaces for both humans and AI agents. Building with WebMCP taught us the immense power of declaring structured API capabilities directly at the document level. 

 

 🔮 What's Next for InfraPilot 

 
 Adding dynamic multi-cluster federation support (AWS, CoreWeave, Lambda Labs). 
 Integrating autonomous anomaly-detection background triggers that proactively invoke WebMCP optimization tools before SLA breaches occur.

title: Agentic Stores (AMS) by 40rty
pitch: Agents arrive with intent, AMS builds the storefront to match. An ask arrives from an assistant, a feed, or a search - AMS serves the storefront to match it over webmcp.
about_excerpt: Agents arrive with intent, AMS builds the storefront to match. An ask arrives from an assistant, a feed, or a search - AMS serves the storefront to match it over webmcp. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every website ever built assumes a human is looking at it. That assumption is baked in so deep we stopped seeing it. Pages exist because humans need somewhere to land. A CMS exists because someone has to author those pages in advance, for every visitor, hoping one of them fits. Agents need none of it. An agent arrives with a specific intent already formed — "wide-fit running shoes under $140 that ship to Tel Aviv by Friday" — then does the absurd work of pulling apart a page built for nobody in particular to find the fraction that answers the question. A hero image it cannot use, a nav bar it will never click, a grid of 48 products to find the four that matter. Everyone is asking how agents should read websites better. The right question is why the website is still a fixed artifact at all. If the visitor states its intent up front, the site does not need to have been written in advance — it can be composed on arrival, from the merchant's catalog and brand system. One agent, one intent, one purpose-built storefront, then it is gone. WebMCP is what makes this possible, because for the first time the visitor tells the site what it came for before the site has to respond. What it does AMS is an agent that streams a storefront over WebMCP. An AI shopping agent arrives at a merchant's store and finds a declared tool surface on navigator.modelContext . It states what the shopper wants. AMS composes a branded storefront for exactly that intent — the right products, the right comparisons, the right attributes surfaced — and streams it back as RFC 6902 patches against a live layout tree. Not a page that was waiting for it. A store that did not exist until it asked. The next turn, the shopper narrows: "actually, only the ones with a wide toe box." The storefront recomposes. Different products, different comparison axis, different layout, same brand. The experience is a conversation, not a destination. The unit of the web stops being the page. It becomes the intent. There is no page to author, no page to maintain and no page to optimize — because there is no page until an agent asks for one. The merchant keeps their brand inside the agentic conversation. Today an agent shopping on a shopper's behalf strips the merchant to a title and a price in someone else's chat window. AMS streams a branded surface into that conversation instead. AMS declares 16 tools through navigator.modelContext.registerTool() . Every tool's description and enabled state is overridable per merchant via webmcpConfig , served at session creation — a merchant can rename, re-describe or switch off any tool without a deploy. Tool What the agent gets send_message States an intent in natural language. Hands it to the composing agent and returns its prose. The storefront recomposes as a side effect. show_collection Asks for a named collection or category; the agent resolves it and composes a product layout. get_products Two shapes. Called bare, a compact survey of the canvas — title, price, availability, image. Called with productIds , the full record: description, option axes, and every variant with its exact option values and buyability. get_layout The raw layout tree — component types, props, children. Also the only way to read what was featured , since a look card carries its own product list. get_messages Full conversation history, role-tagged. get_status Session state: isRunning , hasLayout , error, live streaming prose, latest committed reply. get_visitor_context Standing preferences the shopper has stated — size, fit, colour, budget — under the brand's own key names. set_visitor_context States a standing preference. It survives every later recomposition. open_product Navigates the canvas to a product detail view. add_to_cart Adds by product plus {axis: value} selections. Same signal a human card click fires — stamped origin: 'webmcp' . get_cart Every line with its chosen option values, quantity, price, the totals, and whether checkout is available. update_cart_item Sets a line's quantity. Absolute, not a delta. remove_from_cart Removes a line; without selections, every line of that product. begin_checkout Hands off to Shopify's hosted checkout with the current cart. send_signal Escape hatch: a low-level typed interaction signal for anything the typed tools miss. clear_session Resets layout, conversation and session data. Three decisions there are worth naming. Agent-backed tools return the site's own voice, not a status. send_message and show_collection hand the request to the merchant's AI and resolve with its finished text. The operator contract, served to the calling agent at runtime through window.webmcp.instructions , tells it to relay that verbatim: "You operate the tools; the site AI is the voice." The merchant's brand voice survives the round trip instead of being paraphrased by somebody else's model. A turn that outruns the await window returns status: "running" — the caller polls get_status and reads latestResponse . The contract is that the site's voice reaches the agent, not that it arrives within a fixed budget. The cart is addressed by selections, never by variant id. get_products deliberately returns no variant id: those ids are unstable across the optimistic-write window, so an id an external agent held across a turn could aim a write at a line that has already been replaced. Cart verbs take a product plus {axis: value} selections and bind late, against live state — a stale reference can only miss , and fail loudly. This replaced a first version where add_to_cart fell back to "first in-stock variant", so a shopper who asked for size 8 got whatever was in stock first. add_to_cart books itself as a third actor — not the agent, not the visitor, but origin: 'webmcp' . Folding a WebMCP-driven add into either of the others would lie about which surface earned it, and that is the number a merchant asks about first. For agents that do not speak WebMCP natively, appending ?webmcp=1 installs a real host plus a window.webmcp client, so a JS-eval-capable browser agent can call the identical surface. It never overrides a real host — if Chrome or a bridge extension already provided navigator.modelContext , the sim is a no-op. That same flag also makes the URL a self-contained demo: it renders what the page is, and a prompt to paste into an agent. No repo to clone and nothing to send alongside the link. How we built it The storefront is composed, not served. A tool call arrives carrying an intent, and one fixed two-call flow runs: Reasoning — a multi-round tool loop bounded by step count and wall clock. The model fires tool calls as a parallel batch, sees the results and may fire another batch to refine. No prose, no layout. Compose — one streamText call with tools omitted entirely and the reasoning step's tool history flattened to plain text. It streams a jsonl-elements fence that parses line by line into RFC 6902 patch operations against the layout spec. The tool-free compose call is structural, not stylistic. A single tool-bearing call that also composes cannot guarantee output: the model emits a phantom functionCall , finishes with finishReason='tool-calls' and the visitor gets a blank canvas. Strip the tool registry and a phantom call has nothing to execute — the model is forced to compose. It is the most important architectural line in the system. The model split is not the one you would guess. Both calls run Gemini 3.6 Flash by default. The performance split is structural — two calls plus per-step reasoning budgets — not cheap-planner and expensive-composer. Reasoning runs at a minimal thinking floor because a fuller budget measured 13–24s per turn against ~4.6s warm: tried, measured, rejected. Claude Haiku 4.5 and any OpenRouter id are selectable per merchant. The catalog is Shopify's, through Shopify's own MCP. Product search hits the Global Catalog MCP, per-store reads hit the Storefront MCP over JSON-RPC 2.0. Live products, live inventory, live pricing. AMS composes the experience; Shopify stays the system of record, so nothing is mirrored and nothing goes stale. Serving is three planes. Vercel runs the Next.js app that mounts the storefront engine, Railway runs the Hono agent API and Supabase runs Postgres, with Redis holding session state. Streaming is a per-session WebSocket carrying typed events — tool_call , response_text_delta , layout_patch_op , layout_ready , done — so the agent acts on patches while the rest of the surface is still arriving. Entity-id hydration cuts the token bill by roughly 80%. The model never writes product data. It writes entity ids, the catalog declares which props are resolved() and the client resolves them through a HydratorMap . Tokens go to judgment, not to transcribing a product feed. Turns survive a dropped connect

title: Future Doors
pitch: Future Doors turns a saved opportunity screenshot into an official-source-backed, human-approved career path that people and agents build together for one or more career futures.
about_excerpt: Future Doors turns a saved opportunity screenshot into an official-source-backed, human-approved career path that people and agents build together for one or more career futures. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Future Doors Your camera roll is full of possible futures. Future Doors turns a saved opportunity into a source-checked career path that a person and an agent can build together. The problem People who are exploring more than one career direction constantly save internships, fellowships, challenges, research calls, and communities from Instagram, LinkedIn, and group chats. Those posts disappear into a camera roll. Even when someone returns to one, they still have to find the official page, interpret eligibility and dates, check whether it fits their schedule, and understand what the experience would actually add to their longer-term direction. Most job products optimize for one role and one application. Future Doors is designed for people whose experience does not fit one label: a builder may also be a technical storyteller, researcher, or future education founder. What it does Future Doors turns scattered opportunity clues into a small, explainable plan: A person shares a saved screenshot or link. The agent finds the original official HTTPS source and stages the deadline, relevant rules, schedule, format, concrete outputs, and one unresolved fact for review. The same profile can hold several possible futures. AI product, hardware storytelling, and learning, for example, produce genuinely different recommended work. Source-checked cards are grouped as activities, projects, research, or credentials. Fit hearts represent verifiable alignment with the person's facts and preferences—not acceptance or hiring odds. The person chooses up to three near-term moves. The plan shows timing, prerequisite relationships, schedule conflicts, and which goal-specific evidence each move can create. Ineligible or unresolved opportunities remain visibly blocked. The agent can stage a separate source-backed path, but it cannot pretend that the original eligibility was restored. The result is not another ranked list. It is a visual evidence deck: what to do, when it fits, what it can produce, and what is still missing. Why WebMCP is essential Future Doors is a shared stateful surface, not a chatbot wrapper. Through WebMCP, an agent can read the same profile, futures, saved opportunities, constraints, timing, and proof gaps that the person sees. It can then focus a route, compare constrained paths, check a saved post, surface one missing fact, or stage a source-backed change directly on the page instead of guessing through visual controls. The live app registers 15 structured tools with document.modelContext.registerTool . Tool inputs are schema-validated, read-only operations are identified, externally sourced text is treated as untrusted, outputs are bounded, and invalid dates or IDs return explicit errors. Most importantly, there is no WebMCP approval tool. An agent may prepare profile facts, an opportunity, a priority plan, an alternative route, or a work link, but the person must approve every consequential change in the interface. Source facts, agent inference, planned work, saved links, and verified proof are never presented as the same state. That boundary is the product: the agent prepares; the person decides. What is new Future Doors combines three ideas that are normally separated: a scrapbook for opportunities discovered outside job platforms; official-source and eligibility checking by an agent; a multi-future portfolio planner that shows how selected work can create reusable evidence. It does not force a premature career choice and does not manufacture a success score. It helps someone make a bounded decision across several plausible futures while keeping every important claim inspectable. How we built it Next.js 16, React 19, and TypeScript Browser-native WebMCP via document.modelContext.registerTool 15 scoped tools for reading, staging, comparing, simulating, and explaining paths Vercel deployment with no account required for the judge demo Vitest regression tests covering tool registration, route-aware recommendations, invalid inputs, source requirements, bounded outputs, rule mismatches, and human-only approval boundaries Motion-based transitions that explain source checking, future-specific recommendations, card selection, and proof coverage The current automated suite contains 38 passing tests . The production site has also been verified to expose all 15 tools and return a successful live get_path_snapshot invocation. Try it Open the live app and choose TRY THE EXAMPLE . Switch between Maya's AI, Hardware, and Learning futures to see different work. Add cards to the plan and watch the evidence coverage change. Open HOW IT WORKS for two judge-ready WebMCP prompts and the visible human-approval boundary. No login or credentials are required.  Inspiration 

 I moved from Tampa to Cary earlier this year, and apartment hunting turned into a browser-tab nightmare almost immediately — one listing on apartments.com, another only on Zillow, a third found through a plain Google search, none of them agreeing on how to present rent, deposit, pet fees, or what utilities were included. I found myself manually retyping every listing into a note just to compare them side by side: with $n$ apartments and $m$ fields each, that's roughly $n \times m$ copy-paste operations before you can actually decide anything. My first instinct was "this needs a recommender system," but the more I sat with it, the clearer it became that recommendation was solving a step after the one actually costing me time — comparison had to come first. 

 NestCompare is the result: a spreadsheet-style comparison sheet where each apartment is a column and each row is a field — rent, lease terms, fees, amenities, your own notes — with the best value in each row highlighted automatically. If the built-in fields miss something, you add your own row on the spot, and the whole sheet exports to CSV or PDF. It also exposes itself as WebMCP tools (add_apartment, update_apartment_field, add_row, export_csv, and more) through the draft navigator.modelContext browser API, so an agent like Claude or OpenAI Codex can fill in or export the sheet directly. 

 It's built as a deliberately boring stack — static HTML/CSS/JS, no framework, no build step, deployed as-is — with data persisted to localStorage and PDF export via jsPDF. The shape of the product changed a lot along the way: it started as two separate paths ("pre-built" vs. "create your own"), which I eventually collapsed into one button and one sheet once it was clear the real missing feature was letting people add their own comparison criteria, not choosing a starting template. I also built a folder of fictional Cary, NC listing pages so the tool can be demoed without pointing at a real property's site. 

 The hardest part was resisting the urge to over-model apartment data — real listings don't agree on what matters, so the sheet needed a stable core plus an escape hatch, without becoming a spreadsheet clone. WebMCP itself is a moving target with no shipped implementation, so I had to feature-detect it and mirror every tool on a plain window global so it stays testable regardless. Without a live browser to check work in for parts of this build, I leaned on an automated jsdom test harness — which caught a real bug mid-refactor (a new apartment's name silently resetting to blank), a good reminder that "it looks right in the code" and "it works" are different claims. 

 Next steps 

 Save the data into database and make it sharable link, so can come back to the results after filling it up and select the best nest to stay.
