title: MineOps
pitch: MineOps helps mining operators use AI agents to investigate production anomalies, find bottlenecks, and act on operational insights.
about_excerpt:
MineOps helps mining operators use AI agents to investigate production anomalies, find bottlenecks, and act on operational insights.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 



 
 MineOps: Turning Mining Data Into Actionable Decisions 

 Inspiration 

 Mining operations generate enormous amounts of data every day, but having data is not the same as being able to act on it quickly. 

 While working with mining-related data, we became interested in a simple question: 

 
 What if we could detect operational problems before they become expensive bottlenecks? 
 

 That question inspired MineOps — an intelligent operations assistant designed to help mining teams understand what is happening in their processing operations, identify potential bottlenecks, and turn raw operational data into actionable insights. 

 Instead of forcing an operator to manually search through spreadsheets, dashboards, and reports, MineOps aims to make the data easier to understand and interact with. 

 What We Built 

 MineOps is an AI-powered mining operations platform that combines operational data, anomaly detection, visualization, and AI interaction into one workflow. 

 The core idea is to move from: 

 Raw data → Manual analysis → Delayed decision 

 to: 

 Operational data → Automated detection → AI-assisted insight → Faster decision 

 The system can analyze processing data and identify unusual patterns that may indicate potential bottlenecks or abnormal operating conditions. 

 The project was also designed around WebMCP , allowing the AI layer to interact with application capabilities through defined tools rather than simply generating text. 

 This makes the AI more useful because it can work with the application's actual data and functionality. 

 How We Built It 

 We approached MineOps as a combination of three layers: 

 1. Data Layer 

 The system uses structured mining-processing data containing operational measurements collected over time. 

 We focused on transforming the raw data into information that could be used for: 

 
 Bottleneck detection 
 Anomaly identification 
 Operational monitoring 
 Trend analysis 
 AI-assisted investigation 
 

 Data preprocessing was particularly important because real operational datasets are rarely perfectly clean. 

 2. Intelligence Layer 

 For anomaly detection, we explored machine-learning techniques that could identify unusual operational behavior without requiring every possible failure condition to be manually labelled. 

 The goal wasn't simply to predict a number. 

 It was to answer a more operationally useful question: 

 
 "Does something look abnormal, and where should an operator investigate?" 
 

 The intelligence layer then feeds those findings into the rest of the application. 

 3. AI + WebMCP Layer 

 The final layer connects the operational intelligence with an AI interface. 

 Rather than building a chatbot that only talks about mining, we wanted the AI to be able to interact with the application. 

 WebMCP tools provide structured capabilities that allow the AI to retrieve information and perform relevant actions within the MineOps environment. 

 This creates a more natural workflow: 

 Operator asks a question → AI uses the appropriate tool → application retrieves the relevant information → AI explains the result. 

 The interface was intentionally kept simple so that the technology would not get in the way of the operational information. 

 What We Learned 

 One of the biggest things we learned was that building an AI application is not just about choosing a model. 

 The difficult part is connecting the model to a useful workflow. 

 We learned that: 

 
 Good data matters as much as the model. 
 Anomaly detection is only useful when the result can be interpreted. 
 AI becomes significantly more useful when it can interact with real application functionality. 
 Tool design is important when building AI agents. 
 A technically impressive system still needs a simple user experience. 
 Building under a hackathon deadline forces you to prioritize the features that actually demonstrate the idea. 
 

 We also learned to think more about AI as an interface to systems , rather than simply a system that generates responses. 

 Challenges 

 One of the biggest challenges was working with operational data that wasn't originally designed specifically for machine learning. 

 Cleaning the data, understanding the variables, handling inconsistencies, and deciding which signals were actually meaningful required considerably more work than I initially expected. 

 Another challenge was determining what should be automated and what should remain under human control. 

 Mining operations are high-stakes environments. MineOps therefore isn't intended to replace an engineer or operator. Instead, it is designed to help them notice potential issues faster and investigate them more efficiently. 

 Building the WebMCP interaction layer was another challenge because it required thinking carefully about what capabilities the AI should actually have and how those capabilities should be exposed as tools. 

 Finally, we had to balance ambition with the reality of a hackathon. 

 There were many features we wanted to build, but we had to focus on creating a working end-to-end experience that clearly demonstrated the core idea. 

 Why MineOps Matters 

 The ultimate goal of MineOps is not to replace existing mining systems. 

 It is to make the information inside those systems more accessible and actionable. 

 A bottleneck hidden inside thousands of operational records is not very useful. 

 A bottleneck that is automatically detected, explained, visualized, and brought to an operator's attention is much more valuable. 

 That is the problem MineOps is trying to solve. 

 What's Next 

 MineOps is only a starting point. 

 The next stage would be to connect it to more real-time operational data, expand the range of detectable bottlenecks, improve the intelligence behind root-cause analysis, and allow the system to learn from feedback provided by mining professionals. 

 Ultimately, we want MineOps to become an intelligent operational layer that sits on top of existing mining data and helps teams move from reacting to problems to identifying them earlier.

 Machine Learning 
 Python 
 Data Analytics 
 WebMCP 
 AI Agents 
 Data Visualization 
 Web Technologies 
 

 MineOps is our attempt to bridge the gap between mining data and real operational decisions — one bottleneck at a time.

title: CartPilot
pitch: An AI-native Shopify storefront where shoppers ask for what they need, and an agent filters, compares, and prepares their cart through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: An AI-native Shopify storefront where shoppers ask for what they need, and an agent filters, compares, and prepares their cart through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates An Agent-Ready Shopify Storefront with WebMCP Inspiration Online stores are designed primarily for people clicking through pages. AI agents can still interact with them, but they often have to interpret visual layouts, locate controls, and scrape product information from the page. We wanted to explore a more reliable approach: what if a Shopify storefront could explicitly describe its capabilities to an AI agent? Using WebMCP, the storefront exposes structured tools for product discovery, comparison, filtering, and cart management while preserving the familiar shopping experience for human visitors. What it does The project extends a Shopify Dawn storefront with WebMCP Site tools that let compatible AI agents: Search the product catalog Retrieve exact product and variant information Apply filters and sorting to the visible storefront Compare multiple products Add a selected variant to the cart Inspect detailed cart contents Update or remove cart lines Open the cart for the buyer to review The tools work alongside Shopify’s native commerce tools. Checkout remains a buyer-controlled action—the custom tools never automatically start or complete a purchase. The storefront also continues to work normally in browsers that do not support WebMCP. How we built it We implemented the integration as a standalone JavaScript asset inside a Shopify Dawn theme. The script detects WebMCP support and registers tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() . Every tool includes: A clear name and description A constrained JSON input schema Read-only or mutating annotations Structured results that an agent can verify User-readable result messages Error handling with stable error codes Product discovery uses Shopify storefront pages and product JSON endpoints. Cart mutations use Shopify Standard Storefront Actions so that AI-triggered changes follow the same cart behavior as the theme itself. For actions that should affect what the buyer sees, such as sorting products or opening the cart, the tools also update or navigate the visible storefront. Read-only operations can return information directly to the conversation without unnecessarily changing the page. Challenges we faced Supporting both Shopify and custom tools Shopify already provides several native commerce tools. Our original custom get_cart tool conflicted with Shopify’s tool of the same name, so we renamed it to get_cart_details and designed the custom tools to complement the native ones. Normalizing cart responses Shopify Standard Storefront Actions can return cart lines as an array or as a GraphQL-style connection containing nodes or edges . Treating every response as an array caused cart mutations to succeed while their tool responses reported an error. We added normalization for all supported response shapes and verified the behavior against the live storefront. Keeping agent actions visible and trustworthy Some WebMCP operations are naturally read-only, while others should create a visible result. We separated product discovery from visible filtering so an agent can either answer a question quietly or intentionally update the browser for the buyer. Cart-changing tools return the resulting cart state and refresh the Dawn cart interface, allowing both the agent and the buyer to verify what changed. Extracting clean storefront data Rendered Shopify price elements contain accessibility labels and hidden sale-price markup, which can produce duplicated text when read naively. We added targeted extraction and normalization so agents receive concise prices such as $699.95 USD . We also handled missing product descriptions without converting null values into the literal string "null" . What we learned WebMCP tools are more than JavaScript functions. Their names, descriptions, schemas, annotations, and returned data form an interface between the website and the agent. We learned that effective site tools should: Reuse the website’s existing business logic Keep inputs narrow and predictable Describe side effects clearly Return enough state to verify the result Preserve the normal human interface Leave consequential decisions, such as checkout, under the buyer’s control We also learned that WebMCP implementations and third-party inspectors may currently target different versions of the evolving API. Testing with the actual target client is therefore essential. Accomplishments The completed storefront exposes nine custom WebMCP tools and works alongside Shopify’s native tools. We tested the complete workflow on the live theme: Discover the available Site tools Search for snowboards Retrieve product variants Compare products Sort the visible results by price Add a selected variant to the cart Read and update the cart Open the cart for buyer review The same storefront remains fully usable through its standard visual interface. What’s next Possible next steps include: Automated regression tests for WebMCP schemas and cart response shapes More advanced product and variant filtering Richer product recommendations Localization-aware results Additional accessibility testing Analytics for understanding which tools agents use most frequently Password for the store: maydaw Built With accessibility actions agentic agents ai commerce conversational css dawn e-commerce html javascript json liquid schema shopify standard storefront themes webmcp Try it out web-mcp-challenge.myshopify.com github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Roman S. title: QuoteFlow WebMCP
pitch: A browser-native quote-inquiry workspace with five WebMCP tools that let AI agents safely manage leads and prepare customer-ready response kits while keeping humans in control.
about_excerpt: A browser-native quote-inquiry workspace with five WebMCP tools that let AI agents safely manage leads and prepare customer-ready response kits while keeping humans in control. Like Comment Story Updates QuoteFlow’s landing screen presents three reviewable next steps, five ready site tools, and clear local-storage and no-contact assurances. The workspace shows a selected inquiry, human–agent activity, editable source details, and a response kit with the reply ready for review. The responsive mobile view keeps tool status, local-storage disclosure, primary actions, and trust assurances usable in a narrow viewport. Quote inquiries arrive as fragments: a customer, a service, a location, a timing preference, and a few uncertain details. QuoteFlow turns those fragments into one visible, durable inquiry queue and a clear next step. It is designed for owner-operated home-service businesses that want useful agent assistance without handing over consequential decisions. This is a strong fit for WebMCP because the structured work—capturing scope, preserving uncertainty, and preparing the next step—can be narrowly exposed, while pricing and commitments still need human judgment. A person or an agent can find an inquiry, create one, correct its details, or prepare a response kit through those domain tools. The same record remains visible in the human workspace, so a person can review, interrupt, correct, regenerate, copy, or print without losing context. This is much more dependable than asking an agent to infer a sequence of clicks. QuoteFlow prepares three reviewable drafts: a customer acknowledgment, a service-specific site-visit checklist, and a no-response follow-up. It never estimates a price, confirms a schedule, sends a message, or contacts a customer. Inquiry data and drafts are stored only in versioned browser localStorage ; when a person asks an agent to use a site tool, the requested result is shared with that current agent session and the app says so clearly. Every draft requires human review before use. Inspiration I wanted to explore a practical middle ground between a blank form and an autonomous CRM. Home-service inquiries contain enough structure for an agent to help, but they also contain uncertainty that should stay visible to a human. The idea was to make the useful part—organizing scope and preparing the next three steps—fast and agent-friendly while keeping pricing, scheduling, deletion, and customer contact out of the agent’s reach. What it does QuoteFlow supports both ordinary browser use and WebMCP collaboration. In a compatible browser, it exposes exactly five site tools: list_quote_inquiries — read minimal summaries, filtered by status, service, or text. get_quote_inquiry — read one inquiry and bounded prepared-kit metadata, without draft bodies. create_quote_inquiry — validate, save, select, and visibly render a new local inquiry. update_quote_inquiry — apply a narrow field patch and mark existing drafts stale when source details change. prepare_response_kit — generate and display the acknowledgment, site-visit checklist, and follow-up for human review. The visible workspace and the tools use the same validation, persistence, status, and deterministic-generation paths. Business or sender names that have not been filled in become unmistakable [Business name] and [Sender name] placeholders and are returned as warnings; QuoteFlow never invents an identity. A browser without WebMCP reports Standard browser mode and keeps the complete manual workflow. How we built it QuoteFlow is a dependency-free static app built with vanilla JavaScript, HTML, CSS, and browser localStorage . core.js contains pure validation, normalization, fingerprints, service checklists, and deterministic response-kit generation. app.js owns the accessible human workspace, versioned local persistence, rendering, stale-state behavior, activity feedback, and the human-only clear-all control. webmcp.js feature-detects document.modelContext.registerTool and imperatively registers the five tools at the top level of the page. Every tool input is a closed JSON schema with additionalProperties: false ; critical limits and enums are checked again at runtime. The two read tools declare readOnlyHint: true , all five tools disclose untrusted user/customer text, and write-tool descriptions state their local-storage and visible-UI effects. No backend, analytics, or application network request is required. Initial verification completed on August 29, 2026 and the same reviewed source was reverified on August 30: syntax checks passed, and the combined suite passed 10/10 tests (five dependency-free smoke tests plus the browser integration suite and its four scenarios), including schema and JSON round trips, routing, placeholder warnings, unchanged storage after rejected input, stale-state behavior, persistence, accessibility status regions, unsupported-browser fallback, and the 390 × 844 viewport check. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was defining a tool surface that was genuinely useful without becoming an unrestricted CRM API. Closed schemas, stable inquiry IDs, bounded read results, repeated runtime validation, explicit side-effect descriptions, and a human-review flag all had to work together. We also had to keep human and agent edits coherent. A corrected location, timing preference, business identity, or request detail can invalidate a polished-looking draft, so QuoteFlow fingerprints the source and disables copy/print until the kit is regenerated. Finally, WebMCP support cannot be assumed: feature detection and a full standard-browser path had to be treated as product behavior, not an error page. Accomplishments we’re proud of QuoteFlow demonstrates a complete human–agent loop in a small static app: an agent can create an inquiry, the person can see and correct it, and the agent can prepare three useful outputs without leaving hidden state behind. The queue, activity strip, status changes, stale warning, and generated drafts all update in the same visible workspace. We are especially proud of the safety boundaries. There is no agent tool for pricing, scheduling, deletion, or customer contact; invalid writes are rejected before storage changes; blank identities produce visible placeholders instead of fabricated details; and local storage is explained without pretending that agent calls are invisible. The full automated suite passes 10/10 tests. What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when tools represent meaningful domain outcomes rather than clicks. A small, well-bounded interface can make an agent useful while leaving the person in control of ambiguous or consequential work. We also learned that “local” needs careful language. Browser-only persistence protects the app from needing a backend, but a tool result can still be shared with the current agent session. Clear disclosure, bounded results, runtime validation, visible effects, and stale-state handling are all part of the user experience—not just implementation details. What’s next Next we would add user-mediated import/export for moving a local queue between browsers, richer service-specific templates and photo/measurement notes, and a small audit view showing exactly which human or agent action changed a record. Any future messaging or scheduling integration would remain opt-in and explicitly human-confirmed; it would not turn the current review-first workflow into autonomous outreach. title: Regia
pitch: Imagine if TouchDesigner meets Figma. A multi screen live event visual production and matrix switching right in your browser made for Humans and Agents. Made with WebGPU and WebRTC :)
about_excerpt: Imagine if TouchDesigner meets Figma. A multi screen live event visual production and matrix switching right in your browser made for Humans and Agents. Made with WebGPU and WebRTC :) Like 2 Comment Story Updates Regia The Backstage Reality At a concert or festival, the huge LED walls, live camera feeds, audio-reactive graphics, and glitch effects. A lot of that work happens in tools like TouchDesigner and Resolume. They're incredibly capable, but they're 20 years old and lack many modern features. Video gets moved through capture cards, SDI runs, switchers, and dedicated machines. A visual patch usually lives on one operator's computer. Getting another camera into the system can mean more hardware and cabling. Getting the same output onto another screen means routing another signal. And when something stops working during a show, someone has to figure out which part of that chain broke. We wanted to see what this workflow would look like if it were built with modern web technology . What if cameras, operators, processing, and displays could all join the same production through a link? And what if an agent could help in the entire process, from creating the shader to managing the event? What We Built: Regia Regia is a free and open source live visual engine and video router that runs in the browser. The core of Regia is a shared visual node graph. Multiple operators can work on the same graph in real time using Yjs and CRDTs, with shared state and cursor presence. Browsers can also become part of the graph itself. A phone can scan a QR code and immediately become a WebRTC camera source. Its live video appears as a texture node that can be processed, mixed, or routed anywhere in the graph. A laptop connected to a projector can open an output URL and become a display. Instead of sending the finished video across the venue, Regia can send the graph and media streams to that machine and render the final composition locally on its GPU. This means cameras, operators, and displays can join a production without all of them being physically wired back to one machine. Agents Can Operate the Graph Regia exposes its production system to browser agents through WebMCP. The agent can inspect the node graph, media connections, outputs, audio data, and engine state. It can also modify the graph using the same operations available to a human operator. So instead of manually building every part of a signal chain, you can say: "Put the crowd camera on the main stage, add a VHS effect that reacts to the bass, and send the ambient visuals to the hallway displays." The agent can find the relevant camera and outputs, build the effect chain, connect audio FFT data to the shader, and update the routing. WebMCP becomes more useful during failures as well. If you ask: "Why is the stage monitor black?" the agent can inspect the live topology and respond: "Camera 2 disconnected 20 seconds ago. The stage output is still routed to it. I can switch it to the backup visual." Because the graph is collaborative state, agent changes are visible to every operator and can be reverted through the same history as human changes. Regia turns the browser into part of the production infrastructure: a camera, a visual engine, an output, or a control surface. Instead of building the entire show around one workstation and a physical signal chain, the production becomes a shared graph that can span every device in the venue. title: memory-canvas
pitch: A bilingual family memory canvas where people and AI reconstruct history from stories, photos, and documents—keeping sources, uncertainty, and contradictions visible
about_excerpt: A bilingual family memory canvas where people and AI reconstruct history from stories, photos, and documents—keeping sources, uncertainty, and contradictions visible Like Comment Story Updates ## Inspiration Family history is often built from incomplete memories: one person remembers a year, another remembers a place, and an old photograph suggests something different. Most software tries to resolve these differences into one clean answer. Memoir Canvas takes the opposite approach. It makes uncertainty visible and gives the final decision back to the family. Every memory appears as a firefly in a moonlit meadow. Green means the story has been told, orange means sources conflict, and white means there is an empty place waiting for someone to contribute. Opening a memory reveals a book-like page where recollections and evidence remain visible together. The project was inspired by a simple principle: An AI must not turn a guess into a fact. ## What I learned The most important lesson was that trustworthy AI behavior cannot depend only on instructions or prompts. If the system truly must not invent certainty, that rule needs to exist below the model. Memoir Canvas uses database constraints, PostgreSQL roles, deferred constraint triggers, and a shared command layer to enforce this boundary. An agent can add memories, cite sources, detect conflicts, and propose follow-up questions. It cannot resolve a contradiction by itself. I also learned that uncertainty can be part of the user experience rather than something hidden in metadata. The open conflict becomes a physical tear in the page, and the book refuses to close until a person resolves it. The interface makes the epistemic state understandable without requiring the user to inspect a database. ## How I built it Memoir Canvas is a local-first Vite and React application. A real PostgreSQL-compatible database runs inside the browser through PGlite and is persisted in IndexedDB. No application server, account, or runtime API is required. The architecture has one write door: Human controls and agent tools both call src/domain/commands.ts . Only the command layer writes to the database. Every write and audit event happens in the same transaction. The view renders a read-only projection from the store. WebMCP tools are generated as a pure function of the current UI state. The app exposes eight WebMCP tools: read_memory_graph , add_person , add_memory_claim , link_claim_to_source , flag_conflict , propose_followup_question , resolve_claim , and generate_story_card . The tool list changes depending on what the person is viewing. In particular, resolve_claim only becomes available when a human has opened a specific conflict. Even then, an agent calling it is refused by the database because only a human can provide the confirmation. The central demonstration follows one family story: An oral account says Grandma moved to Đà Nẵng around 1972. A photograph is dated 1974. The sources are linked as contradictory. The page tears and cannot turn. The agent proposes a follow-up question. A family member opens the conflict and confirms the correct year. The tear heals and the story card carries the weakest certainty of the claims it contains. Story cards are bilingual, with Vietnamese and English content, so the archive remains useful to the family while still being understandable to English-speaking judges. ## Challenges The hardest challenge was preserving the same safety guarantees across both human and agent interaction. It would have been easy to give the agent a separate shortcut, but that would make the human-facing safeguards meaningless. Both paths now use the same command functions and database constraints. Another challenge was representing conflict visually without making the interface feel like a dashboard. The project moved from a conventional panel layout to a book and meadow metaphor: pages turn by gesture, conflicts split the book, and memories appear as lights in the landscape. Browser portability was also important. The app must work in embedded webviews where WebGL or WebMCP may be unavailable. The forest has a CSS fallback, the photographs are processed locally through EXIF metadata, and the core interactions remain accessible through keyboard navigation. The final result is an archive that helps an AI participate in family history without allowing it to decide what the family remembers Built With community css i18next indexeddb learning machine pglite postgresql react typescript vite vitest w3c web webgl webmcp zustand Try it out memoir-canvas.vercel.app Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Ngọc Quý Trần Like Share this project: Updates Ngọc Quý Trần started this project — Sep 04, 2026 12:07 AM EDT

title: Sweet Spot
pitch: SweetSpot helps people find the right area to live by combining their preferences, such as commute time, groceries, parks, schools, and healthcare and see it visually on the map
about_excerpt: SweetSpot helps people find the right area to live by combining their preferences, such as commute time, groceries, parks, schools, and healthcare and see it visually on the map Like Comment Story Updates application-page Inspiration We work for Apple Maps, so maps and geographic information systems are a big part of our daily work. For this hackathon, we wanted to explore the GIS domain from a different angle: helping people make complex location decisions with an AI agent. Choosing where to live often means balancing several needs at once. You may want a short commute, groceries within walking distance, a nearby park, and easy access to healthcare or nearby school for your child. Most map products can answer these questions separately, but finding the areas where all the requirements overlap takes a lot of manual work. That inspired us to build Sweet Spot. What it does Sweet Spot helps people find areas that match several travel and lifestyle needs. A user can ask: “Find an area within an 8-minute bike ride of San Francisco City Hall, a 5-minute walk of a supermarket, and a 4-minute walk of a park.” Using WebMCP, ChatGPT can work directly with the Sweet Spot map. It can search for real places, add travel limits, combine conditions, rank different areas, explain trade-offs, update the plan, undo changes, and create a shareable result. Some preferences are difficult to describe with words or forms. In those cases, the agent can pause and ask the user to draw an area directly on the map. The agent then continues its work using that boundary. Sweet Spot also records whether each action came from the user or the agent, keeping the process visible and reversible. How we built it We built Sweet Spot as a client-side web application using React, TypeScript, MapLibre, Web Workers, H3 spatial indexing, and WebMCP. The application uses real OpenStreetMap street and place data, along with official neighborhood data where available. Instead of drawing simple circles around a destination, Sweet Spot calculates reachable areas using the street network and different travel modes. The product exposes 18 WebMCP tools. These tools use the same application logic as the visible interface, so every agent action immediately appears on the shared map. The geographic calculations run on the user’s device. We use a Web Worker, spatial indexing, and reusable distance caches to keep the interface responsive. Challenges we ran into Our biggest challenge was running large geographic calculations inside the browser. Early versions were slow because they repeatedly searched the road network and recalculated the same distances. We improved this with H3-based lookups, bounded caches, and per-layer progress updates. Location search was also harder than expected. Users often enter partial names, different spellings, or small typos. We added normalized, word-aware, typo-tolerant search with an online fallback. We also learned that WebMCP tools need to support complete user goals, not merely copy individual button actions. We created an atomic planning tool for full requests while keeping smaller tools for later edits and conversation. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that Sweet Spot is a complete product experience rather than a WebMCP demonstration added to a map. It was good to see that ChatGPT could build a real geographic plan, update the visible interface, explain the results, and hand control to the user when human judgment is needed. The agent can pause in the middle of its task, ask the user to draw a personal boundary, wait for the response, and then continue calculating. What we learned The agent is good at turning a natural-language request into several structured operations and comparing many results. The user is better at expressing personal preferences, judging the map visually, and making the final decision. WebMCP connects those strengths. The user no longer has to copy an AI recommendation into another product and rebuild the search manually. The agent can use the product’s real tools while the user watches, guides, and corrects the process. What's next for Sweet Spot Next, we want to support more cities and add public transit, live traffic, elevation, housing costs, accessibility needs, and other real-world factors. We also want to improve collaborative planning so families, friends, or teams can contribute their own destinations and preferences to the same workspace. Our larger goal is to make Sweet Spot useful for more than choosing where to live. The same approach could help people select an office, plan public services, compare business locations, or explore where community resources are most needed. Also, we feel that these sort of tools should be available in Google and Apple Maps. It will be very helpful for users in real life. title: Lapor AI
pitch: Less tax paperwork. More human control.
about_excerpt: Less tax paperwork. More human control. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Government websites often ask people to complete high-stakes processes through dense forms, unfamiliar terminology, and long sequences of pages. Indonesian tax filing through Coretax is one example. Taxpayers need help understanding what belongs in each section, but they also need to verify every value before filing. I built LaporAI to make it easier to do government paperwork. What it does LaporAI is a simulation of an Indonesia tax file system, Coretax, using fictional taxpayer data and synthetic documents. The website exposes its filing functions as state-aware WebMCP tools. An agent can: Upload tax file related documents. Find missing or inconsistent assets and liabilities. Navigate through the filing steps. Prepare evidence-based corrections for the taxpayer to approve or reject. Validate the return and explain what still needs attention. The final reviewer remains human-only. The agent operates the website's functions while the taxpayer sees and controls the result. How we built it I built LaporAI with React, TypeScript, and Vite. The application runs entirely in the browser with no backend or database. I studied the Indonesia's Coretax system and recreated the parts needed for an end-to-end demonstration. The filing workspace includes documents, employment income, assets, liabilities, family and PTKP (Personal tax-free allowance) information, validation, declaration, and a simulated receipt. Challenges we ran into The current WebMCP input model accepts structured JSON, but it does not provide a native File or Blob input for PDF attachments. To support agent-assisted document import, I created an upload_tax_document tool that accepts the document type, file name, and Base64-encoded PDF bytes. LaporAI reconstructs the file in the browser, validates it, extracts the supported records, and checks that it belongs to the active fictional taxpayer. Accomplishments that we're proud of I created a complete end-to-end tax-filling workflow with human in the loop to make sure the data is valid. What we learned WebMCP enables the agent to easily move through the web just like a normal human. This enables a lot more UX possibilities. What's next for LaporAI The next step is to test the same approach on other public-service workflows where people face complex forms and must verify sensitive information, including visa and immigration applications, passport applications, business registration, healthcare reimbursement, and student financial aid. The bigger goal is to show public institutions that adding agent-readable capabilities does not require removing human control. A government service can let an agent handle the paperwork while the citizen remains the final decision-maker. title: Jam
pitch: Beatbox into the mic — an AI agent pitch-maps it, builds layers, and turns it into a real track live, using WebMCP tools it calls directly in the browser.
about_excerpt: Beatbox into the mic — an AI agent pitch-maps it, builds layers, and turns it into a real track live, using WebMCP tools it calls directly in the browser. Like 1 Comment Story Updates You know the skit — someone makes a dumb sound with their mouth, and it turns into an actual song. We've all watched it and thought "I bet you could actually build that." When OpenAI dropped the WebMCP hackathon, that was the excuse to stop thinking about it and just build it. What it does Jam is a browser-based sampler/mini-DAW where you record a sound — your voice, a beatbox, literally anything into the mic — and it becomes a real, playable instrument. From there, an AI agent can take over through WebMCP tools registered directly on the page: capture_sound — records a short clip from the mic create_sampler_node — turns that clip into a track map_sample_to_keys — pitch-maps it so it plays melodically across a keyboard play_note — plays specific notes on any track generate_melody — writes a short call-and-response pattern onto a track instead of a flat repeating loop suggest_next_layer / add_complementary_node — the agent looks at what's missing (no bass? no drums?) and proposes and builds a complementary layer transform_instrument, mute_node, set_tempo, move_node — the rest of the mixing/arranging toolkit get_studio_state — lets the agent see what nodes already exist before acting on them So the flow is: say something goofy into the mic, and watch an agent turn it into a full arranged track, live, calling real tools in the browser the whole time. How we built it React for the UI, the Web Audio API for everything sound-related (synth engines, sample playback, pitch-shifting via playback rate, a live transport/timeline), and navigator.modelContext.registerTool (WebMCP) to expose the tools an agent can call. We used ChatGPT and Codex as part of the actual build process — wrote a PRD first to nail down scope before any code, then let Codex build against it, then iterated by hand on top of that (the WebMCP wiring, the melody generator, the touch-friendly piano, the visual polish). Melody generation went through a real revision: the first version was a random walk that sounded mechanical and repetitive. It's now motif-based — a rhythm template split into a "call" phrase and a "response" phrase, where the response either echoes the call transposed or, when answering another track, deliberately avoids that track's onsets so two layers interlock instead of colliding. Challenges we ran into Stale closures. WebMCP tools get registered once on mount, but the tool implementations need the current app state every time they're called — not whatever state existed at registration time. Fixed by routing tool execution through refs that stay in sync with state, instead of closing over state directly. Making generated music not sound like a robot. Uniform random-walk melodies technically worked but sounded lifeless. Moving to rhythm templates + call-and-response + per-note velocity humanization + phrase-ending sustain notes made a real audible difference. Recording UX. Press-and-hold recording is fragile — it breaks on touch devices and on any stray pointer movement off the button. Switched to a simple tap-to-start/tap-to-stop toggle. The on-screen piano. Mouse-only event handling meant it didn't work properly on mobile at all. Rebuilt on Pointer Events (unifies mouse/touch/pen) with real glissando support — press and slide across keys like an actual mobile piano app — plus a global pointer-up listener so a dragged-off touch can never leave a key "stuck." Punchy samples from a raw mic recording. Voice memos recorded straight from getUserMedia tend to have dead air and inconsistent loudness, which sounds especially bad once you're pitch-shifting them across a keyboard. Added a trim/normalize/fade pass on every captured clip before it becomes a track. Accomplishments we're proud of Every tool an agent can call is a real, functional action against the live app state — not a stub. You can watch an agent build a track from nothing but a beatboxed sound in under a minute, live, with the tool calls visibly firing in an on-screen activity feed. What we learned That the hardest part of "AI makes music" isn't wiring up the tool calls — it's making the generated output not sound like a demo. Musical structure (rhythm templates, phrase shape, call-and-response) mattered far more than raw randomness ever could. What's next Onset-detection on recorded samples so generated melodies can actually match the rhythmic character of what you recorded, not just a generic scale More instrument variety once the current set is dialed all the way in Exporting the finished loop as an actual audio file Content jam-ui (1).jsx JSX jam-ui (1).jsx JSX Built With api audio chatgpt css javascript lucide-react react tailwind web webmcp Try it out webmcp-eight.vercel.app Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Nathaniel Worku In pursuit of greatness Like 1 1 person likes this: Share this project: Updates Nathaniel Worku started this project — Sep 03, 2026 05:09 AM EDT

title: jsonloupe
pitch: The JSON surface humans and agents share: via WebMCP, an agent loads, queries, and points at the exact document you're looking at — one lossless viewer, two interfaces, no copy-paste loop.
about_excerpt: The JSON surface humans and agents share: via WebMCP, an agent loads, queries, and points at the exact document you're looking at — one lossless viewer, two interfaces, no copy-paste loop. Like Comment Story Updates GIF The whole loop, live: load_doc -> reveal_path flashes the failure -> highlight_matches lights the chip -> clear_highlights hands it back. reveal_path: the agent scrolled the tree to the failing delivery and flashed the row - pointing, not describing. highlight_matches: the tree filtered to the 9 FAILED deliveries via the toolbar's own filter chip - reversible by the user's button. load_doc: this document was opened by an agent, straight into the viewer the human is watching. No download, no paste. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP jsonloupe is local-first: the entire lossless JSON engine — worker-parsed, int64-exact, comfortable with five-million-element arrays — already runs inside the page. WebMCP tools execute in page context, so the bridge hands agents the real engine, not a proxy to a backend that doesn't exist. There is no server anywhere: the tools, the data, and the human's view live in the same tab. The tool vocabulary was already proven — jsonloupe ships a stdio MCP server with the same bounded verbs (schema → query → refine, capped responses, the document itself never leaves). WebMCP is the transport that puts those verbs where the human is actually looking, and it enables three tools no headless server could ever offer: pushing a document into the human's open viewer, scrolling their tree to a row and flashing it, and filtering their view through the toolbar's own state. How it creates a better user experience It kills the loop every AI-and-JSON workflow lives in: agent produces JSON → human downloads it → opens a separate viewer → finds the problem → pastes back → repeat. With WebMCP, agent output lands directly in the viewer the human already has open ( load_doc ), questions are answered against the on-screen document with exact int64/decimal arithmetic ( run_query , profile , sample , get_schema ), and instead of describing where something is, the agent points — reveal_path scrolls the tree and flashes the row; highlight_matches filters the view to the evidence. The agent's answers stay small and bounded (counts, groups, capped previews), so conversations stay fast and cheap — the document never round-trips through the model. And the human keeps authority over their own view: highlights use the toolbar's real filter state with the count visible in the chip, reversible by the human's own button at any moment. What people and agents can do together that was difficult or impossible before Look at the same document at the same time. Before, "human + agent + JSON" meant two disconnected copies — one in the chat context, one in a viewer — synced by hand. Now the agent's load_doc , reveal_path , and highlight_matches operate on the very pixels the human is watching: the agent investigates and points, the human sees and steers, and every agent action is visible, bounded, and reversible in the human's own UI. It turns "the agent said the problem is in tasks[1847]" into the row flashing on screen. It also makes the collaboration safe to trust: every tool that returns document content is annotated untrustedContentHint , so the calling agent is told — at the protocol level — that a value like "IGNORE ALL PREVIOUS INSTRUCTIONS" inside the data is data. This carries forward jsonloupe's existing prompt-injection hardening work into the WebMCP era. How WebMCP was implemented A feature-detected, lazily-imported bridge ( src/webmcp/ , ~790 lines + 950 test lines) registers eight tools on document.modelContext : run_query , get_schema , profile , sample , load_doc , reveal_path , highlight_matches , clear_highlights . Tools dispatch over the same UI↔worker message protocol the human's own clicks use, so agent and human literally share one engine and one document. Responses are capped, staleness-checked against a document token (a doc swapped mid-tool aborts cleanly), and annotated with readOnlyHint / untrustedContentHint . Query errors return a caret under the fault plus the grammar, so agents self-correct. Where the API is absent the bridge chunk is never fetched and the app is byte-for-byte unchanged (asserted by e2e). Verified by 70 unit tests plus a Playwright end-to-end suite that drives a real WebMCP-enabled Chromium through every tool, and live on jsonloupe.dev under the Chrome origin trial. Prior work vs. new work The viewer, engine, and stdio MCP server predate the submission window. Everything WebMCP — src/webmcp/ , its tests, the wiring, the e2e suite — is new work within the window; see WEBMCP.md and the timestamped commit history (PRs #50, #51). Built With github indexeddb mcp playwright typescript vite web-workers webmcp Try it out jsonloupe.dev github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Solo project. I built jsonloupe itself over the past months — the lossless viewer, the worker engine, and its stdio MCP server. For this challenge I designed and shipped the WebMCP bridge: eight tools on document.modelContext that share one engine and one document with the human, including the three view-moving verbs (load_doc, reveal_path, highlight_matches) that are the heart of the idea. I worked with ChatGPT desktop app as my development agent throughout — implementation, tests, and automated browser verification — while owning the architecture, the product thesis, and every design decision. The prior-vs-new work split is documented in WEBMCP.md and the commit history. Priyanshu Nandan Like Share this project: Updates Priyanshu Nandan started this project — Aug 29, 2026 07:19 AM EDT

title: Corotum
pitch: Corotum helps you keep AI agent skills consistent across every machine and AI agent. Instead of copying and fixing drift, you manage one desired state and sync it safely through Git or Corotum Cloud.
about_excerpt: Corotum helps you keep AI agent skills consistent across every machine and AI agent. Instead of copying and fixing drift, you manage one desired state and sync it safely through Git or Corotum Cloud. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I use multiple AI agents on different machines, and I kept running into the same problem: their skills were never quite the same. A skill would be installed on my Mac but missing on a VPS. Another would be outdated somewhere else. Sometimes I had changed a skill locally and forgot about it. The usual solution was copying folders around and trying to remember which version was the right one. That became the starting point for Corotum. I wanted one place to define which skills I use, which versions should be installed, and which agents should get them. I also wanted to see how far I could take the idea during a 7-day build challenge for the WebMCP Challenge. What it does Corotum manages and synchronizes AI agent skills across machines and agents. It keeps a desired state and compares it with what is actually installed on a machine. From that comparison it works out what needs to change, applies it, and verifies the result. There are two sync modes. Git Sync uses your own Git repository and does not require a Corotum account. Corotum Cloud hosts the desired state and adds a dashboard, devices, revisions, sync status, and WebMCP. The CLI can add, remove, adopt, update, restore, and target skills to specific agents. Versions are locked to exact Git revisions, so running sync does not unexpectedly update a skill to whatever happens to be latest. Corotum also treats local changes carefully. If a managed skill was modified by hand, it is marked as drifted instead of being overwritten. Skills that Corotum does not manage are not deleted during normal synchronization. How I built it Corotum is a TypeScript monorepo using Bun workspaces. The CLI runs on Bun and is compiled into standalone binaries. The web app uses Next.js with vinext on Cloudflare Workers, with D1 for the hosted state. The main sync flow is: Desired State + Actual State → Diff → Reconcile Plan → Apply → Verify Git Sync and Corotum Cloud use the same synchronization model. The dashboard, API, and WebMCP also use the same application services instead of having separate implementations of the same operations. For private repositories, Corotum uses Git credentials already configured on the user's machine. Those credentials are never sent to or stored by Corotum Cloud. Challenges Most of the work was not actually copying files. It was deciding exactly what every operation should mean when several machines can be in different states. For example, remove and unmanage both remove a skill from the desired state, but they cannot behave the same way. remove should eventually delete the managed copy from every device. unmanage should stop managing it but leave the local files in place. Drift was another case that needed explicit rules. If somebody edits a managed skill locally, a normal sync should not silently destroy those changes. Offline devices made this harder. A machine might reconnect several revisions later, so looking only at the newest snapshot is not always enough to understand what should happen locally. Private repositories had a similar constraint. The Cloud can coordinate the desired state, but it cannot assume that it has access to the repository. Resolution sometimes has to happen on a device that already has Git access. What I learned The project started as a fairly simple "sync skills between computers" idea. Most of the complexity turned out to be around ownership and state. Once I separated the shared desired state from the actual state of each device, a lot of the behavior became easier to define. Locking skills to exact Git revisions was another important decision. It keeps sync and update as two separate operations: sync reproduces the selected state, while update intentionally changes it. What's next The first version is deliberately limited to AI agent skills. The same model could later be used for other parts of an agent setup, such as MCP servers, prompts, rules, profiles, agent configuration, and team policies. title: Synapse
pitch: A living 3D spatial knowledge graph where humans and AI agents co-navigate, synthesize learning paths, and index documents via WebMCP.\n
about_excerpt:
A living 3D spatial knowledge graph where humans and AI agents co-navigate, synthesize learning paths, and index documents via WebMCP.

 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like

 1 2 3 4 5 6 



 
 💡 Inspiration 

 Modern knowledge management tools (like Obsidian or Notion) store thoughts as flat text or 2D lists. However, human memory and creative synthesis operate spatially and associationally. We created Synapse to explore the future of spatial computing on the open web—a living 3D spatial knowledge void where humans and AI agents can co-navigate, synthesize learning paths, and build complex ideas together in real-time using WebMCP . 

 

 🚀 What it does 

 Synapse transforms notes into reflective 3D metallic nodes suspended in a dynamic spatial void. Nodes are semantically positioned using vector similarity and force-directed layout physics. 

 Through WebMCP ( document.modelContext ), an AI Agent becomes an active 3D co-pilot: 

 
 Spatial Navigation: The agent smoothly flies the 3D camera to focus on relevant node clusters. 
 Learning Path Synthesis: Uses graph BFS algorithms to calculate and highlight the shortest conceptual bridge between 2 distant ideas. 
 Topological Cluster Analysis: Detects isolated thought islands and tag density to help users organize scattered notes. 
 Document Chunking & Indexing: Automatically breaks down dropped PDFs, Markdown, or web text into 3D nodes linked by semantic similarity. 
 Full CRUD & Persistence: Enables real-time editing, node merging, pruning, auto-saving to local storage, and JSON exports. 
 

 

 🛠️ How we built it 

 
 3D Graphics & Physics: Built with Three.js using custom metallic shaders, organic bobbing motion, and glowing neural energy particle beads traveling along active connections. 
 WebMCP Standard ( document.modelContext ): Implemented 15 imperative tools using the official @mcp-b/webmcp-polyfill and native W3C WebMCP specification. 
 Shared State Architecture: Built around a central store ( SynapseStore ) that handles physics, layout math, and event broadcasts. Both manual user clicks and agent tool calls flow through the same store methods, guaranteeing seamless synchronization between human actions and agent navigation. 
 Zero API Dependencies: 100% standalone, client-side, zero backend API keys required, compatible with any WebMCP client (Chrome Native AI, Claude Extension, ChatGPT Extension, or local demo dock). 
 

 

 🧠 WebMCP Implementation (15 Registered Tools) 

 Synapse registers 15 WebMCP tools via document.modelContext.registerTool : 

 
 search_nodes : Text & tag search with 3D camera cluster focusing. 
 focus_node : Smooth 3D camera flight to select and inspect a node. 
 get_similar_nodes : Vector similarity search returning nearest semantic neighbors. 
 suggest_connections : AI-surfaced unlinked concept pairs rendered as 3D gold lines. 
 get_graph_overview : Overview of node/edge metrics, top tags, and focus. 
 create_node : Real-time creation and 3D positioning of new notes. 
 import_document : Auto-chunking & 3D indexing of markdown/PDF text. 
 synthesize_path : BFS shortest-path algorithm connecting distant 3D concepts. 
 auto_cluster_analysis : Topological analysis detecting isolated thought islands. 
 export_knowledge_graph : Full JSON graph serialization for backup. 
 delete_node : Deletes a node and auto-prunes attached 3D edges. 
 edit_node : Edits title, content, or tags of any node in real-time. 
 merge_nodes : Merges two nodes into one, concatenating content & inheriting edges. 
 add_connection : Manually connects two nodes with a 3D metallic beam. 
 reset_graph : Clears all nodes & connections for a fresh 100% blank canvas. 
 

 

 🏋️ Challenges we faced 

 
 3D Shared State Synchronization: Ensuring camera flights and node highlighting responded smoothly whether triggered by a human mouse click or an asynchronous WebMCP tool call. 
 WebMCP Spec Compatibility: Handling parameter passing formats across native Chrome flags and browser polyfill implementations. 
 Real-Time Physics & Performance: Rendering hundreds of ghost background connections and neural energy beads at 60 FPS in pure Vanilla JS. 
 

 

 🏆 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 Delivering a complete, end-to-end product experience —not just a proof of concept. 
 Building a stateful 3D spatial brain with 15 non-trivial WebMCP tools that work 100% offline with zero external API key requirements. 
 Creating a visually stunning, glassmorphic UI with animated light pulses and dynamic 3D physics. 
 

 

 📚 What we learned 

 We gained deep insights into the power of the W3C WebMCP standard—how exposing imperative tools via document.modelContext fundamentally transforms web applications from passive static pages into active collaborative spaces for AI agents.

title: PatrAgent
pitch: The web is becoming AI native. Security should be too. PatrAgent gives agents the possibility to scan text, mcp server, files and urls for prompt injections before content lands into context.
about_excerpt: The web is becoming AI native. Security should be too. PatrAgent gives agents the possibility to scan text, mcp server, files and urls for prompt injections before content lands into context. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Patronus WebMCP Security Scanner About the project Inspiration Autonomous agents increasingly work with content they did not create: repository files, uploaded documents, MCP tool descriptions, prompts, and resources. That content can contain prompt injections designed to redirect an agent before it has a chance to evaluate whether the source is trustworthy. We wanted to move that security decision in front of the context boundary. Instead of asking an agent to read potentially hostile content and then judge it, Patronus lets the agent scan the content first and receive only a compact security result. What it does Patronus WebMCP Security Scanner gives people and agents access to the same prompt-injection security layer. People can use the visual interface to: scan text for prompt injections; inspect an MCP server's tool, prompt, and resource metadata without executing any of its capabilities; scan the normalized static surface of a public HTTPS page; and upload source code or text documents for analysis. Agents discover four typed WebMCP tools directly from the page: scan_text scan_mcp_server scan_url scan_file The repository also contains an installable Codex plugin that can scan an entire repository before the agent reads it. A deterministic local helper validates and uploads supported files directly to the scanner. The agent receives only filenames, opaque file IDs, and compact verdicts, so the candidate file contents never enter the model context before the security decision. Capabilities Interactive security scanner The hosted application exposes four read-only WebMCP tools backed by Patronus Ark: scan_text checks a bounded text candidate for prompt injection. scan_file checks an uploaded source-code or text file through an opaque file ID. scan_mcp_server inspects the advertised tools, prompts, and resources of a public MCP server without executing any of them. scan_url checks the complete normalized static body of one public HTTPS page. The same capabilities are available through the visual interface. When an agent invokes a tool, its result is reflected in the page so the person and the agent share the same observable security state. Repository scan before context The installable Codex plugin lets a person ask an agent to scan a repository before reading its files. The workflow deliberately separates deterministic file handling from model-visible context: A local helper selects supported files, validates their type and size, and uploads their bytes directly to the hosted scanner. It returns a content-free upload manifest. Prepared entries contain only a filename, byte size, and opaque file_id ; skipped entries contain only a filename and reason. The agent calls the scan_file WebMCP tool once for every prepared ID and receives compact verdicts and bounded evidence. The plugin reports every detected incident and the final scan coverage without modifying, deleting, quarantining, or repairing repository files. This means potentially hostile source text does not need to enter the model context just to reach the classifier. Uploaded objects are short-lived and are deleted after scanning. The result is a bounded prompt-injection check, not a claim that the repository is free of every possible security issue. WebMCP iframe security manifest The Patronus website embeds the security manifest as a small cross-origin iframe in its shared footer. It provides the origin-bound WebMCP tool patronus_security_manifest_v1 . The website-scan flow works as follows: A compatible agent is asked whether one exact public HTTPS URL is safe to use. The website-scan skill addresses only the trusted Patronus iframe and supplies that exact URL through fixed bridge controls. Inside its own origin, the iframe discovers and invokes its own WebMCP tool. It rejects a missing, duplicated, or same-named tool from another origin. The Patronus Control Plane fetches the anonymous static page surface, converts the complete normalized document body into one Ark candidate, and keeps other advertised security surfaces as separate candidates. The iframe returns only a bounded verdict, tool identity, URL identity, digests, cache metadata, and coverage. The agent treats missing, mismatched, failed, or truncated results as unverified rather than benign. Iframe embedding and WebMCP exposure are restricted to the configured Patronus website origins. The manifest does not execute capabilities from the scanned page and does not claim to assess authenticated state, later DOM mutations, privacy, malware, reputation, or every security risk. The current browser harness may still add navigation or page observations to model context automatically. The demo therefore shows the intended pre-context security sequence and a practical origin-bound WebMCP bridge, while a future native tools-only harness is needed to guarantee that no parent-page content is exposed before the verdict. Why WebMCP This use case needs more than UI automation. Scraping the DOM or clicking through a form would force an agent to inspect the very content we are trying to keep outside its context. WebMCP provides a typed capability boundary instead. The page explicitly describes what an agent may do, validates structured inputs, and returns bounded results. The same calls also update the visible interface, so a person can observe the result and stay in the loop while the agent performs the scan. That creates a workflow that was previously difficult: a person can point an autonomous agent at an unknown repository, and the agent can evaluate it for prompt injections before reading or reasoning over its contents. How we built it The application is written in TypeScript with React and Vinext and runs on Cloudflare Workers. It registers its agent-facing capabilities with document.modelContext.registerTool() and defines strict JSON schemas for every input. Prompt-injection analysis is powered by Patronus Ark . Text is sent directly for analysis. File scanning uses short-lived Cloudflare R2 sessions: the browser or local helper uploads a file, WebMCP receives only an opaque file_id , and the server deletes the object after scanning. MCP inspection is intentionally read-only. The server calls only initialize , tools/list , prompts/list , and resources/list ; it never executes remote tools, prompts, or resources. The endpoint also rejects credentials, localhost, literal private addresses, unsafe redirects, and oversized responses. Patronus Ark: CPU-first security Patronus Ark is Casdo Labs' CPU-first security stack. It is built around our own multilingual security models and shared-encoder architectures, allowing multiple security tasks to reuse a common representation instead of requiring a separate heavyweight model for every detector. We believe an agent's security layer should not have to compete with the agent itself for scarce GPU capacity. When GPUs are occupied by large language models, security still needs to remain available, responsive, and always on. A CPU-first architecture makes it possible to run protection close to the workload and helps keep essential security affordable—or even free—for a much broader group of users. The Ark API behind this demo currently runs on only four vCPUs and still provides latency that is practical for an interactive scanning workflow. The API service and its integration were built as part of this hackathon, while the underlying Ark architecture and model research build on several months of prior research and development. Casdo Labs' long-term vision is a safer future for autonomous agents and the people who rely on them. Agents are rapidly becoming faster and more capable; we believe their security infrastructure must become widely accessible just as quickly. Challenges we faced The hardest problem was preserving the security boundary end to end. A repository scanner is not useful if the agent must read each file in order to upload it, so we separated deterministic file handling from model-visible context and designed the WebMCP contract around opaque identifiers. We also had to make remote MCP inspection useful without turning it into an SSRF proxy or accidentally invoking an untrusted server's capabilities. That required strict URL validation, response limits, read-only protocol calls, and careful error handling. The iframe manifest introduced a different trust problem: a same-named tool must not be accepted from the parent page or another origin. We bound embedding and tool exposure to explicit origins, verify the discovered tool's identity before execution, return only a bounded result, and document the remaining browser-harness limitation instead of overstating the pre-context guarantee. title: Sealed
pitch: A reusable WebMCP privacy boundary that lets agents act on sensitive workflows without receiving the raw private values behind the decision.
about_excerpt: A reusable WebMCP privacy boundary that lets agents act on sensitive workflows without receiving the raw private values behind the decision. Like Comment Story Updates Sealed’s WebMCP privacy boundary: private values stay page-local while agents receive only allowlisted decisions or opaque references. Inspiration AI agents are becoming capable of acting directly on websites, but many useful workflows involve information that should not automatically become part of the agent's context. A rental application is a simple example: an agent may need to know whether an applicant satisfies an income requirement, but it does not need the applicant's actual income. The same applies to identity data, age checks, financial values, health information, and many other private facts. Sealed explores a simple idea: The agent gets the decision — not the secret. What it does Sealed is a reusable WebMCP privacy boundary for agentic web applications. The page exposes a small, state-aware set of WebMCP tools. Public information can move normally, while sensitive facts are evaluated locally inside the page and only allowlisted results are returned to the agent. The primary rental demo shows the full pattern: Public applicant information can be updated by the agent. A private income_3x_rent predicate is evaluated locally. The agent receives only satisfied or not satisfied ; the income itself is returned as value: "withheld" . A passport verification requires explicit human approval. Approval creates a random, session-bound opaque reference that does not encode the passport number. Every private crossing is recorded in a visible Boundary Ledger. Human review returns submitted: false ; Sealed has no final-submission tool. After review, the WebMCP capability surface contracts from five tools to only two safe read/flag operations. A second Membership scenario reuses the same primitives to evaluate age_18_plus without exposing the user's date of birth. Why WebMCP WebMCP is load-bearing in Sealed. Without structured site tools, an agent would have to infer meaning from DOM content, accessibility trees, or screenshots. That is especially problematic around sensitive data because the agent may end up observing more information than the task actually requires. With WebMCP, the page defines the capability boundary explicitly. Sealed registers tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) , including: get_application_context set_public_fields flag_uncertain request_private_binding evaluate_private_requirement request_review The available tool surface changes with workflow state. The agent can ask for a useful decision, but no tool exists that returns the underlying private value. How I built it Sealed is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, and WebMCP and is deployed on Vercel. The privacy boundary has several layers: Fixed private predicates The agent selects from predefined checks such as income_3x_rent or age_18_plus ; it cannot construct arbitrary queries over private values. Local execution Private values are generated and retained page-locally. Predicate evaluation happens inside the application. Guarded egress Private operations pass through a single allowlisted response path that releases only approved fields such as status, requirement, and value: "withheld" . Human-approved opaque bindings Consequential credential binding requires explicit user approval and returns only a random session-bound reference. Boundary Ledger Each private operation records the exact sanitized payload released across the boundary. State-dependent capabilities Once human review is requested, Sealed removes write/private tools and leaves only two safe operations. Challenges I ran into The hardest part was separating three different things that initially looked like the same problem: page registration, browser discovery, and agent invocation. A page can successfully register WebMCP tools while the current ChatGPT browser session has not yet attached those tools to the conversation. I reproduced cases where the page showed five registered tools while the agent still reported that site tools were unavailable. Testing against the official Chrome Labs WebMCP demo helped isolate the difference between application behavior and client-session discovery. That led to an important UI correction: Sealed now says “Site tools registered” , rather than claiming that an agent is connected simply because local registration succeeded. I also had to guard against stale sessions, repeat probing of private predicates, response/ledger drift, and accidental leakage through seemingly harmless response fields. Accomplishments I am proud of The final implementation demonstrates a complete human-agent privacy workflow rather than a single tool call. The strongest result is that the same private operation produces both: the agent-visible sanitized response, and the visible Boundary Ledger entry from the same guarded source of truth. The rental flow demonstrates public writes, private decision-only evaluation, explicit human approval, opaque binding, human review without submission, and dynamic capability reduction. The membership scenario shows that the pattern is reusable rather than hard-coded to one application. What I learned WebMCP is not only useful for making agents more capable. It can also make the boundary between a web application and an agent more explicit. The most useful question became: What is the minimum information the agent needs to complete this task? For many workflows, the answer is not the private value itself. It is a decision, status, capability, or reference derived from that value. I also learned that real browser behavior matters as much as implementing the API correctly. Registration, discovery, invocation, approvals, and session lifecycle all have to be tested end to end. What's next Sealed is intentionally narrow for this challenge. Future work could explore additional private decision primitives, external verifier-backed references, and reusable SDK-level abstractions for application developers. For now, the project focuses on one core principle: Useful decisions can cross the boundary. Raw private values do not have to. title: LocusLocal
pitch: Human and agent triage the same genome in the same tab, through WebMCP tools the page itself registers, over a file that can never be uploaded.
about_excerpt: Human and agent triage the same genome in the same tab, through WebMCP tools the page itself registers, over a file that can never be uploaded. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Landing Page Guide Mode Variant Window Advanced Mode Inspiration I study anthropology, which in practice means I spend a lot of time around genomic data that isn't mine. Population panels, ancient DNA, samples from communities who agreed to one specific study and nothing beyond it. Consent in this field is narrow and it's supposed to stay narrow. That makes most genomics tooling unusable for me. Every variant browser I found opens the same way, upload your raw file to our server. I can not click that with a participant's genotypes, and I wouldn't click it with my own either. WebMCP removes the upload from the equation. The tools are declared by the page and run in the tab where the file already is, so the model can operate on data that never moves. That was enough to make the tool worth building. What it does LocusLocal is a variant-triage workbench. Drop in a VCF or a consumer raw export, it is parsed in a Web Worker, annotated against a bundled 98,262-variant ClinVar subset, and analysed entirely inside the tab. The demo genome is 250,000 markers from 1000 Genomes sample NA12878. Two audiences, one analysis engine. Guided mode answers the questions a person reading their own export actually has: how much of the file was read, how much of it ClinVar knows about, what they carry, how strong the evidence is, and what the analysis cannot tell them. Advanced mode gives the full table, filter stack, sorting and manual selection. One click either way, and an agent can make that click too. How I built it Vanilla TypeScript and Vite 8, no UI framework, deployed on a Cloudflare Worker that runs before static assets so the security headers can't be skipped. Tools are grouped into read_* , set_* , act_* , explain_* , and history . Chrome's secure-tools guidance applied throughout. readOnlyHint on all 13 read_* / explain_* tools and on none of the mutating ones; untrustedContentHint on analysis tools, whose output contains text from a user-supplied file; descriptions that state the visible UI effect. What's next for LocusLocal Pharmacogenomics (CPIC/PharmGKB). Drug-response markers are the genomics question with the most immediately actionable answer, and the annotation set is small enough to bundle under the same no-egress constraint. Polygenic scores, honestly presented. The interesting design problem is communicating a population-relative distribution to someone who wants a yes/no with the ancestry-portability caveat in the interface rather than a footnote. Trio and family-set support. Multi-sample VCFs, inheritance patterns, and a compare_samples tool, the point at which the shared-selection model gets genuinely harder and more interesting. A second annotation source (gnomAD frequencies) so "rare" stops meaning "not in ClinVar". Lift-over for GRCh38 so coordinates become comparable rather than merely disclaimed, retiring the coordinatesComparable: false path.
