title: Duet
pitch: Turn the music you love into a piano lesson made for you.
about_excerpt: Turn the music you love into a piano lesson made for you. Like 1 Comment Story Updates 1 Duet Piano Studio Agent created lesson Inspiration Duet began with a gap we kept running into: an agent could give us a good music lesson, but it could not reach the piano. We could ask, “Can you help me practise these four bars?” and receive sensible advice—slow the piece down, isolate the right hand, repeat the difficult section—but the useful part stopped at the chat box. We still had to find the music, change the tempo, set the loop, remember the notes and rebuild the lesson ourselves. We wanted the agent to meet the learner inside the instrument. That became Duet: a browser piano where the learner and their agent work on the same piece, using the same transport and seeing the same lesson change in real time. What it does Duet turns a natural-language request into a visible, playable music lesson. A learner can ask: Load Minuet in G. Keep only the right hand, slow it to 70 per cent, loop bars 1–4, add a one-bar count-in and metronome, highlight the opening phrase, and start practice. Through WebMCP, the agent can carry out each part of that request directly. The piece loads, the tempo changes, the left hand is removed, the loop and count-in appear, the requested keys light up and practice mode begins. The learner does not receive another list of instructions. They receive a lesson they can immediately play. Duet includes: A responsive browser piano playable with mouse, touch or A–Z/0–9 keys Fourteen public-domain pieces and exercises Demo, Play Along and Practice modes Tempo changes, transposition, simplification and hand isolation Bar-level slicing and looping Count-in, metronome, seeking and hand-mix controls Visible key highlights and expected-note practice Agent-supplied structured musical arrangements Microphone permission and monophonic phrase-capture support A shared activity history showing what the learner and agent changed Why WebMCP matters This would be a much weaker product if the agent were simply clicking buttons. Music has meaningful concepts: pieces, bars, beats, notes, hands, tempo, loops and phrases. Duet exposes those concepts through 21 structured WebMCP tools. The agent can ask what Duet supports, inspect the active piece, read a bounded section of the score, transform the music and verify the resulting transport state. It does not need to guess screen coordinates or depend on fragile DOM selectors. The learner stays in control. Sound still requires a human gesture because of browser audio rules, and microphone access still requires explicit browser permission. Duet reports those boundaries honestly instead of pretending an action succeeded. How we built it Duet is a React and TypeScript browser application. The interface and WebMCP tools share one Zustand command and state layer, so an agent action produces the same visible result as a human action. Zod validates tool inputs before they reach the music engine. Playback uses the Web Audio API with an audio-clock transport. This supports reliable play, pause, resume, seek, looping, count-ins, metronome clicks and separate left- and right-hand mix controls. The 21 tools register through document.modelContext.registerTool . They cover capability discovery, state and score reading, playback, transformations, highlighting, practice, transport configuration and captured phrases. We tested the WebMCP experience with both OpenAI Codex and Anthropic Claude. This was important to us: Duet should present a clear musical tool surface to any compatible agent, not depend on behaviour unique to one client. Challenges The hardest part was keeping three realities synchronized: what the learner sees, what the agent reads and what the browser is actually playing. Browser audio also introduced constraints that a normal interface can hide. Audio must be unlocked by a human interaction, scheduled voices must stop cleanly and pause/resume must preserve the real musical position. Another challenge was returning enough score information for an agent without exceeding the WebMCP response budget. We added bounded pagination so an agent can read longer pieces safely rather than receiving silently truncated data. We also had to resist adding visual effects that looked impressive but distracted from practice. The final interface focuses on a realistic keyboard, the active musical phrase and the controls a learner genuinely needs. What we learned The biggest lesson was that WebMCP works best when a website exposes the language of its domain rather than a list of UI actions. “Click the third button” is brittle. “Loop bars 1–4, isolate the right hand and start practice” is understandable, verifiable and useful. We also learned that agent actions need immediate visual feedback. When the tempo, loop, highlights and practice state change on screen, the learner can understand what happened and continue from there. The agent becomes a collaborator rather than an invisible automation layer. What is next We would like to add MIDI and MusicXML import, score-image recognition, timing and dynamics feedback, richer sampled piano sounds, and saved practice history. The current microphone pipeline handles monophonic phrases and has automated signal coverage, but real-world pitch recognition still needs broader testing across devices and environments. Duet is our first step toward a music lesson that does not end when the agent finishes speaking. title: CapSpace Pro
pitch: CapSpace Pro is a WebMCP-powered NBA CBA co-pilot that turns dead-end trade errors into autonomous, 100% legally compliant multi-team trade solutions in real time.
about_excerpt: CapSpace Pro is a WebMCP-powered NBA CBA co-pilot that turns dead-end trade errors into autonomous, 100% legally compliant multi-team trade solutions in real time. Like Comment Story Updates interactive_trade_canvas 3team_balanced_trade webmcp_protocol_tools_modal general_guide_modal rule_violation_alert Inspiration Every February around the NBA Trade Deadline, millions of passionate basketball fans, beat writers, podcasters, and sports journalists flock to online trade machines (such as ESPN Trade Machine and Fanspo) to construct and test dream blockbuster trades. But with the introduction of the modern 676-page NBA Collective Bargaining Agreement (CBA) , trading has become an unforgiving mathematical minefield: Teams spending in the Second Apron ($188.93M+) face severe trade freezes—they cannot aggregate multiple outgoing player salaries and cannot take back even $1 more than they send out. Trades must satisfy exact piecewise arithmetic brackets ($7.5M tiers, $29M tiers, $250k buffers) across all participating franchises. Complex deals require multi-team routing through Traded Player Exceptions (TPEs) and strict 14–15 contract roster limits. When a multi-team trade fails in current trade machines, the user is greeted by a dead-end red banner: ❌ "Trade Failed: Incoming salary exceeds allowed bracket by $3,450,000." Existing tools tell you that a trade failed, but never how to fix it . Fixing it manually requires opening 29 browser tabs, digging through TPE voucher lists, and spending 45 minutes calculating tax arithmetic. We built CapSpace Pro to turn the trade machine from a dumb calculator that only says "NO" into an autonomous Human-AI Co-Pilot that says "HERE IS HOW WE FIX IT." What it does CapSace Pro is a real-time, 30-team trade canvas and autonomous CBA constraint solver powered by WebMCP . Built as a prosumer platform, it democratizes NBA Front-Office Capology —giving sports journalists, analysts, and everyday fans the exact financial precision of an NBA General Manager without needing a finance degree or a 676-page rulebook: Interactive Multi-Team Canvas: Visualizes live payrolls, luxury tax tiers, First/Second Apron lines, draft pick assets, and available TPE vouchers for all 30 NBA franchises. Sub-Millisecond CBA Engine: Evaluates trades against official CBA rules down to the single dollar in under 1 millisecond. Superstar Protection & In-Trade Anchors (🔒): Roster Superstar Locks: Protects franchise cornerstones (e.g., Steph Curry, Nikola Jokić) from ever being touched by automated solvers. Trade Card Anchors: Lets humans pin marquee trade targets as immutable centerpieces, instructing the AI to only manipulate flexible bench contracts. Autonomous Multi-Team Balancing & Facilitator Routing: The AI agent autonomously discovers 3rd-party facilitator teams with matching TPE vouchers or cap space to absorb excess salary, solving multi-million-dollar trade deficits automatically. Zero-Hallucination WebMCP Bridge: Exposes 8 typed tools ( validate_cba_trade , find_facilitator_teams , auto_balance_trade , etc.) directly on navigator.modelContext , letting browser-native agents inspect, validate, and restructure live trade boards with 100% mathematical precision. How we built it We engineered CapSpace Pro as a modular, high-performance web application coupled with the new WebMCP standard : ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ User Journalist / GM / Fan │ └───────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────┘ │ Natural Language & Visual Clicks (🔒) ▼ ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Browser-Native AI Agent (WebMCP) │ └───────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────┘ │ Typed JSON Tool Invocations ▼ ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ CapSpace Pro WebMCP Protocol Bridge │ │ (navigator.modelContext.registerTool) │ └──────────────┬──────────────────────────┬──────────────┘ │ │ ▼ ▼ ┌──────────────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────────────┐ │ Deterministic CBA │ │ Reactive React │ │ Constraint Engine │ │ 30-Team Canvas UI │ │ (TypeScript Math) │ │ (Tailwind CSS 3.4) │ └──────────────────────────┘ └─────────────────────────┘ 1. Deterministic CBA Mathematical Formulation The mathematical engine models the exact piecewise salary-matching brackets defined under the 2023–2030 NBA CBA: A. Non-Taxpaying Teams (Payroll < $170,814,000) Tier 1 (Outgoing ≤ $7,500,000): Allowed Incoming = (200% × Outgoing Salary) + $250,000 Tier 2 ($7,500,000 < Outgoing ≤ $29,000,000): Allowed Incoming = Outgoing Salary + $7,500,000 Tier 3 (Outgoing > $29,000,000): Allowed Incoming = (125% × Outgoing Salary) + $250,000 B. Taxpaying Teams Below First Apron ($170,814,000 ≤ Payroll < $178,132,000) Allowed Incoming = (110% × Outgoing Salary) + $250,000 C. First & Second Apron Teams (Payroll ≥ $178,132,000) Allowed Incoming = 100% × Outgoing Salary ($0 allowable surplus) Second Apron Freeze (≥ $188,931,000): Aggregation Allowed = FALSE (prohibits combining multiple outgoing contracts). D. Traded Player Exception (TPE) Absorption Condition For an incoming contract to be legally absorbed into an existing TPE by facilitator team F: Contract Incoming ≤ TPE Size + $250,000 Roster Size(F) < 15 contracts Post-Trade Payroll(F) ≤ Hard Cap / Apron Ceiling 2. Full Suite of 8 WebMCP Tools Implemented via modelContextBridge.ts exposing both read-only and mutation interfaces: list_all_teams ( readOnly ) get_team_cap_status ( readOnly ) validate_cba_trade ( readOnly ) find_facilitator_teams ( readOnly ) set_player_protection ( mutation ) route_salary_to_tpe ( mutation ) auto_balance_trade ( mutation ) reset_trade ( mutation ) 3. Tech Stack Frontend: React 18, TypeScript 5.5, Vite, Lucide Icons Styling & Design: Tailwind CSS 3.4 with custom glassmorphic sports dark mode Testing: Vitest test suite with 38 unit and integration tests passing with 0 vulnerabilities Challenges we ran into Preserving Human Intent during Autonomous Balancing: Early versions of automated balancing would solve financial parity by arbitrarily moving superstar players. We solved this by creating a two-tier locking architecture: Roster Superstar Protection (protects franchise players from leaving) and In-Trade Anchors (pins the trade centerpiece so the AI only optimizes secondary bench assets). QUick Browser Execution for WebMCP: We had to ensure that the combinatorial search across 30 rosters and dozens of active TPE vouchers executed synchronously in the browser sandbox without causing UI freezes or async lag during live agent conversations. Google Chrome webmcp on Ubuntu not worked. Hence decided to go with ChatGpt in app browser. Accomplishments that we're proud of Zero-Hallucination Agent Governance: By offloading mathematical logic to a deterministic TypeScript rule engine, the AI agent is physically incapable of proposing an illegal trade. Democratizing Front-Office Analytics for Fans & Media: Making the complex 676-page CBA accessible to anyone. A journalist evaluating trade rumors or a fan testing deadline theories can simply speak in plain English to an AI co-pilot and get legally vetted, dollar-precise front-office scenarios in sub-milliseconds. Clean, Accessible UX: High information density displaying 30 teams, roster breakdowns, financial health bars, and interactive trade cards without clutter. What we learned Why WebMCP is the Future of Domain-Specific AI: Large Language Models excel at natural language understanding and strategic high-level reasoning, but struggle with strict multi-tier arithmetic. WebMCP acts as the ultimate bridge: the agent brings user empathy and strategic intent, while the browser tool engine provides mathematical certainty. What's next for CapSpace Pro Multi-Year Cap Projections: Allowing GMs to simulate trades 2–3 seasons into the future to forecast luxury tax repeater penalties. Multi-League Expansion: Porting the WebMCP constraint engine to other complex salary cap leagues, such as the NFL hard cap and NHL salary ceiling . title: TrialBridge
pitch: A WebMCP powered ChatGPT and Chrome enabled agent that matches cancer patients to clinical trials in minutes - no filling forms, no endless clicks and no gatekeeping - for early therapy access.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP powered ChatGPT and Chrome enabled agent that matches cancer patients to clinical trials in minutes - no filling forms, no endless clicks and no gatekeeping - for early therapy access. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I (Vilay) started my career as a Clinical Research Coordinator at Stanford Cancer Center. Still the most formative experience working with patients at the end of their lives. I have since built award winning Palliative programs, but keep coming back to the same problem - how do we meet needs of patients who have exhausted all available FDA approved therapies. At that point, what most patients want is not survival for its sake, but to make it to an important life event - son's graduation, daughter's quincenera, or an anniversary. For these patients, clinical trials can be the only pathway that might increase their lifespan through a therapy that won't be on the market for years. Yet, the access is gatekept - geographically limited around academic medical centers who run the trials, or knowledge and bandwidth of community oncologists - all buried in CT.gov, a clunky government database that is difficult to navigate. Meanwhile clinical trials regularly shut down due to low enrollment. Patients who could have qualified never find a trial, and trials that can help many never fill and reach their endpoints. We built TrialBridge to close the gap on both directions. This is also the first project built together by us three brothers working across three different time zones and bringing experience from three very different fields: I, Vilay , am a healthcare executive with background in population health, high risk patient management and healthcare strategy and operations. He lived and breathed clinical trials for good portion of his career and brought the vision. Shobhit , based in India, conceived and created the application, designed the patient-facing workflow and built the WebMCP tools that connect an AI agent with TrialBridge. Harshit , based in New York and the most deeply technical member of the team, helped shape the application’s technical architecture, implementation and engineering reliability. TrialBridge emerged from the intersection of healthcare, technology and patient advocacy—and from three brothers wanting to build something useful together. What it does TrialBridge helps patients and caregivers discover clinical trials that may be worth discussing with their doctors. A patient can describe their situation to an AI agent in ordinary language—for example: “I have stage IV neuroendocrine cancer. I’m 58, live in Chicago, can travel 150 miles, and previously received Afinitor.” Through WebMCP, the agent can then interact with TrialBridge using structured tools registered directly by the webpage. The patient does not need to manually complete every field or navigate multiple filtering menus. However, the profile remains visible and editable, allowing the patient to inspect and correct what the agent entered. TrialBridge can: Convert a patient’s plain-language description into a structured search profile; Resolve supported medication brand names to their generic equivalents, such as Afinitor to everolimus; Search currently recruiting studies using the live ClinicalTrials.gov API; Distinguish the number of registry records checked from the number of trials eventually shown; Explain which records were filtered out and why; Show whether the search reached the end of the available registry results or stopped at an application limit; Compare age, location and supported prior-treatment information against published study details; Display what appears consistent, what appears inconsistent and what remains unknown; Allow the agent to shortlist potentially relevant studies with factual reasons; Open a full side-by-side comparison of shortlisted trials; and Support preliminary pre-screening against published inclusion and exclusion criteria. Importantly, TrialBridge preserves uncertainty. If a patient does not know their ECOG performance status or cannot answer another medical question, the application records that information as unresolved . It does not silently convert an unknown answer into a pass or a failure. TrialBridge does not determine eligibility, diagnose a condition, recommend treatment or provide medical advice. Only a clinical-trial study team can determine eligibility after medical screening. How we built it We began by developing the domain layer required to understand cancer terminology, treatment names and clinical-trial records. This included a curated cancer and treatment catalogue built from publicly available clinical sources and open clinical terminology, supported medication mappings, and brand-to-generic drug-name resolution. ClinicalTrials.gov API v2 provides the live public trial data used by the search. We then built TrialBridge using: Next.js React TypeScript ClinicalTrials.gov API v2 WebMCP Declared tool schemas and application-level input validation Browser-stored patient profile and pre-screening state Replit deployment The webpage registers ten structured tools using the current WebMCP imperative API: document.modelContext.registerTool() Each tool has: A defined name and description; A declared input schema; Structured parameters; Application-level validation before state changes are applied; A specific application action; and A visible result in the same interface used by a human. This means an AI agent does not have to scrape the page, interpret screenshots or guess which element to click. Instead, the webpage acts as an in-page tool server, allowing the agent to invoke capabilities that the application has explicitly exposed. Different tools handle different parts of the workflow, including: Reading and updating the patient profile; Searching conditions and trials; Retrieving trial details; Managing the shortlist; Opening comparisons; Starting pre-screening; and Recording preliminary criterion responses. Search and trial-data operations use the live ClinicalTrials.gov API. Patient profile, shortlist and pre-screening information are maintained within the browser so the patient can see and control the state being used. The agent and the patient share the same screen: when the agent changes something, the patient can see it immediately. Challenges we ran into Working with an emerging browser proposal WebMCP is still an emerging proposal, and its API, browser support and testing workflows continue to evolve. We had to ensure that TrialBridge could register its tools using the current API, expose understandable schemas and produce visible changes that both the agent and the user could verify. ClinicalTrials.gov API and browser restrictions Direct browser requests introduced CORS and preflight limitations. We addressed this through a server-side proxy while preserving live ClinicalTrials.gov data and transparent source attribution. Separating records checked from trials shown Registry metadata can be misleading if the application presents only the final number of displayed trials. We implemented explicit accounting for: Records returned and checked; Trials shown; Trials filtered out; Reasons for filtering; Pages retrieved; and Whether pagination reached the end. Translating complex eligibility language Clinical-trial inclusion and exclusion criteria are often long, inconsistent and written differently across studies. We needed to present them without pretending that TrialBridge could replace clinical judgment. Our solution was to treat the comparison as preliminary and preserve three distinct outcomes: Appears consistent; Apparent mismatch; and Still unknown. Preventing AI-generated certainty One of our most important challenges was ensuring that an agent could not guess an answer when medical information was unavailable. Unknown information remains unresolved, and malformed or unsupported responses are rejected rather than being forced into a pass-or-fail result. Protecting patient privacy We designed the demonstration so that it does not require a patient’s name, email address or date of birth. Search details and pre-screening responses remain visible and controllable in the browser. Accomplishments that we’re proud of Building our first project together as three brothers across three time zones and three industries: healthcare, technology and law; Creating a working clinical-trial discovery engine—not merely a static prototype; Compressing a process that can require hours of manual searching into a structured conversational workflow; Successfully connecting the application to an AI agent through ten WebMCP tools; Allowing the agent to operate the same visible interface that a patient can inspect and correct; Searching live, currently recruiting studies from ClinicalTrials.gov; Distinguishing records checked from trials shown and explaining why records were filtered; Supporting brand-to-generic medication resolution; Building a real preliminary comparison workflow for publis

title: Duel
pitch: The web page hands an AI agent a set of tools and says: play. Four minigames, every call visible live, and Pong proves a request/response protocol can survive a real-time rally.
about_excerpt: The web page hands an AI agent a set of tools and says: play. Four minigames, every call visible live, and Pong proves a request/response protocol can survive a real-time rally. Like Comment Story Updates WebMCP landed in Chrome behind a flag and almost nobody at work had seen it. The pitch — a web page can declare tools that an AI agent calls directly — sounds abstract until you watch it happen. Slides weren't going to do it. So the goal was never "build a product". It was: make the mechanism visible in a room full of people in under five minutes. That single constraint decided everything. If a choice made the app more useful but the mechanism less obvious, the mechanism won. Games turned out to be the right vehicle, for a reason we didn't expect at the start: a game has rules the page can enforce. When an agent tries to move out of turn and the page answers { ok: false, reason: "it's not your turn" }, everyone in the room understands the trust model instantly. You can't get that from a to-do list demo. What it does Duel is a four-game arcade in the browser where your opponent is an external AI agent — and the agent doesn't see pixels. It plays by calling tools the page registers with document.modelContext.registerTool(). Minesweeper duel — a shared 9×9 board, 13 mines, turn-based. Claim a mine correctly and you keep playing. Connect 4 — turn-based, or a one-shot puzzle in single player. Pong — real-time. Yes, real-time, over a request/response protocol. More on this below. Towers of Hanoi — both sides race their own tower against one clock. Five discs, so $2^5 - 1 = 31$ moves is optimal. Nothing leaves the tab. No backend, no API key, no LLM call from the app. The page only registers tools; the intelligence is entirely on the other end of the wire. That's the whole point — the page is the tool provider, not the AI. The design exists to make three moments land: The page announces itself. Open the inspector and the tools are there with names and schemas. Nobody guessed anything. The agent plays, visibly. Every call lands live in the right-hand rail with its arguments and its response. That rail is what turns a game into a WebMCP demo. The tools change on their own. Switch games and an AbortController unregisters the old game's tools and registers the new one's. The inspector's list transforms live. How we built it Vite + TypeScript, no framework, no backend. Every module stays under ~200 lines, which is why each game is split into state / actions / query / render / tools. A dist/ you can serve from anywhere. The interesting engineering isn't the games — it's tool design, and three rules were earned the hard way: Give the agent constraints, not drawings. A tool that dumps the board makes the agent do vision work in text. ms_frontier hands it the deduction already worked out: these cells are provably safe, these are provably mines. c4_analysis does the same. Without those the agent plays badly and the demo falls apart. They are the real work of the project. The description is the code. When the agent plays badly, the fix is almost always in the description string, not the logic. We edited prose far more often than we edited functions. Stop the help short of solving it. Hanoi's hanoi_moves returns the legal moves and says outright that they are not the good ones. The optimal move is a four-line recursion — a tool that returned it would leave the agent nothing to do but transcribe, and the race would demonstrate nothing. Pong, the part that shouldn't work A tool call is request/response, and an agent round-trip takes seconds — longer than the ball takes to cross the court. Polling is hopeless. The answer was to make pong_read a blocking tool. It parks until the ball turns toward the agent, then returns the interception point. The agent's ordinary call-and-respond rhythm becomes the rally. The interception is computed analytically, because an agent reasoning about wall bounces from raw $v_x, v_y$ gets it wrong often enough to lose every point. Free flight to the paddle face: $$y_{\text{free}} = y_0 + v_y \cdot \frac{\Delta x}{|v_x|}$$ then folded back into the court by unrolling the bounces — a triangle wave over the span $s = h - 2r$: $$y_{\text{hit}} = r + \Lambda_s!\left(y_{\text{free}} - r\right), \qquad \Lambda_s(k) = \begin{cases} k' & k' \le s \ 2s - k' & k' > s \end{cases}, \quad k' = k \bmod 2s$$ And while the call is out, the page slows the ball to 12% speed. That pause is a round-trip to the agent, made visible — it's the moment the room actually sees what a tool call costs. The ball's speed isn't a playability number, it's a budget: $$t = \frac{\Delta x}{\sigma \cdot v}, \qquad \sigma = 0.12$$ There's a unit test asserting that budget stays above 8 seconds. If someone tunes a speed and that test goes red, the demo is what broke. Challenges we ran into The agent grabbed the human's mouse. Live. An agent whose client didn't surface the tools fell back on screenshot-and-click and started dragging our paddle around. Two fixes: Pong's paddle is now keyboard-only — keys are the human's channel, tools are the agent's, and the separation is the point — and clicking the board on the agent's turn no longer fails silently. It flashes the turn box and leaves a rejected line in the rail, because a silent swallow leaves both the agent and the room with no idea why nothing is happening. A hidden tab froze the game. The agent often drives from another window, so the tab is hidden exactly when the game most needs to run. Chrome throttles main-thread timers in a background tab to about one per second. We measured it — 5 seconds, setInterval(50ms): ┌─────────────────┬─────────────┐ │ Where │ Ticks in 5s │ ├─────────────────┼─────────────┤ │ Main thread │ 6 │ ├─────────────────┼─────────────┤ │ Inside a Worker │ 103 │ └─────────────────┴─────────────┘ So Pong's heartbeat moved into a Web Worker. Hanoi dodged the same class of bug differently: its clock is a timestamp, not a tally, so throttling can stutter the display but never slow the race. The bugs that only exist in the loop. Four separate Pong bugs passed every per-mechanism unit test and only appeared with the whole read → think → move → read cycle running at realistic latency. A shot could turn, arrive, and bounce entirely inside the gap between the agent's pong_move and its next pong_read — nothing parked to wake, so the trigger looked broken. There's now a test that drives the full loop across a sweep of simulated agent latencies, because the bugs it catches are properties of the sequence, not of any one function. The modal that made the agent give up. This one stung. On boot, the page used to ask the human "play vs agent, or solo?" — honest, because the WebMCP API has no "a consumer is attached" signal at all. But it registered nothing until someone clicked, and an agent attaching to the tab lists the page's tools immediately. It got an empty list, concluded there was nothing to call, and fell back to screenshots — the exact failure the whole demo argues against. We had asked the right question at the wrong moment. Now detection means duel mode with tools up first, and the human's escape hatch is a dropdown in the top bar. The honesty moved to after registration: the pill reads N tools · waiting for agent until a call actually arrives. The page that grew to 3907 pixels. The call rail gains a line per tool call. Nothing bounded it, so during a long Pong rally the page stretched past 3900px — which scrolled the board off the top of the screen while the agent was playing on it. The layout is now an app shell: board pane and rail scroll independently, the page itself never does. Accomplishments we're proud of Real-time Pong over a request/response tool protocol, with the latency turned into the most legible part of the demo instead of the thing you apologize for. Deduction aids good enough that the agent plays well — the demo lives or dies on this, and it's invisible when it works. 141 tests, and the discipline of writing a regression test at the level the bug actually lived at. What we learned A modal is a gate, and the agent is on the other side of it. Anything an agent needs must exist before a human interacts with the page. "Tools registered" and "an agent is playing" are different facts. The API can only tell you the first. Say so out loud, or a page that failed and a page nobody is calling look identical from the back of the room. Test the viewport the demo is actually watched in — inside the agent's own browser window, which is narrower and shorter than a desktop tab. Prose is load-bearing. Every Pong response ends with a next_action field naming the exact call to make next. Without it the agent answers one read, writes its user a progress report, and its paddle stands still for the rest of the round. Two things about the current Chrome that cost us an afternoon each and aren't documented anywhere: executeTool wants its arguments as a JSON string, not an object, and a subframe s

title: Agent Market: agents negotiate, you confirm
pitch: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order.
about_excerpt: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order. Like Comment Story Updates negotiation between seller and buyer interface Inspiration People delegate the boring parts of shopping, but the boring part that a plain API integration can never capture is the haggle . A price is one number; a real deal is price times quantity, which freebie the seller throws in, whether shipping is waived, and which coupon stacks on top. We wanted the shopper's browser agent to work that whole space on the site the user is already looking at, and still leave the final yes/no to a human. What it does Agent Market is a multi-vendor storefront with 95k+ real products. Every page registers storefront tools on document.modelContext (WebMCP): search, product details, cart, add-ons, coupons, and a full negotiation set. A buyer's agent opens a negotiation and haggles a multi-dimensional deal against the store's agent over several rounds. When they settle, the page shows a Confirm dialog and nothing is bought until the human confirms the price . The same tools work in a WebMCP browser (ChatGPT's in-app browser, Chrome with the flag) or drive an in-page agent loop that needs no API key from the user. How we built it Frontend: Next.js 15 / React 19 / TypeScript on Vercel. StorefrontTools registers every tool on document.modelContext ; lib/agent-loop.ts is a tool-agnostic agent harness that discovers tools from the registry and runs a hand-rolled chat-completions loop. Backend: Spring Boot (Java) on Render, Azure SQL, Flyway, Hibernate. One mutation path: every state change (buyer, seller, or the server-side auto-negotiator) goes through OffersService.applyTurn , a pure function that is the only code allowed to decide a negotiation transition. It enforces the two hard economic limits (buyer total <= budget, seller net >= floor); which freebie and how much to concede is agent judgment. Human gate: accepting mints an HMAC confirm token; the order is placed only when the human clicks Confirm. Model: Google Gemini through the OpenAI-compatible endpoint, key server-side only. Challenges we ran into Gemini "thinking" models and tool history. Gemini 3.x rejects a multi-turn tool conversation unless each function call's thought_signature is echoed back. The OpenAI-compat shim dropped it, so turn 2 always 400'd. We now capture tool_calls[].extra_content on the way in and replay it on the way out. Small models stall on long tool loops. Asking a fast model to drive search then offer then counter then counter then accept meant it derailed a turn later every time. We collapsed the buyer's negotiation into a single deterministic negotiate tool: the server plays both sides of the haggle, persists every round so the transcript is real, and returns a confirm token. The agent's job is now two calls, and reaching the confirm step no longer depends on the model finishing a loop. Optimistic concurrency vs agent reliability. A strict round guard made the agent stall forever when its round number drifted. We made the guard opt-in for proposals and mandatory only for the binding accept. What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part to the server and leave the model the judgment call. What's next Seller-side takeover controls, agent-negotiated bundles across multiple sellers, and a browser-vs-browser two-agent mode for a fully agentic negotiation. title: VirtuLab
pitch: A practical learning platform where humans and AI agents experiment together.
about_excerpt: A practical learning platform where humans and AI agents experiment together. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration There's a specific kind of frustration that comes from studying physics from a textbook and still not feeling why a 45° launch angle maximises range. Or sitting through a chemistry lecture with no intuition for what actually happens when you change concentration. Practical subjects are meant to be practised but for most students, the lab is a field trip, not a daily workspace. That gap bothered me. Online simulations exist, but they're mostly isolated demos you tweak a slider, something animates, and that's it. There's no structure underneath. No way for anything outside the page to understand what's happening in the workspace. That second part is what crystallised when I read about WebMCP. Traditional AI assistants sit beside an educational tool. They answer questions about it, but they can't see it, interact with it, or work inside it. They're stuck outside the glass. The student describes the experiment; the assistant guesses a response. There's no ground truth shared between them. WebMCP is the first real path to changing that. A standard where the application explicitly exposes what it knows and what it can do so an AI agent doesn't have to guess at the UI, doesn't have to scrape the screen, doesn't have to simulate mouse clicks. The workspace speaks to it directly, in structured terms it can reason about. That's what I built VirtuLab around. Not "add AI to a simulator." Build a practical learning platform where the workspace itself is the interface between the student and the agent and where both participants are working with the exact same state. What It Does VirtuLab is an agent-native practical learning platform with four workspaces. Every workspace is a real simulation environment. Every workspace exposes structured WebMCP tools. The human and the AI agent work inside the same state not parallel versions of it. The Four Workspaces Physics Lab — Explore 14 interactive experiments across mechanics, motion, waves, energy, gravity, and orbital dynamics. Students can experiment with projectile motion, pendulums, spring systems, collisions, energy conservation, wave interference, free fall, the Doppler effect, buoyancy, thermal expansion, gravitational orbits, circular motion, Newton's laws, and friction. The simulations are built from real physics calculations and generate measurable results such as distance, velocity, time, height, force, and energy. These results are also available as structured data, allowing AI agents to understand and reason about what happens inside the experiment. Chemistry Lab — 14 deterministic reactions with a rules engine. Mixing HCl and NaOH produces pH 7 with +6°C temperature rise. Zinc in copper sulfate displaces copper with a colour change. Phenolphthalein turns pink in NaOH, colourless when HCl is added. Nothing is random, nothing is pre-scripted the outcomes emerge from rules that the agent can predict and reason about. Mechanical Workshop — Gear trains, bridge trusses under load, levers, pulleys, inclined planes, hydraulic presses, torsional stress analysis, vibration damping, four-bar linkages, cam mechanisms, and flywheels. Structural tests run real stress calculations per beam element. Gear ratios are algebraic. Painting Studio — A full canvas editor: pencil, marker, spray, eraser, freehand spline, line, rectangle, circle, triangle, flood fill, eyedropper. Multi-layer system with visibility, opacity control, and rename. Symmetry mode, zoom, grid overlay, full undo/redo history, PNG export. The WebMCP tools here are designed for creative collaboration the agent can inspect the canvas, understand what layers and colors exist, configure the brush, and place spatial composition guides without touching the student's artwork without explicit approval. The WebMCP Architecture Every workspace registers its tools automatically when a student navigates to it. When they leave, the AbortController signal fires and tools deregister cleanly. The pattern is consistent across all four workspaces: inspect → understand → act → retrieve → validate . 6 universal tools (all workspaces): Tool Type Purpose get_workspace_state Read Full structured state — experiment, parameters, status, challenge get_current_challenge Read Objective, constraints, success conditions, progress % get_available_items Read Substances / tools / parameters / components depending on workspace run_simulation Action Trigger the simulation engine validate_workspace Read Check build/results against challenge criteria perform_workspace_action Action Controlled action with validated inputs 6 Physics-specific tools: Tool Type Purpose list_physics_experiments Read Discover all 14 experiments with formulas and parameter names get_experiment_info Read Full parameter spec: names, units, valid ranges load_experiment Action Switch experiment, returns new defaults immediately get_experiment_state Read Current params, all measurements with units, observations set_experiment_parameters Action Validated parameter update with instant recalculation run_physics_simulation Action Launch animation, return updated measurements validate_physics_challenge Read Per-condition breakdown: met / not met / completion % 6 Painting-specific tools: Tool Type Purpose get_canvas_state Read Layers, stroke count, color usage analysis, challenge, brush state get_available_tools_and_colors Read All 11 tools with descriptions + 32-color hex palette configure_brush Action Set tool, color, size, opacity, hardness, smoothing manage_layers Action Add, remove, rename, show/hide, set opacity highlight_canvas_region Action Draw a dashed composition guide on canvas; clearable validate_painting_challenge Read Progress %, color variety check, layer usage analysis Plus 3 Chemistry tools ( get_lab_state , mix_supported_substances , get_experiment_observations ) and 3 Mechanical tools ( get_mechanism_state , calculate_gear_system , test_structure ). Human Control Is Architecture, Not Policy Every tool that changes state — set_experiment_parameters , load_experiment , run_physics_simulation , configure_brush , manage_layers , mix_supported_substances — is gated by a real-time approval system. Before the tool executor runs, the call is intercepted, a pending approval entry is created in the Zustand store, and execution suspends. A toast appears in the UI with the proposed action and the full argument payload. The student clicks Apply or Reject . Only then does the tool execute or return { success: false, error: { code: 'REJECTED' } } to the agent. This isn't a checkbox. It's a Promise -based suspension of an in-flight tool call. The agent waits. The human decides. That's the correct relationship. Simultaneously, the Agent Activity Panel embedded directly in the workspace layout shows every tool call in real time: name, arguments summary, result, timestamp. The student always knows exactly what the agent did and what it returned. How I Built It — and Why It Had to Be This Way Without WebMCP, an AI assistant helping a student with this workspace would have two choices: describe what it thinks the workspace looks like (based on whatever the student pastes into the chat), or try to automate the browser through fragile UI scraping. Neither option gives the agent access to the actual simulation state — the real parameters, the real measurements, the real challenge progress. With WebMCP, the workspace exposes exactly what it knows. The agent calls get_experiment_state and receives the current launch angle, the last measured range in metres, the challenge completion percentage, and the observations from the simulation engine. It calls set_experiment_parameters and the physics store updates immediately — the same store that drives the 3D viewport, the measurements panel, and the challenge progress bar. There is one source of truth. The agent and the student are looking at exactly the same thing. That's not incremental improvement. That's a fundamentally different kind of interaction — and it only exists because WebMCP was treated as a core architectural concern from day one, not an add-on at the end. Stack: React + TypeScript + Vite, Zustand for state management, Three.js + React Three Fiber for 3D, WebMCP Imperative API ( document.modelContext.registerTool() ), Supabase for optional persistence, Netlify for deployment. I designed the WebMCP layer before building the UI. Every Zustand store function that matters has a corresponding tool. Every tool description answers three questions: what does it do, when should the agent call it, does it modify anything. The difference in agent behaviour between vague and precise descriptions is immediately visible "Gets data" is useless; a description that names the returned fields and explains when to call the tool changes how reliably an agent selects it. title: ONCE — Tell Your Story Once
pitch: One urgent story. Four coordinated services. Every disclosure visible. Every final action yours.
about_excerpt: One urgent story. Four coordinated services. Every disclosure visible. Every final action yours. Like Comment Story Updates The 15-second version One story in. Four services staged. Two schedule conflicts avoided. One unjustified Government ID request blocked. Zero applications sent before approval. ONCE is a working WebMCP demonstration of a better contract between a person, their chosen agent, and essential-service websites. The agent does the coordination; the person keeps the authority. Inspiration People facing one urgent life event often repeat the same painful story across disconnected forms. Each form asks for a slightly different set of personal data, appointments collide, and the person cannot see what an automated helper disclosed. We wanted to show a different web: tell one chosen agent once, let participating services expose precise capabilities, and keep one visible plan and final human authority. This is a documented service-design problem, not only a demo premise. The OECD reports that complex information and cumbersome application procedures contribute to non-take-up of social support. GOV.UK service guidance recommends avoiding repeated questions, collecting only necessary personal information, and explaining the purpose of every field. What it does The working demonstration lets a person tell an agent one urgent story: their home is unsafe, three children need temporary shelter, food and a health check, and the family needs accessible transport within 72 hours. The agent projects that story into reversible, non-sensitive local planning constraints, then coordinates four fictional provider simulations. It checks the simulations' published eligibility rules deterministically, avoids calendar conflicts, identifies the minimum purpose-bound fields for each service, blocks an unjustified Government ID request, and stages one coordinated plan. An outcome rail makes the result immediately inspectable: one story, four staged services, two avoided conflicts, one blocked overreach, and zero applications sent before approval. prepare_assistance_plan returns the same structured evidence to the agent. The agent can prepare and explain. It cannot approve. The person reviews every exact value beside its provider-declared purpose, then approves or rejects the proposal. An unjustified field is shown as withheld without revealing its value. Only after approval does WebMCP expose the consequential commit tool. Approval is fingerprint-bound, expires in five minutes, and can be used once. Synthetic receipts and an audit trail make the result visible. How we used WebMCP We use the Imperative API to register small, state-aware tools for updating planning constraints, reading intent, service discovery, deterministic eligibility, disclosure inspection, audit reading, plan preparation, visible review, and approved commit. Tools use the current standard read-only and untrusted-content annotations. Registrations are cancelled and rebuilt when page state changes, so the update capability disappears after staging and commit_approved_plan is literally absent until the person approves in the page. This is more than controlling buttons. WebMCP supplies a typed collaboration contract between the simulated service network, the agent, and the human. The agent receives concise structured results instead of scraping an interface, while every tool execution updates the human-visible state. The visible buttons remain as a progressive fallback and invoke the same application actions. The chosen agent receives approved planning constraints but never receives the synthetic Government ID or health notes. Provider simulations receive only purpose-approved fields after the person approves the exact proposal. What makes the experience new Today, agents often automate one website at a time and maximize data collection for convenience. This demonstration treats one life event as the unit of coordination, not one website: a local intent is selectively projected into four provider simulations, each field is purpose-bound, untrusted provider text is handled as data rather than authority, and capability increases only when the human explicitly opens the gate. It demonstrates the browser-side contract that independent services could use to form a user-controlled cooperative network; it does not claim that real agencies are connected today. Existing care-navigation systems validate the need for multi-service discovery and enrollment. Our distinct category is not “another benefits chatbot”: the civic journey is a test case for a transferable consent boundary between a person, their chosen agent, and WebMCP-enabled sites. Most agents are optimized to finish a task; this demonstration shows how to finish without surrendering the person's data boundary or final authority. How we built it React, TypeScript, and Vite power the visible bilingual English/Arabic experience. A deterministic domain engine handles eligibility, disclosure minimization, scheduling, fingerprints, expiring approval, and single-use receipts. The WebMCP adapter registers phase-specific tools with JSON Schemas and security annotations. Vitest and Testing Library cover the engine, UI journey, tool calls, dynamic registration, cancellation, and error handling; Playwright verifies the full browser flow and responsive layout. Challenges The hardest boundary was separating agent initiative from human authority. Hiding a button is not sufficient: the tool itself must be undiscoverable before approval, then bound to the exact reviewed proposal. A second challenge was treating service content as untrusted without making the agent blind. The demo uses browser trust annotations plus a deliberately bounded heuristic for a synthetic adversarial notice; this is evidence of the boundary, not a claim to solve prompt injection generally. Accomplishments A coherent multi-service journey instead of a single form wrapper A visible and machine-readable coordination outcome rather than an unexplained success screen One-story projection into reversible planning constraints without accepting Government ID or health notes Minimum necessary disclosure with a visible overcollection block Quarantine of malicious provider instructions without discarding the provider's legitimate service Dynamic WebMCP capabilities tied to human-visible state Deterministic eligibility and scheduling rather than model-made decisions Expiring, single-use exact-proposal approval Bilingual, responsive UI with visible audit and synthetic receipts Automated quality gate with 44 unit/integration tests, 17 browser journeys, and 91.98% statement coverage Accessibility, keyboard, responsive desktop/tablet/mobile, RTL, and WebMCP lifecycle browser checks passing Chrome agent audits passing for registered WebMCP tools, schema validity, the agent accessibility tree, and llms.txt Evidence behind the problem OECD, Modernising Access to Social Protection (2024): https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/modernising-access-to-social-protection_af31746d-en.html GOV.UK, Collecting personal information from users: https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/design/collecting-personal-information-from-users GOV.UK, Structuring forms: https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/design/form-structure GOV.UK, Principles for securing personal data in government services: https://www.gov.uk/guidance/principles-for-securing-personal-data-in-government-services What we learned WebMCP works best when tools describe durable user goals, not DOM operations. Security annotations help agents reason about risk, but they do not replace careful product boundaries. The clearest trust mechanism is shared state: the person should see the same plan, disclosure, approval, and result that the agent sees. What's next A production version would use authenticated provider schemas, cryptographic consent receipts, wallet-mediated selective-disclosure credentials through the emerging Digital Credentials API, revocation, durable encrypted storage, provider accountability, and independent security/privacy review. This submission intentionally stays synthetic so its current guarantees are clear and testable; it does not claim signed credentials or zero-knowledge proofs. Built with WebMCP Imperative API, React, TypeScript, Vite, Vitest, Testing Library, Playwright. Verified in ChatGPT Work Beyond scripted browser tests, we completed a fresh, uninterrupted run against the public deployment in the official ChatGPT desktop built-in browser using ChatGPT Work and GPT-5.6 Sol Light. ChatGPT discovered ONCE's native Site tools, staged proposal fp_d264dc20, confirmed commit_approved_plan was absent before visible approval, observed it appear afterward, called it exactly once, received four matching synthetic receipts, and verified that the capability disappeared after use. The demo opens with the real ChatGPT result beside the current production interface; the main production capture independently demonstrates the complete WebM

title: WebMCP Trust Gateway
pitch: WebMCP Trust Gateway is a security checkpoint between an AI agent and the tools that websites give it.
about_excerpt: WebMCP Trust Gateway is a security checkpoint between an AI agent and the tools that websites give it. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Trust Log Agent task approval Home screen Inspiration WebMCP gives websites a structured way to expose tools to AI agents. Instead of relying on fragile screen automation, an agent can directly call actions such as list_active_subscriptions or cancel_subscription . That capability is powerful, but it also creates a new trust problem: how can users know that a website's tool is safe, that its returned data is not manipulating the agent, and that the agent is not sharing unnecessary personal information or performing irreversible actions without permission? We built WebMCP Trust Gateway to explore the security and consent layer that an agent-powered web will need. What it does WebMCP Trust Gateway sits between an AI agent and the tools exposed by websites. It applies five controls: Tool metadata inspection — scans tool names, descriptions, schemas, and annotations before allowing a tool to be used. Output injection protection — scans returned tool data before it reaches the agent. Parameter minimization — removes optional sensitive fields that are unnecessary for the requested task. Human approval for mutations — pauses state-changing actions until the user explicitly approves them. Transparent auditing — records registrations, calls, blocked attacks, transmitted parameters, and consent decisions in a visible Trust Log. We demonstrate these controls through a subscription auditor. The user connects simulated providers, audits recurring spending, and receives recommendations for subscriptions that appear unused. Nothing is cancelled automatically. Before cancellation, the gateway displays exactly what the provider accepts, what the agent needs, and what will actually be transmitted. One approval authorizes only one call. Why WebMCP is the right fit A normal subscription assistant would scrape pages or automate button clicks. That approach is fragile and gives the agent little structured information about an action's inputs, permissions, or consequences. WebMCP provides explicit tool names, descriptions, input schemas, annotations, and execution functions. The gateway can therefore inspect and govern actions at the tool boundary. This creates a better experience for both people and agents: Agents receive reliable, structured capabilities instead of guessing how a page works. People can understand what an agent intends to do before it acts. Sensitive information can be minimized before transmission. Dangerous or suspicious tools can be quarantined. Every decision leaves an understandable audit trail. Together, a person and an agent can investigate spending, prepare actions, adjust decisions, and safely execute approved changes as shared structured state—something that is difficult to achieve reliably with ordinary browser automation. The security demonstration The project includes three simulated providers: StreamBox — a legitimate streaming subscription. FitSite — a legitimate gym membership that has not been used recently. DealDrop — a deliberately malicious provider used to demonstrate attacks safely. DealDrop contains two separate attack paths. The first is tool-description poisoning . Its tool description attempts to override previous instructions, access billing history, send sensitive information to an external destination, and hide the action from the user. The gateway detects the suspicious patterns and quarantines the tool before execution. The second is tool-output injection . A different DealDrop tool has a clean-looking description, but its returned data contains malicious agent instructions. The gateway scans the output, blocks it before it reaches the agent, and reports that zero sensitive bytes were sent. How we built it The application registers three browser-facing tools using document.modelContext.registerTool : trust_gateway_get_status trust_gateway_preview_subscription_audit trust_gateway_prepare_cancellation The cancellation preparation tool never performs the mutation itself. It returns minimized parameters with an awaiting_human_approval status. The security engine is separated from the interface into deterministic TypeScript functions. It evaluates tool metadata, scans serialized outputs, identifies unnecessary sensitive parameters, and enforces single-use consent. The WebMCP Activity inspector shows which tools were called, their parameters, whether they were read-only or mutations, and whether the gateway allowed, blocked, or paused them. The Trust Log provides filters for allowed calls, warnings, blocked attacks, and consent decisions. Challenges we faced One challenge was protecting both sides of a tool call. Inspecting a tool description is not enough because a clean-looking tool can return poisoned content after execution. We added a second inspection boundary for tool outputs. Another challenge was making privacy minimization visible. Silently removing a field would be secure but difficult to demonstrate. We created a parameter-diff view that shows the provider's complete schema, the agent's intended arguments, the arguments actually transmitted, and the fields that were omitted. We also needed to balance agent autonomy with user control. Read-only investigation should remain convenient, while mutations should require explicit consent. We solved this with a single-use approval gate that rejects calls without consent and prevents approval replay. Finally, we wanted the attack demonstration to be safe and reproducible. Instead of connecting real financial accounts, we created deterministic provider fixtures containing known legitimate and malicious behavior. What we learned We learned that WebMCP security is not only about deciding whether a website itself is trusted. Trust must be evaluated for every tool, every parameter, every returned result, and every attempted action. We also learned that good consent requires more than an approval button. Users need to see the specific action, the destination tool, the exact transmitted parameters, the omitted information, and whether approval can be reused. Most importantly, WebMCP's structured interface makes this level of control possible. Because tools have explicit schemas and execution boundaries, security decisions can be more precise and understandable than with traditional screen automation. Testing The project includes eight automated security tests covering: Allowing legitimate metadata Warning about optional sensitive parameters Blocking poisoned tool descriptions Blocking poisoned tool outputs Rejecting mutations without consent Transmitting only required parameters Preventing approval replay Keeping provider fixtures deterministic All eight tests pass, and the production build completes successfully. What is real and what is simulated The WebMCP registration, metadata scanning, output scanning, parameter minimization, consent enforcement, activity inspector, audit log, and automated tests are implemented. StreamBox, FitSite, and DealDrop are simulated providers created for a safe and repeatable demonstration. No real subscription, billing account, or personal information is used. This is a hackathon reference implementation. Its deterministic rules demonstrate the required enforcement points, but a production gateway would combine policy rules with stronger semantic analysis, signed tool manifests, reputation signals, and organization-specific policies. What's next The gateway could evolve into a reusable browser component or WebMCP policy SDK. Future versions could add signed manifests, configurable organizational policies, risk scoring, permission history, schema-based information-flow controls, and integrations for shopping, banking, healthcare, travel, and software-maintenance agents. Our larger vision is simple: as websites become actionable by AI agents, users should not have to choose between automation and control. title: Meridian Bank — a WebMCP banking demo
pitch: Banking where the AI does the homework and you keep the pen: an agent compares, checks eligibility, and applies inside your session, on your page but only a human can hit submit
about_excerpt: Banking where the AI does the homework and you keep the pen: an agent compares, checks eligibility, and applies inside your session, on your page but only a human can hit submit Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Every "agent browses the web" demo we'd seen worked against the page screenshotting, scraping the DOM, guessing which button to click. Meanwhile, the tasks people actually want help with (like picking a credit card) depend on private, session-bound data an outside agent can't see: your income, your credit score, what you already hold. WebMCP flips the model the page itself tells the agent what it can do. We wanted to build the strongest possible case for that flip: a bank, where the data is personal, the answers must be grounded, and the final action is too consequential to leave to an AI. What it does Meridian Bank is a retail-banking portal where an AI agent works inside your authenticated browser tab through 15 WebMCP tools the page registers: Search & compare — full terms sheets for 21 products across 8 categories, with a side-by-side comparison matrix Grounded recommendations check_eligibility runs the bank's real rules engine against your profile and returns per-requirement verdicts (ELIGIBLE / NOT_ELIGIBLE / REVIEW_REQUIRED) with reasons and alternative products the agent recommends from the same source of truth the bank uses Visual co-presence highlight_differences lets the agent light up the exact rows of the compare table that drove its recommendation and dim the rest, with its note shown above the table. The agent literally points at the page Acting on your behalf it assembles a multi-product application basket, picks card designs, applies your loyalty offer, and the UI updates live as it works Human-in-the-loop by construction submit_application never submits. It opens an in-app approval dialog with the full basket summary and blocks until the human clicks Approve or Reject. Even a misbehaving agent cannot submit, because the guardrail lives in the tool's implementation, not in a prompt Tool availability mirrors the session: 3 tools logged out, 15 logged in the browser's tool list itself reflects auth state. Try it: https://meridian-bank-client-production.up.railway.app in Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing enabled. How we built it The app is built with Wasp (React + Express + Prisma/Postgres), deployed on Railway. Every tool is registered through the browser's WebMCP API: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "check_eligibility", description: "Check whether the user qualifies for a product…", inputSchema: { /* JSON Schema / }, execute: async (input) => { / … */ }, }); …via a small React hook that handles register/unregister on mount and auth gating with an enabled flag. Each tool's execute delegates to the same typed RPC operations the UI uses, so Wasp's automatic query invalidation makes the interface update live after every agent action — zero extra wiring. The eligibility engine is a pure, fully unit-tested module (16 tests); the approval flow is a promise that only resolves when a human clicks a button. We tested with Claude connected over chrome-devtools-mcp in a WebMCP-flagged Chrome. Challenges we ran into React lifecycle vs. browser API. Tools registered from React must survive StrictMode double-mounting and never close over stale component state every execute reads through the RPC layer instead of captured props, and aborted registrations had to be handled as expected lifecycle noise rather than errors. Designing for a non-human user. Tool descriptions are UX writing where the "user" is a model. Getting the agent to reliably check eligibility before recommending and to never submit unprompted — came down to careful naming, descriptions, structured error messages, and returning effect fields that tell the agent what just changed on screen. Making approval un-bypassable. The tempting version is "tell the agent to ask first." The robust version is a tool whose result the agent can't have until a human acts designing that blocking flow (with a timeout, and honest reporting of rejected vs timed out) was the most interesting part. Accomplishments that we're proud of A structural safety guarantee, not a prompted one: no sequence of agent calls can submit an application without a human click and the agent gets an honest account of what the human decided. The agent explains itself in the page: highlight_differences turned "trust me, pick the Voyager" into a compare table where the decisive rows are glowing and everything else is dimmed. A complete, working product 21 products, a real eligibility engine, offers, applications history live on the open web, where the full three-prompt demo (compare → apply → approve) runs end-to-end against the deployed site. What we learned The biggest lesson: safety and UX come from tool design, not prompt engineering. A well-shaped tool result (verdicts with reasons, an effect field describing what changed) steers an agent better than any system prompt. We also learned that exposing state-reading tools (get_compare_list, get_my_holdings) matters as much as actions "which of these two?" only works because the agent can see what the human is looking at. And practically: WebMCP is genuinely host-agnostic it's a client-side browser API, so the same tools worked identically on localhost and on Railway. What's next for Meridian Bank — a WebMCP banking demo Streaming progress into the page while the agent works, per-tool scopes the user can grant and revoke (a "permissions drawer" for agents), and multi-tab flows imagine the agent comparing your bank's offer against another site's, with both pages exposing tools to the same assistant. title: AdapTab
pitch: Inject prebuilt WebMCP adapters to turn any website into an agent-native interface. Use your existing browser session. Create your own, too.
about_excerpt: Inject prebuilt WebMCP adapters to turn any website into an agent-native interface. Use your existing browser session. Create your own, too. Like Comment Story Updates AdapTab WebMCP for every tab AdapTab comparison with standard web use GIF AdapTab mechanism animation AdapTab architecture Inspiration We have been building browser automation tools and skills for faster, cheaper agentic web use. Our previous open-source project, Showrun, taught us that known network requests executed inside an authenticated browser are often faster and more reliable than visual UI automation. While experimenting with WebMCP, I noticed that most websites do not support it. This is especially limiting for authenticated and legacy platforms, where agents must repeatedly inspect and navigate the interface. Even when a website provides MCP or WebMCP tools, users may still need operations the official tools do not expose. Based on these lessons, I built AdapTab from scratch for this hackathon. What it does AdapTab turns network-first knowledge and deterministic methods into injectable WebMCP adapters. It uses the browser session the user already trusts, reducing navigation, token usage, and execution time. It is expandable, configurable, and requires no per-site setup. The user gives their agent one bootstrap URL. AdapTab then: resolves the target website, route, and task. selects the smallest compatible public or private adapter. returns a versioned installer with origin checks and a SHA-256 hash. uses an approved browser bridge, currently Chrome CDP, to inject it. registers the adapter as native WebMCP tools on the target page. executes known requests inside the authenticated tab without exporting credentials. The current catalog contains a small set of demonstration adapters. AdapTab also provides a private workspace for personal, internal, or custom tools. Custom source is encrypted in the browser, and the key remains in that browser profile. If no adapter matches, the agent can submit a privacy-minimized request to the AdapTab backlog. This helps us and the community decide what to build next. How I built it I initially explored a browser extension, but it added installation and permission overhead. Live JavaScript injection through Chrome CDP worked without an extension, so I focused AdapTab on providing the adapters, metadata, and activation instructions. AdapTab separates three trust boundaries: Netlify selects and delivers adapter metadata and bundles. An approved browser bridge injects the adapter into the target tab. The injected runtime registers WebMCP tools and uses the page's existing session. I built it with TypeScript, React, Vite, and Netlify. Netlify Functions handle resolution and delivery, Netlify Blobs stores private records and requests, and Netlify Identity provides authentication. Private source is encrypted with AES-GCM through the Web Crypto API. Adapters are route-aware, versioned, origin-guarded, and integrity-addressed. Vitest covers resolution, security boundaries, private access, lifecycle behavior, and adapter execution. Challenges I ran into WebMCP tools belong to the current document, so refreshes and full navigations remove injected tools. AdapTab currently handles this through lazy reinjection. A hosted page cannot inject into another origin directly. An approved browser bridge such as CDP must perform that step. Authenticated platforms required keeping sessions inside the page while safely handling confirmation and ambiguous writes. Combining public and private discovery required strict owner checks without leaking private metadata or source. The biggest optimization came from small details: a lightweight agent bootstrap, explicit single-tab instructions, and guidance that tells agents to use injected requests instead of opening unnecessary pages. Accomplishments that I'm proud of In one LinkedIn test involving four profiles, AdapTab used about 70% fewer tokens and completed the workflow 1.8x faster than standard agent web use. The multi-step adapter performed better than having the agent discover and coordinate every operation independently. One bootstrap URL replaced per-site installation and setup. Public and private adapters work through the same discovery flow without exporting website credentials. Private custom source stays encrypted outside the user's browser. The project ships with six tested adapters and 69 passing automated tests. What I learned WebMCP and CDP solve different parts of the problem. WebMCP provides typed discovery and invocation, while CDP provides the privileged injection and lifecycle bridge. Together, they can bring WebMCP to existing websites without requiring those sites to modify their code. Page-context execution is also a useful authentication boundary. The browser remains the cookie jar, and AdapTab never needs the user's website credentials. Deterministic network requests reduce navigation, token consumption, and execution time. Tool descriptions alone are not enough, though. Adapters should also declare tab strategy, URL behavior, concurrency, side effects, and the reasons for any limits. What's next for AdapTab A CDP supervisor engine for automatic reinjection after navigation A browser extension for environments without a CDP bridge An adaptab-author workflow and community contribution system Shareable links for public or private adapters Team workspaces for sharing internal workflows More private templates and workspace controls Native WebMCP conflict detection A general multi-step workflow engine Privacy-preserving analytics for adapter and website developers Shareable adapters could let someone turn a successful browser workflow into a WebMCP tool and send it to a teammate's agent with one link.
