title: Median Viz
pitch: Data visualization is designed for humans, making it hard for AI agents to understand what actions are supported in a page. I built Median Viz using LinkedIn demographics to explore a different model
about_excerpt: Data visualization is designed for humans, making it hard for AI agents to understand what actions are supported in a page. I built Median Viz using LinkedIn demographics to explore a different model Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration One day, while my wife and I were watching a video from USAFacts, she wondered aloud how the animated data visualizations in the video were created. I started explaining the usual process—acquiring and cleaning the data, processing it, and then building dashboards with the right dimensions, filters, and pivots. Halfway through the explanation, I realized it might be easier to just build an example application that shows her how they work. That became Median Viz . I started with a few animated Plotly visualizations—a pie chart, a bar race, and a U.S. map—then turned them into a small web application, open-sourced it on GitHub, and deployed it on Vercel. When the WebMCP Challenge was announced, my cofounder and I were also exploring how to analyze LinkedIn Ad Set demographics for client campaigns. The two ideas suddenly connected. Instead of asking an AI agent to infer what a visualization means from the page alone, what if the application could tell the agent exactly what data, analytical capabilities, constraints, and current state were available? That became the /studio experience in Median Viz: a workspace designed so that humans and agents can understand and work on the same analysis through WebMCP. What it does Data visualization tools are usually built as human-operated dashboards for exploring complex data across different dimensions. They can be powerful, but they are also difficult for AI agents to understand because the agent has to infer which filters, dimensions, metrics, and actions the application actually supports. I built Median Viz Studio using LinkedIn Ad Set demographics as the example domain. Through WebMCP , the application exposes its analytical capabilities directly to ChatGPT. The agent can discover what dimensions are available, understand the current workspace, configure an analysis, apply filters, animate changes over time, and explain the results in plain language. The key idea is that the human and the agent are not working in separate experiences. They operate on the same live workspace . A filter selected by the human immediately becomes context for the agent, while a WebMCP action taken by the agent is reflected in the same controls and visualization the human sees. How we built it Median Viz is a Next.js/React application using Plotly for interactive and animated visualizations. The /studio route models a LinkedIn-style B2B audience analysis workflow using the supported demographic dimensions, including Job Function, Seniority, Industry, Company, Company Size, Region, and others. For the public demo, I use representative LinkedIn B2B audience-performance data for a fictional company, Northstar Media , with metrics such as CPC, CTR, impressions, spend, and conversions. The Studio exposes seven semantic tools through WebMCP : three read-only tools that let the agent inspect the dataset, workspace, and current result, and four guarded mutation tools that let it configure an analysis, apply filters, control animation, or reset the view. These tools operate on the same underlying workspace capabilities used by the human interface rather than manipulating Plotly or DOM elements directly. The application also preserves domain rules. For example, LinkedIn demographic dimensions are reported independently, so the system will reject an invalid request such as comparing Job Function directly with Seniority rather than inventing an unsupported intersection. Time-series animation is represented as shared workspace state, and the Agent Activity panel makes WebMCP-driven changes visible to the user. Challenges we ran into One of the main challenges came directly from a problem we were already thinking about in our startup: how do you keep human and agent actions in sync when both can change the same workspace? I wanted a filter or view selected by the user to immediately become context for the agent, while also making sure an agent action did not overwrite a newer human change. There were also important domain constraints to preserve. LinkedIn demographic dimensions are reported independently, so an analysis such as Job Function × Seniority is not valid. I wanted Median Viz to reject requests the underlying data cannot support rather than letting the agent invent an answer. Similarly, derived metrics such as CPC and CTR need to be calculated from aggregated values rather than by averaging row-level ratios. Finally, because this is a public demo based on a problem we encounter with real customer campaigns, privacy was a hard requirement. The public Studio uses representative demo data and fictional identities , so no real customer information is exposed. Accomplishments that we're proud of The accomplishment I’m most proud of is getting to a working experience where a human and an agent can genuinely collaborate in the same analytical workspace . A user can change a filter manually, ChatGPT can immediately understand that new state, and an agent action is reflected back in the same visualization and controls. This also gave my cofounder and me a concrete model for how we could use WebMCP in our own analytics products: expose the capabilities and constraints of the application directly to agents instead of asking them to infer everything from the interface. I was also happy with the way animation evolved. The human gets a visual, time-based experience, while the agent gets structured state it can reason over. Taking the project from an experiment, through WebMCP integration, to a deployed application and a working public demo was especially rewarding. What we learned Start with the problem, not the protocol. WebMCP became useful once I focused on the human-agent collaboration problem rather than trying to find places to add tools. Designing good WebMCP tools feels more like designing a product capability API than exposing UI controls. An agent works better with structured state and evidence than when it has to infer meaning from a screenshot or DOM. Domain constraints are a feature. Giving an agent explicit boundaries can make it both safer and more useful. Shared state matters more than tool count. The most interesting interactions happened when a human action became immediate context for the agent, and vice versa. What's next for Median Viz Explore additional multidimensional datasets beyond advertising , with examples from domains such as travel, retail, and other areas where interactive visual exploration is useful. Add richer annotations and storytelling , especially around animated and filtered views, so the application can help explain why a change matters rather than only showing that it happened. Explore better ways to analyze and compare independently reported demographic dimensions without violating the underlying data semantics —for example through side-by-side views, sequential filtering, or coordinated comparisons rather than unsupported intersections. Extend the human-agent collaboration model beyond the demo, including longer analytical workflows where humans and agents progressively refine the same workspace. title: Suede Agent Studio WebMCP Storefront
pitch: Agents discover services, inspect exact contracts, and run free previews in the browser while people control purchases.
about_excerpt: Agents discover services, inspect exact contracts, and run free previews in the browser while people control purchases. Like Comment Story Updates Why WebMCP fits A service marketplace asks people and agents to make the same decisions: find a service for a job, understand its inputs and price, and decide whether to proceed. An agent that only sees a visual page has to infer buttons, fields, and changing layouts. Suede Agent Studio exposes the storefront as four structured tools in the visitor's current browser page: find_services, get_service, preview_service, and buy_service. The tool set stays constant as the catalog grows. Agents search by intent, then inspect the selected service instead of loading a separate tool definition for every listing. A better experience for people and agents The agent handles discovery and contract reading. The person can review the service's exact price, input schema, review policy, data handling, and worked example before deciding whether to act. Creator-authored catalog text is marked as untrusted content, and returned results are bounded. The demo follows a concrete purchasing-operations task: find a service that compares a purchase order with an invoice, inspect PO Match Gate, and run a free preview using synthetic documents. The worked example illustrates a $15 discrepancy. The actual preview is explicitly a dry run: it records a run and returns a receipt without model inference, payment, or settlement. It is not presented as a fresh model-generated discrepancy analysis. How WebMCP was implemented The existing Next.js, React, and TypeScript application was extended with page-scoped WebMCP tools on /agents and /a/[slug]. Browser registration and same-origin tool execution live in StorefrontTools.tsx; typed tool contracts and result formatting live in src/lib/webmcp. Discovery and contract inspection are read-only. Preview is correctly labeled as a write because it records a durable run. The separate purchase route retains server-side authority, validates origin and request size, applies rate limits, checks service availability, and rechecks the exact accepted price before spending prepaid workspace credit. Purchase receipts preserve the run identifier and charged amount. The public demo does not execute buy_service. Challenges and lessons The central design challenge was making useful agent actions available without turning catalog text into instructions or treating a preview as a purchase. Explicit tool contracts, bounded results, untrusted-content markers, and server-side price checks make those boundaries inspectable. A dry run still changes state when it records a receipt, so preview is labeled as a write even when no funds move. Work completed during the challenge Suede Agent Studio predates the challenge. This entry focuses on its WebMCP storefront extension added after August 25, 2026. The public MIT-licensed repository preserves the pre-WebMCP baseline and separate feature and hardening commits, with an implementation map and reproducible validation instructions in CHALLENGE_EVIDENCE.md. The September 1 verification passed type checking, lint, the production build, and 70 focused WebMCP tests. Try it Open https://agents.suedeai.ai/agents in ChatGPT's in-app browser or a compatible Chrome browser with WebMCP enabled. Ask the agent to find a service for comparing a purchase order with an invoice, inspect po-match-gate-mkgu0, and run its free dry-run preview using synthetic documents. Do not buy anything. The preview receipt should show status done, totalCostUsdc 0, settled false, and mode dry-run. README.md, DEMO_SCRIPT.md, and CHALLENGE_EVIDENCE.md in the public repository provide the full walkthrough and local setup. The remade 2:29 live-interface demo is https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZR1At7lX6-E . title: Guardian Travel WebMCP
pitch: A travel itinerary website built for AI agents to read, not just humans to click. Structured WebMCP tools replace brittle UI guessing with grounded site-provided data.
about_excerpt: A travel itinerary website built for AI agents to read, not just humans to click. Structured WebMCP tools replace brittle UI guessing with grounded site-provided data. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Modern travel websites are designed for humans, not AI agents. A traveler can easily understand the difference between a confirmed flight, a hotel booking, an open dining intention, and a rainy-day backup plan. An AI agent that relies on UI scraping, DOM parsing, or screenshots has a much harder job: nested cards, visual chips, labels, and ambiguous text can easily be misread. We wanted to explore a different approach: Websites should expose tools to agents, not force agents to guess the UI. Guardian Travel WebMCP turns an existing travel itinerary into an agent-native website that exposes structured read tools directly through WebMCP. We do not generate the trip. We make the existing trip readable and adaptable for AI agents. What it does Guardian Travel exposes three read-only WebMCP tools: get_trip_summary get_day_itinerary get_rain_backup These tools let an agent retrieve authoritative, site-provided itinerary data without scraping the interface. For example, when the user asks: “It’s raining tomorrow afternoon. What’s my backup plan?” the agent can call: get_trip_summary get_day_itinerary with relative: "tomorrow" get_rain_backup with relative: "tomorrow", period: "afternoon" The result is grounded in the itinerary itself. In our demo, the outdoor plan is My Khe Beach and the site-provided backup is a generic café or SPA intention — not an invented business name. How we built it The project is a lightweight, dependency-free web application using: HTML5 CSS Vanilla JavaScript WebMCP through document.modelContext The page detects whether a native WebMCP host is available. When running in a supported native host, the three tools are registered directly with document.modelContext . For ordinary browsers that do not yet expose WebMCP, the site includes a small in-page compatibility shim so the interface and demo workflow can still be inspected without changing the tool definitions. The real native WebMCP path was validated in Google Chrome 152 using the native ModelContext implementation. All three tools were discovered and successfully invoked without the shim. Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was making the difference between an entity and an intention explicit. A travel page may contain a real hotel booking, a confirmed flight, or simply text such as “eat seafood tonight” or “coffee / SPA if it rains.” A human understands that immediately. An agent scraping the UI may not. We therefore designed the tool responses to preserve these distinctions and to fail closed when information is unavailable rather than inventing details. Another challenge was validating the emerging native WebMCP implementation across browser environments. We kept the native path authoritative while using a graceful fallback only for unsupported browsers. Accomplishments that we're proud of A real native WebMCP host discovers all three tools. All three tools are callable through document.modelContext . The project requires no DOM scraping. Rain-backup queries return only site-provided structured data. The tool layer is read-only and deterministic. The entire public challenge project is only a small set of static files with no backend or API keys. The project is fully open source under the MIT License. What we learned The most important lesson was that agent-friendly websites should not depend on agents reverse-engineering presentation layers. Humans need rich visual interfaces. Agents need explicit semantic capabilities. WebMCP gives websites a way to support both. Instead of treating the web page as something an agent must visually decode, the site itself can provide the agent with the correct tools and structured context. What's next for Guardian Travel WebMCP The current challenge version is intentionally read-only and focused. Future directions could include: richer place details controlled itinerary updates permissioned write tools cross-day adaptation mobile synchronization real-time travel assistance Any future write capability would remain explicit and permission-gated. For this challenge, we kept the scope small: three real tools, one clear travel use case, and no UI guessing. pitch: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface.
about_excerpt: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration For as much as marketers have optimized for conversion, they haven't been able to cut through the number one reason that people leave open carts. they're not ready to buy. It had just happened to me while shopping for a microphone: I started at one site, then realized I needed more information to determine which was going to be the best fit. What if the shopping interface could have met me where I was at--researching the options, ranking the matches, explaining its rationale, and then designing a search result layout to fit its conclusions? That's just one glimpse of how web-interfaces of the future will adapt to their users' needs through a Live Canvas. What it does Each demo walks you through a conventional user interface, and then cordons off a bounded portion of it as WebMCP to redesign (the Live Canvas) The Storefront demo lets the agent curate the search results with a toolbox of approved card presets and badges. This constrained design is a good fit for the untrusted nature of the public internet, keeping users safe from XSS attacks. The Dashbord demo scales the idea up by giving you an entirely blank page. It imagine how the future of CRM / ERP dashboards might function. Prompt the agent to onboard you, collaborate on a vision with the agent as you would with your analytics team, and the end result is an entirely personal dashboard of controls, visualizations and reports. The Distribution demo scales the idea outwards by asking whether you distribute a Live Canvas as part of conventional component libraries. It demonstrates what a future Datatable component could be, with the ability to generate bespoke reports and save them to your browser - all without backend engineering or ai-vendor lock-in. How we built it The architecture north star is "agent composition, application execution". The application exposes its UI primitives through WebMCP. The agent supplies a composition, and then the live canvas renders that composition using application-owned components. This solution prevents data from leaking out of the organization's security boundary, and also prevents token bloat. Challenges we ran into and accomplishments that we're proud of There are two large challenges that required creativity: The largest challenge was discoverability. WebMCP is not bidirectional: an agent can invoke tools, but there's no mechanism for the website to initiate a conversation. The past 30 years of the web have trained users for the affordance of buttons and forms. I built a new set of visible prompts and verbs to communicate to surface the new modality which was an interesting accomplishment, but does highlight an apparent shortcoming in the standard. The second challenge is the built-in approval flow of agentic browsers. ChatGPT would auto-deny requests to access the user's simulated library to make recommendations, e.g. In the short term, this is solved with instructional text to ask for permission in advance. However, what WebMCP needs is a built in consent layer where tools are tied to required consent artifacts. What we learned WebMCP shows great potential to break interfaces out of the "ai chatbot jail". What's next for Live Canvas The most likely next step is to select an existing open-source component library and use it to build the first end-to-end WebMCP UI framework. That would turn the Live Canvas from just a demo pattern into a production-hardened implementation.  Inspiration 

 It started with a familiar frustration. I save dozens of links every week — articles,
 posts, videos, threads — and revisit almost none of them. The bookmarks pile up,
 the tabs multiply, and most of what I carefully saved disappears into a graveyard
 of good intentions. 

 But the problem isn't saving. It's retrieval . And retrieval is exactly what AI
 is built for. 

 When I discovered WebMCP — an open standard that lets websites expose structured
 tools directly to AI agents — I realized I could bridge both sides of that gap.
 Not just build a smarter bookmark manager, but make my personal library natively 
 accessible to any AI agent, without plugins, without API key sharing, without
 configuration. Just open the page, and your AI can search your library. 

 What I Built 

 SavedPocket is a personal AI library for saving and rediscovering content from
 across the web. It supports one-click saving via a Chrome extension, bulk import
 from WhatsApp chat history, and automatic AI analysis that generates a summary,
 tags, and category for every saved item. 

 The WebMCP layer exposes six tools at /webmcp : 

 
 search_library — semantic vector search across your entire saved library using
natural language (finds results by meaning, not just keywords) 
 get_item — retrieve full details of a saved item including AI-generated summary,
tags, extracted content, and notes 
 get_recent — list the most recently saved items in reverse chronological order 
 save_url — save a new URL directly to your library via AI agent; AI analysis
and summarization run automatically after saving 
 list_collections — browse all curated collections in your library 
 get_collection_items — retrieve all items inside a specific collection 
 

 This means an AI agent can not only read your library but also write to it —
 asking ChatGPT "save this page for me" actually saves it to SavedPocket. 

 With SavedPocket open in a browser tab, ChatGPT can call these tools directly
 using WebMCP — no setup required on the AI side. 

 How I Built It 

 Stack: Next.js 15 (App Router), PostgreSQL with pgvector , Drizzle ORM,
 deployed on Render. 

 Semantic search runs entirely on-device using Xenova/multilingual-e5-small 
 — a quantized ONNX model loaded via @huggingface/transformers . Embeddings are
 stored as 384-dimensional vectors in PostgreSQL and indexed with HNSW for
 sub-linear approximate nearest-neighbor search: 

 similarity ( q , d ) = 1 − q ⋅ d | q | ⋅ | d | 

 Every saved item is embedded once and cached in the database. At query time, only
 a single embedding is computed (the user's message), then matched against stored
 vectors using the cosine distance operator <=> . This means search performance
 is independent of library size. 

 The WebMCP endpoint follows the MCP protocol over HTTP, handling initialize ,
 tools/list , and tools/call methods. The Chrome extension additionally
 discovers WebMCP endpoints across the web using /.well-known/mcp.json , enriching
 saved items with structured content where available. 

 Challenges 

 Memory constraints on a shared server. The ONNX model takes ~50–60 MB of RAM, 
 and the first embedding inference on a cold server adds a transient spike. Running
 on a 512 MB instance caused OOM crashes early on. The fix was baking the model
 into the Docker image at build time and tuning Node.js GC with --max-old-space-size . 

 Idempotent startup seeding. The demo user and seed data are created
 automatically on every deploy via a startup hook. Getting this to be truly
 idempotent — handling existing users, collections, and items without constraint
 violations across deploys — required careful use of onConflictDoNothing and
 matching upserts to the actual database unique constraints. 

 WebMCP discovery in the Chrome extension. Fetching /.well-known/mcp.json 
 from arbitrary origins introduces CORS and timing complexity inside a service
 worker. A 3-second timeout with graceful fallback to HTML scraping kept the
 extension reliable across sites that don't yet speak WebMCP. 

 What I Learned 

 WebMCP flips the model. Instead of AI agents scraping the open web or requiring 
 users to paste content into a chat window, websites can declare what they offer
 and let agents consume it cleanly. SavedPocket is a small demonstration of what
 that future looks like applied to personal knowledge — a library that any AI can
 search, the moment you're logged in. 

 The standard is early. Most sites don't expose WebMCP endpoints yet. But the
 infrastructure is there, and the pattern is simple enough that adoption can move
 quickly. I came away convinced this is how the agent web will actually work.

"Enter FlyWhisperer. FlyWhisperer is a highly accessible, voice-first travel agent that completely bypasses visual UI clutter. Instead of clicking through screens, users simply press one large button and say: 'Find me the cheapest flight from Berlin to London next Friday.'" 

 The Tech Magic (WebMCP)
"What makes FlyWhisperer unique is how it's built. Instead of a traditional standalone backend, it is built natively on the WebMCP standard and hosted via ChatGPT Sites. When the user speaks, the AI agent dynamically discovers our WebMCP tool, securely pulls real-time flight data, strips out all the marketing noise, and instantly reads back only the best option in clear, conversational audio—or displays it in ultra-high-contrast, WCAG AAA-compliant text." 

 The Impact
"We aren't just building another travel app. We are showcasing how the WebMCP standard and AI can translate the web's most complex data into an inclusive, human-centric experience, giving visually impaired users their travel independence back." 

 What it does
FlyWhisperer is an accessible, voice-first flight assistant designed for visually impaired and low-vision travelers. Instead of forcing users through cluttered booking forms and ads, it lets them simply speak or view ultra-high-contrast text to find and compare the cheapest flights effortlessly. 

 How we built it
We built FlyWhisperer natively around the WebMCP standard and hosted it via ChatGPT Sites. The conversational agent leverages built-in Speech-to-Text and TTS capabilities to discover and invoke our custom WebMCP tool, which securely queries, parses, and sanitizes live flight data. 

 Challenges we ran into
Handling large, complex flight payloads was our biggest hurdle. We had to strictly sanitize the data within our WebMCP worker to prevent prompt injection, preserve LLM token context, and translate technical airline jargon into natural, spoken English. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of
We successfully proved that WebMCP can transform an overwhelmingly visual, complex task into an intuitive, eyes-free experience that adheres strictly to WCAG AAA accessibility standards. 

 What we learned
We gained deep insights into WebMCP tool discovery, edge tool calling, and how to design prompt boundaries specifically optimized for voice output and assistive technologies.

title: 5 of 23
pitch: Fill the form. Keep the rest.
about_excerpt: Fill the form. Keep the rest. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Most forms ask for more personal information than they actually need. I wanted to test a simple idea: could an agent help finish a form without getting a free pass to read an entire profile? That became 5 of 23. The name is literal. The demo profile has 23 fields, but the sample application only needs five of them and an over-18 check. The point is not to make form filling faster at any cost. It is to make the boundary visible: what is needed, why it is needed, and who gets to release it. What it does The agent can inspect the application requirements and see what is missing without receiving the raw profile. For the age requirement, it calls an allow-listed is_adult check and gets a boolean result instead of a date of birth. It then requests the five fields required by the form. The request appears in the page, but it does not grant access. I approve or reject each field in the interface. Once the approved values have been applied, the form reaches 6/6 requirements and the temporary write capability disappears. There is still no submit tool. Final review remains a separate UI action. If that review is approved, the page exposes a local packet marked submitted: false . Revoking city removes the value, clears the reviewed copy and makes the old tool handle fail because it belongs to an earlier consent version. Everything in the demo is synthetic. It does not send an application anywhere. Why WebMCP This flow depends on the agent and the person sharing the live state of the same page: requirements, missing answers, approved scope, consent version and review status. WebMCP gives the agent a semantic tool surface instead of making it scrape buttons and labels. More importantly, the page can register a capability only while that capability is valid. The available tools change with consent, and the callbacks check the consent version again when they run. That is why this is not a chat box added to a form. The agent works out what the task needs and carries out the approved part. The person controls disclosure and review. The page enforces the boundary. How I built it I built the project in React and TypeScript with Vinext and Vite. The page registers its tools at the top level with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) so a compatible browser can discover them directly. A deterministic in-browser state engine owns the synthetic profile, form progress, disclosure requests, approvals, consent versions, receipts and reviewed packet. The normal interface and the WebMCP callbacks use that same store. The schemas use narrow enums, reject extra properties and bind dynamic writes to the current consent version. The prototype has no application API, database, login, analytics, payment flow or external submission handler. That kept the build focused on the consent model rather than infrastructure. The source code is public under the MIT License . Challenges I ran into The hard part was not the happy path. It was keeping six states separate and understandable: request, approval, application, review, revocation and stale authority. Dynamic tools also needed two layers of protection. A tool has to disappear when its authority disappears, but its callback must still reject an old handle that was fetched before the change. I also had to keep the proof honest: a mocked test is useful, but it is not the same thing as a real browser discovering and invoking the final page. What I am proud of In the local end-to-end browser run, the available tool count moved 8 → 9 → 8 → 9 → 8 as consent and review changed. The minimum path completed 6/6 requirements using 5 of 23 fields and one boolean age check. The other 18 fields stayed sealed in the tool/UI flow. Revoking city returned the form to 5/6 , left 4 of 23 fields disclosed, removed the reviewed-packet tool and rejected its old handle. The deterministic suite passed 14/14 tests , along with typecheck, lint, the production build and the recorded npm audit. The demo data lives in the public client bundle, so “sealed” describes the exercised interface and tool behavior, not source-code secrecy. This is a synthetic prototype, not a claim of production-grade security or measured user impact. What I learned Tool discovery is only the start of an agent-native product. The more interesting question is when a capability should exist, how small its scope can be, and what should happen to authority the moment consent changes. I also learned that privacy needs visible negative evidence. A good demo should show not only what the agent can do, but what it cannot read, cannot approve and can no longer use after revocation. What's next I would add property-based tests around redaction and stale versions, a small policy language for purpose and expiry, and a proper accessibility review of the consent controls. The next product question is whether people clearly understand the difference between a request, a grant and a reviewed local packet. title: Handrail WebMCP
pitch: A WebMCP server that gives AI agents safe, reliable access to web workflows
about_excerpt: A WebMCP server that gives AI agents safe, reliable access to web workflows Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI agents should eventually help streamline day-to-day store operations, but a tool should never become a way to circumvent orders, refunds, price adjustments, etc., without restraint. With Handrail I aim to add more control by allowing the agent to investigate orders and propose actions that the merchant can ultimately approve and execute. What it does Handrail is a browser based store operations console. Agents can search orders, customers, policies, inventory, shipping, products, and sales data using WebMCP tools. When the agent needs to perform an action like issue a refund or cancel an order, the agent cannot mutate the data. Handrail does validation and creates a parameter approved ticket. The merchant approves the action in the application and only then can the agent execute the same parameters. The guided demo shows the refund for an order ORD-1042 and shows validation failures and request protections against requests that are mismatched or replayed. How I built it Handrail was built using Vite to speed up development and deployed as purely a browser based React application. Handrail also provides a fallback interface when WebMCP tools are not available as it registers 14 WebMCP tools. The safety flow is implemented in the application logic: agent suggestion → approval → exact parameter match → one time execution → confirmation All demo data is held in memory, so it can be safely reset without a backend or payment integration. Challenges I ran into The biggest challenge was still making the approval step more meaningful than just a confirmation must be checked. An approval should be for the actual amount, the actual order and the actual operation, not a statement like an agent is going to “do this later”. I dealt with this by freezing the canonical parameters for each ticket, validating them again at the time of ticket execution, preventing ticket replay, enforcing expiry, and recording both successful actions and denials in an activity log. What I learned Executable actions and audit receipts make sense between reaching out and approval. The executive semantics of an actual execution are very important when it comes to safe agent tooling, and this is more important than having a label like “read-only” or “write” on that action. Managing multiple medications shouldn't require patients to become pharmacology experts. A single new medicine can introduce an interaction that's easy to miss.
We built SafeDose AI — RegimenGuard to turn complex medication information into understandable safety insights — and with WebMCP , allow AI agents to work directly with structured medication context. 

 
 The agent investigates. SafeDose provides context. The human decides. 

 🛡️ What it does 

 SafeDose is an agent-native medication safety workspace that helps users: 

 
 💊 Manage their current medication regimen 
 ⚠️ Detect potential drug interactions 
 📊 Understand an overall regimen safety score 
 🔴 Distinguish critical risks from cautions and safer combinations 
 🔎 Search structured medication information 
 👥 Support caregiver and medication-management workflows 
 
 

 🤖 Powered by WebMCP 

 SafeDose exposes three focused, read-only agent tools :
 search_medication 🔎 — Find medication information
 get_current_regimen 💊 — Understand the user's current regimen
 check_regimen_safety 🛡️ — Check a candidate medication against that regimen 

 Instead of repeatedly copying medication lists into an AI conversation, compatible agents can work with SafeDose's structured capabilities directly. 

 Agents investigate — they don't prescribe or modify medications. 

 🛠️ How we built it 

 SafeDose combines:
 React + TypeScript ⚛️ → application

 Google AI Studio ✨ → AI-assisted development 
 GitHub 🐙 → source control 
 Vercel ▲ → live deployment 

 We also built an Agent Activity interface to make WebMCP capabilities visible and understandable. 

 🧩 Challenges we ran into 

 Our biggest challenge was bridging two worlds:
 Human UI ↔ WebMCP ↔ AI Agent 
We worked through evolving WebMCP browser APIs, tool registration, deployment, agent discovery, and medication-data integration. 

 Healthcare also raised an important design question: How much authority should an AI agent have? 
Our answer was deliberate — read-only tools and human-controlled decisions. 

 🏆 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We're especially proud that SafeDose isn't simply “another healthcare chatbot.” 
We transformed an existing medication-safety experience into an agent-native web application , while preserving a polished interface for traditional users. 

 Most importantly, WebMCP addresses a genuinely contextual problem: 

 
 It's not only “What does this medication do?” 
It's “What does this medication mean alongside everything I'm already taking?” 
 

 🧠 What we learned 

 WebMCP showed us that the future of AI on the web isn't necessarily putting a chatbot on every website. 

 It's about making websites themselves understandable and actionable to agents. 
And in healthcare, powerful AI doesn't always mean maximum autonomy.
 Good agents also know where their authority ends. 

 🚀 What's next for SafeDose AI — RegimenGuard 

 Next, we envision:
💊 Medication reconciliation 
👨‍⚕️ Pharmacist-review workflows 
👨‍👩‍👧 Caregiver collaboration 
📅 Smarter medication planning 
♿ Improved accessibility 
🤖 Expanded WebMCP capabilities with human approval 

 Our goal is simple: 

 SafeDose AI — Your regimen. Your agent. Safer decisions. 🛡️ 

 Disclaimer: SafeDose is a prototype decision-support tool and does not replace professional medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment.

about_excerpt: PawPilot is a WebMCP-powered pet-care agent that turns natural language into action Like Comment Story Updates PawPilot — Project Story Try the live agent demo Live agent demo: https://agent-6a965dc9f0937d545273e692--pawpilot-webmcp.netlify.app This is the agent-facing PawPilot deployment used for the demo experience. The underlying WebMCP capabilities, server-side validation, human approval boundary, and persisted care-plan workflow remain part of the PawPilot application. What inspired me PawPilot started with a simple question: What if talking to a pet-care website could feel as natural as talking to an assistant? Pet care is full of information—profiles, routines, products, services, and care plans—but people are still expected to click through pages and menus to make something happen. I wanted to see what would happen if the website could actually understand what an agent needs to do. So I built PawPilot around my dog Dojo and started turning a normal pet-care website into something an agent could actually work with. That became my experiment with the agentic web: PawPilot. Why WebMCP matters to me WebMCP changes the interaction model from People → Pages → Buttons toward People → Agents → Capabilities. That idea really clicked for me. Instead of an agent having to guess what a website can do by looking at text and buttons, PawPilot explicitly tells the agent what capabilities are available. PawPilot exposes six structured WebMCP tools through document.modelContext: get_pet_profile get_daily_needs find_pet_services find_pet_products save_care_plan list_care_plans The result is a website that can participate in an agent conversation instead of just waiting for a person to navigate it. What people and agents can do together A person can simply ask: “Build Dojo a care plan for today.” From there, the agent can use PawPilot's structured capabilities to retrieve Dojo's profile, understand his daily needs, find relevant services or products, and prepare a proposed care plan. But I didn't want “agentic” to mean “the agent gets to do whatever it wants.” The important boundary is the write operation. PawPilot does not allow the OpenAI agent to silently save a care plan. The person gets to see what is being proposed and explicitly chooses Confirm & Save. Only then does the server issue a short-lived approval token tied to that exact pet and exact plan before accepting the database write. So the collaboration loop becomes: User request → Agent discovers capabilities → Agent prepares action → Human reviews → Human approves → Server verifies → Action is saved That separation between what an agent can discover, what it can execute, and what a human must authorize became one of the most important parts of PawPilot for me. I didn't stop at the website — I built a Safari WebMCP Bridge While I was building PawPilot, I ran into another question: what happens when the browser experience around WebMCP isn't there yet? Instead of treating that as a reason to stop, I built a PawPilot WebMCP Bridge Safari Web Extension alongside the application. This part matters because I wasn't trying to fake native WebMCP support. The extension is deliberately a browser-side inspection, compatibility, and testing layer. PawPilot's own WebMCP registration and server-side authorization remain the source of truth. The extension can detect native WebMCP through document.modelContext, discover tools with getTools(), and, when the runtime supports it, invoke executeTool(). It also treats write-capable tools differently and requires explicit confirmation before executing them. I gave the extension its own little developer workspace too: an in-page PawPilot WebMCP Console, a Safari-friendly popup dashboard, live tool and toolchange monitoring, runtime and Permissions Policy diagnostics, background event history, and structured report export. I also ran into one of those very real browser problems that doesn't show up in a clean architecture diagram. Safari/WebKit was giving me a WebKitBlobResource failure around report downloads. I changed the exporter to use a data: URL instead of Blob URLs and URL.createObjectURL(). That made the export path Safari-safe and taught me something I probably wouldn't have learned by only testing in one browser. The extension is kept separate under safari-extension/ specifically so it can inspect PawPilot without modifying the existing WebMCP registration. That separation was intentional: the bridge can tell me what the browser actually supports instead of pretending native support exists when it doesn't. And then PawPilot needed somewhere to remember what happened I also didn't want the care-plan part of the demo to be a fake screen that only looked like it saved something. PawPilot uses a Netlify-hosted database with Drizzle migrations to persist care plans. The application has a database migration for the care_plans data, and the server-side tool layer performs the validation and persistence after the approval boundary has been satisfied. That gives the demo a complete path from agent request to real application state: WebMCP capability → validated operation → human approval → authorized server write → persisted care plan That was important to me because I wanted the “action” in agentic web to actually mean something. The agent isn't just generating text about a care plan; PawPilot can turn that approved plan into saved application state. How I built it PawPilot is a Next.js application deployed on Netlify with a browser-native WebMCP layer. The WebMCP client registers the six tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(), including descriptions, JSON input schemas, read/write annotations, and executable handlers. Tool execution is routed through the application's server-side validation layer rather than trusting browser-provided parameters. The OpenAI interaction layer uses the same centralized tool catalog for its agent-facing read capabilities, while save_care_plan remains UI-controlled. This keeps the WebMCP surface and application implementation aligned instead of creating a separate set of business rules for every integration. The Safari WebMCP Bridge lives separately under safari-extension/ so it can inspect PawPilot without modifying the application's existing WebMCP registration. Its content script handles discovery, diagnostics, events, and controlled execution; the popup provides the developer-facing controls; and the background script keeps bridge event history. The care-plan persistence path uses the Netlify database and Drizzle migration already in the project. The database write remains behind the same server-side approval and validation boundary as the rest of the application. Browser testing: real WebMCP calls I tested PawPilot with WebMCP enabled in Microsoft Edge and Google Chrome. I didn't want to stop at seeing a WebMCP object on the page. The six tools were exposed through document.modelContext, discovered with getTools(), and actually invoked through executeTool() against live PawPilot implementations. The Safari extension gives me another way to inspect that capability surface and see what the browser/runtime is actually exposing. That distinction matters: PawPilot isn't just an HTTP API with “WebMCP” written on top of it. The website exposes structured capabilities through the WebMCP surface, and those capabilities connect to real application behavior and persisted state. Challenges WebMCP is an emerging standard, which meant I had to learn while building. Browser support and developer tooling are still evolving, and testing exposed differences between environments. I ended up separating several things that are easy to blur together: The website registering its capabilities The browser exposing those capabilities The agent discovering and using them The server validating and executing the underlying operation The database persisting the approved result The human deciding whether a consequential action should actually happen Building the Safari Bridge made that separation even clearer. A browser tool shouldn't quietly pretend that native support exists. It should tell you what is really happening and give you useful diagnostics when it doesn't. Safety and trust PawPilot is a demo of controlled agentic action, not autonomous pet-care decision making. Read operations can be performed through structured tools. A care-plan write requires explicit human confirmation and a server-generated approval challenge tied to the exact proposed payload. Approval tokens are short-lived and single-use within the active server instance. The demo does not claim user identity or authentication. The approval mechanism is an action-authorization boundary for this demo, not an identity system. I wanted that distinction to be clear rather than hiding it behind impressive-sounding AI language. title: ReturnReady
pitch: ReturnReady turns scattered receipts and work records into an evidence-linked, review-ready Australian tax return draft, using WebMCP to prepare, verify, and resolve gaps.
about_excerpt: ReturnReady turns scattered receipts and work records into an evidence-linked, review-ready Australian tax return draft, using WebMCP to prepare, verify, and resolve gaps. Like Comment Story Updates Start with a sparse FY2025-26 evidence draft, then complete it manually or let Codex populate structured facts through WebMCP. Codex records 3 disposals while preserving AAPL’s user attestation and BTC’s warning. Generated Review Pack with unresolved warning Inspiration This started with my own tax return. Most of it was prefilled, but my foreign shares and crypto weren't - so I was the one who had to get all of it in. That meant logging into each broker, exporting my holdings (every platform in its own format), and then typing each position in by hand. It's tedious, easy to get wrong, and it's the same job every year. The hard part was never the tax treatment. It was moving structured facts out of a pile of exports and into one draft I could actually review, without losing track of where each number came from or which ones the paperwork couldn't answer. That's the gap ReturnReady goes after. ReturnReady is a small WebMCP experiment: I attach synthetic evidence to Codex, Codex pulls the structured facts out (outside the page), and the app exposes a few narrow tools for recording and checking those facts. I still review everything and fill in anything the evidence can't prove. What it does ReturnReady opens on a sparse FY2025–26 draft with a bit of prefilled PAYG context. From there you can add deductions and disposals yourself, or ask Codex to do it through WebMCP. The demo walks through: 40 hours of work-from-home, at the prototype's fixed rate, giving a visible $28 deduction MSFT and AAPL foreign-share disposals a BTC disposal with the transaction fee left out on purpose The evidence doesn't contain AAPL's acquisition details, so validation raises a blocker instead of making the numbers up. You supply those facts yourself as a user attestation, which stays visibly separate from anything backed by a document. Once the blocker is cleared, ReturnReady builds a review pack, keeping the unresolved BTC warning and logging every action along the way. One thing worth being clear about: ReturnReady organizes evidence. It doesn't lodge returns, give tax advice, work out the authoritative tax, or claim your return is complete. The gains and losses are amounts I worked out myself and entered; the app records and checks them, it doesn't calculate them. Why WebMCP Normal browser automation has to read the DOM, guess what each control does, and poke at fields from the outside. ReturnReady skips all of that. It exposes six tools with tight JSON Schemas: get_return_draft record_deductions record_disposals record_acquisition_details validate_review_pack generate_review_pack Both the agent and the manual UI go through the same controller and the same domain logic. So WebMCP speeds up data entry without getting around validation, provenance, idempotency, or the audit trail and if WebMCP isn't available, the manual workflow still works on its own. How I built it ReturnReady is a static React app in strict TypeScript, built with Vite, no backend. It registers its tools imperatively with document.modelContext.registerTool() . Every tool checks its input against an allow-list at the schema boundary, then checks it again inside the handler. The page never sees the attached files or the raw document text. No tool takes a file path, a URL, a selector, executable content, or arbitrary JavaScript. All the bundled evidence and values are synthetic. For tests, Vitest and Testing Library cover the domain rules, the security boundaries, tool annotations, bounded outputs, idempotency, and making sure a human and the agent get the same result. Playwright runs the whole manual workflow end to end for accessibility. Challenges I ran into The main one was keeping a single trustworthy workflow across two ways in. Early on, validation triggered by the agent could look different from validation triggered by a human. I fixed it by deriving the modal and the review pack from shared controller state, and added a regression test that runs the real WebMCP handler against the rendered UI. The other challenge was one I felt as a builder: the page deliberately never touches the raw files. Part of me wanted to just let the app accept an upload and parse it, that's the obvious and easy path. But that's exactly the boundary that makes this trustworthy, so keeping all the file handling outside the page stayed non-negotiable, even when it made the build feel more restrictive than it had to be. I also kept the scope tight on purpose. ReturnReady shows the recorded facts and a fixed-rate deduction result, but it doesn't try to calculate capital gains or guess at missing acquisition data. Accomplishments that I am proud of 6 small WebMCP tools instead of handing over the whole browser one shared domain layer behind both the manual and agent paths provenance that clearly separates documentary evidence from user attestation invalid or conflicting calls get rejected cleanly, with no change to state repeat calls are idempotent, they don't pile up duplicate records a review pack that carries unresolved warnings through instead of hiding them a fully synthetic demo anyone can reproduce What I learned WebMCP earns its keep when it exposes what things mean, not when it turns every button into a tool. A small, semantic surface lets the agent move fast while the app keeps hold of the parts that matter: validation, state changes, and deciding what the person actually needs to review. What's next for ReturnReady More evidence categories, better review exports for an accountant, and a few real calculation methods so the amounts don't all have to be worked out by hand first, all while keeping raw-file interpretation outside the page and the same trust boundary intact. title: Cooktree
pitch: Give an AI the kitchen. Keep the keys. CookTree hands an agent thirteen functions and withholds four — your card, your address, your order history, your spend limit.
about_excerpt: Give an AI the kitchen. Keep the keys. CookTree hands an agent thirteen functions and withholds four — your card, your address, your order history, your spend limit. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Agent Native Meal Planning, built for humans and agents. Inspiration There are only two ways to let an AI act for you on a website today. Hand it your browser, and it inherits your entire logged-in session — every page, every saved card. Or issue it a token, which outlives the session and can be replayed somewhere you'll never see. There is no third option that says "just a little bit." WebMCP is that third option, and we wanted to build the smallest thing that makes the difference obvious. Meal planning turned out to be perfect: it's a dependency graph pretending to be a list, and a grocery account holds exactly the things an agent has no business touching — a card, an address, an order history, a spend limit. What it does Tell CookTree what you want for dinner. It plans the week, works out what's already in your kitchen, dedupes ingredients across dishes, rounds up to real pack sizes, and gives you a list of things to actually buy. Twenty-one ingredient requests collapse into sixteen ingredients and eight purchases. Say "drop the mapo tofu" and it returns the diff — three lines gone, −$14.70 — not a page you have to re-read. Say "I used up the garlic" and the buy list grows to match. Describe a dish it has never heard of, in English or Chinese, and it generates a real recipe with quantities, cookware, and a photograph, then plans it through the same engine as the built-in dishes. Then ask it to change your delivery address. It can't. Not blocked, not password-protected — the site never registered that function. Thirteen tools exist; that isn't one of them. How we built it One static HTML file, no build step. Thirteen tools defined once in §4 TOOLS[] and registered individually with document.modelContext.registerTool(), falling back to navigator.modelContext and to provideContext({tools}) where registerTool is absent. Every tool body — and every button in the UI — routes through a single invoke(name, args) function, so there is no separate agent path that can drift out of sync with what people see. Clicking an ingredient fires explain_shortage; clicking a dish fires plan_week. It all shows up in the on-page agent console as tool calls, because it is all the same layer. Two Vercel Functions sit behind it so provider keys never reach the browser or the repo: one turns free text into a plannable dish (DeepSeek for the recipe, Nano Banana 2 Lite for the photo, in parallel), the other turns shortages into live Shopify Global Catalog listings and real merchant carts. We chose the tool set with one question per candidate: if this fired a hundred times by mistake, what happens? Nothing → expose. A draft gets messy → expose. A retailer handoff is created → expose, but gate it on a human. Money moves → keep the final action on the retailer's page. The account becomes someone else's → never expose. That last answer is why update_delivery_address, update_payment_method, read_order_history and update_spend_limit have no tool. Challenges we ran into The spec is still moving. The context object has lived on both document and navigator during the draft, and both spellings are still in the wild, so we probe for both. registerTool returns a promise, which a synchronous try/catch will not catch — a registration failure could leave the status pill claiming success. We trusted the model's numbers once, and shouldn't have. A generated recipe asked for 3 g of onion. An onion is a 200 g pack. Now the site validates every quantity against its own pack sizes and says in the console when it corrects one. The model is a source, not an authority. A hardcoded string nearly lied to the judges. The console header shipped with 8 tools registered, which JavaScript overwrites at load. When we opened the live site in ChatGPT's plain browsing — which reads rendered text without executing the page — it reported eight tools. Anything that doesn't run the script saw the wrong number. Deployment split in half. GitHub Pages auto-deployed but has no /api routes; Vercel had the routes but kept serving a stale build, because the Vercel GitHub App was installed on the account without being authorized for this repository. Diagnosing that took a cache-busting fetch and reading response headers, not guessing. Accomplishments that we're proud of We verified the argument in someone else's agent. ChatGPT's Cloud Browser opened the live site, enumerated all thirteen tools by name, and called get_kitchen successfully. Then we asked it to change the delivery address, and it came back with: → update_delivery_address {"address":"42 Mission St"} ✕ no such tool — 13 registered, this is not one of them the site never exposed it · a click-agent would open Settings and change it That refusal is not our demo script talking to itself. A real third-party agent tried, and the site had nothing to give it. We're also proud that checkout stops where it does. CookTree sends product names and quantities to Shopify, gets back real listings and real merchant carts, and then stops — the person pays on the merchant's own page. That boundary is the design, not an unfinished edge: a version of this that took payment would be a version that had to hold a card. What we learned Splitting is what buys the site choice. The interesting granularity isn't categories, it's scope. get_order_status is registered — it covers handoffs this agent created in this tab. Reading the retailer account's order history is a different scope and has no tool. The same noun splits into an exposed half and a withheld half, and you only get that by registering functions instead of handing over a session. And an honest boundary: this is least privilege, not a security perimeter. An agent that already has DOM access can go around all of it. The point isn't that the site is armored. It's that a cooperating agent never needs that access in the first place, and the site — for the first time — gets to define the surface it's willing to support. Cooking is just the version you can understand in ninety seconds. The mechanism matters most in banking, health portals, and internal admin consoles, where the list of things a site must not hand over is long. What's next for Cooktree Make the Agent/Manual switch real. Right now it only disables the chat box. The spec's registerTool(..., { signal }) means a site can revoke its tool layer with an AbortController — so the toggle could genuinely withdraw all thirteen tools and drop the pill to zero. A site that can choose what to expose should also be able to choose when. Surface the withheld set as a first-class thing. Today the four unregistered functions are visible in the account panel and in the docs. They should be part of the protocol conversation: a site should be able to tell an agent "this exists and I'm not giving it to you," so the agent can say so to the user instead of failing blind. Take it somewhere with real stakes. The same shape — a small set of typed functions, a human gate on the one that reaches outside, and a withheld list you can point at — is what a bank or a patient portal would need. Groceries were the version we could ship in three days. title: The Commons
pitch: A shared idea board where people and AI agents post, link, and upvote ideas together in real time - through 7 registered WebMCP tools, not scraping or screenshots.
about_excerpt:
A shared idea board where people and AI agents post, link, and upvote ideas together in real time - through 7 registered WebMCP tools, not scraping or screenshots.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Agents are getting good at driving a browser like a person would — click, type, scroll, screenshot, repeat. That works, but it's slow and brittle, and it treats the agent like a guest who has to guess at a UI built for someone else. WebMCP flips that: the page itself can say, in plain terms, "here's what you're actually allowed to do here." We wanted to build something small enough to finish quickly but real enough to show what that unlocks — a space where a person and an agent aren't just co-existing on the same page, they're editing the same shared thing, together, in view of each other. 

 What it does 

 The Commons is a shared idea board about the future of the open web. A person can post an idea, tag it, upvote it, or link it to another idea through the normal UI. An AI agent visiting the same page in a WebMCP-enabled browser gets seven registered tools — add_idea , list_ideas , search_ideas , connect_ideas , upvote_idea , remove_idea , get_board_summary — that operate on the exact same board. Every tool call the agent makes shows up instantly in an on-page activity feed, and agent-authored ideas are visually distinct (teal) from human ones (amber), so provenance is never ambiguous. Because the board lives on a shared backend rather than in localStorage , two different people (or a person and an agent) genuinely see and build on each other's contributions in the same session. 

 How we built it 

 The frontend is a single static index.html — no framework, no build step — that registers its tools with document.modelContext.registerTool() on load, each with a name, a plain-language description, and a JSON Schema input contract. Read-only tools ( list_ideas , search_ideas , get_board_summary ) are marked with readOnlyHint: true . The execute function for every tool calls the same small REST API that the human-facing UI calls, so there's exactly one source of truth for board state, mutated by two different actors. The backend is a small Express server with a JSON-file store, deployed on Railway; the frontend is deployed separately on Vercel and points at it via a configurable API base URL. The page polls the API every few seconds so a person watching sees an agent's edits without refreshing. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Getting the mutation model right took a couple of passes — early on the WebMCP tools and the UI's own click handlers each had their own copy of the board, which meant an agent's edit wouldn't show up until a manual refresh. Routing every mutation, human and agent alike, through the same API call fixed that and made the "co-creating in real time" story actually true instead of just visually implied. 

 What's next 

 Multiplayer presence (showing who's currently viewing the board), letting the agent read why a person upvoted something before adding a related idea, and exposing the same tool set to iframed origins via exposedTo so a partner site could embed The Commons and let its own visitors' agents contribute too.

title: MG Guide | Agent-Native Follow-Up
pitch: A WebMCP-native meeting follow-up workspace where agents prepare action, state, and draft artifacts while people keep final send authority.
about_excerpt:
A WebMCP-native meeting follow-up workspace where agents prepare action, state, and draft artifacts while people keep final send authority.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Platform context: the competition surface stays bounded while MG MCP and the broader MG Guide platform remain adjacent context. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Current WebMCP experience: ACTION → STATE → ARTIFACT turns meeting context into a human-reviewed follow-up draft. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 WebMCP build architecture: ChatGPT browser discovers 3 native tools backed by a bounded synthetic MG Guide workflow. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Platform context: the competition surface stays bounded while MG MCP and the broader MG Guide platform remain adjacent context. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Current WebMCP experience: ACTION → STATE → ARTIFACT turns meeting context into a human-reviewed follow-up draft. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 WebMCP build architecture: ChatGPT browser discovers 3 native tools backed by a bounded synthetic MG Guide workflow. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Platform context: the competition surface stays bounded while MG MCP and the broader MG Guide platform remain adjacent context. 
 
 1 2 3 4 



 
 MG Guide | Agent-Native Follow-Up 

 MG Guide started from a practical problem we see in relationship-driven sales: the meeting may happen virtually, but the real work often starts after the call ends. 

 Someone still has to remember what mattered, connect the conversation to the right relationship, determine the next step, and prepare a thoughtful follow-up. That work matters because relationships are personal, but it can also become repetitive and fragmented across meetings, notes, CRM systems, inboxes, and different tools. 

 We have been building MG Guide as part of a broader effort to create a governed AI workspace that can work behind salespeople and sales teams without taking judgment or relationship ownership away from them. 

 
 Our goal is simple: let AI help prepare the work, while the person remains responsible for the relationship. 
 

 For The WebMCP Challenge , that idea took on a new form. 

 What WebMCP changed for us 

 Before this challenge, MG Guide already had a meeting follow-up workflow and the broader foundation we had been building around meeting context, relationship context, follow-up planning, and governed AI workflows. 

 WebMCP gave us a new way to think about how an AI agent could interact with that experience. 

 Instead of building a separate interface just for an agent, or asking an agent to interpret buttons and page structure, we could let the website itself clearly expose the actions that were safe and useful for an agent to perform. 

 That led us to a simple model: 

 
 ACTION → STATE → ARTIFACT → HUMAN CONTROL 
 

 The agent can help process the meeting, understand the current follow-up state, and retrieve the prepared follow-up draft. The person still reviews the result and decides what happens next. 

 That became one of the most important lessons from the project: 

 
 The website itself can become a shared workspace between a person and an AI agent. 
 

 What we built for the challenge 

 For the WebMCP Challenge, we meaningfully extended the existing MG Guide experience with a browser-native WebMCP layer. 

 The live MG Guide page now exposes exactly three capabilities to a compatible browser agent: 

 
 ACTION — process the meeting follow-up 
 STATE — understand where the follow-up currently stands 
 ARTIFACT — retrieve the draft that was prepared 
 

 This creates one shared experience instead of one interface for the person and another interface for the agent. 

 When everything is clear, MG Guide can prepare a useful follow-up draft. 

 When the relationship is unclear or ambiguous, the system stops and asks for human review instead of guessing. 

 That distinction matters to us. In relationship-based work, a good AI system should know not only when it can help, but also when it should stop. 

 
 Agent can prepare. Only a person can review and send. 
 

 What we learned 

 This challenge changed how we think about agent-native software. 

 The page can be the shared contract 

 One of our biggest takeaways was that an AI agent does not always need its own separate interface. 

 The same page a person uses can expose a small, intentional set of capabilities that an agent can understand and use. That keeps the human and the AI working from the same experience instead of creating two disconnected versions of the workflow. 

 Safe refusal is part of good design 

 We intentionally built an ambiguous-contact scenario into the demo. 

 If MG Guide cannot confidently connect the meeting to the right relationship, it does not continue automatically. It stops. 

 That may look like less automation, but for us it represents better automation. 

 Trust is especially important when AI is working around relationships, financial conversations, customer information, and follow-up communication. 

 Human control should be designed in from the beginning 

 We did not want “human in the loop” to be a sentence we added at the end of the project. We wanted it reflected in the experience itself. 

 The agent can prepare context, state, and a draft, but the final customer-facing action remains with the person. 

 That boundary became one of the clearest principles of the project. 

 Browser behavior matters more than we expected 

 We also learned that making an agent-capable web experience reliable is not only about the AI. 

 Browser behavior, tool discovery, origin boundaries, caching, and how the page is served all affect whether the experience actually works for a person and an agent together. 

 That pushed us to think more seriously about the browser as part of the agent environment, not simply as a screen. 

 Where this is leading us 

 The WebMCP Challenge also surfaced a bigger idea for the future of MG Guide and the governed AI ecosystem we are building around our sales teams. 

 This challenge primarily demonstrates an outbound pattern: 

 
 MG Guide exposes safe capabilities from our governed environment to a browser agent. 
 

 But we are increasingly interested in the opposite direction too. 

 What happens when a salesperson finds useful information somewhere else on the web and wants to intentionally bring that information back into their governed AI workspace? 

 For example: 

 
 useful research before a meeting; 
 a company website; 
 an article relevant to a relationship; 
 publicly available information about a business; 
 information a salesperson intentionally selects while preparing for a conversation. 
 

 We do not want that to become uncontrolled web scraping or automatic memory collection. 

 Instead, we see an opportunity for a governed intake experience . 

 The person could intentionally select information, identify why it matters, and bring it into MG Guide with context about where it came from and what it is allowed to inform. 

 That information could then become evidence available to the governed AI environment without automatically becoming permanent memory or authorizing an external action. 

 WebMCP and a future Chrome extension companion 

 This is also where a browser extension becomes interesting to us. 

 On websites that support WebMCP, we would prefer to use the structured capabilities the site intentionally exposes. 

 But many websites will not expose WebMCP immediately. A future Chrome extension companion could provide a user-controlled bridge. 

 The salesperson could choose the information they want to bring into MG Guide, explain what they want to use it for, and send it through the same governed intake boundary. 

 Conceptually: 
 WebMCP-enabled website
→ structured information selected through the site's declared capabilities
→ governed intake
→ MG Guide
 Website without WebMCP
→ information explicitly selected by the person through a browser extension
→ governed intake
→ MG Guide
 
 In both cases, the important part is not simply collecting more information. 

 The important part is preserving: 

 
 where the information came from; 
 why the person brought it in; 
 what workflow it is allowed to support; 
 whether it should remain temporary or become durable context; 
 and what actions still require human approval. 
 

 That is becoming an important part of how we think about building AI for real sales teams. 

 The larger vision 

 MG Guide is ultimately one piece of a broader governed AI ecosystem we are building to work behind salespeople and sales teams from a virtual perspective.

title: Study Map
pitch: Learn anything as a map you and ChatGPT draw together.
about_excerpt: Learn anything as a map you and ChatGPT draw together. Like Comment Story Updates Live: https://hungson175.github.io/study-map/ · Code: https://github.com/hungson175/study-map I study most days, and I build software one small piece at a time. I want to learn the same way. Mind maps that arrive finished have never worked for me. NotebookLM is good, but a complete map is someone else's map: I read it once and keep nothing. I want one that opens only where I got curious and ends up holding my own notes, so next time I can just glance at it. So Study Map does not fill everything in at once. The page's guide tells the agent to draw a few nodes and stop. I select a node, pin a question, and only that branch grows. Working together. WebMCP is what makes this simple. The page hands the agent what it needs as tools: the map, my selection, my open questions. It draws and it researches; I drag, rewrite, delete and write in my own notes. It can also refuse, when there is no room beside a node, rather than write over my work. Same canvas, both of us, no screenshots in between. Built. An MIT retrofit of Excalidraw. The page registers 17 tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . The one that took by far the most work is how_to_use : read-only, recomputed from the live canvas, it is the page teaching the agent how to run this kind of session — a few nodes, then stop and wait for the person, then grow only what they asked about. That guideline is really the product. The other sixteen tools just carry it out. The demo is me using Study Map to learn WebMCP itself. title: ROBO BRIDGE MCP
pitch: Browser robot arm demo. Build structures with an AI Agent through WebMCP tools. Place bricks, plan structures and more!
about_excerpt: Browser robot arm demo. Build structures with an AI Agent through WebMCP tools. Place bricks, plan structures and more! Like Comment Story Updates Main Overview, with robot arm, and train on the final built bridge Built Simple Wall Building Bridge Building Rubiks Cube Pushing the "MORE BRICKS" button Building a Checkerboard Bridge Hologram View Train testing the bridge Train testing the bridge 2 Inspiration I loved building with lego for years, and wanted to see what it would look like if a robot could build with bricks in an interactive simulation. Thought this was a bit ambitious, it is buggy in areas, but hopefulyl it shows what future interactive games could look like with WebMCP. What it does ROBO BRIDGE MCP is a browser-based robotics simulator built around a robot arm and a shared construction environment. Through WebMCP, the AI can inspect the workspace, plan structures, control the robot, place bricks, request more materials and react to changes made by you in the scene. There are over 31 native WebMCP tools available for controlling the robot, planning, placing the bricks, and modifying the environment. When testing it out, ask your agent to explore the tools, and iterate with it to build different structures. I was suprised when i asked it for a checkerboard pattern and rubiks cube that it nailed it! How I built it The simulator runs entirely in the browser using Three.js in a static website with no server-side processing. A shared build area, inventory and revision state are used by both the Human and the AI agent. You decide what to build, and the agent plans on how to build it and which tools to use. The WebMCP tools are used to trigger code that drives the robot movement to place bricks. I tried to get the agents to do the full robot joint commands and it took too long, so it essentially controls the TCP and gripper of the robot, and inverse kinematics handles the rest to position the robot joints within its workspace. Challenges The hardest part was getting the robot arm to build structures AND adapt if the user would place a brick in the middle of its plan. I also had to make the interaction fast enough for a natural live demonstration while keeping placement validation deterministic. So a real robot arm wouldnt move that quickly, but you can play around with the speed settings in the menu. (Note some larger builds may take a while, even with 1 second brick pick-and-place cycle time, the planning and number of bricks will greatly increase the time the build takes) What I learned WebMCP is awesome! This live demo game opens up a lot of possibilities. Hopefully i can get it to build larger buildings, streets and towns later on. You could also potentially control a real robot arm through the browser. Or even its own dedicated web game, where people can connect their agents to it to build cool stuff.
