title: Spokes - a collaborative map to help with coordination
pitch: Spokes turns "where should we go?" into one live map. Everyone adds their needs, some kept private, and places rule themselves out in real time. Your agent can assist you or fully negotiate for you.
about_excerpt: Spokes turns "where should we go?" into one live map. Everyone adds their needs, some kept private, and places rule themselves out in real time. Your agent can assist you or fully negotiate for you. Like Comment Story Updates Social media banner for Spokes Spokes — Devpost submission Live: https://spokes.alainschlesser.com/ Inspiration Groups are bad at picking somewhere to go, and the reason is structural rather than social. The needs that decide the answer are scattered across people and arrive piecemeal: a dietary restriction here, a budget there, a veto that lands after everyone else has settled, and at least one reason nobody wants to say out loud. A search results page optimises a single query. A group chat collects messages. Neither keeps a shared model of what the group has actually asked for, and neither lets a sensitive constraint count toward the decision without being explained to everybody first. That last part is what made this worth building for WebMCP specifically. A personal agent already knows things about its user that the user would rather not broadcast to five friends. Until now the only way to put that knowledge to work was to hand it to a shared service. I wanted to find out whether an agent could advocate for someone inside a live page, as that person and within an authority they granted, while the reason itself never left their client. What it does Three people open one planning room from a link. They see the same live map and the same brief of what the group has asked for so far. Each person states what matters in a single composer bar and chooses who may see it before they speak . A need can be shared, private, or agent-only. The server evaluates a private need and peers see only its effect on the count. An agent-only need stays with your agent and never reaches the server at all. The app suggests the next thing worth asking about from the data itself, never from a built-in list of categories. Every need becomes a row you can set aside. Press and hold a row and the map shows the room without that need, live. The cost of a need becomes visible instead of argued about. The room recomputes which places still work after every move, and it counts what is merely unverified separately from what actually failed. Missing data is drawn as its own state rather than quietly dropping a place. When nothing satisfies everyone, Spokes does not name who is blocking. It privately offers each person a quantified way out. The organizer sees "widen the area from 800 m to 1.2 km, brings back 4 places". The person who stated a need sees "let this need be nice-to-have, +12 places". Consent is explicit and confirmed on the page. Once the group agrees, the composer gives way to arrival: a travel mode and a one-tap handoff to the map app everyone already has. Alongside all of it, your personal ChatGPT can act in the same session through WebMCP. It can catch up on what changed while you were away, inspect places, put one forward, rule one out, or grant an adjustment. Your agent can assist you, or negotiate for you outright. How I built it A TypeScript monorepo (pnpm). Fastify and a Postgres event log sit behind a WebSocket realtime channel. The front end is React and Vite with MapLibre GL over keyless OpenFreeMap tiles. TypeBox contracts are shared by both sides behind a hashed contract-manifest gate. Place data is a one-time OpenStreetMap extract of Berlin Mitte. The WebMCP surface is 22 tools registered imperatively on document.modelContext at page load, 10 for negotiation and 12 spatial. Each is a narrow function with closed enum schemas, readOnlyHint and untrustedContentHint annotations, and a capped result budget. The page works fully without WebMCP. The tools are an additional way in. Four decisions did most of the work. Two protocols over the WebMCP substrate. WebMCP itself only carries tool names and schemas. So the first sync_session call returns a capability manifest that teaches the agent a domain-independent negotiation protocol (identity, revision sync, privacy tiers, requirements, stances, adjustments, consent, agreement) and a spatial-destination domain layered on top. Server-owned identity and per-viewer projections. Actor identity comes only from the bearer token. No tool argument accepts an actor id. Every event is stored once and projected per viewer, so unauthorised fields never appear in another participant's HTTP body or WebSocket frame. The test suite asserts this at the wire, not at the function boundary. Revision discipline instead of pretend realtime. Every mutation carries the agent's last-seen revision. A stale one returns a structured sync_required with a delta instead of acting on old state. That fits an agent that participates in bursts far better than a subscription it never really holds. Consent an agent cannot forge. An agent may recommend a grant, but a change beyond what the user delegated only stages . Staging mints a single-use code delivered on the participant's own realtime channel. The applying command must carry it back, and the code never appears in any tool result. Eligibility, minimal-conflict-set detection and the impasse counterfactuals are all deterministic. No model is allowed to invent a feasibility fact. 364 automated tests across three lanes: 222 unit, 128 three-user API, and 14 Playwright specs driving three isolated browser contexts. Challenges I ran into Privacy that is neither a lie nor a hole. The rule I settled on is that a private need's effect is always public and its content never leaves its owner. Both halves matter. Hiding the effect would make the count inexplicable, and leaking the content is the whole thing I was avoiding. It took a real redesign to stop routing private predicates through shared state "just for rendering", and a wire-level test suite to prove I had. Proving a human consented, honestly. My first cut let a bearer token commit an agreement over plain HTTP without ever touching the page. The realtime-only nonce closes that. It still is not proof a human clicked, because the realtime channel authenticates with the same token. Rather than overclaim, I wrote the residual threat model down in KNOWN-LIMITATIONS.md . Keeping the interface domain-agnostic. It is hard not to type a domain word into a heading. What saved it was a rule on the server side. The server returns the facets present across the current result set, each with a mandatory unknown count, and the client renders whatever it gets. There is no domain branch anywhere in the front end, which is also what lets a human and an agent reason over the same vocabulary. Deployment, on the last evening. I had prepared a Coolify deployment and abandoned it at the gate. Its Traefik has documented WebSocket failures on compose stacks, and the room is a WebSocket. The January 2026 disclosure put eleven critical CVEs in a control plane that runs as root. Its baseline would have claimed a quarter of a 4 GB box before Postgres started. The existing compose file was already a correct production stack. It needed twenty lines of Caddy in front, not a PaaS. That deploy went out with nineteen minutes to spare, after a self-inflicted detour in which a redeploy overwrote the host's generated Postgres password and stranded the database behind credentials nothing had written down. Two rendering bugs that looked like design problems. Vite's dependency optimiser broke MapLibre's worker, so the basemap never drew. A CSS animation setting transform silently overwrote a positioning translate and threw pins at their anchors. Both cost hours before either was understood. Accomplishments that I'm proud of An agent that can advocate for a constraint it never discloses. The agent screens places locally and returns per-place verdicts. The council folds them into eligibility, and peers see the aggregate effect with no route back to the cause. That is the capability I most wanted WebMCP to make possible, and it works. Press and hold. Holding a need shows the map without it, live, and releasing restores it. It turns an argument about whether a need is reasonable into a number you can see, and it is the one gesture everybody understood without being told. An impasse resolver that refuses to assign blame. When nothing satisfies everyone, the room offers each person a private, quantified route out, phrased as a consequence rather than an instruction. Honest unverified state. Missing data renders as a hollow pin and a separate count. A place is never silently dropped for lacking a value, and unknown is never drawn as failure. Two independent adversarial reviews: a protocol-invariant audit and a cross-family model review of the server, then two further reviews of the rebuilt client. The privacy and agreement-integrity findings were fixed and are covered by tests. I published the deferred items instead of hiding them. What I learned An agent is not a fast user, and modelling it as one produces bugs. It participates in bursts, disappears, an
video_title: Spokes: collaborative coordination assistant · WebMCP Challenge 2026 explainer video
video_transcript_excerpt: Picking a place with friends pays for boring reason. The needs live in different heads. They arrive one at a time and one of them is something somebody will not say out loud. Spokes puts the whole group on one live map and it lets you bring your own assistant. It starts with a sentence. I tell chat GPT what the group is trying to do. Because Spokes talks to assistants directly, the assistant can work on the product on my behalf. Pick the area, set up the room, hand back the invite. Nobody learned an app, nobody filled in a form. Show the code and the others are in. Sarah would like to sit outside. She adds it. Everyone's map settles. The places that still work stay bright, the rest fade where they stand. Press and hold her need and the map shows the room without it. What a need costs becomes a number you can see instead of something to argue about. Joe has a need he would rather not explain. He marks it private. The room learns only that a private condition ruled some places out, not what it was, not whose. And now nothing works for everyone. This is where a group chat goes quiet. Spokes does not wait and it does not name who is blocking. It offers each person a private way out with a number attached. Joe sees what comes back if his need became optional. Sarah sees the same for sitting outside. I see what a wider area brings back. Each decides alone. Joe leaves his, nobody asks him why. Sarah lets hers go and the room opens up again. For some places, the information is hollow. The map does not know enough about them and it says so instead of guessing. This is where an assistant earns its place. I ask it to find out. It reads menus and websites and records what it finds in the room. Hollow pins fill in for everyone. It cannot see what Joe needs because it only knows what I know, but everything it does learn, the whole group gets. I have the assistant put forward a place it just checked. The court lands with everyone. Sarah looks and rules it out. The assistant notices the room moved, takes the veto into account, and suggests another. This time everyone is in. Only a person can settle it, and only once everyone has said so. An assistant can help you decide. It never decides for you. And then off you go. Pick how you're getting there and hand off to the map you already use. One room needs to count without being shown a way out for everyone instead of blame, and an assistant that works inside the room as you. Finds what the map cannot and keeps what you keep. Spokes.

title: Quorum
pitch: Scheduling, negotiated by your agent — approved by you. Humans and AI agents vote, counter-propose, and converge on a meeting time together via WebMCP, with every agent action visibly logged.
about_excerpt: Scheduling, negotiated by your agent — approved by you. Humans and AI agents vote, counter-propose, and converge on a meeting time together via WebMCP, with every agent action visibly logged. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Group scheduling is a negotiation over everyone's constraints - and it's still done by making humans click checkboxes in polls. When WebMCP launched, we realized the missing piece was never a smarter poll: it was letting each person's AI agent join the negotiation itself . Quorum is our answer: scheduling, negotiated by your agent - approved by you. What it does Quorum is a meeting scheduler where humans and agents are equal participants in the same live session. Humans get a normal UI: candidate times, yes/maybe/no voting, counter-proposals. Agents get seven WebMCP tools registered by the page itself - they can read the event state, join on their human's behalf, vote with reasons, counter-propose new times, and rank the slots. Every action lands in a shared negotiation log tagged HUMAN or AGENT , and only the human organizer can accept proposals or lock in the final time. Agent proposes; human approves. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Scheduling is a multi-step, stateful interaction - exactly where screen-scraping agents fail. With WebMCP, the page tells agents what's possible via typed, self-describing tools. In testing, an agent that had never seen the app correctly chained four tools on the first try (read state -> join -> vote with a conflict note -> report the winner) purely from the tool descriptions. What people and agents can do together that wasn't possible before A mixed negotiation - some parties human, some agents - on the same page, in real time, with full mutual visibility. Before WebMCP, agents couldn't reliably operate voting UIs built for humans, and sites had no way to declare what actions they support. Quorum shows the new shape of the open web: agents handle the tedium, the audit trail keeps trust, and humans keep the final word. How we built it Vanilla JS frontend + Express backend, live-synced over server-sent events. Every WebMCP tool executes the same functions the human UI uses , tagged via: "agent" - one code path, one audit trail: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "submit_availability", description: "Submit availability for candidate slots on behalf of your user…", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { responses: { type: "array" } }, required: ["responses"] }, execute: async ({ responses }) => submitAvailability(responses, "agent"), }); Deployed on Vercel; Upstash Redis keeps event state consistent across serverless instances, with a per-stream Redis poll so every open tab stays live. The visual design was created in Claude Design and implemented as a hand-written design system. Challenges we ran into - Serverless broke our state. Events lived in memory; on Vercel, an SSE stream landed on a different instance and couldn't find the event. We added a storage layer (Upstash Redis in production, in-memory locally) and cross-instance live updates via polling. - The WebMCP API surface is still moving (document.modelContext vs the earlier navigator.modelContext), so we wrote a small adapter that registers against whichever exists. - Tool descriptions are prompts. Agents chained our tools correctly only after we rewrote descriptions to say when to call each tool and what to fetch first. Accomplishments that we're proud of - **A never-before-seen agent used our app correctly on the first try.** In our final test, a Gemini-backed agent autonomously chained four tools - read the event state, joined as a new participant, voted with a conflict note attached to the right slot, and reported the winning time - guided by nothing but our tool descriptions. That's the whole WebMCP promise, working. - **One code path for humans and agents.** Every WebMCP tool executes the exact same functions the human UI calls - so the audit log, validation, and permissions are identical no matter who acts. No parallel "agent API" to drift out of sync. - **Trust as a first-class feature.** The negotiation log tags every action HUMAN or AGENT in real time, organizer-only tools are genuinely scoped, and an agent can never finalize a meeting on its own. - **A one-click seeded demo event**, so any judge can see a mid-negotiation session - votes, an agent counter-proposal, a live log - in under ten seconds, then take over as the organizer. - **Shipping the full journey in days**: idea -> working local app -> designed UI -> deployed on Vercel with Redis-backed state that survives serverless cold starts. What we learned - **Tool descriptions are prompts.** Agents started chaining our tools correctly only after we rewrote descriptions to say *when* to call each tool and what to fetch first ("Call this first to understand the current state"). Designing for a model reader is a real skill, and WebMCP makes it part of frontend work. - **The trust problem matters more than the automation problem.** The feature people react to isn't that agents can vote — it's seeing exactly what an agent did on your behalf, and knowing the final decision always needs a human. - **Serverless changes your assumptions.** Our in-memory state worked perfectly until the first live SSE request landed on a different instance. Moving to Redis-backed storage with cross-instance live updates taught us to design for "any request, any instance" from the start. - **Build for a moving standard defensively.** WebMCP's surface has shifted between Chrome previews (`document.modelContext` vs `navigator.modelContext`), so a small adapter layer saved us from breaking on every browser update. What's next for Quorum - **Calendar integration**, so your agent votes from your real availability instead of being told your constraints. - **Agent-to-agent negotiation rounds** - agents exchange counter-proposals automatically until they converge on a shortlist, and humans only see the final choice to ratify. - **Invites addressed to agents**: send an event link straight to someone's assistant, which handles everything and pings its human only for approval. - **Richer constraints in tools** - recurring meetings, time-zone fairness scoring, and "must attend / optional" roles that agents can reason about. title: CoHabby Living
pitch: A compatibility-first roommate finder where your browser agent does the structured work through six WebMCP tools, and you keep every human decision.
about_excerpt: A compatibility-first roommate finder where your browser agent does the structured work through six WebMCP tools, and you keep every human decision. Like Comment Story Updates The last click stays human: Confirm demo introduction moves the state to v9. Demo confirmed. No real message was sent. compare_shortlist lays two people side by side across six dimensions of daily life. Warm is the chosen tone for the first hello. Public proof: MIT license, public repository, immutable tag, and the live footer's exact deployed revision ba55c557358a. Six WebMCP tools registered on one page: five change what the person sees, one is read-only. READY · v1 is the state both of them share. prepare_introduction drafts a first hello from facts already on the page. The person edits every word; no site tool can confirm or send. Synergy Lens: explain_synergy_match opens Maya's 92 read, 88% profile evidence, and three practical reasons the household rhythms fit. Approval is not a tool. The agent stages the living plan; only the person clicks Yes, use these choices. State moves v2 to v3. find_compatible_rooms brings Maya, Jordan, and Sam onto the page, person first, home as context. Whole-card selection stays human. Inspiration Finding a roommate is easy. Finding someone you can actually live well with is hard, and it shapes daily life for a lot of people: traveling nurses, single parents, new graduates, retirees, interns. Rooms are easy to list. Compatibility is what nobody helps with. CoHabby puts the person first and the room second. I also believe good technology should make people more human, not more mechanical. WebMCP made that concrete: the page can hand an agent real tools and still keep the meaningful decisions on the human side of the screen. CoHabby is already a live product with real users on the web , iOS , and Android . This challenge build is a separate, new codebase, but the problem it targets and the people it serves are the same. What people and agents do together Six small WebMCP tools share one page with the person: get_living_context reads the visible state (the only read-only tool) stage_living_brief stages a living plan from everyday habits find_compatible_rooms brings Maya, Jordan, and Sam onto the page, person first explain_synergy_match opens the Synergy Lens: a 92 score, 88% evidence, three practical reasons compare_shortlist lays two people side by side across six dimensions of daily life prepare_introduction drafts an editable first hello from facts already on the page Three actions are deliberately not tools: approving the plan, editing the hello, and confirming the introduction. The public tests assert that apply_living_brief and confirm_introduction do not exist. The agent prepares everything. The last click stays with the person. Why WebMCP fits Roommate matching is structured work with a few consequential decisions in between. WebMCP lets the page describe each step precisely, so the agent completes it reliably instead of guessing at the UI, and every result renders where the person can see it. Agent and human read the same state, which advances visibly from v1 to v9. How I built it Next.js and TypeScript. Every tool has a strict JSON Schema input (bounded enums, patterns, additionalProperties: false ) and a separate output schema, so nothing reaches the agent that a person could not see. Each call runs under a combined abort signal: cancel it and it rolls back to its checkpoint and commits nothing. A tool resolves only after the page acknowledges the new state has rendered, so "done" always means "visible." The live footer prints the deployed revision, the repo is MIT, and the judged source is pinned to an immutable tag. Fixtures and Synergy scores are fictional demo data, and the film says so. This WebMCP app is entirely new work created during the submission period (repository started Sept 1, 2026; every commit is dated inside the window). It shares no code with CoHabby's existing web and mobile products. Only the brand, the mission, and the roommate-compatibility concept pre-date the challenge; CHALLENGE_WORK.md in the repo documents the separation. Challenges and what I learned The hardest call was the human boundary. Making everything a tool would have looked more autonomous. It also would have let an agent introduce you to a stranger without asking. The hardest engineering was render acknowledgement: agents move faster than browsers paint, and a tool that returns before its result is on screen creates a page the person and the agent disagree about. The lesson: small, bounded tools with visible results beat one clever tool, and the best agent-native page is the one where you can tell exactly what the agent did and what you decided.  IntentCart 🛒🤖 

 AI researches. You decide. 

 IntentCart is an agent-native collaborative shopping experience built with WebMCP . 

 Instead of endlessly searching through products, users can simply describe what they want. For example: 

 
 “Build me a coding setup for college under ₹70,000.” 
 

 The AI agent can then research products, compare options, create a shopping plan, and calculate the total budget — while keeping the human in control of the final decision. 

 💡 Inspiration 

 Online shopping can involve searching through dozens of products, comparing specifications, checking prices, and trying to stay within a budget. 

 I wanted to explore a different experience where an AI agent could actually interact with the shopping website and help with the research and planning, instead of just acting like a chatbot. 

 🚀 What IntentCart Does 

 IntentCart provides 8 native WebMCP tools : 

 
 🔎 Search products 
 📋 Get product details 
 ⚖️ Compare products 
 🛒 Add products to cart 
 ❌ Remove products from cart 
 🛍️ View the cart 
 💰 Calculate the budget 
 🧠 Create a shopping plan 
 

 For example, the agent can create a complete college coding setup while staying within a ₹70,000 budget. 

 Each recommended product includes a “Why Selected” explanation so the human can understand the recommendation. 

 👤 Human Approval 

 The AI does not automatically make the final shopping decision. 

 The agent creates a proposal first. The human reviews the products, reasons, and budget, then explicitly clicks: 

 “Approve & Add to Cart” 

 Only after approval are the products added to the collaborative cart. 

 This creates a simple principle: 

 
 AI handles the research and planning. Humans make the final decision. 
 

 🔧 How It Was Built 

 IntentCart was built using: 

 
 React 
 TypeScript 
 Vite 
 WebMCP 
 Native browser WebMCP APIs 
 HTML5 
 CSS3 
 

 The application uses a shared cart state so that changes made through the website and WebMCP tools remain synchronized. 

 An Agent Activity timeline also shows tool activity as the agent interacts with the application. 

 🧩 Challenges 

 One of the biggest challenges was designing a shared state that could work consistently between the normal UI and agent tool calls. 

 Another important challenge was creating a safe approval flow where the AI can propose actions without automatically making purchasing decisions . 

 I also had to handle WebMCP tool registration carefully to avoid duplicate registrations during React development and remounts. 

 🏆 What I'm Proud Of 

 
 Native WebMCP tool integration 
 Agent-accessible shopping capabilities 
 Human approval before cart changes 
 Real-time shared cart state 
 Product comparison and budget planning 
 Clear visibility into agent activity 
 

 📚 What I Learned 

 This project helped me understand how to build for the agent-native web . 

 Instead of designing only for humans clicking buttons, I learned how to expose meaningful application capabilities as structured tools that AI agents can use. 

 I also learned that good agent experiences need a balance between automation and human control . 

 🔮 What's Next 

 Future versions could include: 

 
 More personalized shopping preferences 
 Larger and real-world product catalogs 
 Smarter recommendations 
 More advanced comparison features 
 More granular human approval controls 
 Multi-user collaborative shopping

title: Benchkeeper
pitch: Community events are an important for social causes and supporting the local community. Benchkeeper uses WebMCP to help organizers plan these events and protect key bookings, and reveal trade-offs.
about_excerpt: Community events are an important for social causes and supporting the local community. Benchkeeper uses WebMCP to help organizers plan these events and protect key bookings, and reveal trade-offs. Like Comment Story Updates Many communities have these local events to support different causes to raise funds or just do stuff in the community like repairing community parks to clean up from emergencies and more. These community events require different skills for example a repair event, a clean up event etc. These different community events require different skills from different people. However it's really hard to plan these events particularly if one person doesn't show up. Rebuilding the schedule means deciding which promises can still be kept. I built "Benchkeeper" to help these community organizers work through their decisions with a browser agent. WebMCP lets the agent work with explicit scheduling constraints and shares a proposal directly for the organizer. What Benchkeeper is a sort of planning desk for small community events. Organizers can add repair requests, manage volunteer availability, reserve break or walk-in time, and protect promised appointments. Through ten browser-native WebMCP tools, an agent can inspect the event, explore cancellations, propose a revised schedule, and explain why an item cannot fit. The organizer can compare the current and proposed plans, see who moves or loses a slot, and review the tradeoffs before applying anything. The tools cannot apply a plan or release a protected appointment. Those actions remain in the organizer’s interface. Benchkeeper also supports spreadsheet intake, undo and redo, JSON backups, and printable schedules. It sends no messages to visitors, and manual planning works without WebMCP. How I built this. We built the interface with React, TypeScript, and Vite, using Zod to validate tool inputs and imported data. A deterministic, bounded scheduling search considers repairer skills, availability, visitor time windows, parts readiness, and protected appointments. The WebMCP tools and human interface use the same application state. Revision checks reject stale edits, and approval is tied to the exact proposal being reviewed. Event data is stored in the browser tab’s sessionStorage, with downloadable backups. Cloudflare Workers serves the app; there is no event-data backend or embedded chatbot. We used Vitest, Playwright, and axe-core for automated checks, alongside real native WebMCP execution tests. Challenges Browser implementation differences made WebMCP integration more involved than registering a tool catalog. We had to test actual execution and handle differences in argument formats. Scheduling also exposed a subtle distinction: keeping someone’s appointment at exactly the same time is different from keeping that person booked at all. We refined the planning preferences and comparison reports to make that tradeoff explicit. Keeping human edits, agent proposals, and saved state consistent required careful handling of stale reviews and browser Back navigation. Accomplishments that we're proud of I built a complete cancellation-and-recovery workflow where an agent’s proposal appears in the same desk the organizer uses. Protected appointments stay fixed during replanning, excluded requests have concrete explanations, and organizers can preview the cost of making room for another item. I also tested the scheduler against thousands of small, exhaustively checked cases and kept discovered failures as regression tests. Native WebMCP execution was tested separately from the clearly labeled scripted rehearsal. What we learned Useful agent tools need clear consequences as well as clear inputs. Organizers need to know whose appointment changed, why a request was excluded, and whether a proposal still reflects the latest event. I also learned that a passing build does not establish a working product. Native browser execution, keyboard navigation, printed schedules, and saved-state recovery each exposed issues that needed their own checks. What's next My next priority is testing Benchkeeper is to run it on a small clean up operation for a school in my area. the current examples is synthetic so doing something good in the community and using this seems like a good next step. Then the feedback should guide if this was useful to them. For now, the tool works for pre-event planning tool, and its bounded search does not guarantee the best possible schedule. There is also a bigger opportunity with other industries to help with planning and coordination particularly with health-care, education, plumbing and more. title: PersonalWebMCP
pitch: Teach a website workflow once. Reuse it as a personal WebMCP tool.
about_excerpt: Teach a website workflow once. Reuse it as a personal WebMCP tool. Like Comment Story Updates extension overview Teaching workflow Tools overview Project Story Inspiration WebMCP gives websites a reliable way to expose named, typed capabilities to agents. But the web will not become fully agent-ready at once. Many sites expose no tools, some expose only part of what a user needs, and even a well-designed site cannot anticipate every personal routine or preference. That led me to a simple question: why should only website developers be able to define capabilities for agents? I wanted to explore a user-owned layer for WebMCP. Instead of repeatedly asking an agent to rediscover the same buttons and fields, a person could demonstrate a workflow once, decide what should vary, and save the result as a semantic tool. On a WebMCP-enabled site, that same layer could personalize and combine the site's native tools rather than replacing them. What it does PersonalWebMCP is a Chromium extension that lets users create their own WebMCP tools on the websites they use. The extension works in three main ways: Teach a missing capability. The user performs a normal browser workflow, reviews the captured actions, and chooses which values become typed agent inputs and which remain remembered preferences. Personalize and compose existing capabilities. PersonalWebMCP discovers tools already exposed by the website and can combine them with taught actions as one higher-level personal tool. Keep capabilities understandable and repairable. Every saved tool has a name, description, JSON Schema input contract, origin and path scope, provenance, workflow graph, health state, and revision history. The saved capability is registered into the visible page through document.modelContext.registerTool() . A compatible agent discovers it beside the website's native tools and invokes it with structured input. The two central demonstrations show both sides of the idea: A legacy supplier portal exposes zero WebMCP tools. I teach an invoice-search workflow, expose vendor and min_amount as inputs, and an agent later invokes personal_open_latest_unpaid_invoice from another section of the portal. A furniture configurator already exposes five native WebMCP tools, but it lacks an Add to project action. I teach only that missing action, combine it with the native tools, remember my preferred configuration, and expose only quantity to the agent through personal_prepare_my_studio_workspace . How we built it I built PersonalWebMCP as a TypeScript and pnpm monorepo. The product is a WXT Manifest V3 extension with a React side panel, a service worker, an isolated content script, and a small MAIN-world runtime. That separation matters because WebMCP is page-scoped: document.modelContext belongs to the webpage, while extension content scripts normally run in an isolated JavaScript world. The MAIN-world runtime performs WebMCP discovery, registration, invocation, and tool lifecycle management. The content script carries validated messages across the page boundary, while the service worker owns compilation, execution, local persistence, scope, receipts, confirmation state, and repair history. The extension uses the WebMCP API directly: document.modelContext.getTools() discovers website-owned and registered personal tools. document.modelContext.registerTool() registers personal_ping and every saved personal capability. document.modelContext.executeTool() invokes native dependencies inside composite tools. abort signals and tool-change events manage registration and invocation lifetimes. The compiler converts a raw interaction trace into a reusable capability contract and workflow graph. It retains semantic evidence such as accessible names, roles, labels, landmarks, routes, and form relationships while excluding sensitive controls. Personal tools are stored locally and registered only when their origin, path, health, and prerequisites match the visible page. The companion demo site is built with Next.js and React. It supplies deterministic environments for testing a site with no WebMCP, a site with native tools, and a hybrid workflow. The extension remains the product; the hosted pages are controlled evaluation surfaces. Challenges we ran into The first challenge was the browser execution boundary. Registering a tool from an extension is not the same as registering one in ordinary page code, because the service worker and isolated content script cannot directly use the page's document.modelContext . Building a small, validated bridge between those worlds was necessary for genuine WebMCP registration. The second challenge was ensuring the result was more than a macro recorder. A literal recording tends to preserve unstable details such as a result row, changing price, or generated record ID. The compiler had to separate task intent from recorded outcome, let the user choose parameters versus preferences, restore the correct starting context, and expose a typed semantic contract to the agent. Navigation and lifecycle behavior were also difficult. Personal tools must appear on the correct origin and path, follow the active browser tab, refresh after saving, and withdraw or re-register as the page changes. Experimental browser behavior made real Chrome testing essential; a successful TypeScript build alone could not prove the WebMCP lifecycle. Finally, repair requires restraint. Automatically selecting a vaguely similar element may be worse than stopping. The implementation uses semantic evidence, visible outcome checks, versioned revisions, and guided approval when a replacement is ambiguous. Accomplishments that we're proud of A user-created tool is genuinely registered through WebMCP, discovered by an agent, invoked with structured arguments, and produces a visible result. The legacy demonstration goes from zero native tools to a reusable personal capability without requiring the user to write JavaScript or JSON Schema. The configurator demonstrates that PersonalWebMCP remains useful after WebMCP adoption: it combines five website-owned tools with one user-taught action as a single personalized capability. Personal tools retain provenance, local scope, typed contracts, execution receipts, health, and repair history instead of becoming opaque browser scripts. The same extension interface supports inspection, teaching, composition, execution, and repair while keeping the agent's actions visible to the user. What we learned The most important lesson was that WebMCP is not merely a cleaner way to automate clicks. Its value is the contract between a page and an agent: a stable name, a useful description, typed inputs, execution semantics, and a meaningful result. I also learned that native and personal capabilities are complementary. Website developers are best positioned to expose safe, general primitives. Users are best positioned to describe the higher-level routines and preferences that matter specifically to them. A personal capability layer can connect those two levels. Building the extension also made the WebMCP lifecycle very concrete. Registration context, abort signals, navigation, tool discovery, schema quality, scope, and error messages all directly affect whether an agent can use a capability reliably. What's next for PersonalWebMCP The next priority is making the compiler and semantic execution engine reliable across a broader range of real websites, beyond the controlled fixtures. I would also like to add intent-first teaching, where the user describes the desired capability before demonstrating it, and PersonalWebMCP asks only for the missing actions or choices. Other directions include portable tool export and synchronization, richer repair learning, multi-site compositions, stronger review controls for consequential actions, and support for more WebMCP-compatible browsers and agents. Longer term, frequently created personal tools could also help website teams understand which native capabilities their users actually want. title: TrustScore Atlas
pitch: The open, source-cited registry of businesses, built for agents and people. Every value carries the government register that published it and the date it said so.
about_excerpt: The open, source-cited registry of businesses, built for agents and people. Every value carries the government register that published it and the date it said so. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Somewhere right now, someone is asking an AI whether a company is real. In most of the world there is no structured answer. Across much of Africa, South Asia and Latin America, company data exists only in fragmented public lists: PDFs, portals and scanned registers that never meet. Uganda, our reference country, publishes a dozen business registers (city trading licences, tax agent lists, the procurement portal, product certifications, sector regulators), each with its own identifier, format and outage schedule. A lender doing KYB, a procurement officer checking a bidder, or an agent asked "is this company real?" all repeat the same manual, unrecorded work. The businesses themselves have nowhere to see or correct what the public record says about them. Global aggregators work only where registers are already structured. We tested the alternative before building: the same question through web search dug through PDFs, anchored on a 2024 licence, and confused two legal entities. That answer is what most of the world gets today. What it does Atlas harmonises public registers into one business record with field-level provenance. Every value is a statement: source, source reference, date pulled, licence and precedence. Records are resolved across registers by issuer-unique identifiers (tax identification numbers merge; name matches stay candidates, never merges). Four deterministic, versioned scores (Formality, Activity, Compliance Signals, Procurement Readiness) are computed from the evidence and always report coverage: how many registers were checked, found, and not yet checked. No language model produces a number; scores are explained by templated evidence rows a person can click through to the register. Unknown is shown as unknown, never as zero. Today: 79,078 businesses across 2 country packs, 9 of 13 registers loaded, over 600,000 sourced statements and 300,000 stored scores. Uganda is the reference pack (8 of 12 registers); Kenya's central-bank licensee directory is the second, proving the contract is portable. A country is a pack: declarations for its registers, identifier schemes and boundaries plus small adapters, forkable by anyone. WebMCP. The site registers its tools with document.modelContext , scoped to the route (four on the home and search pages, more on a business page with atlas_id defaulting to the record on screen, all ten on /tools; tool sets change on navigation via toolchange ). Read tools (search_businesses, get_business, get_evidence, score_business, explain_score, find_segment, list_sources) carry readOnlyHint , and every result containing register-derived text carries untrustedContentHint so agents treat it as data, not instructions; results are structured, bounded and paginated with context-bound cursors. Write tools (start_claim, submit_correction, label_linkage, report_issue) each require human confirmation: where the browser cannot prompt in-page, the tool stores an unconfirmed request and returns a link to a plain form the person must submit, and unconfirmed requests expire and never count. The claim and report forms are declarative tools ( toolname , toolparamdescription ). The same implementations are served over a read-only remote MCP endpoint, and the /tools page runs every tool from the page itself in any browser, no flag needed. Humans and agents together. An agent answers "is this bidder real, and has it delivered public contracts?" with cited register rows, and "no evidence in checked registers" is an honest answer. A business owner then claims their record: the agent starts the claim, the person confirms on the page, the claim is verified by publishing a string on the business website (or a link mailed to a domain a register published), a maintainer approves it in a moderation queue that shows exactly what the approval rests on, and the next regeneration publishes the operator-verified value above the register value, with its own source beside it. Corrections never overwrite a regulator's word. How we built it SvelteKit on Cloudflare Workers; three D1 databases (records, statements, scores) regenerated by a transactional pointer swap; R2 for raw snapshots and Parquet bundles with Frictionless data packages; KV caching keyed by regeneration and deployment; a Python pipeline (adapters with a six-check conformance suite, probabilistic linkage with Splink, versioned rubrics) scheduled with GitHub Actions, with an identity-churn guard. Personal contact details in registers are dropped at parse time. Apache-2.0 code, CC-BY-4.0 data. Challenges we ran into Chrome 152 does not expose in-page confirmation for write tools, so we built a page-confirmation fallback that keeps a human in every write. Registers disagree about where a business is, so location is resolved as a unit from one winning source rather than field by field. A register's export job failed on the publisher's side mid-build; the pipeline now records that source as failed with both dates and regenerates from everything that succeeded, so one outage never blocks the rest. Accomplishments that we're proud of Tested in ChatGPT's built-in browser (GPT-5.6 Sol): the site tools arrow lists the tools, and the ask about a real company came back cited register by register, with identifiers and dates from this week, in under four minutes (screenshots in the README). The verified-claims loop is live end to end: domain-proved claims, evidence documents, a gated moderation queue, and operator statements that outrank scraped values at the next regeneration. And the whole thing runs on free-tier infrastructure with open data downloads. What we learned Agents are honest exactly when the data layer is: give them provenance and coverage and they say "not checked" instead of guessing. Deterministic scores plus clickable evidence beat any generated number. And a register that fails must be shown as failed, because stale data dressed as fresh is worse than a gap. What's next for TrustScore Atlas More country packs through the same declarations, cross-country search, and the operator-verified claims loop running at scale. Built for the places where the answer used to be a guess. Trust Score Atlas.

title: PrzedWysylka | WebMCP Lab
pitch: A browser-local FA(3) workbench where an agent can prove a repair while approval remains a visible UI decision.
about_excerpt: A browser-local FA(3) workbench where an agent can prove a repair while approval remains a visible UI decision. Like Comment Story Updates 1 The production workbench after WebMCP has staged and validated a two-value repair. Inspiration Invoice XML is boring until one malformed value stops a real workflow. Poland's FA(3) format is strict and large. Inspecting it by eye is difficult. An agent is useful when the fault is two placeholder values buried inside an official template. That does not mean the agent should quietly decide that the repaired document is acceptable. I built PrzedWysylka WebMCP Lab to test a narrower contract. The agent should do the mechanical work against the state already visible in the browser. The reviewer should see the source and proposed bytes. The same screen should show the validation result and final page control. What it does The app opens an official parameterized FA(3) template at Revision 0. The template is intentionally invalid. Its two placeholders fail canonical XSD validation. The page registers exactly six WebMCP tools: get_workspace_status list_official_assets read_official_asset select_official_asset stage_exact_replacements validate_workspace During the demo, the agent selects the template and validates Revision 0. It reads the relevant source lines, then stages two exact replacements. After validating the pending proposal, the page displays its diff and a SHA-256 proof bound to those proposed bytes. There is no WebMCP approval or rejection tool. The review buttons stay in the visible interface. In the demo workflow, I click Approve changes myself. The store creates Revision 1 and runs canonical validation again. An ordinary browser still gets the complete manual workbench. It also gets an honest WebMCP unavailable status instead of a polyfill pretending that the native API exists. Why WebMCP fits this job Without WebMCP, an agent would have to scrape diagnostics from the DOM and infer which file or revision is active. It would then scroll through XML and type into an editor. That is fragile. A remote MCP server would create another copy of state outside the review surface. Here, each tool calls the same asset registry and validator used by the UI. It also uses the page's replacement engine and workspace store. The agent receives bounded structured results. The reviewer watches the same state change in the page. WebMCP is the working interaction contract rather than a decorative endpoint. The missing capabilities matter too. Approval and rejection are not registered as WebMCP tools. Neither are upload, download or submission. The accurate claim is narrow: approval is a visible UI action and is absent from the WebMCP surface. The app does not claim to identify who operates the browser. How I built it The frontend uses React 19 with TypeScript 6 on Vite 8. It feature-detects document.modelContext and registers imperative tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() . The definitions have static descriptions and JSON input schemas. Callback inputs pass through Zod before they reach application state. The callbacks reuse existing application services instead of maintaining an agent-only model. Validation runs in the browser through libxml2 compiled to WebAssembly. The deployed app has no application backend or account system. It also has no analytics and no customer upload path. Every successful tool response is limited to 1,500 serialized characters. Catalog results are paged. Source cursors preserve the locked files' CRLF/LF/bare-CR delimiters. A caller cannot place a cursor inside a UTF-16 surrogate pair. Validation returns the complete finding count with compact summaries and explicit truncation metadata. Proposal proof is owned by the store. validate_workspace hashes the exact content snapshot it checked. The record includes the asset and proposal IDs plus the base revision. It also stores the document generation, validation result and proposed SHA-256. Approval fails closed if any part of that identity is stale. Challenges Registering six functions was the easy part. Keeping async work tied to the same browser state took most of the effort. Cancellation exposed a subtle bug. A dependency could ignore its AbortSignal and resolve late, after the caller had already cancelled. I had to invalidate pending work immediately and check state again after every awaited boundary. A cancelled validation can no longer persist a result or revive an obsolete proof. Byte fidelity caused a different class of failures. Many official files use CRLF, while some contain bare carriage returns. Normalizing line endings made a source excerpt look harmless but broke exact replacement. The reader now slices the original decoded text and returns a recoverable cursor without splitting newline pairs or Unicode surrogate pairs. Evidence also needed a hard boundary. The deterministic Playwright suite uses an injected, standards-shaped harness. That proves callback behavior but not native browser support. A separate production smoke uses Chrome's real document.modelContext ; it records nativeModelContext: true and injectedHarness: false . The report does not pretend that an automated Playwright click was a human approval. Verification The native production smoke registers all six tools and executes every callback. It confirms that the WebMCP surface contains no approval tool. Every proof location resolves to the same value, from proposal preflight through the final applied draft: a41799c158deca1bca74e1a158a0748f401721b0ed4b5731ef1a38cfa087c3f0 The offline corpus gate checks all 55 locked first-party records. Browser WASM validation agrees with an independent xmllint gate on 28 expected-valid and 16 expected-invalid FA(3) records. The committed suite covers shared state and cancellation. It tests proposal gating and the visible approval path as separate boundaries. Other checks exercise the ordinary-browser fallback. Responsive layouts and Axe audits run too. The evidence files are committed under docs/assets/ . They record the exact browser build and production artifact identity used for the smoke instead of relying on a screenshot label. What I learned WebMCP works best when a page exposes capabilities it already owns. Creating a parallel agent backend would have weakened this project because the reviewer and agent could disagree about selection or revision state. I also learned that small protocol details become product behavior very quickly. Output limits and cancellation are not cleanup tasks. Neither are cursor semantics or proof identity. If any one of them is vague, the approval screen can look trustworthy while referring to old or incomplete work. What's next The same approach could support other regulated schemas where an agent prepares a repair but the final review stays visible. User-provided documents would require a separate privacy design and threat model before I add an upload path. The six-tool competition surface will remain narrow. title: Chapa - engineering impact you and your agent shape together
pitch: Your repos show what you shipped. Chapa shows the engineer behind them: a live, verifiable impact badge that AI agents can understand, explain, compare, and evolve with you.
about_excerpt: Your repos show what you shipped. Chapa shows the engineer behind them: a live, verifiable impact badge that AI agents can understand, explain, compare, and evolve with you. Like 4 Comment 2 Story Updates Chapa meets WebMCP: the live developer-impact site becomes agent-operable. 19 tool registrations, reads open, writes human-approved. 18 distinct tools across 4 surfaces: discovery, profiles, verification, and the badge studio; all callable from the page itself. Agents propose, humans approve: simulate and preview freely, but nothing persists without explicit human confirmation. Try it live at chapa.thecreativetoken.com. Point any WebMCP-capable agent at the site or scan the QR. Inspiration Your repos show what you shipped. They do not show the engineer behind them. A CV can say "reliable," "consistent," or "quality-focused," but those are claims. Chapa tries to turn the work itself into evidence. Chapa analyzes 12 months of engineering activity and builds an Impact Profile across four core dimensions: Delivery, Quality, Consistency, and Breadth. An optional fifth dimension, Craft, appears when a developer provides a report from an AI coding tool. The profile includes a developer archetype, composite score, and trend over time. An internal confidence score adjusts the composite when data is incomplete. GitHub can be the starting point, but the profile is not limited to GitHub. Chapa can combine activity from GitLab, Bitbucket, Codeberg, and enterprise-managed GitHub accounts uploaded through the Chapa CLI. The result is a live SVG badge that can sit in a README and evolve as the developer's work evolves. Badges marked Verified metrics carry an HMAC-SHA256 signature, so their verification records can be authenticated and tampering detected. But there was a problem. The badge could show your engineering impact, but it could not explain it. Why is Quality 62? What caused the score to fall this month? What would happen if Delivery improved by ten points? How does this profile compare with another developer's? A static badge cannot answer those questions. An agent can. Why WebMCP WebMCP changes Chapa from something an agent can merely look at into something an agent can understand. Behind the badge is structured state: dimension scores, normalized submetrics, archetype, confidence, trend history, verification data, and badge configuration. Trying to infer that state from the DOM would be fragile and incomplete. With WebMCP, Chapa exposes the underlying model directly. An agent can call explain_dimension and receive the score, formula, normalized submetrics, and an improvement tip. It can call get_impact_history to reason about changes over time, or compare_profiles to compare two developers dimension by dimension. The agent is no longer interpreting pixels. It is working with the same engineering model that produced them. Creator Studio made the fit even stronger. Studio was already terminal-first: users type commands such as /set colorPalette indigo or /preset holographic . That command registry already defined Chapa's mutation vocabulary. WebMCP became another interface to the same system rather than a separate agent API. Human clicks, terminal commands, and agent tool calls all converge on the same underlying actions. What people and agents can do together Understand the profile Instead of searching through panels, you can ask: "Why did my score drop this month?" The agent can inspect the impact history, explain the affected dimensions, and answer using the same numbers Chapa displays. suggest_improvements runs Chapa's existing insight engine against the real profile, so recommendations come from the developer's own activity rather than generic advice. Explore what could change simulate_score lets an agent change hypothetical dimension values and calculate the resulting composite score, tier, and delta. Nothing is persisted. That means the agent can answer questions like: "What happens if I improve Quality to 80?" before anything changes. Compare engineering profiles compare_profiles validates another public handle, loads both profiles, and returns the delta for every dimension. What previously required opening two profiles and comparing them manually becomes a structured question an agent can answer. Understand verification explain_verification explains what a Chapa signature proves, what it does not prove, when the verification record expires, and whether it uses the current or legacy format. Verification becomes something a person can actually understand rather than just a cryptographic status indicator. Shape the badge Creator Studio contains seven visual style categories. Instead of navigating controls, a developer can describe what they want: "Make it minimal, remove the glow, and use the terminal preset." The agent translates that intent into the same /preset and /set commands a person would type. Those commands appear in the Studio transcript as they execute. The agent does not get a secret mutation path. It uses the same one the human does. Human control stays at the boundary The most important design decision was deciding what the agent should not control. Agents can inspect, explain, compare, simulate, preview, and restyle freely. Persistence is different. save_badge_config creates a proposal in the UI and waits for the developer to approve it. The agent can help shape the result; the human decides when it becomes real. In production, confirmation persists the configuration, invalidates the badge cache, and updates the public share page and live SVG. In judge demo mode, confirmed saves remain local. How I implemented WebMCP Chapa registers 19 WebMCP tool registrations across four surfaces, using 18 distinct tool names because Creator Studio and public profiles both register explain_dimension . Landing page ( / ) get_site_capabilities , find_profile Creator Studio ( /studio and /studio?demo=1 ) list_style_options , apply_badge_style , apply_preset , preview_badge , reset_badge_config , save_badge_config , simulate_score , suggest_improvements , explain_dimension Public profile ( /u/{handle} ) get_impact_profile , get_impact_history , verify_badge , compare_profiles , explain_dimension , get_embed_snippet Verification page ( /verify/{hash} ) get_verification_record , explain_verification A shared useModelContextTools hook registers each catalog on document.modelContext . A catalog signature keys registration so updated definitions register cleanly, and an AbortController removes tools when the component unmounts. In Creator Studio, Quick Controls, terminal commands, and WebMCP calls all resolve to command text and pass through the same executeCommand registry. This keeps the terminal transcript, React state, live preview, and pending save configuration on one shared mutation path. Trust and safety Public profile and verification tools are read-only. Any tool that may return user-controlled text, such as a display name from a source platform, sets untrustedContentHint to true . Free-text values are length-bounded and control characters are removed at the tool boundary. The server also removes private data before it reaches the browser. For example, a profile's confidence value and penalty reasons never enter the React Server Component payload for a visitor viewing another developer's profile. verify_badge strips confidence again at the client boundary as defense in depth. A feature flag named webmcp_enabled controls the entire WebMCP surface. A database value can override the environment configuration, allowing the tools to be disabled without a deployment. Challenges One of the most useful bugs I found was not in a tool. It was in the trust model around one. explain_dimension is used in two contexts. In Creator Studio, the data belongs to the developer viewing it. On a public profile, some of that data originates from another developer. The original tool factory hardcoded the trusted annotation. Nothing exploitable was exposed because no user-controlled text was present in the current submetrics. But the next field containing something like a repository name could have crossed the boundary incorrectly. I changed the factory so trust context is a required parameter. Each caller now has to declare what it knows. The second challenge appeared in badge caching. Because badge content can be localized, it was possible for the rendered locale and cache key locale to disagree. An English badge could therefore end up in a Spanish cache slot. I replaced those independent decisions with a single resolveBadgeLocale entry point that returns both the localized strings and the corresponding cache key. The caller can no longer accidentally pair one locale with another locale's cache entry. What I am proud of WebMCP did not become a parallel control plane bolted onto Chapa. The agent uses the same domain model and, in Creator Studio, the same command registry as the person using the interface. That gives Chapa a clear collaboration bounda

title: Second Mayor: build a city with your agent
pitch: Your favorite city builder now has room for a second mayor. Bring your agent along to advise you, plan neighbourhoods, or build the city of your dreams with you.
about_excerpt: Your favorite city builder now has room for a second mayor. Bring your agent along to advise you, plan neighbourhoods, or build the city of your dreams with you. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I wanted to play a city-builder with an AI agent. I love this type of game. Since my childhood I've been a huge fan of SimCity, and more recently Cities: Skylines. I didn't want to watch a demo of an agent filling in a city. I wanted real work between me and an agent. The hackathon was short, so I needed a game I could build on instead of starting from zero. So I went looking for a city builder I could open up, and found IsoCity: open source, TypeScript, MIT licensed, and built on plain canvas with no game engine underneath. That meant I could reach into the game state directly and wire WebMCP into it. What it does I've added a new mode to IsoCity. It's called Co-Mayor. It creates a portal for your little agent! With this portal, you have two modes: Advisor and Co-Mayor. The first mode, Advisor, lets you ask your agent questions about your city. He can advise you on anything. If you're wondering why your city seems unsafe, ask him! Why are you losing money? Ask him. If there are traffic problems, ask him. The second mode is Co-Mayor, and it's a step up from the first one. This time your agent can make changes to your city! For example, when you start a game, just ask him to draw roads optimised for revenue at the top of the map. He will gladly help you do this. WebMCP is the only way this works. The whole game is drawn on a canvas, so an agent that clicks buttons and reads the page sees nothing at all. Tools are not a shortcut here, they are the only way in. And because every build goes through a plan I approve, the agent can do real work in my city without me losing control of it. How I built it The base game is IsoCity by amilich, MIT licensed. Next.js, TypeScript, HTML5 Canvas. I played it first. I wanted to know what a mayor actually does in this game, because that list was going to become my list of tools. You zone land, connect it with roads, keep power and water running to it, set a tax rate, fund departments, and then watch what breaks. My goal was to expose as much as possible through WebMCP. Not only the actions, but the situation: the terrain, the budget, so he can understand what's right and what's wrong. Everything YOU already read to make a judgment on your city should be exposed to WebMCP. In total there are 22 tools exposed. Then I looked at what the game already gave me. IsoCity keeps its state and its actions in one React context. Place a tile, bulldoze, set the tax rate, fund a department, change the speed, make the map bigger. The buttons in the UI call these functions. So I did not have to build an action layer. Every button was already a tool the agent could use, if I gave it a way to ask. Then I made the list of tools before I wrote any. Two columns. What I want the agent to see, and what I want it to change. I did the seeing column first, and that turned out to be most of the work. For seeing: the land around a point, the city stats, what is going wrong right now, and its own status. For changing: nothing happens directly. The agent proposes, and the plan waits. I did not want an agent editing my city behind my back. Then I wrote the code. src/context/AgentContext.tsx handles the plan: propose, ghost, confirm, undo. src/hooks/useWebMCPTools.ts registers everything with document.modelContext.registerTool . The tools read the game through a live ref, not React state, so the agent always sees the city as it is right now. Reading was the harder half. The map is a canvas, so there is nothing in the page for an agent to look at. It only knows what I hand it. get_problems is where most of that went: buildings with no power or water, traffic, fires, abandoned tiles, empty zoned land, and notes on what the city wants. Without it the agent builds in the wrong place and feels sure about it. Challenges I ran into I ran into multiple challenges. The most obvious one is that React is not a game engine. The game state changes every tick, so the agent needs to read live information from the game. I fixed it by letting the tools read through a live ref rather than the rendered state. Another challenge was testing locally. I kept thinking everything was broken. The issue was that ChatGPT couldn't reach localhost, so I had to use the ChatGPT in-app browser. An AI can also do many random things, so I had to guide my agent and point it in the right direction. I had to rename some tools so it wouldn't get confused. It would send plans far bigger than the game could take, then have no idea why they came back smaller. So the limit is published now: get_tool_catalog and get_agent_status both report 'maxPlanTiles: 200', and propose_placements answers with truncated and 'droppedForCap' so the agent can see exactly what got cut. Applying a plan was where everything broke. Plans sometimes applied themselves before I approved them. Plans sometimes did things that should not have been legal in the first place. Part of it was WebMCP delivering the same call twice, so confirm_plan now keeps applied plans in a cache and returns 'alreadyApplied' instead of building the same thing again. The agent did not know what it could afford. It once decided on a plan when I had no money left. It destroyed my city more than once. That is not the agent being stupid, that is me not giving it the game's constraints. A lot of the work turned into passing the current context down: what state the game is in, what the rules are right now, what is affordable right now. That is also why undo had to be good. Applying a plan compares the grid before and after, so undo puts back what actually changed. It only touches a tile if that tile still looks the way the agent left it. If you built a school on top of the agent's road, undo leaves your school alone. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I'm proud that I can play a city-builder with an AI. This hackathon let me dig deep into WebMCP and into the game itself. I learned a lot, and the result is playable and fun to play with an agent. What I learned Tool descriptions are the most important thing in WebMCP and MCP. Every time my agent did something weird, the fix was mostly in the tool descriptions. The number of tools matters just as much. When I started, I tried to add as many tools as I could. The more I worked on this project, the more tools I deleted, to keep things small and working. What's next for Co-Mayor Today the agent starts fresh every time. I want him to remember the city between sessions: what we built together, what we already tried, what you like. A co-mayor who forgets your city every morning is not much of a partner. So a real memory system for the agent. Next I want the agent to disagree with me. Right now he does what I ask. It would be more interesting if he could say a plan is a bad idea and explain why, and I have to convince him or change my mind. title: CapexIQ
pitch: Know if it pays for itself, before you buy it.
about_excerpt: Know if it pays for itself, before you buy it. Like Comment Story Updates Hero/landing page of CapexIQ A depiction of the target audience of CapexIQ A brief look at the CapexIQ basic assessment The result dashboard of CapexIQ A look at the cumulative cash flow chart at the result dashboard Case comparison and export feature in CapexIQ A brief look at the advanced mode in CapexIQ How it all started I think it began during my internship. It was the consultancy’s first-ever turnkey project. A brownfield, Super Specialty Cardiology Unit, being opened in the suburbs, and luckily I got my hands on the project. It was the Biomedical Equipment planning that had the first tinkling of CapexIQ. Back then, I used to call it simply the ROI Calculator. If you were to comb through the code on GitHub, you might still find remnants of it somewhere around in the initial planning documents. Once we had sorted out the equipment that was to be needed for the project, I was asked to figure out when we would hit break-even, when would we get the returns on our investments, and so on. To be a little more honest, they basically asked me, “Figure out, when will we make our money back?” The fancy terms were merely my additions. And so began the journey to figure out how to do so. The consultancy allowed me to connect with various veteran managers across the Indian healthcare sector. That gave me a serious glimpse into how the industry calculated ROI for their capital-intensive clinical investments. The idea for them was very simple, or so I learned from my conversations with them and inspection of their Excel models. Each manager, especially veterans, had their own Excel models, some more advanced than others, some more traditional, ignoring inflation and depreciation, while some focused on NPV and IRR, but none were as comprehensive as they could be. It wasn’t that these managers couldn’t figure out on their own how to include inflation, payer mix, or even adjust for seasonal changes. They could, but it wasn’t worth the time. Approximations could work, so they said. As an intern, I usually had one or two tangents of projects, and a whole day to myself to take it all to perfection. And so I did. I made the most ambitious Excel model that I could make, taking into account every little thing I could. Assisted by AIs, I must say my productivity was through the roof. Usually, you’d be stuck finding what you need in government standards, a dense 1,500-volume, split across 4 sections. But times are different; a needle in a haystack is nothing for models of today’s age. And so there I was, a humble Excel titled ROI Calculator, beefed up to multiple pages, interlinked with formulas. I was very proud of it. And so was my supervisor. And hence the consultancy kept it, their own ROI Calculator. But I wished to make it more accessible. After all, I wondered how many times hospitals may have cancelled some high-CAPEX purchase like CT or MRI, especially in my country where the doctor-to-population ratio is 1:811. Maybe if they had hands on a better tool to predict their chances, maybe some would dare? Would go ahead with a purchase and reduce the burden on India’s public health infrastructure. With my discussions with managers, I realised there was no standard template they could use. Everyone had their own models, their own idea of what a discount rate should be. So there needed to be something standard, something that could be used as a foundation and adapted to their needs, something that reflected the current market condition and realistic assumptions reflecting the Indian market. And so I made CapexIQ, a transparent, open-source, and reliable calculator that provides managers the flexibility to go as deep into building their clinical investment case as they want. There was yet a small accessibility issue still, but more on that later. The Building I think when I started with the build of CapexIQ, I had a subscription to Claude, which was almost about to end. I used Claude Code to plan out my build. Using my Excel model as a base, we drafted out how the website would look, what variables we would use, we designed the dashboard, and used deep research agents to ground our assumptions in trusted sources. Once that was done, I shifted to Codex. I’d like to point out, in all of the building process, no frontier model was used. Since I could either afford Claude Pro or ChatGPT Plus, I primarily relied on GPT-5.5 Low and then Luna High-Max when it came out. I was exceptionally blown away with Luna. At High or Max, it delivered substantial performance, could do parallel running tasks, without making an exceptional dent in my usage. That allowed me to push further with my building efforts. I designed a new system, all thanks to Codex. I proudly call it “Cascading Parallelism.” Essentially, I’d start with a plan, which would be the one where I would spend a substantial amount of my time. Once that was done, I’d divide my plan into sections that can run in parallel. I would then instruct the parallel agents to cascade, to start another thread with a prompt that builds up on their work. Suppose there are 6 stages, A to F. And A and B can run in parallel, while C, D, E, and F relied on the work they did. (Each of A to F are different agents, who each used subagents as they wished.) So: A —> C —> D —> F B —> F This approach allowed me to stop becoming a copy-and-paste tool, starting and inspecting agents’ work. I couldn’t have achieved this level of orchestration in Claude Code. And I am very happy with this way of building. It makes me spend time where I need to spend it, planning, and I can then come back hours later when all of it is done. This also helps my managerial sense, for this allows me to maximise the output I receive per agent hour. I created a small system while I used Claude (which I later found was more ubiquitous than I had earlier anticipated). Agents would read intro , a brief Markdown file that introduced them to the project, made them aware of where the project spec was located, where the directory was located, instructed them to write in 'handoff.md' once they were done, and maintain an issue tracker. The spec list would have all the information related to work phases, so all I had to do was start an agent, and the rest of the context was always available for them. However, this was crude and still required me to intervene after every agent was done. This was simplified tenfold when I moved to Codex. The orchestration between agents was seamless. I did learn that as long as your planning is immaculate, the bugs you encounter later on do decrease quite a bit. As long as you have an idea as to how each bit of your software should act, and you can plan it out, agents have no issue executing your vision. And all of this by lower-end models running for a very usage-conscious user. The Accessibility Issue and WebMCP I sent out the early version of CapexIQ to all the managers I had earlier connected with and requested them to try it out, either on one of their previous cases or a new one if they had. Some did get back to me, praising how easy it was. They especially loved that they could export their data in a well-formatted Excel. I am glad they did. I was proud of that feature, and I knew how much it means to managers to have their Excels neatly embedded with formulas. A sentiment I wholeheartedly agree with. They did mention they could never dig deeper again. Payer mix, life cycle, was often untouched by them. It was a problem. I was thinking of converting CapexIQ into a plugin or maybe building a semantic extractor where they could just upload their PDFs and my algorithm could do its best to extract useful data from it, but none of it would be perfect. And then I came across the WebMCP challenge on X. The prizes may be enticing, but for me, this would solve the accessibility issue that I was facing! I went on to inspect what it meant, had a conversation with my agents as to how compatible it would be and how we could integrate it with CapexIQ. And oh, how happy I was to see how it could make using the product so much easier for my target audience. It wasn’t that the managers could not fill the form. It was maybe a little more than that. Form filling is one thing; during work, there are so many things an operations manager has to go through. Maybe they wouldn’t bother with it, or maybe, as one pointed out to me, “We are not finance guys, we don’t know how to assume so many different variables.” For me then, WebMCP acts as a solution to my clientele. I tried my best to make CapexIQ as accessible as I could. Every variable has a tooltip attached to guide users as to what it means, how to fill it, and where to find its source. But I guess it becomes tedious to go through HIS (Hospital Information System) for every other variable. And so, WebMCP solved all of that.
